title: Patient perception of robotic-assisted spine surgery.
authors: Watkins V RG, Skaggs DL, Mikhail C.
abstract: Patient behaviors related to pursuing robotic-assisted spine surgery remain poorly characterized. This study evaluated patients' perceptions of robotic-assisted spine surgery and behaviors related to seeking robotic-assisted care. We surveyed 116 adult spine patients at initial consultation (n = 101) or postoperative follow-up after confirmed robotic-assisted surgery (n = 15). Questions assessed perceived attributes of robotic-assisted versus traditional surgery, comfort, surgical preference, willingness to recommend robotic spine surgery, perceived robotic involvement, and whether patients had actively sought surgeons using robotics. Analyses included descriptive statistics, 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and exploratory subgroup comparisons. Patients perceived robotic-assisted surgery as more accurate (65%) and less invasive (63%), with smaller incisions (74%) and shorter surgery (53%) and recovery times (46%). Robotic and traditional surgery were most commonly perceived as comparable in pain (56%) and radiation exposure (51%). 69% believed a robot could perform most or all of the surgery; 60% would recommend robotic spine surgery, and 56% were somewhat or very comfortable with robotics. For otherwise identical surgeries, 73% (85/116, 95% CI 64.6-80.5%) reported no preference, 16% preferred robotic assistance, and 11% preferred surgery without robotics. Of 94 yes/no respondents, 6 (6.4%, 95% CI 3.0-13.2%) reported actively seeking a surgeon using robotics. The other 22 selected "Not Applicable." Although perceptions were generally favorable, most patients had no preference regarding robotic assistance, and few reported actively seeking surgeons using robotics. Robotic availability was not a prominent stated selection factor in this small, single-center sample.

title: Association of popliteal artery wall index with cartilage morphology and loss in knee osteoarthritis: data from the FNIH Biomarkers Consortium.
authors: Eshraghi N, Pooyan A, Mirghaderi P, Alipour E, Kocher P, Pishgar F, Tan Z, Yuan C, Balu N, Guermazi A, Chalian M.
abstract: To evaluate MRI-derived popliteal artery wall index in relation to knee cartilage volume and 24-month cartilage loss in the Foundation for the National Institutes of Health (FNIH) Osteoarthritis Biomarkers Consortium cohort. This observational cohort study included 594 participants with one indexed knee each. Mean wall index was calculated by averaging values derived using the Fully Automated and Robust Analysis Technique for Popliteal Artery Evaluation across all evaluable axial cross-sectional images reformatted from the sagittal three-dimensional dual-echo steady-state MRI volume. Fully adjusted models, including relevant clinical and imaging covariates, evaluated cross-sectional and change-on-change associations with regional cartilage volume. Mixed-effects and sensitivity analyses assessed robustness. At baseline, each 10-percentage-point higher mean wall index was associated with lower lateral femoral cartilage volume (β = -67.4 mm3; 95% CI, -126.4 to -8.3; p = 0.025) and thickness (-0.091 mm; 95% CI, -0.162 to -0.021; p = 0.011). Each 1-SD increase in mean wall-index change was associated with greater medial tibial (β = 0.53 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.95; p = 0.012) and lateral femoral (β = 0.35 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.01 to 0.69; p = 0.048) cartilage-volume loss. The medial tibial association was supported by mixed-effects, robust, rank-based, and baseline-adjusted sensitivity analyses. A greater 24-month increase in mean wall index was associated with greater concurrent medial tibial cartilage-volume loss. Mean wall index derived from standardized 3D DESS knee MRI may provide complementary information about concurrent cartilage loss, although further longitudinal studies are needed to establish its clinical significance.

title: Wnt1 controls subchondral bone remodeling and osteoarthritis progression.
authors: Xie W, Donat A, Jiang S, Pan H, Augustin R, Schoberwalter T, Gerriets C, Sevecke J, Erdmann C, Schröder S, Alimy AR, Behrens I, Ocokoljic A, Zhao W, Luther J, Yorgan T, Schinke T, Frosch KH, Rolvien T, Baranowsky A, Keller J.
abstract: Despite mounting evidence emphasizing the role of abnormal subchondral bone remodeling in the progression of osteoarthritis (OA), clinical translation has produced disappointing results. Here, we demonstrate an increased expression of Wnt1, a key Wnt ligand with potent osteoanabolic effects, during OA progression in human and murine subchondral bone. Temporarily overexpressing Wnt1 in osteoblasts in the early phase after anterior cruciate ligament transection (ACLT)-induced OA has no effect on cartilage degeneration; however, it contributes to increased subchondral bone mass and alleviates subchondral bone loss. In contrast, late-phase induction of Wnt1 in osteoblasts exacerbates OA severity by inducing aberrant subchondral bone sclerosis, where inflammation-induced secreted frizzled-related protein 2 (Sfrp2) in the subchondral bone potentiates the harmful effects of Wnt1. Moreover, mice with a global inactivating Wnt1G177C mutation, which clinically causes osteogenesis imperfecta type XV, display low subchondral bone mass, are resistant to ACLT-induced subchondral bone loss and exhibit attenuated OA progression. Taken together, these findings identify a pathophysiological role for Wnt1 in subchondral bone remodeling and OA progression that could represent a promising therapeutic target.

title: Task-specific Humeral Head Translation Is Associated With Neuromuscular Recruitment Deficits in Multidirectional Shoulder Instability.
authors: Weng YH, Weng YC, Huang TS, Yang JL, Lin JJ.
abstract: Background Multidirectional shoulder instability is a common clinical challenge, particularly in adolescents and young adult females. It can impact daily function and athletic performance. However, evidence regarding the relationship between humeral head translation and muscle recruitment patterns in this population remains unclear. Questions/purposes This study aimed to (1) compare humeral head translation between patients with multidirectional instability and controls, as well as among clinical subgroups characterized by anterior, inferior, and posterior instability; (2) examine shoulder muscle activity across groups, including variations within clinical subgroups; and (3) investigate the relationship between humeral head translation and muscle activation levels during three standardized isometric tasks. Methods From an initial screening of 37 patients and 35 controls, 19% (7) of patients and 14% (5) of controls were excluded based on predefined criteria (shoulder pain 0.50. Results Compared with controls, patients with multidirectional instability demonstrated greater humeral head translation across all tasks, exceeding the MDC threshold in controls versus patients for anterior translation (mean ± SD 0.4 ± 0.3 mm versus 2.6 ± 1.1 mm, mean difference 2.2 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.8 to 2.6]; p Conclusion Patients with multidirectional instability exhibit task-specific increases in humeral head translation exceeding the MDC, driven by distinct neuromuscular deficits. Subgroup analyses show that patients experience the greatest translation during tasks corresponding to their predominant direction of instability. Future studies should evaluate the longitudinal efficacy of rehabilitation protocols in modifying abnormal translation patterns and improving clinical outcomes across different subgroups. Clinical relevance From a foundational science perspective, our findings indicate that traditional, generalized shoulder strengthening is insufficient for multidirectional instability. Instead, rehabilitation should utilize direction-specific interventions tailored to each patient's predominant instability pattern, targeting underperforming muscles to mitigate abnormal joint translation and restore dynamic glenohumeral stability.

title: Preoperative depressive symptoms predict long-term mortality and early functional recovery after osteoporotic hip fracture: a 3-year cohort study.
authors: Gao F, Tu C, Chen Y, Bei M, Chen Y, Li R, Xu S, Chen L, Liu G, Yang M, Wu X.
abstract: Depressive symptoms are common in older adults with osteoporotic hip fracture, but their impact on long-term outcomes remains unclear. In this cohort study, preoperative depressive symptoms were associated with increased 3-year mortality and poorer early functional recovery. These findings highlight the importance of psychological assessment in the management of fragility fractures. To investigate the association between preoperative depressive symptoms and postoperative mortality and functional recovery in older adults with hip fracture. This secondary analysis was based on a prospective cohort of patients aged ≥65 years undergoing surgical treatment for hip fracture. Depressive symptoms were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) within 24 hours of admission, with a cutoff score of ≥5. Mortality and functional recovery were evaluated at 30-day, 120-day, 1-year, and 3-year follow-up. Cox proportional hazards models and multinomial logistic regression were used after adjustment for potential confounders. Among 1092 patients, 93 (8.5%) had PHQ-9 ≥ 5. Preoperative depressive symptoms were not associated with short-term mortality but were independently associated with increased 3-year mortality (HR = 1.57, 95% CI: 1.05-2.36). Patients with PHQ-9 ≥ 5 had significantly poorer functional recovery at 30-day, 120-day, and 1-year follow-up, whereas no independent association was observed at 3 years. Preoperative depressive symptoms were associated with increased long-term mortality and poorer early functional recovery. These findings support the role of early psychological assessment in perioperative risk stratification.

title: Outcomes of a Multidisciplinary Lower Limb Fracture Care Pathway in a Tertiary Hospital: A 3-Year Experience of 1073 Geriatric Patients.
authors: Zhang C, Tan T, Chu Z, Lee-Moeung C, Yam M.
abstract: Geriatric lower limb fractures place a significant burden on tertiary healthcare systems. This study evaluates the outcomes of a fast-track, multidisciplinary lower limb fracture care pathway implemented at a tertiary hospital in Singapore. This study aims to describe and compare the functional outcomes, mortality, and the comparative impact of time to surgery (TTS) across different geriatric lower limb fractures (knee, femur shaft, and ankle) within the pathway, using hip fractures as a benchmark. A retrospective cohort study was conducted of patients ≥ 65 years old with non-pathological, surgically-treated lower limb fractures admitted to a tertiary institution between December 2020 and April 2024. Primary outcomes included postoperative functional status assessed via Modified Barthel Index (MBI) scores and perioperative complications, while the secondary outcome was 12-month mortality. Multivariate regression analyses evaluated predictors influencing these outcomes. The cohort predominantly consisted of hip fracture patients (82.2%), with knee (7.3%), ankle (5.4%), and femur shaft (5.1%) fractures comprising smaller groups. At 12 months, there were no significant differences in mortality across fracture types (overall mortality: 7.2%). Functional outcomes, measured by MBI scores, showed significant improvement over 12 months, with no significant difference between fracture types (p = 0.32). Multivariate analysis identified younger age, female gender, higher pre-fracture MBI scores, and lower clinical frailty scores as positive predictors of 12-month functional outcomes. Early surgery (< 48 h) was significantly associated with better 12-month functional outcomes in knee fracture patients. TTS (< 48 h) significantly influenced mortality outcomes in hip fractures only. These findings describe comparable functional outcomes and mortality across fracture types and outcomes observed for a broader range of lower limb injuries beyond hip fractures are favorable under a coordinated multidisciplinary care pathway.

title: Open Repair of Patellar Osteochondral Fracture With Absorbable Sutures

title: Need for removal of flexible intramedullary nails used to treat femoral shaft fractures in children: an observational study of 55 children with a minimum of 5-year follow-up.
authors: Nietosvaara NR, Kosola J, Nietosvaara Y, Puhakka J, Helenius I, Laaksonen T.
abstract: Background and purpose Removal of flexible intramedullary nails (FIN) in children with femoral shaft fractures has been considered unnecessary when nails are left unbent flush to the bone. We aimed to evaluate the frequency and timing of nail removal on demand. Methods This is an observational follow-up study including consecutive 3-14-year-old children with femoral shaft fractures treated during 2011-2018 with FIN. The instruction was to leave the distal ends of the nails unbent above the distal femoral physis. Alignment of the fracture and position of the nails were assessed after nailing and during follow-up. Data on nail removal rates and timing was collected with at least 5 years of follow-up. The outcomes for children with correctly placed nails were compared with those with nails that were too long, defined as cut at or below the distal femoral physis evaluated from postoperative radiographs. Results 55 consecutive children were included. All fractures healed in satisfactory alignment. FINs were too long in 24 patients (20 distally, 4 proximally). Hardware was removed in 37 (67%) children at a median of 2.4 years from surgery because of pain (range 0.3-9.3). Removal occurred in 21/24 of those with too long nails, and in 16/31 patients with correctly applied FIN, RR 1.7 (95% confidence interval 1.2-2.5, P = 0.005). Conclusion Half of the children with unbent FIN placed flush to the bone in femoral shaft fractures had removal of nails. Extending the nail to or below the distal femoral growth plate leads to hardware removal in nearly all cases, mainly due to pain.

title: Multicenter external validation of CT-based deep learning for proximal femoral fracture classification and quantitative fracture-line assessment.
authors: Shimizu T, Kusunoki K, Nishida Y, Che X, Nakamura S, Arita K, Ohashi Y, Sugawara Y, Ishizu H, Yokota S, Yamada K, Iwasaki N.
abstract: Objective To develop and externally validate a CT-based deep learning CAD system for proximal femoral fracture classification and fracture-line angle quantification and to preliminarily evaluate its clinical utility in a reader study. Materials and methods In this multicenter retrospective study, coronal CT images from four institutions were used for training (259 patients, 19,844 annotated images) and internal validation (91 patients, 92 hips). External validation included 200 patients from independent institutions scanned with CT systems from two vendors. A ResNet-50-based convolutional neural network was used to perform fracture region segmentation, fracture classification, pelvic fracture detection, and fracture line angle estimation. The diagnostic performance and fracture-line angle agreement were evaluated using internal and external validation datasets. An exploratory reader study involving six readers was conducted to assess the effects of CAD assistance. Results Overall classification accuracy was 95.7% (κ = 0.944) internally and 91.5% (κ = 0.887) externally; F1-score ranges were 0.927-0.982 and 0.667-0.952, respectively. The fracture-line angle mean absolute errors were 4.54° and 6.26°, approaching the interobserver errors between orthopedic specialists (3.64° and 5.18°), with corresponding ICCs of 0.817 and 0.736, respectively. In the exploratory reader study, residents showed higher sensitivity with CAD assistance for non-displaced femoral neck fractures (0.78 vs. 0.47), with high specificity. Conclusion This multicenter CT-based CAD system demonstrated accurate and generalizable fracture region segmentation, proximal femoral fracture classification, and objective fracture line angle quantification across independent datasets. The proposed approach has the potential to support diagnosis and preoperative assessment of proximal femoral fractures.

title: Knotless Hip Labral Repair With Tensioning Set Up by Intentional Slack
authors: Kang R, Mardaus K.

title: Influence of peri-implant soft tissue thickness on marginal bone loss following immediate implant placement in the anterior maxilla: A retrospective comparative study.
authors: Kadkhodazadeh M, Alam M, Golkar M, Naghshbandi T.
abstract: Marginal bone stability is a critical determinant of the long-term success and esthetic harmony of dental implants. Peri-implant soft tissue thickness (STT) has been proposed as a biological factor influencing crestal bone remodeling. This retrospective comparative study aimed to evaluate the relationship between peri-implant STT and marginal bone loss (MBL) following immediate implant placement in the anterior maxilla after one year of functional loading. Fifty immediate implant sites from 50 patients were retrospectively analyzed. Based on mid-buccal soft tissue measurement, implants were classified as thin (STT ≤ 1 mm; n = 22) or thick (STT > 1 mm; n = 28) phenotypes. Clinical parameters, including probing depth, bleeding on probing, plaque index, keratinized tissue width, and pink esthetic score, and radiographic parameters (MBL) were extracted from patient records. MBL was measured on standardized periapical digital radiographs taken immediately after surgery and at one-year follow-up using a custom positioning index. The mean age of participants was 57.88 ± 11.16 years. MBL was significantly higher in the thin soft tissue group (1.34 ± 0.19 mm) compared with the thick tissue group (1.00 ± 0.20 mm; p < 0.0001). STT exhibited a strong negative correlation with MBL (r = -0.749, p < 0.0001). Other variables showed no significant intergroup differences. No significant difference in MBL was observed between implant systems. Within the limitations of this retrospective study, peri-implant soft tissue thickness was identified as a key determinant of marginal bone preservation after immediate implant placement in the anterior maxilla. Thicker mucosa was associated with significantly reduced bone resorption and more stable peri-implant esthetic outcomes after one year.

title: Imaging and diagnosis of overuse shoulder injuries in overhead athletes.
authors: McGill KC, Davies M, Feuerriegel GC, Sweetwood K, Wong LH.
abstract: Shoulder overuse injuries are highly prevalent among athletes participating in overhead sports such as baseball, tennis, swimming, and volleyball, where repetitive high-velocity loading imposes unique biomechanical demands on the glenohumeral complex. These injuries span a broad spectrum, including rotator cuff tears, subacromial/subdeltoid impingement, superior labrum anterior-to-posterior (SLAP) lesions, long head of the biceps tendinopathy, glenohumeral instability, internal impingement, glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD), and Little League shoulder. Accurate diagnosis requires an understanding of sport-specific biomechanics, particularly the extreme forces generated during the late cocking and early acceleration phases of throwing, which produce characteristic injury patterns such as posterosuperior partial articular-sided rotator cuff tears and type II SLAP lesions via the peel-back mechanism. Imaging plays a central role in diagnosis and management. Radiographs remain the initial study for evaluating osseous anatomy and acromial morphology. MRI is the principal modality for soft-tissue assessment, while MR arthrography offers superior sensitivity for intra-articular pathology, including labral and partial articular-sided rotator cuff tears. Musculoskeletal ultrasound provides dynamic, cost-effective evaluation of tendons and bursae, and 3D CT or zero-time echo (ZTE) MRI is essential for quantifying glenoid bone loss in the setting of instability. Because many imaging findings are present in asymptomatic athletes, careful clinical correlation is essential. This review summarizes the imaging features, diagnostic pearls, and limitations of current modalities for shoulder overuse injuries in overhead athletes.

title: Higher pre-treatment expectations are associated with less pain and better physical function and quality of life after physiotherapy for knee osteoarthritis.
authors: Konings-Pijnappels A, van der Steen MC, van Bekkum F, van Doesburg C, den Boer WA, Young JJ, Vlieland TV, Janssen R.
abstract: To examine the association of pre-treatment expectations with clinical outcomes of physiotherapy in individuals with knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Observational study, using data from the Good Life with osteoArthritis Denmark (GLA:D®) physiotherapy program executed in one region in The Netherlands. Before treatment, patients' characteristics and their expectations of (1) pain and (2) function were recorded (5-point Likert scales; 1= a lot - 5= very little to none). In addition, Pain (NRS Pain), physical functioning (KOOS-12) and quality of life (QoL) (EQ-5D-5L) were measured before and directly after treatment. Expectation scores were categorized into high (scores 1-2) or low (scores 3-5) and four expectation groups were constructed: 1) High pain and function expectations, 2) High pain expectations only, 3) High function expectations only, 4) Moderate/Low pain and function expectations. Linear and logistic regression analyses examined the association between expectation groups and outcomes, with the Moderate/Low pain and function expectations group serving as reference. Data from 871/1442 participants (60%) was complete and included in the analyses. Having both high pain and function expectations showed an association with pain (regression coefficient B -0.740; 95% confidence interval (CI) -1.073 to -0.407), physical functioning (B 3.265; 95%CI 1.589 to 4.940) and QoL (B 0.045; 95%CI 0.024 to 0.066) after treatment compared to having moderate/low pain and function expectations. The intermediate groups showed higher QoL after treatment compared to the moderate/low pain and function group (B 0.040; 95% CI 0.004 to 0.075 and B 0.040; 0.008 to 0.073 respectively). Having higher patient expectations for both pain and function was consistently associated with better outcomes of exercise therapy for KOA. More research into the possible role of clinicians in assessing and/or modifying pre-treatment expectations is needed.

title: Foot Morphology Asymmetry, Gait Biomechanics, and Trunk Muscle Activation in Adolescents With Major Thoracic Idiopathic Scoliosis: A Cross-Sectional Study.
authors: Huang Y, Lin B, Wang D, Lin Y, Yang Y, Wang X, Liao B, Zhang X.
abstract: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) of the major thoracic type-characterized by a right thoracic primary curve with compensatory adaptations-carries a significant risk of progression. While spinal and pelvic biomechanics have been extensively examined, the influence of foot morphology and distal gait compensation in this subgroup remains poorly understood. This study aimed to investigate foot asymmetries and their association with gait deviations in individuals with major thoracic AIS. A total of 23 patients with major thoracic AIS and 23 age-matched healthy controls were enrolled between October 2022 and October 2023. Each participant underwent a multimodal biomechanical assessment, which included bilateral foot morphology evaluation (arch index, foot length, heel width, hallux valgus angle, arch length, and metatarsal widths) via a 3D laser scanner, three-dimensional gait analysis synchronized with force plates, and surface electromyography (sEMG) of core trunk muscles during natural walking. Between-group differences in left/right ratios for foot and gait parameters were analyzed using independent t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests. Correlations between foot morphology, spinal parameters, and gait parameters were also examined. Compared with controls, the AIS group demonstrated significant foot asymmetries, including elevated left/right ratios for the arch index (p = 0.03) and heel width (p = 0.03). Kinetic analysis revealed a significantly reduced left/right ratio for the maximum ankle coronal (eversion) moment (p < 0.01). Kinematically, the AIS group exhibited altered knee angle ratios at initial contact (p = 0.03) and a decreased knee range-of-motion ratio (p < 0.01). sEMG indicated a significantly higher internal oblique activation ratio in the AIS group (p = 0.04). Correlation analysis revealed that spinal parameters and foot morphology asymmetries were significantly correlated with asymmetric trunk muscle activation and altered lower limb biomechanics, with positive and negative associations depending on the specific parameters. This cross-sectional study suggests that major thoracic AIS is associated with foot morphology asymmetry, altered ankle and knee biomechanics, and asymmetric trunk muscle activation during walking. The observed associations between foot structure asymmetry, lower-limb biomechanics, and trunk muscle activation support the presence of interconnected biomechanical adaptations along the spine-pelvis-foot axis.

title: Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine Innovative Techniques in Knee Preservation: Osteotomy about the Knee: The Advent of Patient Specific Instrumentation (PSI).
authors: Lezak BA, Alaia MJ.
abstract: Purpose of review Osteotomy about the knee corrects lower extremity malalignment to unload the diseased compartment or for combined procedures to optimize outcomes. Planning from 2D radiographs and freehand execution can leave a gap between planned and achieved correction. Patient-specific instrumentation (PSI) uses CT- or MRI-derived 3D models to produce custom cutting guides and plates that carry the preoperative plan into the operating room. This review summarizes the evidence on PSI for osteotomy about the knee, covering accuracy, safety, versatility, efficiency, and patient-reported outcomes. Recent findings PSI reproduces planned coronal and sagittal corrections to within about 1°, and comparative studies and meta-analyses show improved accuracy and fewer outliers compared with conventional technique, though some studies find no advantage in experienced hands. A 2026 meta-analysis found PSI-guided high tibial osteotomy required fewer fluoroscopic images and was about 20 min shorter than conventional technique, with no difference in complication risk. These gains appear after roughly 10 cases. PSI allows a single guide to correct coronal alignment and posterior tibial slope together and supports double-level osteotomy and concomitant ligament or meniscal procedures. Patient-reported outcomes improve with either PSI or conventional technique; PSI shows an early advantage at 3 to 6 months that is gone by final follow-up. PSI improves the accuracy and efficiency of knee osteotomy and reduces radiation exposure, with complication rates similar to conventional technique. Its greatest value is in complex multiplanar and slope-correcting osteotomies, combined procedures, and for surgeons earlier in their osteotomy experience. Cost, manufacturing lead time, guide-related soft-tissue exposure, and the lack of long-term outcome data remain limitations. Prospective studies with longer follow-up are needed to determine whether PSI's technical precision produces more durable clinical results.

title: Autologous Bone Plug Harvest and Reimplantation for Tibial Tunnel Management in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction
authors: Yan D, Fang D, Wu D, Zhang Y, Zhao Q.

title: Association between surgery-oriented standardized clinical pathways and postoperative delirium in geriatric hip fracture patients: A retrospective cohort study.
authors: Zhao Z, Yu J, Lan Y, Yang B, Tan Q, Wen Z, Yao Y, He C, Fang X.
abstract: Elderly hip fracture patients are at high risk of postoperative delirium (POD). The association between surgery-oriented standardized clinical pathways and POD incidence remains poorly clarified. This study aimed to explore the association between surgery-oriented standardized clinical pathways, internal fixation clinical pathway(IFCP), versus arthroplasty clinical pathway(ARCP), and POD occurrence in elderly hip fracture patients. This retrospective cohort study examined the medical records of patients aged 65 years and older who underwent hip fracture surgery at a tertiary medical facility from January 2022 to December 2025. Patients were divided into groups according to the surgery-oriented standardized clinical pathways they received: those with extracapsular fractures who underwent intramedullary nailing were assigned to the IFCP group, and those with intracapsular fractures who underwent hip arthroplasty were assigned to the ARCP group. Multivariate logistic regression and propensity score matching (PSM) analyses were utilized to evaluate the association between surgery-oriented standardized clinical pathways and POD. Subgroup analysis was subsequently conducted to explore potential interactions further. A total of 693 patients were included in this study, with a POD incidence of 15.01% (104/693) during the postoperative hospitalization period. Before matching, the incidence of POD was significantly lower in the ARCP group than in the IFCP group (9.92% vs. 20.61%, P < 0.001). This significant difference persisted after matching (11.54% vs. 18.85%, P = 0.020). Multivariate logistic regression confirmed that the ARCP was independently associated with a reduced risk of POD (OR = 0.40, 95% CI: 0.24-0.67, P < 0.001). Surgery-oriented standardized clinical pathways showed a statistically association with POD risk among elderly hip fracture patients. The ARCP exhibited a lower observed incidence of POD compared with the IFCP.

title: Analysis of factors hindering the prevention of perioperative hypothermia in elderly patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty: A qualitative study.
authors: Dou C, Sun Y, Dai K, Wei M, Li J, Qu K, Hu Q, Zhang H.
abstract: Elderly patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty (THA) have a high incidence of perioperative hypothermia due to anesthetic suppression of thermoregulation, prolonged surgical duration, and diminished endogenous thermoregulatory function, which can lead to poor outcomes. Effective prevention of hypothermia is a critical clinical issue; however, previous studies have lacked in-depth analysis of comprehensive continuous management and practical barriers. This study aimed to identify barriers to the prevention of perioperative hypothermia in elderly THA patients. A qualitative study design was employed, conducted from January to February 2026 at a Grade III Level A hospital in the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Using purposive sampling, anesthesiologists (n = 5), anesthesia nurses (n = 5), and operating room nurses (n = 5) were recruited as participants. Semi-structured face-to-face interviews were conducted, and data were analyzed using content analysis with the assistance of NVivo 12.0 software. A total of 3 themes and 5 subthemes were identified: (1) System and process level: The warm chain management process requires improvement, and the allocation of key warming resources needs to be strengthened; (2) Human resources and team atmosphere level: Nursing staffing needs to be reinforced, and a positive organizational culture requires cultivation; (3) Multidisciplinary collaboration and continuous improvement level: The multidisciplinary collaboration platform and continuous improvement system remain inadequate. Diverse factors hinder the prevention of perioperative hypothermia in elderly THA patients. Managers should implement improvements across three dimensions-system processes, human resources and team atmosphere, and multidisciplinary collaboration-to explore perioperative temperature management strategies and promote quality improvements in hypothermia prevention and control.

title: All‐Arthroscopic Staged Matrix‐Induced Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation for Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus

title: Agreement between FRAX-based treatment decisions with and without bone mineral density and factors influencing discordance in Sri Lanka.
authors: Gnanathayalan SW, Bulugahapitiya U, Sumanatilleke M, Athukorala T, Chandrasekaran M.
abstract: In 309 Sri Lankan adults referred for DXA, FRAX with and without BMD showed moderate agreement (κ = 0.57) in treatment recommendations, with 82.5% concordance. Discordance was more frequent in older individuals and those with FRAX without BMD values near intervention thresholds. Increasing age and lower BMD independently predicted discordance, highlighting the influence of BMD on treatment classification and risk estimates generated by FRAX. Background The Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX) estimates an individual's 10-year fracture probability using clinical risk factors, with bone mineral density (BMD) as an optional contributor. The objective of this study was to evaluate the level of agreement between treatment recommendations generated by FRAX with BMD and FRAX without BMD, using Sri Lankan intervention thresholds. Methods A cross-sectional analysis was conducted among adults aged 40-90 years who were referred for dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) for osteoporosis screening at a tertiary hospital in Sri Lanka between 2023 and 2024. FRAX probabilities were calculated using the Sri Lankan model, both with and without femoral neck BMD. Participants were categorized into treatment or non-treatment groups based on national thresholds. Concordance was defined as identical treatment recommendations from both FRAX approaches. Clinical variables were compared between concordant and discordant groups. Agreement between treatment recommendations was quantified using Cohen's kappa statistic. Results Of the 309 participants included, 88.0% were women. Treatment was recommended for 94 individuals (30.4%) using FRAX with BMD and 84 individuals (27.2%) using FRAX without BMD. Overall concordance was 82.5% (255/309). Agreement between FRAX with and without BMD was moderate (Cohen's kappa = 0.57, 95% CI 0.47-0.68, p 60 years (p Conclusion FRAX calculations with and without BMD demonstrated moderate agreement in treatment recommendations, with reduced concordance among older adults and in those with FRAX without BMD around intervention thresholds. These findings suggest that incorporation of BMD can meaningfully alter FRAX risk estimates and treatment recommendations in these populations. However, these findings are applicable to individuals referred for DXA assessment and may not be generalizable to the broader Sri Lankan adult population.

title: Where does your allograft tissue come from? Allograft use in reconstructive orthopaedic surgery: A review of the NHSBT provision of musculoskeletal allografts in the UK.
authors: Telford J, Cornish E, Spalding T, Barkatali B.
abstract: The use of musculoskeletal (MSK) allografting techniques in reconstructive surgery of the knee is well established, with the most common application being in revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. However, the journey from donor to recipient is poorly understood by orthopaedic surgeons. NHSBT Tissue Service in Liverpool is one of the largest tissue banks in Europe and provides MSK allograft tissue to hospitals in the UK, though it is not the sole provider. All stages of the process, from donor identification to distribution are tightly regulated by the Human Tissue Act 2004 to provide MSK allografts which retain the biomechanical properties required, whilst also being at an extremely low risk of disease transmission. This is achieved through a rigorous donor selection process and protocols for the harvesting, shaping, preservation, decontamination, sterilisation, packaging and storage of tissues This review describes NHSBT protocols for MSK allograft provision attained via publicly available data, correspondence with NHSBT staff and a tour of the facility in Speke, Liverpool. In addition, a review of the literature was performed to establish international practice, and the effect methods of retrieval, processing and storage can have on disease transmission and biomechanical properties. This review describes the production of MSK allografts by NHSBT in the UK.

title: The Latarjet with Anterior Capsular Shift for Anterior Shoulder Instability in Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome: A Case Series.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Bailey EP, Sullivan CM, Hardrick JC, Seilern Und Aspang J, Grundman H, Wagner ER.
abstract: Background Shoulder instability in patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS) remains a complex issue. Patients undergoing surgical management are at increased risk for complications and recurrence. The Latarjet procedure with anterior capsular shift provides bony stability and may be a viable option for patients with hEDS who have predominant anterior shoulder instability; however, outcomes remain poorly reported in the literature. Methods A retrospective case series from a single institution analyzed patients with hEDS and anterior-predominant shoulder instability who underwent the Latarjet procedure with anterior capsular shift between November 2019 and December 2024. Demographics, comorbidities, prior surgeries, and peri-operative details were collected. The primary outcome was recurrent shoulder instability. Secondary outcomes included range of motion (ROM), patient reported outcome measures (PROMs), and other complications. Collected PROMs included Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain, the Shoulder Subjective Value (SSV), and the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score. Results A total of 19 shoulders in 18 patients were included with a mean follow-up of 38.2 months (range 12-73 months). All patients had a diagnosis of hEDS with an average Beighton score of 8 and 63% of shoulders having previously failed shoulder stabilization surgery. Only one complication of graft fracture postoperatively was reported with the patient undergoing revision Latarjet, which successfully stabilized the shoulder. There were no instances of recurrent shoulder instability reported. Both PROMs and ROM demonstrated statistically significant improvement from pre-operative values including forward flexion, abduction, internal rotation, VAS, and SSV. VAS pain improved from 5.2 to 0.5, SSV from 41 to 88, and the mean postoperative ASES score was 92.8 (P Conclusion In appropriately selected patients with hEDS and anterior-predominant shoulder instability, Latarjet with anterior capsular shift was associated with improved range of motion, pain, and patient-reported outcomes with low complication rates. Level of evidence Level IV, Case Series, Treatment Study.

title: Targeting Medial Leg Pain in Athletes: Distinguishing Between Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome and Tibialis Posterior Tendinopathy.
authors: Millar AN, Hynes K, Knapik DM.
abstract: Purpose of review To examine the clinical overlap between medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS) and tibialis posterior tendinopathy (TPT) in athletes with exercise-induced medial lower leg pain. Current evidence regarding anatomy, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, imaging, and management is reviewed to improve diagnostic accuracy and highlight emerging concepts regarding posterior tibial tendon (PTT) involvement in athletes traditionally diagnosed with "shin splints." Recent findings Although MTSS remains the most common diagnosis for exercise-induced medial tibial pain, growing biomechanical and imaging evidence suggests PTT pathology may be more prevalent than previously recognized, particularly in athletic populations. MTSS and TPT share overlapping symptom location, gradual onset, and activity-related pain, contributing to potential misdiagnosis. Despite these similarities, important distinctions exist in physical examination findings, foot biomechanics, imaging characteristics, and treatment strategies. Additionally, evolving concepts surrounding progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD) have better defined the relationship between PTT pathology and medial foot and ankle instability. The broad clinical diagnosis of "shin splints" may encompass a subset of athletes with unrecognized TPT. Careful assessment of PTT function, foot alignment, and lower extremity biomechanics should complement evaluation of medial lower leg pain athletes. Improved recognition of TPT may facilitate earlier diagnosis, guide appropriate rehabilitation, prevent progression to PCFD, and identify opportunities for future prospective studies directly comparing MTSS and TPT in athletic populations.

title: Surgical Treatment of Trans-ulnar Basal Coronoid Fracture-Dislocations: Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes in 34 Patients at a Mean 4-Year Follow-up.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Marinelli A, Riva M, Coliva F, Villari E, Brunello V, Guerra E.
abstract: Background Trans-ulnar basal coronoid (TUBC) fracture-dislocations represent a highly unstable pattern of elbow injury, characterized by a fracture through the base of the coronoid process that separates it from both the olecranon and the ulnar metaphysis. In TUBC fracture-dislocations, anatomic reduction and stable fixation of the coronoid are critical for restoring elbow function. The purpose of the present study was to evaluate the clinical and radiographic outcomes of patients surgically treated for TUBC fracture-dislocations. We analyzed fracture morphology, associated lesions, surgical approaches, coronoid fixation techniques, complications, and potential prognostic factors associated with inferior clinical outcomes. Materials and methods A retrospective review was performed of all patients surgically treated for TUBC fracture-dislocations at a single institution between 2012 and 2025 with a minimum clinical and radiographic follow-up of 12 months. Preoperative computed tomography scans were assessed to characterize fracture morphology and associated lesions. Clinical evaluation included elbow range of motion, Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Broberg and Morrey (B&M) score, QuickDASH, and Single Assessment Numeric Evaluation (SANE). Radiographs were reviewed to assess fracture healing and radiographic complications. Results Thirty-four patients were included, with a mean age of 51.8 years. Mean clinical and radiographic follow-up were 48 and 43.1 months, respectively. A radial head fracture was present in 28 patients. At final follow-up, mean elbow flexion-extension arc was 117.2°. Mean forearm rotation arc was 154.2°. Mean MEPS and B&M scores were 92.3 and 90.5 points, respectively, whereas mean QuickDASH and SANE scores were 14.8 and 85.6 points, respectively. Coronoid comminution (≥ 3 fragments) was associated with higher odds of a non-excellent MEPS ( Conclusions TUBC fracture-dislocations are complex injuries characterized by substantial variability in fracture morphology, in which accurate reduction and stable fixation of the coronoid are considered essential for achieving favorable outcomes. Most patients in the present series achieved satisfactory functional outcomes, with good or excellent MEPS results in more than 90% of cases. However, the overall complication rate remained substantial (44.1%) with a reoperation rate of 11.8%. A key finding of this study was that coronoid comminution was associated with poorer functional outcomes and higher odds of non-excellent MEPS results.

title: Subscapularis Healing and the Associated Impact on Outcomes Following Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Kevin Sungwook Lee AL, Rohl MR, Moor M, Baessler AM, Stephens SP, Badman BL.
abstract: Background The role of subscapularis repair following reverse shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA) remains controversial, particularly regarding restoration of internal rotation and postoperative function. While prior studies have compared repair versus non-repair, few have evaluated postoperative tendon integrity using ultrasound. Without direct assessment of tendon healing, functional differences cannot be reliably attributed to repair status. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the relationship between subscapularis healing and clinical outcomes following rTSA. Methods A retrospective review of prospectively collected data was performed of patients undergoing primary lateralized rTSA from 2022-2025 by a single surgeon. Patients underwent subscapularis repair with optional augmentation. Subscapularis repair was classified as healed or non-healed based on ultrasound evaluation at minimum 10-weeks. Patients with at least 1-year follow-up and postoperative ultrasound evaluation of the subscapularis were included. Patients with preoperative fractures or full-thickness subscapularis tears were excluded. Outcomes included VAS pain score, ASES score, SST score, range of motion, strength testing, and complication rates. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between augmentation and healing, adjusting for ultrasound timing and sex. Multivariable linear regression assessed the association between healing and postoperative ROM at 12 and 24 months, adjusting for preoperative motion and posterosuperior rotator cuff integrity. Significance was set at p Results Of 235 patients who underwent subscapularis repair, 126 shoulders (118 patients) met inclusion criteria. Healing was observed in 100 patients (79.4%). Healed repairs were significantly associated with augmentation (84.9% vs. 67.5%, p = .025), however, this association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for ultrasound timing and sex (p = .113). Healed tendons demonstrated lower VAS pain (0 vs 1, p = 0.014) and ASES scores at 24 months (92 vs. 85, p = .022), though these differences are below the MCID. Internal rotation was improved at 12 months (6 vs. 4, p = 0.017). Healing was not independently associated with forward elevation, abduction, external rotation, or internal rotation at 12 or 24 months after multivariable adjustment. Complications occurred in 7.0% of patients with healed repairs and none with non-healed repairs (p = .343). Conclusion Sonographically intact subscapularis repairs following lateralized rTSA were associated with greater internal rotation at 1-year, however it was not independently associated with postoperative ROM after adjustment. This study represents one of the largest cohorts of sonographically evaluated subscapularis repairs following RTSA. Further investigation of biologic augmentation strategies may help improve subscapularis repair outcomes in rTSA. Level of evidence Level III; Retrospective Cohort Comparison; Prognosis Study.

title: Sensorimotor representation in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis compared with healthy controls: Proprioception, tactile acuity, left-right judgment, and motor imagery.
authors: Çetin S, Alaca N, Yilgor C, Alanay A.
abstract: Objective Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is increasingly recognized as involving central sensorimotor alterations beyond structural spinal deformity, yet multiple sensorimotor domains have not been assessed comprehensively within a single AIS sample. This study aimed to compare tactile acuity, proprioception, left/right judgment, and motor imagery between adolescents with AIS and healthy controls, and to explore the associations of these sensorimotor domains with postural, body image, and health-related quality-of-life outcomes. Methods In this cross-sectional case-control study, 41 adolescents with AIS and 42 healthy controls were assessed for tactile acuity, proprioception, left/right judgment, motor imagery, and pressure pain threshold, alongside body image, perceived spinal appearance, and quality of life. Results Adolescents with AIS showed elevated paraspinal two-point discrimination thresholds at right T10, right L4, and left L4 (all adjusted p ≤ 0.040), but not at left T10, greater spinal repositioning errors in all four tested directions (all adjusted p ≤ 0.005), and poorer external visual motor imagery (adjusted p = 0.023). No between-group differences were found for left/right judgment or pressure pain threshold (all adjusted p > 0.05). Proprioceptive measures showed the strongest discriminative ability (lumbar right lateral flexion and lumbar flexion repositioning errors: AUC = 0.802 and 0.794, both p Conclusion Adolescents with AIS showed impairments in tactile acuity, proprioception, and external visual motor imagery relative to healthy controls. These cross-sectional findings suggest that sensorimotor alterations may be relevant when designing rehabilitation strategies for this population, but they should be interpreted cautiously and do not establish causality. Larger longitudinal and neuroimaging-based studies are needed to clarify these relationships.

title: Propensity-Matched Comparison of Stemless and Stemmed Anatomic Total Shoulder Arthroplasty in Patients Over 70 Years of Age.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Abdelshaheed J, Beleckas CM, Garcia JR, Obeid T, Grand ZA, Chatterji R, Mark D, Kamm D, Levy JC.
abstract: Background Stemless anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty (aTSA) has gained popularity for glenohumeral osteoarthritis due to improvements in bone preservation, flexibility with humeral head reconstruction and revision advantages. Since bone quality may impact stemless component fixation, routine use in older adults has been questioned. This study aimed to compare clinical and radiographic outcomes of stemless and stemmed aTSA in patients over the age of 70. Methods A retrospective review of a single surgeon's shoulder arthroplasty repository identified patients aged ≥70 years who underwent primary aTSA for glenohumeral osteoarthritis with an intact rotator cuff between 2007 and 2023 with two-year follow-up. Patients treated with a stemless humeral component (CS Edge; Enovis, Austin, TX) were propensity score matched 1:1 to patients treated with a stemmed humeral component (Altivate Anatomic Short Stem or Turon Standard Stem; Enovis, Austin, TX) based on age, sex, and glenoid wear pattern. Deltoid tuberosity index (DTI) was measured on preoperative radiographs as a measure of osteoporosis for all patients. Clinical outcomes including the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score, Simple Shoulder Test (SST), Single Assessment Numeric Evaluation (SANE), Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain and function scores, range of motion, patient satisfaction, and willingness to undergo the procedure again were evaluated at two-year follow-up. Postoperative radiographs were evaluated for humeral component radiolucent lines, glenoid loosening, and medial calcar resorption. Results A total of 176 patients met inclusion criteria following propensity score matching: 88 stemless and 88 stemmed aTSA patients. There were no differences in age, sex, or glenoid wear pattern between cohorts. High rates of osteoporosis were observed similarly in both groups, as DTI measurements met the criteria for osteoporosis in 45 of stemmed and 35 of stemless patients (54% vs 43%, P = .2). At two-year follow-up, both groups demonstrated excellent clinical outcomes with high patient satisfaction and willingness to undergo the procedure again, with no differences amongst the two groups. Radiographic findings demonstrated no cases of humeral component radiolucent lines. The stemless cohort demonstrated significantly lower rates of glenoid radiolucent lines (0/63 [0%] vs. 6/62 [10%]; P = .013) and calcar resorption (13/63 [21%] vs. 24/62 [39%]; P = .027). A total of 3 complications requiring revision to reverse shoulder arthroplasty were identified, none related to humeral loosening. Conclusion Stemless aTSA in patients 70 years and older was associated with excellent clinical outcomes with high patient satisfaction comparable to stemmed aTSA at early follow-up, despite high rates of osteoporosis as measured by DTI. Level of evidence Level III; Retrospective Cohort Comparison; Treatment Study.

title: Prolonged prophylactic antibiotic regimens may reduce periprosthetic infection in megaprosthetic reconstruction: a case series.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Stauss R, Bugdoll F, Graulich T, Tuecking LR, Savov P, Ettinger M, Omar M.
abstract: Introduction Megaprosthetic reconstruction (MPR) is associated with a substantially higher risk of periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) compared to primary total joint arthroplasty. However, evidence guiding the optimal duration of antibiotic prophylaxis remains limited, and institutional practices vary considerably. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the incidence of PJI, antibiotic-related complications, and surgical outcomes in patients undergoing MPR followed by a prolonged prophylactic antibiotic regimen. Materials and methods This retrospective single-centre study included patients undergoing MPR between May 2020 and November 2022 at a tertiary sarcoma referral centre. All patients received a standardised postoperative 12-week prophylactic antibiotic regimen consisting of two weeks of intravenous ampicillin/sulbactam followed by 10 weeks of oral rifampin and levofloxacin. The primary outcome was the incidence of PJI. Secondary outcomes included surgery-related complication and revision rates, antibiotic-related adverse events, and mortality. Results A total of 47 patients were included into the study, of which 83% underwent MPR for oncologic conditions. The overall PJI rate was 2.1% at a mean follow-up of 39 months. Surgery-related complications occurred in 4.3%, and the revision rate was 4.3%. No antibiotic-related adverse events were documented during inpatient treatment or follow-up. All-cause mortality was 21.3%. Conclusions In this retrospective case series, a low incidence of PJI was observed in patients undergoing MPR followed by a standardised 12-week prophylactic antibiotic regimen. Thus, these findings might support the notion that extended prophylaxis could be a safe and effective strategy in high-risk patients undergoing MPR. However, the study design, limited sample size and absence of a control group restrict the conclusions that can be drawn from these findings, and comparative prospective studies are required to determine the effectiveness of prolonged antibiotic prophylaxis following MPR.

title: Prior Clostridioides difficile Infection Is Associated with Infectious Complications Following Total Shoulder Arthroplasty.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Paul BR, Patel JR, Moore ML, Hassebrock JD, Tokish JM, Deckey DG.
abstract: Background Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) has been associated with postoperative complications and periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) after hip and knee arthroplasty but has not been studied in total shoulder arthroplasty (TSA). This study evaluated the association between CDI within two years before TSA and postoperative infectious complications. We hypothesized that prior CDI would be associated with increased odds of PJI, with the greatest odds when CDI occurred closest to surgery. Methods Patients undergoing TSA were identified in a national claims database. Patients with CDI within two years before surgery (n = 782) were propensity score-matched 1:4 to controls (n = 3,098) on demographics, comorbidities, insurance, surgical year, and care setting. The primary outcome was two-year PJI. The CDI cohort was stratified by timing before TSA (0 to 3, 3 to 6, 6 to 12, and 12 to 24 months). Outcomes were compared using chi-square testing and logistic regression. Results Two-year PJI rates were higher in patients with prior CDI (4.6% versus 2.8%; odds ratio [OR] 1.7 [95% CI 1.1 to 2.5]; P = .016), with the greatest odds when CDI occurred within three months before surgery (8.9%; OR 3.4 [1.7 to 6.6]; adjusted P = .002). Prior CDI was also associated with higher odds of subsequent CDI within two years (16.1% versus 1.9%; OR 10.1 [7.3 to 13.9]; adjusted P Conclusion Prior CDI is associated with increased odds of PJI following TSA, particularly when CDI occurs within three months of surgery, as well as with subsequent CDI. These findings suggest that CDI history may help identify higher-risk patients, and surgeons may consider CDI history and timing during preoperative planning.

title: Pericapsular nerve group versus quadratus lumborum block for hip surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Adio AA, Moser AM, Barros A, Khela H, Schweppe E, Sheth NP.
abstract: Introduction The pericapsular nerve group (PENG) block and the quadratus lumborum block (QLB) are both used to provide analgesia after hip surgery, but their comparative efficacy remains uncertain. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing PENG and QLB. Materials and methods PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar were searched through March 2025 for RCTs comparing PENG and QLB in adults undergoing hip surgery. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Random-effects meta-analyses (DerSimonian-Laird estimator with Knapp-Hartung adjustment) pooled standardized mean differences (SMD) for pain, mean differences in intravenous morphine milligram equivalents (MME) for opioid consumption, and risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes. Heterogeneity was quantified with I². Prespecified subgroup analyses (surgical population and QLB approach) and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were performed. Results Seven RCTs (554 patients; 283 PENG, 271 QLB) were included. PENG showed a non-significant trend toward lower early (~ 2 h) resting pain (SMD - 0.25; 95% CI - 0.60 to 0.09; I²=55%). No significant differences were found for resting pain at 24 h (SMD - 0.40; -1.44 to 0.64; I²=92%), pain on movement at 24 h (SMD 0.08; -0.27 to 0.43; I²=0%), or cumulative opioid consumption (mean difference - 0.50 intravenous morphine milligram equivalents; 95% CI - 5.92 to 4.93; I²=84%). Conclusions No clear difference between PENG and QLB was demonstrated for pain, opioid consumption, or safety after hip surgery. The available evidence is insufficient to establish superiority between the techniques, and the early-pain and motor-sparing signals favoring PENG should be regarded as uncertain. Larger standardized randomized trials are required. Level of evidence Level I, systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

title: Patient, surgeon, and institutional variation in implant selection at first-time aseptic revision knee arthroplasty: a registry-based study from the National Joint Registry for England, Wales, Northern Ireland, the Isle of Man, and the Channel Islands.
authors: Tyas B, Hewitt C, Deehan D, Baker P.
abstract: Background and purpose We aimed to characterize temporal trends in implant selection, estimate associations between patient, surgeon, and institutional characteristics and implant choice, and quantify surgeon- and institution-related variation at first-time aseptic revision knee arthroplasty (rTKA). Methods This retrospective registry-based study used National Joint Registry data from England, Wales, Northern Ireland, the Isle of Man, Guernsey, and Jersey. Elective aseptic revisions of primary total knee replacements undertaken between January 1, 2009 and September 30, 2023 were included. Outcomes were metaphyseal fixation device (MFD) use, hinged-construct use, absence of intramedullary stem fixation, and mobile-bearing use. Temporal trends were described. Multilevel regression models estimated associations between patient, surgeon, and institutional characteristics and implant selection, as well as surgeon- and institution-related variation. Results The study comprised 12,950 patients (12,950 knees), with procedures undertaken by 1,250 surgeons across 402 institutions. The use of MFDs increased from 8.5% in 2009 to 37% in 2023. High-volume surgeons had greater odds of MFD use (odd ratio [OR] 1.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.27-2.23; P Conclusion Implant selection changed substantially over time and varied with patient factors and surgeon/institutional context. Measured factors explained few of the examined implant decisions, highlighting substantial practice variation and the need for clearer evidence-based guidance to support implant choices in this setting.

title: Novel Application of Fish-Derived Acellular Matrix in Dural Repair and Scalp Reconstruction Following Subdural Empyema.
authors: Akari A, Evans A, DeJesus R.
abstract: Subdural empyema is a rare intracranial infection characterized by purulent accumulation between the arachnoid and dura mater and has a reported mortality rate of 12.2%. Management includes antibiotics and control of the infection source, commonly through craniotomy and debridement of necrotic tissue. A 51-year-old male with uncontrolled diabetes presented with a chronic necrotic scalp lesion, right hemiparesis, and a left-sided subdural empyema with overlying osteomyelitis. After serial washouts and debridement of nonviable tissue, reconstruction of the dura mater and scalp was required. This case describes the surgical management and first use of Kerecis, a fish-derived acellular matrix, for dural reconstruction. The scalp was additionally reconstructed with a fasciocutaneous anterolateral thigh (ALT) free flap. Postoperatively, the patient demonstrated neurological recovery, a well-perfused flap, and resolution of infection. This case highlights the successful use of Kerecis in reconstructing a devitalized segment of dura. It represents a promising means of clinically and radiologically successful means of dura reconstruction in infected fields that have undergone aggressive surgical debridement and antibiotic treatment.

title: Neglected posteromedial elbow dislocation managed with implant-free bony and soft-tissue reconstruction.
authors: Shakeel MA, Gadwal P, Mittal N, Patil R.

title: Musculoskeletal Pain Management in Physically Demanding Work: Workplace Practices, Social Relations, and Opportunities for Adjustment.
authors: Andersen DR, Nielsen KJ, Andersen JH, Christiansen DH.
abstract: Purpose Musculoskeletal pain is common in physically demanding occupations and contributes to work-related disability. Despite longstanding ergonomic interventions targeting individual risk factors, pain persists, highlighting the role of cultural and organizational conditions in how pain is managed and reported. This study examines workplace-embedded pain-management practices in Danish healthcare and slaughterhouse settings and their implications for pain reporting. Methods Eight workplaces with varying pain prevalence were purposively sampled from a prior survey. At each site, ten semi-structured interviews were conducted and complemented by ethnographic fieldwork. Data were thematically analyzed to examine how employees managed pain and how practices varied across sectors and workplaces. Results Employees combined endurance, self-care, mutual support, and openness about pain, with practices shaped by workplace conditions. In slaughterhouses, endurance predominated within tightly structured, high-paced production systems where pain was normalized. Informal support coexisted with endurance but did not necessarily enable self-care or open discussion. In healthcare, endurance coexisted with self-care and mutual support, facilitated by flexible task allocation, team-based work, and norms legitimizing discussion of pain. Higher pain reporting occurred in workplaces characterized by greater openness, suggesting that reporting reflects not only pain experience but also the social conditions under which pain can be expressed. Conclusions Musculoskeletal pain management is shaped by cultural, organizational, and sectoral conditions. Interventions should address workplace norms, social support, and flexibility in work organization alongside individual and ergonomic factors to support sustainable work participation.

title: Mid-term outcomes of medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction using suture tape in paediatric and adolescent population: a case series.
authors: Youssef K, Vampertzis T, Gangadharan R, Rad D, Bailey M, Wadia F.
abstract: Background Suture tape medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) reconstruction avoids tendon graft harvest, but outcomes in children are poorly reported. This study evaluated functional outcomes and complications in children and adolescents with recurrent patellar instability. Methods A retrospective cohort of 56 patients (77 knees; 40 female; mean age 14.3 years, range 8.2-17.7) underwent isolated suture tape MPFL reconstruction for recurrent instability at a tertiary centre between 2020 and 2025. Minimum follow-up was 6 months. The primary outcome was the Paediatric International Knee Documentation Committee (Pedi-IKDC) score at ≥6 months (available for 58 knees). Secondary outcomes were recurrent instability, extensor lag and other complications. Results The mean Pedi-IKDC score improved from 49.6 (SD 13.9) to 79.6 (SD 16.9), a mean gain of 30.0 points (p Conclusion Suture tape MPFL reconstruction improved the Pedi-IKDC score by 30.0 points, more than three times the minimal clinically important difference, with recurrent instability (6.5%) comparable to tendon graft reconstruction in children and no physeal complications. Extensor lag (26.2%) was common but resolved with physiotherapy in all but one knee. Suture tape is a reasonable graft-free option; comparative studies are needed.

title: Hip Strength Recovery Over 1-Year Following Arthroscopic Surgery for Femoroacetabular Impingement Syndrome.
authors: Johnston M, Chan JZ, Halliwell C, Remedios S, Wong I.
abstract: Femoroacetabular impingement syndrome (FAIS) is associated with hip muscle weakness and altered neuromuscular function, which may persist despite surgical intervention. Although patients undergoing arthroscopic surgery for FAIS often report improvements in pain and function, recovery of hip muscle strength following surgery remains poorly characterized particularly beyond the early postoperative period. The purpose of this study was to characterize changes in hip muscle strength and patient-reported outcomes 1 year following arthroscopic surgery for FAIS. Retrospective case series of prospectively collected clinical data. Patients who underwent hip arthroscopy for FAIS between 2019 and 2022 were included if they completed standardized preoperative and 1-year postoperative strength assessments. Isometric hip flexor, extensor, abductor, internal rotator, and external rotator strength were measured using handheld dynamometry. Patient-reported outcomes were assessed using the International Hip Outcome Tool-33. Within-participant changes were analyzed in males and females using paired t-tests, with effect sizes and 95% CIs reported. Fifty-two participants (mean age 40.1 [13.5] y; 69% female) were included. At 1-year, females strength increased across all muscle groups (P = .01- < .001), where males did not have a statistically significant improvement in any strength measure. More than 70% of female participants exceeded their preoperative strength levels across all movement directions, although substantial interindividual variability was observed. On average, International Hip Outcome Tool-33 scores improved by 30 points (P < .001). Females undergoing arthroscopic management of FAIS demonstrate improvements in muscle strength with no differences in males. The postoperative strength recovery values reported here may provide clinicians with descriptive reference points for monitoring recovery following arthroscopic management of FAIS, although these values should not be interpreted as validated rehabilitation thresholds.

title: Functional and Magnetic Resonance Imaging Outcomes After Cell-Free Collagen Matrix Treatment for Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus: A Multicentered Retrospective Clinical and Radiological Study.
authors: Simon R, Upadhyay R, Abraham AS, Arunkumar G, S R A, Vishavadia P, Jose DP, Rajan A.
abstract: BackgroundOsteochondral lesions of the talus (OLTs) are challenging to treat due to the limited regenerative capacity of hyaline cartilage. Emerging cell-free scaffolds such as ChondroFiller offer a single-stage, minimally invasive option; however, evidence regarding their clinical and radiological outcomes in ankle lesions remains limited.MethodsThis multicenter retrospective cohort study included 21 patients with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-confirmed OLTs (Hepple grades III-V) treated arthroscopically with ChondroFiller between October 2023 and October 2025. Autologous cancellous bone grafting was performed in cases with subchondral defects. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the foot and ankle outcome score (FAOS) and visual analog scale (VAS), while cartilage repair was evaluated using the magnetic resonance observation of cartilage repair tissue (MOCART 2.0) score on postoperative MRI at a minimum follow-up of 6 months. Statistical analysis included paired comparisons and correlation testing.ResultsAt a mean follow-up of 20.7 ± 7.8 months, significant improvements were observed in all clinical parameters. Mean FAOS improved from 52.7 ± 11.3 preoperatively to 85.0 ± 7.7 postoperatively (P IV retrospective case series .

title: Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes of Suture Anchor Repair versus Transarticular Kirschner Wire Fixation of the Acromioclavicular Joint in Acute High-grade Dislocation: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Hirunthanawiwat T, Benjawongsathien K, Sutthapakti B, Reingrittha P, Larpjitkusol P, Laoruengthana A.
abstract: Background For high-grade acromioclavicular (AC) joint injury, repairing the AC ligament complex in addition to coracoclavicular (CC) stabilization provides superior biomechanical and functional outcomes. Rigid AC fixation, such as transarticular wires or hook plates, yields reliable outcomes but may be offset by complications. Therefore, this study compared the clinical and radiographic outcomes of an alternative AC stabilization with Suture anchor repair versus K-wire fixation. Methods A prospective randomized trial was conducted in 32 patients with acute AC dislocation. Patients were randomized (16 per group) to Suture anchor repair or transarticular K-wire fixation, both with the same nonbiologic CC suspensory technique. In the Suture anchor group, a single 2.8-mm anchor was inserted into the distal clavicle to repair the superior AC capsuloligamentous complex. The primary outcome was the Constant-Murley Score (CMS); secondary outcomes were the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) shoulder scores, percentage coracoclavicular distance (%CCD) change, and complications, assessed at 4, 8, 16, 24, and 52 weeks. Repeated measurements were analyzed using multilevel Gaussian regression with Bonferroni adjustment, and differences were interpreted against published minimal clinically important difference thresholds. Results All 32 patients completed 52-week follow-up. The Suture anchor group included 3 Rockwood type IIIB and 13 type V, while the K-wire group included 8 type IIIB and 8 type V. The Suture anchor group had higher CMS at 4 weeks (mean difference, 12.7 points; 95% CI, 8.7-16.6), 8 weeks (7.9; 95% CI, 4.0-11.9), and 16 weeks (5.3; 95% CI, 1.4-9.3) (all P ≤ .003), with no difference at 24 or 52 weeks. ASES and UCLA scores were higher in the Suture anchor group at 4 and 8 weeks only (all P Conclusion While AC stabilization with suture anchor repair provided faster early functional recovery and K-wire fixation better maintained radiographic reduction, both techniques yielded comparable functional outcomes from 24 weeks and onward. Additionally, these findings should be limited to AC joint dislocation with primarily vertical instability, and the choice between techniques should be individualized. Level of evidence Level I, Randomized Controlled Trial, Treatment Study.

title: Classification-Dependent Prevalence of Lumbosacral Transitional Vertebrae on Whole-Spine CT: Castellvi vs. Jenkins in a Polish Trauma Cohort.
authors: Jankowski J, Maślanek N, Glin M, Jasiewicz M, Pawełczyk A, Polguj M, Radek M.
abstract: Study designRetrospective cohort study.ObjectivesDespite the clinical significance of spinal anatomical variability, robust epidemiological data on its prevalence remain limited. This study aimed to characterize segmental and morphological spinal variations in a Polish adult trauma cohort undergoing whole-spine CT, with emphasis on lumbosacral transitional vertebrae (LSTV), and to compare LSTV prevalence and subtype distribution according to the Castellvi and Jenkins classification systems.Materials and MethodsA single-center retrospective analysis of 499 consecutive adult trauma patients undergoing whole-spine CT (2022-2024) was performed. Vertebral segmentation was established for each case, and transitional anatomy was assessed across all spinal junctions. LSTV was classified using both the Castellvi and Jenkins systems to allow comparison of classification-dependent prevalence estimates.ResultsStandard C7-T12-L5-S5 segmentation was observed in 67.94% (339/499) of cases, with 14 distinct segmentation patterns identified overall. Transitional features were most frequent at the lumbosacral junction, followed by sacrococcygeal (26.25%; 131/499), the thoracolumbar (11.82%; 59/499), cervicothoracic (7.01%; 35/499), and craniocervical (0.20%; 1/499) junctions. LSTV prevalence differed markedly according to the classification system, being 26.85% (134/499) according to Castellvi and 92.59% (462/499) according to Jenkins.ConclusionLSTV prevalence in this Polish trauma cohort lies in the upper range of previously reported values using the Castellvi classification. The marked discrepancy between the Castellvi and Jenkins systems highlights fundamental differences in defining transitional anatomy, with the Jenkins classification capturing a substantially broader spectrum of morphologies, particularly through its distance-based Type I criterion. The exceptionally high prevalence obtained with the Jenkins system raises questions regarding the discriminatory value of this threshold and warrants further clinical validation.

title: CT-Based Morphology and Outcomes After ORIF of Humeral Head Articular Fractures.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Gavaskar AS, Ayyadurai P, Srinivasan P, Tummala NC.
abstract: Background Articular fractures of the humeral head encompass a spectrum of injuries. CT-based assessment of the extent of articular injury may influence reduction, functional outcomes, and avascular necrosis (AVN), but its association with outcomes after open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) remains incompletely understood. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 109 patients with humeral head articular fractures treated between 2010 and 2023 and classified fractures into five types using preoperative CT. Outcomes were analysed in 78 patients undergoing ORIF (mean age, 43 years; range, 20-68; SD, 11). Functional scores, reduction quality, and AVN incidence were compared across fracture types; complications and reoperations were recorded. Age and sex adjusted Constant scores (CS) and QuickDASH scores were assessed at a mean follow-up of 62 months (range, 24-122; SD, 18) after index ORIF. Exploratory multivariable analyses evaluated associations between fracture type and functional outcomes after adjustment for selected patient and injury characteristics. Reduction quality was graded as anatomical, acceptable, or poor using predefined radiographic criteria. Post-arthroplasty functional outcomes were analysed separately. Results Union was achieved in 72 of 78 patients (92%). Mean CS was 69 (range, 28-100; SD, 18) and mean QuickDASH was 29 (range, 2.3-61.4; SD, 14). Functional outcomes differed among fracture types (CS and QuickDASH, both p Level of evidence Level III, Retrospective Cohort Comparison, Prognosis Study.
