title: Barriers and facilitators for collecting spine registry data in rehabilitation practice: Interpretive description of perspectives from patient, clinicians, and policy-makers in Canada.
authors: El Chamaa A, Walton D, J van der Wees P, Cruijsberg J, Staal JB, Rushton A.
abstract: Background Routine collection of patient-reported and clinical data is central to clinical registries and is increasingly promoted to support quality improvement, shared decision-making, and research in spinal pain. However, registry implementation may be burdensome and poorly aligned with everyday clinical practice. Little is known about how patients, clinicians, and policymakers in Canada experience these efforts. Objectives To explore barriers to and facilitators of routine data collection and registry implementation from the perspectives of patients, clinicians, and policymakers in Canadian spinal pain physiotherapy. Methods A qualitative study was conducted within a larger bi-national project on registry implementation. This abstract reports Canadian findings. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with patients with spinal pain (n = 6), physiotherapy clinicians (n = 6), and policymakers (n = 6). Participants were purposively sampled to capture variation in age, sex, practice settings, and leadership roles. Using interpretive description and Reflexive Thematic Analysis, transcripts and field notes were coded into themes. Patient partners refined the interview guide and reviewed findings. Results Across groups, sustained participation depended on balancing burden with value. Time, workflow disruption, and lack of feedback threatened engagement, whereas a registry was viewed as valuable and a way to improve care beyond individual encounters. Patients wanted tools that were short, flexible, and linked to care. Clinicians supported registries that added clear value with minimal effort. Policymakers valued registries for quality improvement but raised concerns about privacy, inequity, and punitive use of metrics. Conclusions Spinal pain registries should be easy to use, integrated into clinical workflows, and provide visible feedback to sustain engagement.

title: Ultra-High-Field (7T) knee MRI: review of technical considerations and current evidence, with experience from an institutional clinical series.
authors: Boudabbous S, Branco DF, Tscholl PM, Delattre BMA, Rubbia-Brandt L, Bouredoucen H, Poletti PA, Hannouche D, Lövblad KO, Kurz FT.
abstract: Background Ultra-high-field, 7 Tesla (T) MRI provides higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and enables high-resolution 3D and quantitative imaging. Its role in musculoskeletal (MSK) knee imaging is emerging but not yet standardized. Purpose To review current 7 T knee MRI techniques and evidence, detail key technical/physics considerations, and to report a single-center clinical experience through a descriptive study. Methods Up to date narrative synthesis of the literature organized by qualitative (morphologic) and quantitative applications, complemented by experience from a retrospective single-center series of consecutive 7 T knee examinations. Results Literature shows that 7 T imaging can improve conspicuity of cartilage, meniscus, ligaments, and bone microarchitecture with isotropic 3D acquisitions; quantitative methods (T2/T2*, Ultrashort Echo Time (UTE), Glycosaminoglycan Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer (gagCEST), 23 Na, T1rho) show promise but require rigorous B0/B1 correction and Specific Absorption Rate (SAR) management. Our experience demonstrated that 7 T imaging was clinically feasible and well tolerated in a cohort of 131 patients (mean age 33.8 ± 10.5 years ranging from 16 to 63 years) and provided a potential and a subjective increase in diagnosis confidence in selected scenarios, particularly in postoperative meniscus assessment and conservative ACL follow-up. Conclusion 7 T knee MRI is feasible and potentially impactful in specific indications; however, stronger comparative data, protocol harmonization, and quantitative validation are needed.

title: Risk Period for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Rupture During Skiing: A Multicenter Epidemiological Study.
authors: Amini F, Hardy A, Behr J, Morin V, Noailles T.
abstract: Background Alpine skiing carries a substantial risk of knee injuries, particularly anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures. Despite improvements in equipment and safety standards, ACL injuries remain frequent and are influenced by modifiable and unmodifiable risk factors. Identifying temporal and situational patterns may support more effective prevention strategies. Hypothesis ACL ruptures in recreational skiers occur more frequently early in ski vacations and earlier in the ski day, reflecting insufficient neuromuscular adaptation. Study design Multicenter retrospective observational study (2024-2025 season). Level of evidence Level 4. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted between January and April 2025 in 3 sports medicine centers in France. Patients with magnetic resonance imaging scan-confirmed ACL rupture sustained during recreational skiing within the preceding 3 months were included. Data were collected using a standardized questionnaire assessing injury timing, skiing experience, injury mechanism, and environmental conditions. Descriptive statistics were used. Results A total of 138 patients were included; 68.1% were female, with a mean age of 33 years. ACL injuries occurred predominantly at the beginning of ski vacations (46%) and before midday (64.6%). Most injuries involved intermediate or expert skiers (83.3%). Falls and changes of direction were common injury mechanisms. Injuries occurred more frequently (58.3%) under average or poor snow conditions, whereas visibility showed no clear association. Associated injuries were observed in 36 (28.5%) patients and were mainly vertical tears of the medial meniscus. Specific lesions were also identified, including 3 ramp lesions (8.3%) and 3 lateral meniscal root lesions (8.3%). Conclusion ACL ruptures in skiing occur most commonly early in ski vacations and during the morning, particularly among intermediate and expert skiers. These findings underscore the role of neuromuscular readiness, fatigue-independent factors, and environmental conditions in ACL injury risk. Clinical relevance Prevention strategies for skiing-related ACL injuries should prioritize early-session and early-vacation interventions, including structured warm-up routines, progressive skill adaptation, and neuromuscular training. Targeted prevention programs, particularly for female and higher-level recreational skiers, may reduce the incidence of severe knee injuries.

title: Real-time instance segmentation of spine endoscopy images using a YOLO-V11 deep convolutional neural network.
authors: Jung HJ, Nam NE, Lee C, Lim Y, Choi WC, Lee J, Kim G, Kim H, Lee SK, Kang J, Kim TS.
abstract: Background and objectives Spine endoscopic surgery requires precise anatomical recognition and real-time bleeding detection to enhance surgical safety and efficiency. However, most existing computer vision studies do not offer real-time multi-class segmentation of the entire scene. This study aims to develop a real-time instance segmentation model based on YOLO-V11, capable of automatically identifying surgical instruments, critical anatomical structures, and bleeding sites in spine endoscopy. Methods The model was trained and evaluated using 2,181 annotated frames (training 1,741 / validation 216 / held-out test 224) from spine endoscopy images, covering nine key categories: instruments, bone, ligamentum flavum, dura, soft tissue, vessels, fat, the radiofrequency ablation wand, and bleeding focus. The segmentation model's performance was evaluated across various YOLO-V11 variants. Results Across five random seeds per variant on the same NVIDIA A100 GPU, YOLO-V11 l achieved the highest mask mAP50, defined as mean average precision at an intersection-over-union threshold of 0.50, with a value of 0.7735 ± 0.0030 (mean ± SD, n = 5). It also maintained real-time inference, reaching 270 ± 35 frames per second (FPS) with a per-frame latency of 3.75 ± 0.51 ms. All five variants exceeded 30 FPS, the widely accepted real-time threshold for surgical imaging. The model demonstrated high precision in segmenting vital structures such as the dura and ligamentum flavum and accurately identified bleeding regions. Conclusion This research contributes to AI-driven surgical guidance systems, with potential applications in robotic-assisted spine surgery. The developed model enables real-time navigation, improving intraoperative decision-making and enhancing surgical outcomes. In particular, our YOLO-V11-based framework extends prior single-structure or lower-frame-rate multi-element approaches by delivering real-time multi-class instance segmentation of instruments, anatomical structures, and bleeding sites in spine endoscopy, with explicitly quantified inference latency.

title: Osteoarthritis year in review 2026: Imaging.
authors: Fukuda T, Jarraya M, Roemer F, Guermazi A.
abstract: Objective To narratively review the literature on osteoarthritis (OA) imaging published between March 2025 and March 2026 and to identify current trends and emerging directions in imaging-based OA research. Methods PubMed was searched for original English-language human in vivo studies published during the period. Trends by imaging modality and target-joint distributions were analyzed. For narrative synthesis, studies were selected subjectively by consensus among the authors based on methodological novelty, clinical or trial relevance, contribution to understanding OA pathophysiology or progression, and potential future impact. Results Of 1,910 publications identified, 1,035 specified a target joint. Approximately 70% investigated the knee, followed by the hip. Radiography and ultrasound yielded the most records, encompassing heterogeneous applications such as trial eligibility and image-guided procedures. Although publication counts for these modalities have gradually declined in recent years, those for MRI have remained stable. Semiquantitative MRI analysis linked worsening bone marrow lesions and Hoffa-synovitis to greater cartilage loss, and suggested differing associations between injection type and subsequent structural progression. Quantitative MRI studies linked cartilage T2 to BMI in a population-based cohort, while muscle radiomics predicted incident knee OA. Among emerging technique, magnetic resonance fingerprinting (MRF) provided rapid cartilage T2 mapping, and [18F]NaF PET-MRI linked increased metabolic activity at enthesis to worse knee-related outcomes. For clinical-trial eligibility, MRI detected exclusionary abnormalities in 10% of otherwise DMOAD-eligible knees. AI-related publications gradually increased, with applications including prediction of future total knee replacement (TKR) and automated tissue segmentation. Conclusion Studies highlight the use of imaging for longitudinal assessment of structural progression, clinical-trial eligibility, and quantitative tissue characterization. MRI remains central to understanding disease mechanisms and progression, while emerging techniques such as MRF and [18F]NaF PET-MRI broaden quantitative and metabolic assessment. AI may support prediction of future TKR and automated cartilage morphometry.

title: Musculoskeletal injury epidemiology among football players in Africa: A systematic review of injury incidence, patterns and associated factors.
authors: Jimoh FA, Adepoju AM, Afolabi ST, Bolarinwa AM.
abstract: Background Football is widely played across Africa, yet evidence on the epidemiology of musculoskeletal injuries among African football players remains fragmented across countries, populations, and competitive settings. Differences in injury definitions, surveillance methods, and exposure measurement further limit comparison between studies. This systematic review synthesised the available evidence on musculoskeletal injury epidemiology in African football. Methods PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Database, and Google Scholar were systematically searched from inception to the final search date, supplemented by backward citation searching. Studies investigating musculoskeletal injuries among football players in Africa were eligible for inclusion. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Methodological quality and risk of bias were evaluated using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and Quality In Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tools, as appropriate. Owing to methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively. Results Twenty-six studies were included. Sixteen studies contributed 18 incidence estimates, ranging from 2.2 to 289 injuries per 1,000 athlete-exposure hours, while 10 studies reported prevalence estimates ranging from 4.1% to 81.6%. Tournament surveillance studies generally reported higher incidence than season-long studies, and match incidence exceeded training incidence where both were reported. Lower-extremity injuries predominated, particularly at the ankle and knee, while sprains or ligament injuries, contusions, and muscle-related injuries were the most frequently reported injury types. Previous injury or recurrence was the most consistently identified associated factor. Conclusion Musculoskeletal injuries are common in African football, but substantial methodological heterogeneity limits direct comparison of estimates. Standardised injury surveillance and stronger prospective research are needed to improve the evidence base and support context-specific injury prevention. Prospero registration number CRD420261444997.

title: Effects of Talar Osteochondral Lesion Location and Size on the Ankle Joint: A Finite Element Analysis With Cadaveric Validation.
authors: Aslan L, Subasi O, O'Neill C, Winckelmans D, Kerkhoffs GMMJ, Kwon JY, Waryasz G, Ashkani-Esfahani S, DiGiovanni CW.
abstract: BackgroundOsteochondral lesions of the talus (OLTs) are frequently treated with bone marrow stimulation, but failure rates increase as lesion size enlarges. Operative decision-making is largely based on lesion diameter, with limited quantitative biomechanical evidence addressing how lesion size and anatomic location together influence ankle joint mechanics. This study evaluated how OLT size and anatomic location might affect cartilage stress distribution under physiologic loadingMethodsTwelve fresh-frozen ankle specimens underwent weight-bearing computed tomography (WBCT) under a standardized 70-kg (~686-N) axial load in the neutral position in the intact state and following sequential creation of 6-, 8-, 10-, 12-, and 15-mm osteochondral defects. Specimens were assigned to one of three clinically relevant talar zones: centromedial (zone 4), centrolateral (zone 6), or posteromedial (zone 7; n = 4 per zone). Subject- and lesion-state-specific finite element models were generated from the neutral-position WBCT data sets and subsequently analyzed computationally in 15° plantarflexion, neutral position, and 15° dorsiflexion. Maximum and average talar cartilage von Mises stresses were calculated.ResultsCartilage stress increased nonlinearly with progressive lesion enlargement. Significant stepwise increases were most consistently observed in zones 4 and 6, particularly during plantarflexion and dorsiflexion, with prominent increases across the 8- to 12-mm range. Zone 7 demonstrated more modest changes, with no significant sequential increases. Stress escalation was less pronounced in the neutral position.ConclusionProgressive OLT enlargement produced nonlinear increases in talar cartilage stress, with the magnitude and timing of stress escalation varying across lesion locations and ankle positions. Stress escalation was most pronounced in zones 4 and 6 across the 8- to 12-mm range, whereas zone 7 demonstrated more modest changes. These findings suggest that lesion location and the associated mechanical environment may provide additional biomechanical information beyond lesion size alone; however, they should not be interpreted as establishing new clinical treatment thresholds.Level of Evidence:5.

title: Biomechanical Evaluation of Crossed Screw Fixations With Different Head Designs for First Tarsometatarsal Joint Arthrodesis.
authors: Ortmayr J, Benca E, Dornyi T, Hirtler L, Veljkovic A, Schuh R, Zandieh S, Windhager R, Willegger M.
abstract: BackgroundMidfoot arthrodesis is used to treat deformity, instability, and degenerative conditions. Headless compression screws may reduce hardware prominence and soft tissue irritation. We compared the biomechanical properties of conventional and headless compression screws in a modified Lapidus first tarsometatarsal joint (TMTJ) arthrodesis model.MethodsTen matched human lower extremity pairs were randomly assigned to first TMTJ arthrodesis using either 2 crossed headed 4.0-mm cannulated compression screws (HS) or two 4.0-mm cannulated headless compression screws (HLS). After bone mineral density (BMD) assessment, specimens were cyclically loaded from 0 to 31 N for 1000 cycles. Dorsal angulation and construct stiffness were measured during cyclic loading and subsequent loading to failure.ResultsMean stiffness during ultimate load testing was 58.91 ± 31.33 N/mm for headed screws and 68.36 ± 84.29 N/mm for headless screws (P = .842). Mean yield load was 115.80 ± 61.94 and 67.79 ± 35.90 N (P = .101), and mean ultimate load was 142.10 ± 65.24 and 83.02 ± 60.77 N (P = 0.064), respectively. No significant difference in dorsal angulation was observed. Mean BMD was 0.547 ± 0.222 g/cm² for headed screws and 0.533 ± 0.204 g/cm² for headless screws (P = 0.897). Bone mineral density positively correlated with construct stiffness in the headless screw group during several loading cycles, but not in the headed screw group. No significant correlations were found between BMD and yield or ultimate load.ConclusionHeaded and headless crossed screw constructs showed no statistically significant differences in stiffness, yield load, ultimate load, or dorsal angulation. However, the numerical difference in ultimate load favored headed screws. Headless compression screws may offer clinical advantages through their low-profile design, but further biomechanical and clinical studies are warranted.Clinical Relevance:Headless and headed screws showed no statistically significant differences in this cadaveric first tarsometatarsal joint model, although headed screws achieved higher mean failure loads. Their low-profile design may reduce hardware prominence and soft tissue irritation while maintaining adequate primary fixation stability.

title: Biomechanical Comparison of Triple and Quintuple Percutaneous Achilles Tendon Lengthening Techniques: A Short Report.
authors: Zhu M, Marty EW, Myerson MS, Li S.
abstract: Background Triple hemi-section percutaneous Achilles tendon lengthening is a widely used technique for the treatment of Achilles tendon contracture. This cadaveric study compared a novel quintuple hemi-section technique with the traditional triple hemi-section technique to assess their effects on Achilles tendon lengthening and ankle dorsiflexion. Methods Seven matched pairs of above-knee specimens were randomly assigned for either triple or quintuple hemi-section Achilles tendon lengthening. A constant 45-N load was applied throughout the procedure. Following completion of the tenotomies, tensile load was progressively increased until either maximum ankle dorsiflexion or Achilles tendon rupture occurred. Tendon lengthening, ankle dorsiflexion angle, load at maximal dorsiflexion, or tendon rupture were compared between the 2 groups. Results Mean tendon lengthening was 24.20 mm in the quintuple hemi-section group and 11.22 mm in the triple hemi-section group ( P = .24). Mean ankle dorsiflexion was 12.61° and 9.19°, respectively ( P = .46). Achilles tendon rupture occurred in 4 specimens (57%) in the quintuple group and in 5 specimens (71%) in the triple group ( P > .99). Conclusion In this paired cadaveric biomechanical study, with the numbers available, no significant difference could be detected between the experimental quintuple and the traditional triple hemi-section techniques in Achilles tendon lengthening or ankle dorsiflexion. Although numerical differences were observed, their clinical significance remains uncertain and should be evaluated in larger biomechanical and clinical studies. Clinical relevance This study provides biomechanical comparison of a novel quintuple hemi-section technique and the traditional triple hemi-section technique for percutaneous Achilles tendon lengthening. Although no significant differences were observed, these findings provide preliminary data to guide future clinical studies evaluating whether additional hemi-sections improve equinus correction while maintaining safety.

title: Anterior subcapital realignment osteotomy for unstable slipped capital femoral epiphysis: a retrospective consecutive series of forty five hips.
authors: Sodhai V, Patwardhan S, Shyam A, Khairnar T.
abstract: Purpose The optimal management of unstable, high-grade slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) remains controversial due to the need to balance anatomical realignment with preservation of femoral head vascularity. This study aims to evaluate the outcomes of anterior subcapital realignment osteotomy (ASRO) as a reproducible alternative for unstable SCFE. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted of 45 consecutive moderate-to-severe unstable slips managed with ASRO between 2013 and 2023. Patients were classified as unstable based on Loder's classification, acute (n = 7) or acute-on-chronic (n = 38) based on duration of symptoms, and moderate (30-60°, n = 28) or severe (> 60°, n = 17) slip using the Southwick angle. Functional outcomes were assessed using the Harris Hip Score (HHS) and pain using the Faces Pain Scale-Revised (FPS-R). Results The cohort included 31 males and 14 females with a mean age of 13.7 years (SD 1.1) and mean follow-up of 38 months (range 24-64). Mean BMI was 28.3 (SD 2.9). Southwick angle improved from 54.1° (SD 16.1) preoperatively to 13.7° (SD 2.4) postoperatively (p Conclusion ASRO provides reliable anatomical correction and favourable short to mid-term functional outcomes in unstable, moderate to severe SCFE. The observed rate of AVN was comparable to that of SSD. This approach avoids surgical hip dislocation and may represent a reproducible alternative to the SSD approach.

title: What matters more in the time to flap: injury-to-flap or definitive-fixation-to-flap?
authors: Mundy LR, Coto SD, O'Hara NN, Wolinsky P, Obremskey WT, Potter BK, Beltran MJ, Scolaro JA, Sprague S, Slobogean GP, Gitajn IL, PREP-IT Investigators.
abstract: Objectives To determine the optimal threshold between injury, first debridement, and fixation-to-flap that minimizes infection risk in adult patients who sustained an open fracture requiring acute flap coverage. Methods Design: A retrospective, secondary analysis using data from two prospective randomized controlled trials (XXX and XXX trials) to evaluate infection and time to flap coverage. Setting Multinational clinical trial at 25 institutions. Patient selection criteria This secondary analysis included patients 18 years and older, who underwent definitive fracture fixation with an implant, and operative debridement within 72 hours of injury. Patients also had to receive a free or pedicled flap for acute injury management, rather than for wound dehiscence or infection. Outcome measures and comparisons Infection rate at 3-months was assessed using Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) criteria with a sensitivity analysis at 12-months. Time from injury-to-flap, first debridement-to-flap and definitive fixation-to-flap intervals were evaluated using multivariate logistic regression models while adjusting for demographic and clinical factors. Included covariates were selected based on a stepwise procedure, using the Akaike Information Criterion, and on their clinical or sociodemographic relevance. Results The analysis included 138 patients. 32 patients (23.2%) developed an infection and 106 did not (76.8%). The two groups were similar with regards to demographic and injury-related characteristics, with a mean age of 44.9 years (standard deviation [SD] 16.0) in the group of patients with a primary infection versus 44.8 years (SD 16.0) in those who did not develop an infection. Seventy-five percent of patients with a primary infection were male compared to 63.2% in the other group. Mean time to flap was 9.7 days (range 0.0 - 30.0). Multivariate analysis showed that a flap within 7 days following injury (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.09-0.74, p=0.01) or first debridement (OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.12-0.89, p Conclusions This study suggests that limiting the time from injury and first debridement to flap to less than 7 days was associated with decreased risk of infection. However, infection was not found to be associated with time from definitive fixation-to-flap. Level of evidence Level III.

title: What I Wish My Surgeon Knew: Caring for the Young Atypical Patient.
authors: Zook VR.

title: What Are the Long-term Outcomes of Periacetabular Osteotomy in a United States Cohort?
authors: Maroyan A, Mendola LC, De Silva S, Matheney T, Millis MB.
abstract: Background Periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) is an effective and common hip-preserving procedure used to treat symptomatic acetabular dysplasia of the hip. Evidence regarding long-term outcomes after PAO remains limited. Information regarding long-term outcomes may be important in developing reasonable expectations for both patients and surgeons to facilitate effective therapeutic decision-making. Questions/purposes (1) What is the likelihood of long-term hip preservation and the level of pain at a minimum of 25 years of follow-up after PAO? (2) What clinical and radiographic factors were associated with patients having a poor result, which we defined either as having THA or a WOMAC score of ≥ 10 points at the most recent survey? (3) What were the outcome scores of patients who underwent THA after PAO, and how did these scores compare to the scores of the preserved hips and to the scores of age-related norms? Methods We retrospectively evaluated the cohort of the first 142 patients (171 hips) who underwent PAO performed by one surgeon to treat symptomatic dysplasia between 1991 and 1998. Twenty-three percent (33 of 142) of patients (37 hips) were lost to follow-up. This included six patients (6 hips) who had died, 23 patients (26 hips) who could not be located, and four patients (5 hips) who did not complete questionnaires. Seventy-seven percent (109 of 142) of eligible patients (134 hips) returned complete questionnaires at a median (range) of 27 years (25 to 33) after PAO. Our analyzed group included 87% female patients (95 patients, 117 hips) and 13% male patients (14 patients, 17 hips). The median (range) age at surgery was 25 years (9 to 45). The median (range) time of review after PAO was 27 years (25 to 33). The 53 hips that had undergone THA were reviewed at a median (range) of 11 years (1 to 28) after the THA. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to assess survivorship free from conversion to THA. Hips were postoperatively evaluated using the pain subscale of the WOMAC index. We characterized a poor clinical outcome as either having a preserved hip with a WOMAC pain score of ≥ 10 or undergoing THA. All patients who were analyzed returned questionnaires; some were seen in person with images. Factors associated with a patient having a high (poor) WOMAC score for pain or undergoing THA were evaluated using a multinomial logistic regression model using generalized estimating equations. Results Of patients analyzed, 60% (81 of 134) of hips remained preserved. Forty percent (53 of 134) of hips had undergone THA at a median of 22 years after PAO. The survivorship free from conversion to THA at 25 years after PAO was 70% (95% confidence interval [CI] 62% to 78%), and the median (range) level of pain was 1 (0 to 20) of 20 points. After controlling for potentially confounding variables including sex, preoperative lateral center-edge angle and anterior center-edge angle, and postoperative lateral center-edge angle, we found that the following factors were associated with increased odds of having either a poor (≥ 10 points) WOMAC pain score or conversion to THA: preoperative joint space width ≤ 2 mm (HR 7.3 [95% CI 2.8 to 19.2]), labral tear noted intraoperatively (HR 2.8 [95% CI 1.3 to 5.8]), age at surgery > 21 years and Conclusion While a majority of hips can be preserved with good function at a mean of 27 years after PAO, our findings suggest that surgery should be considered as soon as the diagnosis of symptomatic dysplasia is made, given that older age at the time of surgery was independently associated with later THA or a WOMAC pain score of ≥ 10. If a patient develops painful arthrosis after a PAO, THA should be offered and expected to provide function comparable to age-related norms. Prospective registry-based multicenter studies of patients treated for symptomatic hip dysplasia are indicated to improve outcomes. Level of evidence level III, therapeutic study.

title: Voluntary wheel running attenuates mechanical hypersensitivity but transiently prolongs gait impairments in male and female mice with unilateral osteoarthritis.
authors: Florea R, Hestehave S, Nwankwo O, Andreoli L, Wright A, Géranton SM.
abstract: Objective Physical activity is a first-line therapeutic intervention for managing osteoarthritis-related pain and functional impairment. However, the growing literature questions the long-term relevance of exercise-induced improvements in patients, while pre-clinical research evidence-base is limited by reliance on stressful, forced exercise paradigms which do not reflect voluntary engagement. Here, we investigated the effects of voluntary wheel running on the pain experience in mice with joint pain. Design We investigated the impact of free access to a running wheel on sensory, functional and affective outcomes following unilateral intra-articular injection of monoiodoacetate (MIA) into the knee joint of 8-week-old male and female C57Bl/6J mice (n=14/16). Mice were single-housed and randomly assigned to remain sedentary or have unrestricted access to a wheel from at least two weeks before MIA. Behavioural outcomes were assessed longitudinally over an eight-week post-injection period. Results Mean daily running distance decreased from 3.01 to 0.69 km in males and from 3.90 to 1.69 km in females by day 5 after MIA. Following a short-lived recovery, males showed a progressive decline, while the rebound in activity was sustained in females throughout the observation period. Voluntary wheel running attenuated MIA-induced secondary mechanical hypersensitivity, with higher mechanical withdrawal thresholds in active than sedentary mice, most obviously during the pain-like maintenance stage (day 40: males: 0.08g; 95%CI 0.040 to 0.126; females: 0.125g, 95%CI 0.029 to 0.222). Conversely, wheel running transiently delayed full gait recovery, with between-group differences in stance symmetry and duty factor during early recovery in both sexes (males day 20: stance: -11.8%; 95%CI -21.25 to -2.27; duty factor: -5.4%; 95%CI -10.53 to -0.35; females day 12: stance: -22.0%; 95%CI -32.48 to -11.51; duty factor: -15.9%; 95%CI -22.97 to -8.83). Finally, wheel access had little effect on anxio-depressive-like behaviours or cognition, but reduced faecal output and influenced body weight. Conclusions In this animal model of MIA-induced osteoarthritis, voluntary wheel running was associated with improvements in secondary mechanical hypersensitivity, despite a transient and acute worsening of several gait impairments. These findings highlight the importance of assessing multiple behavioural domains in preclinical studies and underscore the complexity of exercise-induced effects on pain and function.

title: Unplanned Reoperation and Patient-Reported Outcomes After Operative Treatment of Intraarticular Glenoid Fractures.
authors: McGlone PJ, Funk K, Ambrose M, Chiu A, Gruver-Williams A, Wise A, Kim J, Shear BM, O'Hara NN, O'Toole RV, Eglseder WA.
abstract: Objectives To determine the proportion of patients undergoing unplanned reoperation and to report patient-reported outcomes after operative treatment of intraarticular glenoid fractures. Methods Design: Retrospective case series. Setting Single trauma institution. Patient selection criteria Adults with operatively managed intraarticular glenoid fractures (OTA/AO 14F) from 2007 to 2024 were screened for eligibility. Patients were included if they had at least 182 days of clinical follow-up, at least 182 days of telephone follow-up, or underwent an unplanned reoperation within 182 days of the index surgery. Outcomes measures and comparisons The primary outcome was unplanned reoperation related to the glenoid injury. The secondary outcome was the SANE score, ranging from 0 (worst) to 100 (best). Results Fifty-four patients were included; mean age was 40 years (range, 20-73 years) and 74% were male. Twenty-six patients completed the SANE outcome assessment at a median of 9.3 years after surgery (IQR, 5.1-13.9 years; range, 0.6-21.9 years). The overall cohort had a median clinical follow-up duration of 7.7 months (IQR, 4.6-14.5 months; range, 0.4-77.9 months). Unplanned reoperation occurred in 15 of 54 patients (28%; 95% CI, 18%-41%). The median SANE score was 98 (IQR 76-100). Conclusions In this case series of 54 patients, operative treatment of intraarticular glenoid fractures was associated with unplanned reoperation in 28% of patients. Twenty-six patients completed SANE outcome assessment at a median of 9.3 years after surgery, with a median score of 98. These findings suggest that operative fixation of intraarticular glenoid fractures can result in favorable patient-reported outcomes, although patients should be counseled regarding the possibility of reoperation. Level of evidence Therapeutic, Level IV.

title: Treatment of Single-level Thoracolumbar Tuberculosis by Bilateral Percutaneous Endoscopic Debridement and Percutaneous Pedicle Screw Fixation: A Retrospective Cohort Study With 2-year Follow-up.
authors: Liu Y, Du H, Du H, Yin S.
abstract: Background To evaluate the efficacy of bilateral percutaneous endoscopic debridement (BPED) with percutaneous pedicle screw fixation for single-level thoracolumbar tuberculosis with 2-year follow-up. Materials and methods This retrospective cohort study included 62 patients with single-level thoracolumbar tuberculosis from January 2023 to December 2024. Of these, 32 underwent BPED with percutaneous pedicle screw fixation (BPED group), and 30 received open anterior debridement with posterior fixation (control group). Clinical outcomes (ie, visual analog scale [VAS], Oswestry Disability Index [ODI]) and radiographic parameters (ie, local kyphotic angle, fusion status) were assessed. Subgroup analyses stratified by lesion level (thoracic vs lumbar) were performed. Results BPED showed shorter operative time (mean difference, 29.99 min, 95% CI: 19.45-40.53), less blood loss (mean difference, 468.64 mL, 95% CI: 445.21-492.07), shorter hospital stay (mean difference, 3.44 days, 95% CI: 2.52-4.36), and no transfusion requirement (vs 40% in controls) (all P P P > .05). VAS and ODI were lower in BPED group at 3 months ( P Conclusion BPED offers favorable perioperative outcomes and comparable short-term efficacy to that of open surgery for single-level thoracolumbar tuberculosis. Larger prospective studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these findings.

title: The Illusion of Scale: Divergent Orthopaedic Trauma Outcomes Across Large Healthcare Databases.
authors: Croen BJ, Zhuang T, Jagiella-Lodise O, Soma S, Dehghani B, Donegan D, D'Alleyrand JC, Mehta S.
abstract: Objectives To compare demographic characteristics and postoperative complication rates between the TriNetX and PearlDiver national databases across three common orthopaedic trauma procedures. Methods Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting National United States electronic health record and administrative claims databases (TriNetX and PearlDiver). Patient selection criteria Adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent open treatment of proximal femur fracture (PFFx)(CPT 27236), femoral shaft intramedullary nail (fIMN)(CPT 27506), or tibial shaft intramedullary nail (tIMN)(CPT 27759) between 2015 and 2020 were identified. Outcome measures and comparisons Demographic characteristics and postoperative surgical site infection, transfusion, anemia, acute kidney injury, urinary tract infection, pneumonia, wound dehiscence, and pulmonary embolism were compared between databases at 30, 60, and 90 days. Results TriNetX and PearlDiver identified 61,110 and 91,106 patients undergoing open treatment of proximal femur fracture (PFFx), 35,130 and 21,478 undergoing femoral shaft intramedullary nailing (fIMN), and 34,945 and 24,742 undergoing tibial shaft intramedullary nailing (tIMN), respectively. At 30 days, TriNetX demonstrated higher PE incidence than PearlDiver following PFFx (1.6% vs 0.2%), fIMN (2.4% vs 0.9%), and tIMN (1.1% vs 0.2%), whereas pneumonia incidence was lower (3.9% vs 4.7%, 2.9% vs 4.5%, and 1.7% vs 3.2%, respectively; all p Conclusions TriNetX and PearlDiver produced different demographic characteristics and complication rates following proximal femur fracture fixation and femoral and tibial shaft intramedullary nailing, suggesting that database-specific characteristics may influence reported outcomes. Level of evidence Level III.

title: Survival Prediction Models for Metastatic Bone Disease: A Comprehensive Review of Development, External Validation, and Clinical Applicability.
authors: Lin T, Wang Q, Tan L, Da W, Min L.
abstract: Accurate survival estimation fundamentally guides treatment strategy for metastatic bone disease, balancing durable surgical reconstruction against palliative care. Over three decades, predictive tools have evolved from static classical scores into sophisticated nomograms and machine learning algorithms, integrating patient reserve, tumor biology, metastatic burden, and treatment context. In this comprehensive review, we systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science and identified 25 studies reporting the development or external validation of multivariable survival prediction models, encompassing classical scoring systems (Tokuhashi, Tomita, Bauer, Katagiri), nomograms (SORG), Bayesian networks (PATHFx), and machine learning algorithms (SORG-MLA, BMETS). While this methodological evolution improved individualized prognostication in derivation cohorts, external validation studies reveal a critical disconnect: algorithmic complexity does not guarantee clinical transportability. Our synthesis identifies several recurrent sources of this transportability failure, primarily temporal calibration drift from evolving systemic therapies, anatomic site mismatches between spinal and appendicular disease, and selection biases inherent to surgical versus radiotherapeutic cohorts. Consequently, a substantial gap persists between methodological sophistication and actual bedside applicability, and routine clinical deployment of these tools remains premature until these foundational deficits are systematically addressed. Bridging this gap requires shifting from universal prediction tools toward context-specific, prospectively validated models with routine temporal recalibration.

title: Surgical Site Infection After Posterolateral Lumbar Fusion: Incidence and Risk Factors in a Nationwide Database.
authors: Mastrokostas PG, Schwartz LB, Said M, Mastrokostas LE, Mizuno M, Singh R, Jagtiani P, Xavier J, Monas A, Elmenawi K, Houten JK, Varthi A, Vaccaro AR, Schroeder GD, Kepler CK, Monsef JB, Razi AE, Ng MK.
abstract: Background Posterolateral lumbar fusion (PLF) is a widely performed procedure for degenerative lumbar spine disease, yet postoperative surgical site infection (SSI) remains a consequential complication. The aim of this study was to estimate the national 90-day incidence of SSI following PLF and identify independent predictors of 90-day SSI. Materials and methods We performed a retrospective cohort study of adults undergoing PLF in the PearlDiver Mariner database from 2016 to 2023. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors of 90-day SSI, adjusting for demographic, procedural, and comorbidity variables. Significance was set at P Results Among 291,435 PLF procedures, 14,725 (5.1%) developed a 90-day SSI. SSI occurred in 4.0% (6,105/151,951) of single-level PLF cases and 6.2% (8,620/139,484) of multilevel cases. Multilevel fusion significantly increased infection risk compared with single-level PLF (odds ratio [OR] 1.47, P P P P P P P P P P P P P Conclusion Ninety-day SSI after PLF was more frequent following multilevel fusion and among patients with substantial cardiometabolic, hematologic, and behavioral comorbidities.

title: Sports Trauma in Athletes with Impairment.
authors: Ford K, Leonardi C, Ehn M, Uihlein M, Willick S.
abstract: Purpose of review Trauma in athletes with impairment is an under-reported aspect of Para sport. This review article aims to present current data regarding characteristics of acute sports trauma in winter and summer Para sport participants and considerations for management of acute injury. This includes recommendations for trauma prevention and preparedness, assessment and management on the field of play, and extrication from Para sport equipment. Recent findings Injury surveillance systems help characterize risk factors for acute sports trauma and inform injury prevention programs. Concussion and injuries to the head and face are common in Para sport. Winter sports such as Para alpine skiing and sled hockey have high rates of acute sports trauma. While summer sports generally have higher rates of repetitive use injuries, some sports such as blind football, Para cycling, wheelchair rugby, judo, and goalball have higher rates of acute traumatic injuries. There are many important factors to consider when assessing field of play, extrication, emergency evaluation, and care-coordination considerations. Winter sports such as Para alpine skiing and sled hockey have high rates of acute sports trauma. While summer sports generally have higher rates of repetitive use injuries, some sports such as blind football, Para cycling, wheelchair rugby, judo, and goalball have higher rates of acute traumatic injuries. There are many important factors to consider when assessing field of play, extrication, emergency evaluation, and care-coordination considerations.

title: Sound-limb propulsive impulse after lower-limb amputation increases with amputation level but is not driven by peak ankle power.
authors: Ribeiro DM, de Menezes RL, Gervásio FM, de Santana ML, Chieregato Matheus JP.
abstract: Individuals with lower-limb amputation are thought to compensate for reduced prosthetic push-off by generating additional propulsion in the sound limb, but whether this originates at the ankle remains unclear. We compared propulsive impulse (PI), peak ankle power generation (A2), ankle positive work (APW) and related variables in 87 participants: 31 unimpaired controls, 30 with transfemoral amputation (TFA) and 26 with transtibial amputation (TTA), all fitted with prostheses through Brazil's public health system under a standardised protocol. Three-dimensional gait analysis provided ground reaction forces, ankle kinetics and spatiotemporal parameters. PI increased monotonically from Control to TTA to TFA and remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons and after adjustment for gait speed. In contrast, A2 was lower in both amputee groups than in Control; this reduction persisted after adjustment for gait speed only in TFA. APW, a time-integrated measure more directly comparable to PI, likewise did not follow the PI gradient. PI and A2 remained moderately correlated within every group, and the greater PI was attributable mainly to a longer propulsive phase rather than greater propulsive force. These findings indicate that the greater sound-limb propulsive impulse is not accompanied by increased peak ankle power generation or ankle positive work, although some ankle contribution cannot be excluded; whether it involves redistribution of mechanical output to more proximal joints remains a plausible hypothesis for future work. Prosthetic and rehabilitation strategies focused narrowly on restoring ankle push-off power may therefore not, by themselves, normalise sound-limb loading, particularly after transfemoral amputation.

title: Shorter Versus Longer Fusion in Adult Spinal Deformity Surgery: Proximal Junctional Fracture Risk and Patient Selection.
authors: Kawabata A, Hashimoto J, Motoyoshi T, Utagawa K, Matsukura Y, Oyaizu T, Hirai T, Onuma H, Egawa S, Yamada K, Morishita S, Kusano K, Otani K, Shindo S, Yoshii T.
abstract: Study DesignRetrospective cohort study.ObjectivesTo compare proximal junctional fracture (PJFx) and PJFx-related revision after shorter versus longer proximal fusion in adult spinal deformity (ASD).MethodsASD patients aged 65 years or older with upper instrumented vertebra (UIV) from T8 to L1 were reviewed; shorter proximal extent was UIV T11-L1 and longer extent UIV T8-T10. Propensity score matching used nine covariates spanning demographics, frailty, bone quality, and preoperative alignment. Outcomes were analysed as proportions and as time-to-event data with death as a competing risk; the same matching was applied to a T9/T10 versus T12/L1 contrast.ResultsAmong 324 patients, follow-up was similar between groups (p=0.582). PJFx-related revision was more frequent after T11-L1 UIV (16.8% vs 5.9%; OR, 3.25; 95% CI, 1.44-7.58; p=0.003), as was PJFx (40.3% vs 28.3%; OR, 1.71; p=0.028). Five-year cumulative incidence of revision was 17.6% versus 6.2% (log-rank p=0.001; adjusted hazard ratio, 2.73; 95% CI, 1.34-5.55). In the 100 matched pairs both outcomes lay in the same direction but were imprecise (revision: OR, 2.33; 95% CI, 0.84-7.41). The excess revision rate after T12/L1 (OR, 2.76; p=0.030) was attenuated after matching and imprecise (OR, 1.40; 0.38-5.59).ConclusionsA thoracolumbar UIV was associated with higher rates of PJFx-related revision, which persisted after adjustment for frailty, bone quality, surgical strategy, and alignment. The matched estimate lay in the same direction but was imprecise. The apparent excess after a T12/L1 UIV was attenuated after matching and too imprecise to draw a conclusion, and remains exploratory.

title: Robot-assisted total hip arthroplasty for Crowe type II or higher hip dysplasia.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Asai H, Osawa Y, Takegami Y, Funahashi H, Ido H, Imagama S.
abstract: Purpose Robot-assisted total hip arthroplasty (RATHA) offers superior implant accuracy, but its efficacy for highly deformed hips remains unclear. This study compared the RATHA outcomes of patients with Crowe types II-IV and I osteoarthritis. Methods We evaluated 25 hips that underwent RATHA for Crowe types II-IV osteoarthritis (Crowe II-IV group). Propensity score matching (age, sex, and body mass index) was used to select 75 matched hips with Crowe type I osteoarthritis (Crowe I group). The outcomes included component positioning, distance from teardrop to femoral head centre, operative data, complications, and Harris Hip Scores. Results The absolute navigation errors of the groups did not differ significantly (Crowe II-IV: radiographic inclination [RI] 1.6 ± 1.7°, radiographic inclination [RA] 1.7 ± 2.1°; Crowe I: RI 1.3 ± 1.3°, RA 1.4 ± 2.0°). However, the vertical distance from the teardrop to the femoral head centre was significantly greater for the Crowe II-IV group than for the Crowe I group (23.6 ± 6.4 mm vs. 19.8 ± 4.4 mm, P = 0.001). A vertical distance of > 28 mm was observed for four Crowe II-IV cases (16%), but not for the Crowe I group. The postoperative Harris Hip Score and complication rates did not differ significantly. Conclusions RATHA for Crowe type II-IV osteoarthritis achieved accurate implant alignment comparable to that for Crowe type I. However, superior displacement of the hip joint centre occurred in 16% of severe cases, suggesting caution for inferior acetabular osteophytes. The similar complication rates support the clinical utility of RATHA even for severe deformities.

title: Return-to-Work Clearance After Primary Rotator Cuff Repair: A Systematic Review of Time-, Function-, and Job-Demand-Based Criteria.
authors: Hasan M, Ghadir M, Najami A, Ghantous S, Berkovich Y.
abstract: Background Return-to-work (RTW) outcomes after rotator cuff repair (RCR) are widely reported, but the criteria used to authorize occupational return remain unclear. Methods Six databases were searched from inception to July 26, 2026, for studies of adults who underwent primary RCR that reported occupational outcomes or clearance processes. Approaches were classified as time-based, function-based, job-demand-based, combined, individualized/subjective, or not reported. Results Thirty-six reports representing 32 cohort groups were included. Clearance processes were unreported in 59.4% of cohorts (n = 19), combined in 21.9% (n = 7), individualized/subjective in 9.4% (n = 3), and predominantly time-based in 9.4% (n = 3). No cohort reported a purely function-based or job-demand-based algorithm with predefined, reproducible thresholds. No study directly compared alternative clearance strategies. Conclusions Occupational recovery was commonly measured, but authorization criteria were usually absent or insufficiently reproducible. Prospective studies should evaluate transparent, validated, occupation-specific clearance criteria rather than RTW timing alone.

title: Residency Diary: The White Whale.
authors: Friedman LGM.

title: Progressive collapsing foot deformity: advances in weightbearing CT imaging and three-dimensional assessment.
authors: Bouredoucen H.
abstract: Progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD) is a three-dimensional deformity characterized, to varying degrees, by hindfoot valgus, midfoot or forefoot abduction, medial column collapse, peritalar subluxation, and valgus instability of the ankle. Conventional weightbearing radiographs remain the cornerstone of imaging assessment, whereas weightbearing computed tomography (WBCT) enables multiplanar and three-dimensional analysis of osseous alignment and articular relationships under load. This narrative review summarizes WBCT-based methods for the assessment of PCFD, including two-dimensional measurements, three-dimensional alignment parameters, articular distance and coverage mapping, diagnostic performance, and automated segmentation methods. WBCT enables quantification of the different components of the contemporary A-E classification and is valuable for assessing peritalar subluxation and lateral impingement. The Foot and Ankle Offset provides a reproducible measure of global alignment, whereas middle facet subluxation and regional mapping more directly characterize local abnormalities in peritalar relationships. Available evidence indicates that class D parameters contribute to distinguishing symptomatic PCFD from asymptomatic flatfoot morphology. However, published diagnostic thresholds remain dependent on the populations and methods used and should not be interpreted in isolation as diagnostic or therapeutic criteria. Automation substantially reduces the time required for three-dimensional analyses, and initial predictive models demonstrate the feasibility of quantitative preoperative planning. However, interchangeability between methods, external validation of thresholds, establishment of normative values, and longitudinal associations with symptoms and clinical outcomes remain insufficiently established. WBCT should therefore be considered complementary to conventional radiographs and MRI. Its principal contribution lies in the multiplanar and three-dimensional characterization, under weightbearing conditions, of the osseous and articular components of PCFD.

title: Osteoporosis management after distal radius fracture in a Korean multicenter cohort: persistent treatment gap and the pitfall of repeat surgery as a surrogate for refracture.
authors: Im JH, Park IJ, Roh YT, Lee JY.
abstract: After a wrist fracture, osteoporosis evaluation and treatment provide an opportunity for secondary fracture prevention. In a Korean multicenter study of surgically treated distal radius fractures, we found that a substantial proportion of patients had no recorded osteoporosis pharmacotherapy and that counting repeat surgeries as refractures can overestimate their frequency, highlighting important clinical and methodological limitations of real-world fracture data. Background Distal radius fracture (DRF) is an early manifestation of osteoporosis and provides an opportunity for secondary fracture prevention. However, real-world data on post-fracture osteoporosis management remain limited, and the validity of using repeat surgical procedures as a surrogate for refracture in clinical data warehouse (CDW) studies is uncertain. Methods We conducted a retrospective multicenter cohort study of 449 patients aged ≥64 years who underwent surgical treatment for DRF across nine hospitals in Korea (2018-2024). Osteoporosis treatment, bone mineral density (BMD) evaluation, and repeat surgical procedures were extracted from the CDW. Repeat surgeries were reclassified using a procedure code-interval approach. Results Osteoporosis pharmacotherapy was recorded in 64.8% of patients, with 47.7% having their first recorded prescription after fracture. Among post-fracture initiators, 82.7% had their first recorded prescription within 30 days. Overall, 35.2% had no recorded osteoporosis pharmacotherapy during follow-up. Although BMD examinations were ordered in all patients, structured T-score data were available for only 72 of 891 BMD examination records (8.1%), precluding assessment of treatment eligibility at the individual patient level. Nine patients (2.0%) underwent repeat surgery; after operational reclassification, four events (0.9%) were classified as events consistent with refracture. Simple enumeration of repeat surgery therefore yielded more than twice the number of events classified as consistent with refracture. Conclusions DRF surgery represents an important opportunity for osteoporosis evaluation and treatment initiation, although a substantial proportion of patients had no recorded pharmacotherapy during follow-up. In CDW-based studies, repeat surgery alone is an unreliable surrogate for refracture, highlighting the need for chart-level validation of database-defined fracture events.

title: Operative Strategies for Treating Tibial Plateau Fractures in Patients Aged 55 Years and Older: A Five-Year Comparison of Acute Total Knee Arthroplasty with Open Reduction and Internal Fixation, Conversion Total Knee Arthroplasty, and Total Knee Arthroplasty for Osteoarthritis.
authors: Wahid M, Bellamy J, Hoskins W, Zaidi Z, Gusho C, Scott CEH, Chen AF.
abstract: Objectives To compare outcomes of acute total knee arthroplasty (TKA) for tibial plateau fracture in patients aged 55 years and older with matched patients undergoing open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), conversion TKA after failed ORIF, and primary TKA for osteoarthritis. Methods Design: Retrospective cohort study with propensity score matching. Setting Federated multi-institutional electronic health records database (TriNetX United States Collaborative Network). Patient selection criteria Patients aged ≥55 years with tibial plateau fracture treated with acute TKA, ORIF, or conversion TKA after failed ORIF were identified. A separate cohort undergoing primary TKA for osteoarthritis without fracture history was identified as a non-traumatic comparator. The study period was restricted to January 1, 2005 through December 31, 2020 to ensure a minimum of five years of potential follow-up for all included patients. Outcome measures and comparisons The primary outcome was revision surgery at 5 years, defined as conversion to TKA after ORIF and as revision TKA after arthroplasty. Secondary outcomes were a composite "return to the operating room (OR)" outcome (selected major reoperations), periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), surgical site infection (SSI), aseptic loosening, manipulation under anesthesia (MUA), and periprosthetic fracture. Three 1:1 propensity score-matched comparisons were performed (acute TKA versus ORIF; acute versus conversion TKA; acute TKA versus primary TKA for osteoarthritis), with risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) calculated. Subgroup analyses were stratified by age (55-70 years; ≥70 years). Results After matching, 1,321 patients per cohort were compared in the primary acute TKA versus ORIF analysis. Mean age was 66.1 years in the acute TKA cohort and 66.6 years in the ORIF cohort (range, 55 to 90 in both), and 65.3% and 66.7%, respectively, were female. Acute TKA had higher 5-year revision rates than ORIF (7.0% versus 0.8%; RR 8.36, 95% CI 4.50-15.56; P Conclusions In patients aged 55 years and older, acute TKA for tibial plateau fracture was associated with higher risks of revision and complications compared with ORIF. Revision and complication rates after acute TKA were comparable with those after conversion TKA following failed ORIF but higher than those after primary TKA for osteoarthritis. Acute TKA should be reserved for patients at highest risk of ORIF failure requiring subsequent conversion to TKA. Level of evidence Level III, therapeutic study.

title: Menopausal Hormone Therapy History is Associated with Improved Postoperative Ambulatory Recovery in Postmenopausal Women with Hip Fragility Fractures.
authors: Fox BQ, Kocher SD, Brown C, Olexa M, Ford A, Wittstein J, DeBaun M, Pean C.
abstract: Objectives To compare changes in ambulatory status after hip fracture surgery in women with and without a history of systemic menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) use. Methods Design: Retrospective cohort. Setting Single center academic Level 1 trauma center. Patient selection criteria Patients were included if they were female, >=50, received surgery for OTA/AO 31-A (intertrochanteric/peritrochanteric), 31-B (femoral neck), and 32-A (subtrochanteric) fragility fractures from December 2022 to September 2025, and had minimum 3-month follow-up data. Outcome measures and comparisons Patients were categorized into "Ever User" and "Never User" groups based on MHT exposure documented in electronic records. Primary outcomes were postoperative ambulatory status, categorized using a six-level functional scale, and return to baseline ambulation, measured as a binary variable at 30 and 90 days postoperatively. Secondary outcomes included 30- and 90-day hospital readmission and six-month all-cause mortality. Comparisons of outcomes were made between cohorts following adjustment for age, American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grade, baseline ambulatory status, and dementia diagnosis. Results Among 358 included female patients, Ever Users (n=80) and Never Users (n=278) demonstrated similar ages (mean:80.6, range:60-100 vs. mean:78.8, range:50-101; P=0.14) and baseline ambulatory independence (48.8% vs. 46.0%, P=0.76). At 30 days, cohorts demonstrated similar rates of return to baseline function (25.3% vs. 23.4%; P=0.85). At 90 days, Ever Users demonstrated higher rates of independent ambulation (17.5% vs. 9.1%; P=0.029) and return to baseline status (53.8% vs. 35.8%; P Conclusions In women undergoing fragility hip fracture surgery, history of menopausal hormone therapy use was independently associated with improved return to baseline ambulation by 90 days postoperatively. These findings suggested prior menopausal hormone therapy exposure may confer functional benefits extending beyond fracture prevention. Level of evidence III (Retrospective Cohort Study).

title: Investigation of optimal placement of locking attachment plate in periprosthetic femoral fractures : a biomechanical comparative study.
authors: Omori K, Baba T, Blauth M, Horikoshi Y, Nagata Y, Ishijima M.
abstract: Aims To investigate the biomechanical effects of proximal, diaphyseal, and dual locking attachment plate (LAP) configurations compared with a locking compression plate (LCP)-only construct in a Vancouver type C periprosthetic femoral fracture model under cyclic and monotonic loading. Methods A cementless stem was implanted into synthetic femora to create a standardized Vancouver type C periprosthetic femoral fracture. Four constructs (n = 6 each) were evaluated: proximal LAP, diaphyseal LAP, dual LAP, and a LCP-only control. Axial cyclic loading was applied starting at 600 N with progressive increments up to 1,800 N (maximum 6,500 cycles), followed by monotonic loading to failure. Primary outcomes were cyclic load to first fracture line and monotonic failure load. Composite bone distance and fracture line locations were also assessed. Results Cyclic load to first fracture line did not differ among constructs (all p > 0.05). Under monotonic loading, proximal LAP (mean 4,850.2 N (SD 1,026.9)) and dual LAP (mean 4,593.6 N (SD 930.3)) demonstrated higher failure loads than diaphyseal LAP (mean 3,226.1 N (SD 423.0)) and the LCP-only control (mean 3,266.7 N (SD 676.5)) (p = 0.014 to 0.042), with no significant difference between proximal and dual LAP constructs. Composite bone distance increased progressively during cyclic loading. Fracture lines clustered near the fourth hole in the proximal LAP configuration and near the second hole in the diaphyseal and dual LAP configurations. Early fatigue failure occurred in the proximal LAP (2/6), diaphyseal LAP (1/6), and control (2/6) groups, whereas no specimen failed during cyclic loading in the dual LAP group. Conclusion This biomechanical study demonstrates that proximal and dual LAP configurations provide higher static failure strength than diaphyseal LAP or LCP-only constructs, while resistance to early cyclic fracture was similar among configurations. The absence of early fatigue failure in the dual LAP configuration indicates a mechanical advantage when anatomical placement allows.

title: Global Research Landscape of Recurrent Osteoporotic Vertebral Compression Fractures: A Bibliometric Analysis of Risk Factors, Prevention, and Prediction (1993-2024).
authors: Jin H, Ma J, Yang S, Wang H.
abstract: Objectives Recurrent osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures (ROVCFs) remain a clinical challenge because they are associated with pain, spinal instability, and disability, particularly in older populations. This study presents a bibliometric and visual analysis of global research on risk factors, prevention, and prediction related to ROVCFs from 1993 to 2024. Methods The Web of Science Core Collection was searched on January 10, 2025, for English-language Articles and Review Articles published from 1993 to 2024. VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and the R package bibliometrix were used to analyze publication and citation characteristics, collaboration networks, keyword co-occurrence patterns, thematic clusters, and keyword citation bursts. Results A total of 381 eligible publications on risk factors, prevention, and prediction related to ROVCFs were included in the analysis. Annual publication output generally increased over the study period, particularly after 2008. China, the USA, and Germany were the most productive countries, while Chang Gung Memorial Hospital, Capital Medical University, and Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine were leading institutions. Spine, European Spine Journal, and Osteoporosis International were the top publishing journals. Within the present dataset, Chen Hao and Lin Wei-Che had the highest h-index values, followed by Chen Zhi. Keyword co-occurrence analysis revealed seven major research clusters: (1) osteoporosis-related risk factors, (2) percutaneous vertebroplasty (PVP)-related factors, (3) intravertebral clefts (IVC) factor for cemented vertebrae, (4) anti-osteoporosis drugs for refractures, (5) predictive model validation, (6) adjacent vertebrae refractures, and (7) kyphotic deformity. Keyword-burst analysis highlighted growing research attention to bone mineral density, management, prevention, vertebroplasty, and kyphoplasty. Conclusion This bibliometric analysis delineated the global research landscape and thematic structure of ROVCF research. The major themes involved osteoporosis-related risk factors, vertebral augmentation-related factors, intravertebral clefts, anti-osteoporosis treatment, adjacent vertebral fractures, kyphotic deformity, and prediction-model development. Further multicenter research is needed to evaluate and externally validate refracture-risk prediction approaches.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Opioid and Glucocorticoid Use on Complications in Hallux Valgus Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
authors: Wang J, Ibrahim KG, Panchbhavi V, Nguyen P, Iyer S, Patel SJ, Panchbhavi V.
abstract: Background This study examined whether preoperative exposure to glucocorticoids, opioids, or their combination is associated with increased postoperative complications after hallux valgus (HV) surgery. Materials and methods A retrospective cohort analysis of the TriNetX Research Network identified adults who underwent HV correction. Patients were grouped by preoperative glucocorticoid use, opioid use, combined use, or neither (control), with exposure assessed in 2 windows: 1-90 and 90-365 days preoperatively. Each of the 6 exposure-timeframe comparisons was separately propensity score matched on demographics and comorbidities. Significance was set at P Results Combined glucocorticoid and opioid use was associated with sepsis at 1-90 days ( P = .005) and with infection and stiffness at 90-365 days ( P ≤ .007). Isolated opioid use was associated with infection in both windows, acute kidney injury at 1-90 days, and sepsis at 90-365 days. Isolated glucocorticoid use was associated with pneumonia and stiffness at 90-365 days. Absolute risk differences were small (0.7% to 2.0%; numbers needed to harm 49 to 141). Most outcomes, including thromboembolic, cardiovascular, and mortality outcomes, did not differ; only glucocorticoid-associated stiffness and pneumonia and opioid-associated acute kidney injury remained significant after Bonferroni correction. Conclusion In this retrospective database study, preoperative opioid and combined exposure were associated with small absolute increases in specific complications, most consistently infection; isolated glucocorticoid exposure was associated with pneumonia and stiffness, findings vulnerable to confounding by indication. Because dose, duration, and patient-level co-occurrence of outcomes were unavailable and residual confounding is likely, these findings are hypothesis generating.

title: Effects of Health Behaviour Change Interventions on Pain Intensity, Functional Disability, and Safety Behaviour Among Nurses with Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials.
authors: Lian Y, Dou J, Jia H, Ma G, Dapari R, Zeng Q, Liang S, Rahman AA.
abstract: Purpose To systematically evaluate and synthesise the effects of health behaviour change interventions on pain intensity, functional disability, and safety behaviours among nurses with work-related musculoskeletal disorders. Methods This study adhered to the PRISMA 2020 reporting guidelines. Six electronic databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, EMBASE, and Ovid MEDLINE) were searched for randomised controlled trials published before 16 February 2026. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for randomised trials and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach via GRADEpro. Primary meta-analyses used fixed-effect models in Review Manager 5.4; supplementary random-effects analyses estimated 95% prediction intervals. Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q test and the I 2 statistic. Sensitivity and subgroup analyses were conducted where appropriate. Results Ten randomised controlled trials comprising 1,208 nurses met the inclusion criteria. In the primary fixed-effect analyses, health behaviour change interventions reduced pain intensity (SMD = -0.32; 95% CI: -0.49 to -0.15; P = 0.0003; I 2 = 61%) and functional disability (SMD = -0.66; 95% CI: -0.83 to -0.50; P 2 = 84%) and improved safety behaviours (SMD = 1.04; 95% CI: 0.87 to 1.22; P 2 = 89%). Supplementary random-effects analyses showed that the effects on pain and functional disability were no longer statistically significant, while the effect on safety behaviours remained significant. Conclusions This review identified associations between health behaviour change interventions and improvements in pain, functional disability, and safety behaviours among nurses with work-related musculoskeletal disorders. However, due to methodological bias, study heterogeneity, and short follow-up periods, the evidence remains limited. Trial registration CRD420251042168 (PROSPERO).

title: Effectiveness and Safety of Prophylactic Inferior Vena Cava Filters in High-Risk Hip Fracture Patients: Clinical implications of an early retrieval strategy.
authors: Kim CH, La CW, Kim JW.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of prophylactic inferior vena cava (IVC) filter in patients with hip fracture who were at high risk for pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE). Methods Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting Single-center Level I Trauma Center. Patient selection criteria Patients older than 50 years who sustained a low-energy hip fracture (AO/OTA 31A, B, and 32A) and underwent prophylactic IVC filter insertion before hip fracture surgery between 2005 and 2025 were included. Prophylactic IVC filter placement was selectively performed in patients with either objectively confirmed deep vein thrombosis on preoperative screening or absolute contraindications to mechanical and pharmacological venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Those who had multiple trauma at the time of injury, a clinical follow-up duration ≤6 months after surgery, or undergone IVC filter placement following a confirmed diagnosis of PTE based on pulmonary computed tomography or lung perfusion scanning were excluded. Outcome measures and comparisons The primary outcome was the rate of newly developed symptomatic PTE. Secondary outcomes included IVC filter-related complications, retrieval rates, and 30-day mortality. Results One hundred fifty-six patients were included in the prophylactic IVC filter group (39 men 25.0%], 117 women [75.0%]; mean age, 75.8 ± 11.1 years; femoral neck [AO/OTA 31B], n = 71 [45.5%]; intertrochanteric [31A], n = 75 [48.1%]; subtrochanteric [AO/OTA 32A], n = 10 [6.4%];mean indwelling time, 9.1 days; retrieval rate, 88.5%). Among these patients, no cases of newly developed symptomatic PTE were observed (0%), whereas the incidence in the overall hip fracture cohort (n=4,568) was 0.44%. Filter-related complications occurred in 3.9% of patients (minor tilting, 2.6%; vessel adhesion, 1.3%), with no major mechanical failures such as migration or perforation. Although no thrombi were detected at insertion, 4.5% of the patients had trapped thrombi at the time of removal. The 30-day all-cause mortality rate was 1.3% (2/156) in the prophylactic IVC filter group, compared with 1.5% (67/4,568) in the overall hip fracture cohort. (p=0.845). Neither death in the prophylactic IVC filter group was attributed to PTE or an IVC filter-related complication. Conclusions In this study's selected extreme pulmonary thromboembolism risk cohort, including patients with CT-confirmed preoperative DVT, those clinically expected to undergo prolonged perioperative immobilization, or those with contraindications to prophylactic anticoagulation, such as GI bleeding, prophylactic inferior vena cava filter served as an effective and safe temporary bridge therapy rather than a routine prophylactic strategy. Level of evidence Prognostic Level III.

title: Earlier and More Criteria-Based Return to Sport After Pediatric Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in North America Compared With the Asia-Pacific Region: A Systematic Review.
authors: Lim JI, Binte Mirza Irwan NH, Tan SHS, Hui JHP, Lim AKS.
abstract: Purpose To compare the management and rehabilitation strategies for pediatric anterior cruciate ligament injuries between North America and the Asia-Pacific region. Methods Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, a comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library was performed for studies published between January 2020 and August 2025. Articles were included if they described pediatric anterior cruciate ligament rehabilitation protocols for patients 18 years and younger. Included studies consisted primarily of retrospective studies, cohort studies, case series, technical notes, and cross-sectional studies (Levels II-IV). Data were extracted on bracing use and duration, weight-bearing status, range-of-motion restrictions, sports progression, and return-to-sport criteria. Results Forty studies were included (27 North America, 13 Asia-Pacific). Bracing was used frequently in both North America (86%) and Asia-Pacific (72%), with North American protocols often specifying duration (2-6 weeks) or criteria-based discontinuation, whereas Asia-Pacific protocols frequently omitted details. Early range-of-motion restoration was advocated in both regions (North America 85%, Asia-Pacific 91%), although restrictions were applied when meniscal repair was performed. Both regions supported early weight-bearing regardless of surgical technique. Both regions shared similar timelines for running and jogging restrictions; however, North American centers (60%) introduced sport-specific drills earlier between 3 and 6 months. Return-to-sport clearance was delayed beyond 9 months in most protocols (North America 46%, Asia-Pacific 62%). North American center, however, showed more flexibility with 46% allowing return-to-sport clearance before 9 months. North American centers more often incorporated functional criteria (50%) alongside time-based measures, whereas Asia-Pacific centers relied primarily on time-based thresholds. Conclusions Early rehabilitation protocols after pediatric anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction were similar between North America and the Asia-Pacific region with respect to bracing, weight-bearing, and range-of-motion practices. However, return-to-sport progression differed because North American centers more frequently introduced sport-specific activities earlier and more commonly incorporated functional criteria in addition to time-based thresholds, whereas Asia-Pacific centers more often relied on time-based clearance and delayed sport-specific progression. Level of evidence Level IV, systematic review of Level II to IV evidence.

title: Cortical button versus suture anchor fixation in distal biceps tendon repair: a comparison of objective four-plane strength and functional outcomes.
authors: Lopiz Y, Guijarro J, Checa P, García-Fernández C, Marco F.
abstract: Purpose To compare four-plane isometric strength, function and complications between cortical button and suture anchor fixation in distal biceps repair, and to explore the influence of surgical delay. Methods Twenty-eight men (mean age, 44.2 years) underwent single-incision repair with a cortical button (n = 16) or suture anchors (n = 12) between 2020 and 2025. At a mean follow-up of 46 months, we assessed isometric strength in four planes with a hand-held dynamometer (relative to the uninjured side), range of motion, QuickDASH, Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Oxford Elbow Score (OES) and complications. A sensitivity analysis included only patients followed for ≥ 24 months. Results Mean strength was 93.8% (flexion), 100.1% (extension), 90.3% (supination) and 97.2% (pronation; median, 94.2%); all planes except extension remained below the uninjured side (P ≤ 0.016). Strength did not differ between techniques in any plane, also in the sensitivity analysis. Functional scores were high in both groups, with small differences in favour of suture anchors that should be interpreted with caution (MEPS 100 vs. 95.0, P = 0.022; QuickDASH 1.3 vs. 5.5, P = 0.046; OES 47.4 vs. 43.4, P = 0.069). Repair after 21 days (n = 6; exploratory) was associated with weaker flexion (85.4% vs. 96.1%, P = 0.024). No reruptures occurred; three patients (10.7%) had transient neurapraxia. Conclusion No significant strength differences were found between techniques, although the small sample cannot exclude clinically relevant differences and fixation was confounded with treatment era. A small supination and flexion deficit persisted after both techniques.

title: Computed Tomography Scan Zone-of-Injury Modeling Predicts Need for Definitive Soft-Tissue Coverage and Complications in Open OTA 42A-C Tibial Shaft Fractures.
authors: Vu NH, Esper GW, Goldstein AR, Ganta A, Barrera J, Hacquebord J, Konda SR.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the ability of a CT-derived soft-tissue zone-of-injury (ZOI) model to predict the need for soft-tissue (ST) coverage in open 42A-C tibial shaft fractures and compare its discriminatory performance with the Gustilo-Anderson (GA) classification for fracture-related complications. Methods Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting Urban, multi-site academic center, 2014-2024. Patient selection criteria Patients with operatively treated open OTA 42A-C tibial shaft fractures, preoperative tibial CT imaging, and ≥6-month follow-up were included. Outcome measures and comparisons The primary outcome was the need for ST coverage (skin-graft, dermal matrix, local flap, free flap, or amputation). Secondary outcomes included ST- and fracture-related complications. CT-derived ZOI measurements, demographics, and injury characteristics were entered into a multivariable regression with stepwise elimination to develop a CT-derived ST coverage model (CTzoi-STC), which was compared with GA classification and with a model without CT-derived data. Patients were further stratified by risk for secondary outcome comparisons. Results 122 patients (40.5 years (range 18-72), 95 (77.9%) male, GA I: 19 (15.6%), II: 30 (24.6%), III: 73 (59.8%); III: 73 (59.8%), of which IIIA: 62 (84.9%), IIIB: 8 (11.0%), IIIC: 3 (4.1%)) met inclusion criteria, with 37 (30.3%) requiring ST coverage. The final CTzoi-STC model, which included longitudinal free air extent on CT scan, wound size, and wound location (tibial third), demonstrated higher discrimination for predicting ST coverage compared with GA classification (AUC 0.845 vs 0.731, p = 0.041). A model without CT-derived data (GA classification, wound size, and wound location) had an AUC of 0.829 (p = 0.654 vs CTzoi-STC). Free air extent remained independently associated with ST coverage after adjustment (OR 8.1, 95% CI 1.4-47.2, p = 0.021). Using the Youden-derived cutoff (0.278), 30 of 47 high-risk patients (63.8%) required ST coverage compared with 7 (9.3%) of low-risk patients.
