High-risk patients had higher rates of nonunion (40.4% vs 16.0%, p = 0.003), fracture-related infection (38.3% vs 17.3%, p = 0.010), and ST coverage failure (14.9% vs 0.0%, p Conclusions For open tibial shaft fractures, a CT-derived soft-tissue zone-of-injury model incorporating longitudinal free air extent, wound size, and wound location more accurately identified patients requiring soft-tissue coverage and those at risk for soft-tissue- and fracture-related complications than the Gustilo-Anderson classification. Free air extent on CT was an objective, independent predictor of soft-tissue coverage, although a model without CT-derived data had similar discrimination. Level of evidence III, Prognostic.

title: Clinical recommendations on monitoring and management of bone health in adults with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy and transition to adult care: A national Delphi consensus study.
authors: Abdelrahman S, McCarrison S, Armstrong DJ, Bubbear JS, Chandler F, Crabtree N, Duncan EL, Gittoes NJL, Javaid MK, Johnson A, Langlands G, Lilleker JB, Padidela R, Saraff V, Selby P, Talla MR, Walsh JS, Willis T, Wood CL, Keen R, Quinlivan R, Wong SC.
abstract: Poor bone health and low-trauma fractures are common in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), reflecting the combined effects of progressive muscle weakness, reduced mechanical loading, delayed puberty and/or hypogonadism, and long-term glucocorticoid exposure. Although paediatric bone health guidance in DMD is well established, adult-specific recommendations remain limited, particularly for individuals who enter adult services having received many years of bisphosphonate therapy during childhood or adolescence. We developed national expert consensus recommendations for the monitoring and management of bone health in adults with DMD, with particular emphasis on transition from paediatric to adult care. Recommendations were informed by review of the literature, a clinician survey, input from adults with DMD and carers, and discussion within a multidisciplinary expert group. A modified Delphi process was undertaken, with 16 clinicians voting on draft statements using a 9-point agreement scale; consensus was defined as at least 80% of participants scoring 7-9. Thirteen evidence-informed expert consensus clinical recommendations were agreed, covering fracture risk assessment, DXA and vertebral fracture monitoring, vitamin D and gonadal status, indications for specialist bone review, initiation and review of osteoporosis therapy, management of possible treatment failure, and structured review of long-term therapy during transition. The recommendations emphasise individualised decision-making, recognising the technical challenges of imaging, limited adult DMD-specific evidence, cumulative treatment burden, and the functional impact of fractures in this population. These consensus recommendations provide a practical framework to support adult neuromuscular and bone clinicians managing bone health in a rare, high-risk and increasingly adult DMD population.

title: Clinical Outcomes of Robot-assisted Endoscopic Lumbar Interbody Fusion Compared With Transforaminal Lumbar Interbody Fusion for Single-level Lumbar Degenerative Disease.
authors: Sun J, Li H, Huang L, Xue J, Zhao Y, Ou Y.
abstract: Background This study compared the clinical outcomes of robot-assisted endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion (RA-Endo-LIF) with those of traditional transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) in patients with single-level lumbar degenerative disease. Materials and methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of 66 patients who underwent surgery for single-level lumbar degenerative disease between July 2023 and January 2025. Patients were assigned to either the RA-Endo-LIF group (n = 35) or the TLIF group (n = 31) based on the surgical technique performed. Data on incision length, operative time, intraoperative fluoroscopy frequency, blood loss, postoperative drainage volume, time to ambulation, and length of hospital stay were collected and analyzed. Clinical outcomes were evaluated pre- and postoperatively using the visual analog scale (VAS), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) scores, and intervertebral disk height. Results Compared to the TLIF group, the RA-Endo-LIF group demonstrated significant superiority related to smaller incision length, reduced intraoperative blood loss, less postoperative drainage, earlier time to ambulation, and shorter hospital stay ( P P P P > .05). Conclusion The RA-Endo-LIF technique offers distinct minimally invasive advantages. It provides short-term pain relief and functional improvement comparable to TLIF. However, its longer operative time and steep learning curve warrant consideration. Further validation through larger sample sizes and long-term follow-up is required.

title: Biomechanical Comparison of Composite versus Screw-Rod Fixation for Posterior C5-C6 Fusion.
authors: Wadhwa H, Castro J, Chan C, Ahmad SH, Li YD, Hu SS, Bruckman K, Mok JM.
abstract: Study DesignBiomechanical.ObjectivesTo compare subaxial cervical stability with a dental composite-plate construct versus lateral mass screw-rod construct.Methods6 fresh-frozen human cadaveric cervical vertebrae (C4-C7) were prepared by stripping all soft tissues. Lateral mass screw fixation was performed bilaterally with standard freehand technique. Dental composite (Filtek) was applied to lamina before placement of a custom minifragment plate. Range of motion (ROM) and rotation to failure testing was performed using a robotic testing system (SimVITRO). Wilcoxon ranked sum test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction was used to compare results with significance set to p<0.05.ResultsThe screw-rod construct (5.1±4.0 deg) and composite-plate construct (4.5±3.2 deg) significantly decreased flexion-extension ROM relative to native state (8.1±1.7 deg, p<0.05). Only the composite-plate construct (2.7±1.9 deg) significantly decreased lateral bending ROM relative to native state (4.7±2.5 deg, p<0.05). Both the screw-rod construct (7.0±4.3 deg) and composite-plate construct (5.7±3.7 deg) significantly decreased axial rotation ROM relative to native state (9.9±5.2 deg, p<0.05). Composite-plate also decreased axial rotation ROM relative to screw-rod, while both constructs had comparable ROM in flexion-extension and lateral bending. Flexion to failure for the composite-plate construct was 7.1 ± 1.7 N-m. Mechanism of failure was the composite cracking off bone.ConclusionScrew-rod and composite-plate constructs significantly decrease ROM compared to the native state and are comparable in stiffness. Failure of composite-plate occurs with composite cracking off undamaged bone surface. A strategy utilizing composite fixation may offer a reasonable alternative to screws for subaxial stabilization.

title: Beyond the Bone: Resuming Daily Life After Surgery or Illness in a Super-aged Society.
authors: Kim TK.

title: Atlas of meniscal cells from different species and characterizing meniscal endothelial and smooth muscle cells.
authors: Zhang M, Huang J, Cai Z, Lin X, Li D, Xu J, Ma R, Sun H.
abstract: Aims The meniscus is a vital biomechanical component of the knee, but a comprehensive understanding of its cellular composition across species is lacking. This study aimed to construct the first cross-species cellular atlas of the meniscus by defining conserved and species-specific cell populations, with particular focus on characterizing smooth muscle cells, to better understand knee joint biology and pathology. Methods We performed single-cell RNA sequencing analysis on meniscal tissues from multiple species, including mice, rats, beagles, goats, and humans, encompassing both healthy individuals and patients with osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or discoid meniscus. This approach enabled detailed cell type classification, marker gene identification, and histological validation through immunohistochemistry and Masson staining. Functional experiments were performed to investigate the role of smooth muscle cell-enriched genes. Results Our analysis revealed nine distinct cell types common across all species. Their proportions varied significantly between species, with rat meniscus showing the closest cellular composition to human. A major finding was the consistent presence of actin alpha 2 (ACTA2)-positive smooth muscle cells, located primarily in the meniscal surface zone, which were significantly reduced in pathological conditions. Intersection of bulk RNA-seq and single-cell data identified three conserved smooth muscle cell-enriched genes ( SPARCL1 , S1PR3 , ARHGAP6 ), functional assays showed that S1PR3 signalling modulates meniscal matrix gene expression (collagen type 1, alpha 1 ( COL1A1 )). Masson staining further confirmed organized smooth muscle fibres in canine and goat menisci. Conclusion This study establishes the first cross-species cellular atlas of the meniscus, identifying both universal and divergent cellular features. The discovery of a conserved smooth muscle cell population that diminishes in disease states, coupled with the identification of S1PR3 as a regulator of matrix gene expression, provides new insight into meniscal degeneration and highlights ACTA2+ smooth muscle cells as a potential therapeutic target for knee joint disorders.

title: Association Between Newly Diagnosed Dyslipidemia and Joint-Specific Incident Osteoarthritis: A Nationwide Propensity-Score-Matched Cohort Study.
authors: Choi BS, Lee H, Bae HC, Yu J, Kang JH, Park SJ, Kim HJ, Park SM, Han HS.
abstract: Objective Whether dyslipidemia raises the risk of incident osteoarthritis (OA) is uncertain given inconsistent prior cohort evidence. We examined the association between newly diagnosed and treated dyslipidemia and incident OA, overall and by joint site. Design Using the Korean National Health Insurance Service database, we identified adults with newly diagnosed dyslipidemia (International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision [ICD-10] code E78 plus a lipid-lowering prescription) between 2007 and 2012, with the same 2-year washout applied to both groups. Participants with dyslipidemia were propensity-score matched (target ratio 1:3), with exact matching on index year, to comparators with no E78 claim during 2007-2012. Incident OA (≥1 inpatient or ≥3 outpatient claims, ICD-10 M15-M19) was assessed overall and for the knee, hip, hand, and multiple joints. Cox regression with robust variance estimates accounting for matched sets provided the primary adjusted estimates, complemented by competing-risk and period-specific analyses. Results The matched cohort included 32,684 participants with newly diagnosed dyslipidemia and 76,375 comparators. Overall OA occurred in 12,594 and 25,089 participants, respectively, corresponding to incidence rates of 51.60 and 43.41 per 1,000 person-years (rate difference, 8.186; 95% confidence interval [CI], 7.136-9.235). The primary adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) for overall OA was 1.133 (95% CI, 1.109-1.159; crude, 1.191), and the 10-year cumulative incidence was 38.62% versus 33.14% (risk difference, 5.48 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.87-6.14). Dyslipidemia was also associated with knee OA (aHR, 1.119; 95% CI, 1.090-1.148), hip OA (1.214; 1.078-1.366), and multiple-joint OA (1.294; 1.113-1.503), with no clear association for hand OA (1.135; 0.837-1.537). For overall and knee OA, the relative associations were stronger earlier in follow-up and weaker after exploratory cut points of 6 and 9.5 years, respectively. Analyses treating death as a competing event yielded similar findings. Conclusions Newly diagnosed and treated dyslipidemia was positively associated with incident clinically diagnosed OA in this nationwide Korean cohort, most consistently for overall and knee OA, although the associations attenuated with longer follow-up. These findings add population-based evidence for an association between dyslipidemia and OA, and further studies are needed to clarify the underlying mechanisms and clinical relevance.

title: Antibiotic Nails Outperform Implant Retention in Preventing Recurrent Infections After Intramedullary Nail Fixation of Tibial Shaft Fractures Complicated by Infection.
authors: Wilhelm ZC, Kommu K, Adler EM, Schermerhorn JT, Arave MD, O'Hara NN, Wilkinson BG, Wise BT, Khoury P, O'Toole RV.
abstract: Objectives To compare infection recurrence rates between patients treated with antibiotic nail versus implant retention for open tibial shaft fractures initially treated with an intramedullary (IM) nail complicated by infection. Methods Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting Level I trauma center. Patient selection criteria Adults with tibial shaft fractures (OTA/AO 42A-C) treated with an IM nail between 2007 and 2023 who developed deep surgical site infections after index fixation were included. Outcome measures and comparisons The primary outcome was infection recurrence within 2 years requiring reoperation and antibiotics. Secondary outcomes included amputation rate, all-cause mortality rate, days in hospital within 1 year of index infection surgery, time to recurrence, and number of surgeries needed after recurrence. The association between treatment and the study outcomes was estimated using Cox proportional hazards models, controlling for potential confounders. Results A total of 96 patients were included, 75 (78%) [62 males; median age 47 years (interquartile range (IQR), 31 to 53)] were treated with conversion to antibiotic nail and 21 (22%) [18 males; median age 36 years (IQR, 27 to 48)] with implant retention. The antibiotic nail group was more likely to have chronic infections, requiring surgery 6 or more weeks after index IM nail fixation (65% vs. 38%, P = 0.03). The 2-year infection recurrence rate was significantly lower with implant removal and antibiotic nail (33%) than with implant retention (54%) (HR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.20 to 0.92; P = 0.03). For the secondary outcomes collected, only the average number of surgeries required after recurrence differed significantly between the two groups, with 3.9 for antibiotic nail and 3.0 for implant retention (IRR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.91; P = 0.04). Conclusions Conversion to an antibiotic nail was associated with lower rates of infection recurrence compared with implant retention. The overall infection recurrence rates of 33% in the antibiotic nail cohort and 54% in the implant retention cohort highlight the challenges associated with treating infection after IM nail fixation of tibial shaft fractures, regardless of treatment strategy. Level of evidence Therapeutic, Level III.

title: Anterior Cervical Diskectomy and Fusion Complicated by Salmonella Infection: A Case Report.
authors: Gattas S, Dardick J, Kashlan R, Judy B, Witham T.
abstract: Background Anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion (ACDF) is a commonly performed spinal procedure with low rates of postoperative infection. Reported infections are typically caused by skin or nosocomial flora, such as Staphylococcus species. Salmonella has been reported rarely after posterior cervical and lumbar spinal procedures but has not been described following an anterior cervical approach. Materials and methods We report a 35-year-old immunocompetent woman who developed a prevertebral abscess on postoperative day 15 following C5-C7 ACDF performed after a traumatic cervical spine injury was sustained abroad. She presented with incision site erythema, swelling, and purulent drainage but remained afebrile with a normal white blood cell count. Imaging demonstrated a rim-enhancing prevertebral fluid collection from C5-C7. She underwent irrigation and debridement with retention of instrumentation. Cultures obtained from purulent fluid overlying the anterior plate grew Salmonella group D and coagulase-negative Staphylococcus . Blood and stool cultures were negative. Results On structured literature search, this represents the first reported Salmonella infection following ACDF or any anterior cervical approach, and the first presenting as a prevertebral abscess. Recent travel and environmental exposure, with probable hematogenous seeding of a recently operated site, may have contributed. Infection occurred without systemic symptoms, underscoring the importance of clinical suspicion despite normal laboratory values. Conclusion Salmonella should be considered a rare potential pathogen in postoperative spinal infection, particularly with relevant exposure history.

title: A Novel Technique to Maintain Skeletal Traction During CT Imaging for Acetabular Fractures with Mechanical Instability.
authors: Champagne AA, Cabell GH, Parsons AW, Harman EJ, Torrey JS, Pean CA, Reilly R, DeBaun MR.
abstract: Maintaining skeletal traction in patients with acetabular fracture dislocations and associated mechanical instability remains a challenge during computed tomography (CT) acquisition. Further, multiple transfers and prolonged periods without traction pose an increased risk for recurrent dislocation episodes following closed reduction while awaiting definitive surgery. In this technical report, a traction apparatus that includes a ratchet strap connected to a digital scale was applied to maintain skeletal traction during CT imaging of acetabular fractures with mechanical instability. A cohort of 15 patients (meanage=44.0 +/- 21.5 years old, 10M/5F, Table 1) was retrospectively reviewed following implementation of the described method with no dislocation episodes during serial CT imaging prior to operative fixation. This technique is low-cost, vendor-agnostic, and does not require additional radiation exposure to trainees or radiologic technologists to manually maintain traction.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Achilles Repair Improves Suture Placement Accuracy and Reduces the Rate of Conversion to Open Repair.
authors: Kwan B, Caywood B, Vincent J, Pyle C.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate whether intraoperative ultrasound (US) guidance during percutaneous Achilles tendon repair using the Percutaneous Achilles Repair System (PARS) improves suture placement accuracy and reduces the rate of intraoperative conversion to open repair compared with repair performed without US. Methods A retrospective comparative study was performed on patients with acute or subacute Achilles tendon ruptures who underwent primary percutaneous repair using PARS by a single surgeon between June 2022 and November 2025 with a minimum of 6 months of postoperative follow-up. Patients were divided into 2 groups: PARS with US guidance (PARS US) and PARS without US (PARS no-US). Suture placement accuracy, intraoperative conversion to open repair, tourniquet times, and postoperative complications were recorded and compared between groups. Results Thirty-nine patients were included: 24 in the PARS US group and 15 in the PARS no-US group. The mean follow-up was 8.5 months (range: 6-12 months) in the PARS US group and 8.9 months (range: 6.4-11.5 months) in the PARS no-US group ( P = .541). Baseline demographics and time to surgery were comparable between groups. The PARS US group showed significantly higher suture placement accuracy compared with the PARS no-US group (98.2% [165/168] vs 76.2% [80/105], P = .005). Three patients (20%) in the PARS no-US group required intraoperative conversion to open repair because of inadequate suture purchase, whereas no conversions occurred in the PARS US group ( P = .049). Tourniquet times were significantly longer in cases requiring conversion to open repair compared with US-guided repairs ( P = .005). Overall tourniquet times were comparable between groups ( P = .324). Complication rates, including wound complications and rerupture, were low and comparable between groups. Conclusions In this single-surgeon retrospective series, US guidance during percutaneous Achilles tendon repair using the PARS system was associated with a significantly higher suture placement accuracy and a significantly lower rate of intraoperative conversion to open repair compared with repairs performed without US. The addition of US did not increase the overall tourniquet time or complication rates. Level of evidence Level III, retrospective comparative study.

title: Three-Point Suspension for Arthroscopic Bankart Repair in the Lateral Decubitus Position.
authors: Zimmerman IC, Reddy A, Stetson WB.
abstract: Arthroscopic Bankart repair remains a common procedure for anterior glenohumeral instability. Proper patient positioning, visualization, and access to the anteroinferior glenoid are crucial for successful labral repair and anchor placement. Controversy persists regarding beach chair versus lateral decubitus (LD) position for shoulder arthroscopy. The literature has shown lower recurrence rates after anterior shoulder stabilization performed in the LD position compared with beach chair. The LD position introduces technical complexities related to suspension use and operative setup. This technical note and video present a reproducible technique for patient positioning, portal placement, and 3-point suspension in the LD position to improve visualization and access to the anteroinferior labrum, glenoid, and axillary pouch during instability procedures.

title: The Impact of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist Use on Clinical Outcomes After Spinal Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authors: Xu X, Zhang X, Cai Z, Yang Y, Lin T, Zhang Z, Meng Y.
abstract: Study designsystematic review and meta-analysis.ObjectiveTo evaluate the association between perioperative glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) use and clinical outcomes after spine surgery.MethodsPubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched through July 31, 2026. Comparative studies of adults undergoing spine surgery with versus without perioperative GLP-1RA exposure were pooled using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and certainty with GRADE.ResultsThirty-six retrospective cohorts involving 435,085 patients were included. GLP-1RA use was not associated with pseudarthrosis at 90 days (RR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.25-3.98), but was associated with lower risk at 6 months (RR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.56-0.68), 1 year (RR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.61-0.69), 2 years (RR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.66-0.89), and 3 years (RR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.69-0.92). Revision risk was lower at 6 months and 2 years. GLP-1RA use was also associated with lower risks of selected systemic, infectious, and wound complications and reduced healthcare utilization, but with higher risks of hypoglycemia and adjacent segment disease.ConclusionsIn separate follow-up-specific analyses, GLP-1RA exposure was associated with lower pseudarthrosis and revision risks at selected intervals and with several other postoperative outcomes. These estimates do not establish a temporal drug effect or distinguish direct pharmacologic effects from weight loss, improved glycemic control, or confounding. Heterogeneity, possible overlapping cohorts, and very-low-certainty observational evidence preclude causal or treatment recommendations.

title: Tensionable Medial Collateral Ligament Reconstruction Using Hamstring Autograft and Bioinductive Implant Augmentation: An Updated Technique.
authors: Minkel K, Hopps K, Fernainy C, Nizar A, Lang S, Gilmer BB.
abstract: The medial collateral ligament (MCL) is the most commonly injured ligament of the knee, where reconstruction is indicated for high-grade injuries, persistent valgus laxity, and multiligament knee trauma. Traditional autograft options, particularly hamstring grafts, offer limited graft volume and suboptimal approximation of native MCL dimensions. We describe an updated version of our previously reported modified Bosworth MCL reconstruction technique to improve graft strength, volume, and healing potential. The technique uses the semitendinosus autograft left attached distally, fixed proximally at an isometric femoral point with a tensionable button to allow for controlled retensioning. Tibial fixation is achieved using knotless all-suture anchors placed with a prepared trough at the native superficial MCL footprint. A type I collagen-poly(L-lactide) bioinductive scaffold is added circumferentially around the double graft to increase construct diameter and provide early mechanical reinforcement while promoting organized biologic ingrowth. Surgical indications, exposure, graft preparation, fixation steps, and key advantages and disadvantages are outlined to support application of the technique. This updated technique seeks to better approximate the native MCL in both size and function while enhancing early stability and biologic incorporation.

title: Surgical Intervention for Massive Lesions (>3cm<sup>2</sup>): Proceedings of the International Congress on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle.
authors: Rubin J, Tham A, Butler JJ, Gauthier P, Kennedy JG, Smyth NA, Murawski CD, Adams SB, Berlet GC, Buda R, Labib SA, Nunley JA, Raikin SM, Andrews CL, Angthong C, Batista JP, Bayer S, Becher C, Boakye LAT, Brown A, Calder JDF, Canata GL, Carreira D, Clanton TO, Dahmen J, D'Hooghe P, DiGiovanni CW, Dombrowski ME, Ehlers M, Ferkel EI, Ferkel RD, Ferrao PNF, Glazebrook M, Gianakos AL, Giza E, Gomaa M, Görtz S, Haleem AM, Hamid KS, Hangody L, Hannon CP, Haverkamp D, Hertel J, Hintermann B, Hogan MV, Hunt KJ, Hurley ET, Karlsson J, Kearns SR, Kerkhoffs GMMJ, Kim HJ, Kong SW, Krebsbach S, Lambers KTA, Woo Lee J, Lee KB, Ling JS, Longo UG, Marangon A, McCollum G, McCullough K, Mitchell AW, Mittwede PN, Nehrer S, Nicolescu R, Niemeyer P, O'Malley M, Ortiz C, Osei-Hwedieh D, Paul J, Pearce C, Pereira H, Phadke R, Popchak A, Prado MP, Reilingh ML, Robert G, Rothrauff BB, Schon LC, Simpson H, Sofka CM, Spennacchio P, Stone JW, Sullivan M, Takao M, Tanaka Y, Thermann H, Thordarson DB, Tuan R, Valderrabano V, van Bergen CJA, van Dijk CN, van Dijk PAD, Vannini F, Vaseenon T, Volesky M, Walls C, Walther M, Wiewiorski M, Xu X, Yasui Y, Hua Y, Yoshimura I, Younger ASE, Zdanowicz U, Zhang Z.
abstract: BackgroundManagement of massive (>3 cm 2 ) osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLT) remains challenging due to extensive subchondral bone loss, uncontained lesion morphology, and limited high-quality evidence guiding treatment strategies. To address these gaps, an international group of experts convened to establish consensus-based recommendations for surgical management of massive OLT.MethodsExperts from multiple countries participated in a structured Delphi consensus during the International Congress on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle (ICCRA) meetings held in 2017 and 2025. Blinded surveys, structured questionnaires, and in-person discussions were used to develop and refine statements supported by literature review and graded evidence. Consensus strength was defined as consensus (51%-74%), strong consensus (75%-99%), or unanimous (100%). Grade of evidence was determined by previously established guidelines.ResultsA total of 8 consensus statements were developed addressing the surgical management of massive OLT (> 3 cm 2 ), all of which achieved strong consensus (≥86%), including 1 statement with unanimous agreement. Bulk allograft transplantation was identified as a primary joint-preserving strategy for large, uncontained, or previously treated lesions. Key technical considerations included complete lesion excision, adequate graft depth, precise graft matching, and stable fixation. Experts emphasized the importance of patient selection, surgical technique, and postoperative activity modification to optimize outcomes.ConclusionThe ICCRA statements provide structured, evidence-informed guidance for the operative management of massive OLT. By defining indications, technical considerations, and expected outcomes for bulk allograft transplantation and alternative reconstructive strategies, this framework aims to support clinical decision-making and promote consistency in the management of this complex and challenging condition.Level of Evidence:V, expert opinion.

title: Structure-based phenotypes of knee and hip osteoarthritis display clinical and genetic differences with potential implications for stratified treatment.
authors: Faber BG, Jung M, Ebsim R, Saunders FR, Hashmi A, Scott S, Gregory JS, Harvey NC, Kemp JP, Smith GD, Judge A, Boer C, Aspden RM, Lindner C, Cootes T, Collins JE, Tobias JH.
abstract: Objective Osteoarthritis is a heterogeneous disease, with diverse structural patterns likely reflecting distinct pathomechanisms. However, scalable imaging-driven approaches to define clinically meaningful phenotypes are limited. This study aimed to identify structure-based osteoarthritis phenotypes incorporating demographic features at population scale and evaluate their clinical and genetic profiles. Method Machine learning models were applied to knee and hip DXA scans from UK Biobank to quantify osteophyte area, minimum joint space width, and B-scores DXA . Imaging and demographic features were clustered using k-means to classify individuals with at least one osteoarthritis feature. Associations with joint pain and total joint replacement (TJR) were evaluated relative to structurally normal controls. Genetic correlations and polygenic risk scores were analysed to characterise shared and differing genetic architecture across phenotypes. Results Among 59,539 participants, a nine-phenotype clustering solution was derived in 28,953 participants with structural features of osteoarthritis, spanning joint-specific and multi-joint patterns. Across the nine phenotypes, prolonged knee pain ranged from 12.2% (95% CI 11.5-13.0) to 61.2% (52.7-69.0), and during follow-up knee replacement from 0.37% (0.25-0.55) to 14.9% (9.9-21.9), with the lowest proportions in the narrower joint space phenotype and highest in knee end-stage. The adjusted odds ratio for knee replacement in knee end-stage versus structurally normal controls was 98.8 (95% CI 55.5-175.9). Hip replacement ranged from 0.21% (0.12-0.35) in narrower joint space to 13.6% (10.7-17.1) in left hip end-stage (adjusted OR versus controls 72.9 [95% CI 50.3-105.6]). Genetic differences included an inverse genetic correlation between wider and narrower joint space phenotypes (rg -0.46 [95% CI -0.91, -0.01]). End-stage phenotypes demonstrated the highest joint-specific polygenic risk scores. Conclusion Population-scale imaging identifies structure-based osteoarthritis phenotypes, encompassing variation in demographics, structural components and severity, with distinct clinical outcomes and genetic profiles. This provides a scalable framework for stratifying osteoarthritis patients. Whether these phenotypes predict treatment response or inform treatment selection remains to be established and further investigation is required.

title: Self-efficacy for safety participation and the association between patient safety engagement behaviours and patient-reported safety outcomes among inpatients in Malaysian public tertiary hospitals.
authors: Mohd Nawawi MH, Mohd Hairon S, Ibrahim MI.
abstract: Introduction Patient engagement is promoted as a mechanism for enhancing hospital safety, yet the psychological and behavioural factors that determine its effectiveness are not fully understood, particularly in low- and middle-income settings. This study investigated the distribution of self-efficacy for safety participation and examined the association between patient engagement behaviours and patient-reported safety outcomes among inpatients in Malaysian public tertiary hospitals. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted between January and April 2025 across four Malaysian public tertiary hospitals. A total of 986 adult inpatients were recruited from medical, surgical, orthopaedic, and obstetrics-gynaecology wards using computer-generated simple random sampling. Validated Malay-language versions of the General Self-Efficacy Scale (GSES), Inpatient Medication-Safety Involvement Scale (IMSIS), and Patient Measure of Safety (PMOS-10) were administered. Self-efficacy scores were categorised into low, moderate, and high levels using pre-specified distribution-based cut-points. The association between patient safety engagement and patient-reported safety outcomes was analysed using Pearson correlation and robust linear regression. Results The mean self-efficacy score was 3.27 (SD = 0.52) on a four-point scale. Using pre-specified cut-points, 61.1% of participants were classified as having high self-efficacy, 37.0% as moderate, and 1.9% as low. A positive correlation was observed between patient safety engagement and patient-reported safety outcomes (r = 0.38, 95% CI [0.32, 0.43], p Conclusion Most adult inpatients in Malaysian public tertiary hospitals reported moderate-to-high self-efficacy for engaging in safety-related behaviours. Greater patient safety engagement, measured specifically through medication-related behaviours, was positively associated with more favourable patient-reported safety outcomes, though the effect size was modest (R² = 0.14). The small subgroup of patients with low self-efficacy highlights the need for tailored approaches to address heterogeneity in patient populations. These findings contribute to the limited evidence base on patient engagement in safety within low- and middle-income settings and support further investigation into strategies that enable patient participation in safer hospital care.

title: Repurposed Reamings for Donor Distribution: The R2D2 Technique for Osteochondral Allograft Transplantation.
authors: Nuelle CW, Ryan PM, Jackson GR, Cook JL.
abstract: Osteochondral allograft transplantation is an established treatment for large symptomatic articular defects of the knee, with functional graft survivorship reportedly improving. However, failure of osseous integration at the graft-recipient site remains a significant cause of treatment failure. This article describes the Repurposed Reamings for Donor Distribution technique-a technique that combines autogenous bone reamings harvested during native bed preparation with bone marrow aspirate concentrate applied into drilled osteochondral allograft subchondral bone tunnels and onto the interface surface to enhance osseous integration.

title: Repair of Posterior Root Medial Meniscus Oblique Tear Repair With Centralized Suture Technique of Inverted Anchors Combined With Fibrin Clot.
authors: Hou P, Meng C, Xu J, Zhao W, Wei Y, Han C.
abstract: Posterior root tear of the medial meniscus is closely associated with meniscal extrusion, which refers to the displacement of the meniscal body beyond the tibial margin. Meniscal extrusion can seriously impair the load-distributing function of the meniscus and is associated with symptoms such as knee joint pain. With the progression of extrusion, it will eventually lead to knee osteoarthritis. Isolated repair of the meniscal posterior root may not be sufficient to alleviate the degree of meniscal extrusion. Therefore, we adopt an arthroscopic centralization technique to reduce medial meniscus extrusion using reverse fixation, combined with platelet-rich fibrin clot to promote meniscus healing and improve prognosis to a certain extent. This technique presents the advantages of high fixation strength, stable anchor implantation, and simple operation.

title: Regional Differences in Publication Volume on Pediatric Sports Knee Conditions Between North America and the Asia-Pacific Regions.
authors: Chong B, Goh RSJ, Tan SHS, Hui JHP.
abstract: Purpose To characterize and compare publication patterns for 5 major pediatric sports knee conditions-anterior cruciate ligament tears, discoid meniscus pathology, osteochondritis dissecans (OCD), patellar instability, and tibial eminence fractures-across North America and the Asia-Pacific regions, examining regional research volume, condition-specific publication patterns, and changes in research output over time. Methods EMBASE, PubMed, and Medline were searched from inception to January 2025. Studies focusing on pediatric populations (≤18 years) addressing the 5 specified knee conditions were included. Publications were classified by geographic region based on recruiting institution country, with North America including the United States, Canada, and Mexico and Asia-Pacific defined according to the World Health Organization regional classifications. Results Of 1100 included publications, North American institutions contributed 907 studies (82.5%) compared with 193 from Asia-Pacific institutions (17.5%). Anterior cruciate ligament injuries dominated research focus globally, comprising 613 publications (56%). Regional differences emerged in condition-specific priorities: discoid meniscus research represented 18% of Asia-Pacific output versus 6.5% in North America, whereas OCD accounted for 26% versus 19%, respectively. Patellar instability and tibial eminence fractures together represented the smallest share of publications (16% combined). Asia-Pacific research showed rapid growth, with 75% of regional publications occurring within the last decade. Conclusions Research output rose across both regions, with North America as the dominant contributor. Anterior cruciate ligament injury was the most studied condition, comprising over half of all publications, followed by OCD, patellar instability, discoid meniscus, and tibial eminence fractures. Marked regional variation in condition-specific focus was observed, with Asia-Pacific institutions contributing proportionally greater output on discoid meniscus and OCD. Clinical relevance North America's dominant research output means that guidelines are largely derived from Western populations, which may limit their applicability in the Asia-Pacific context. These findings highlight the need for internationally collaborative studies to improve generalizability of clinical evidence across diverse populations.

title: Postoperative Opioid Prescribing in Older Adults: A Comparison of Academic and Non-academic Centers Following Short-Segment Lumbar Surgery.
authors: Kaghazchi A, Lunasco L, Ashraf A, Jelkin G, Karnati J, Abid S, Wu A, Ranganathan S, Assi JY, Wallace M, Cheng J, Adogwa O.
abstract: Study DesignRetrospective, propensity score-matched cohort study.ObjectivesTo compare postoperative opioid prescription patterns between academic and non-academic centers among adults aged ≥65 years undergoing short-segment lumbar procedures.MethodsUsing the TriNetX electronic health record database, we identified patients aged ≥65 years who underwent primary short-segment lumbar operations between 2010 and 2022 at academic or non-academic centers for lumbar spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, radiculopathy, or scoliosis. After 1:1 matching, 3,404 patients were included in each cohort. Opioid prescription rates were compared within three postoperative windows: 3-6, 6-12, and 12-24 months. Prescriptions were categorized by medication type, CYP2D6 dependence, and potency.ResultsDuring the 3-6-month postoperative window, patients treated at non-academic centers had lower odds of a documented order for CYP2D6-dependent (OR 0.774, 95% CI [0.683-0.876]), strong-potency (OR 0.787, 95% CI [0.672-0.923]), and moderate-potency opioids (OR 0.817, 95% CI [0.693-0.963]). Their odds were higher for CYP2D6-independent opioids during the 6-12-month window (OR 1.357, 95% CI [1.174-1.568]) and for CYP2D6-independent (OR 1.191, 95% CI [1.055-1.345]) and moderate-potency opioids (OR 1.209, 95% CI [1.059-1.379]) during the 12-24-month window.ConclusionsAcademic centers had higher prescription rates for CYP2D6-dependent, strong-potency, and moderate-potency opioids at 3-6 months, whereas non-academic centers had higher rates of CYP2D6-independent opioids at 6-12 and 12-24 months and moderate-potency opioids at 12-24 months. These comparisons demonstrate institutional variation in postoperative opioid prescribing within each observation window and warrant further investigation into the clinical and organizational factors underlying these patterns.

title: Pediatric and adolescent pathological fractures: Etiological spectrum, biomechanical instability, and individualized treatment strategies - a current concepts review.
authors: Krieg AH, van de Sande M, Balacó I, Salom-Taverner M, Helenius I, Wirth T, Chiari C, Kowalczyk B, Study Group (SG) Tumor of the European Paediatric Orthopaedic Society (EPOS) – Based on the SG-Meeting in Toulouse 2025.
abstract: Pathological fractures in children and adolescents are rare but clinically significant compared with typical low-energy traumatic fractures. These fractures occur when bone with compromised load-bearing capacity fails, due to a focal lesion, systemic bone fragility, or external insult. Pediatric bones differ from adults in greater plasticity, thicker periosteum, and ongoing growth, resulting in unique age-specific features in etiology, biomechanics, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. This review brings together current evidence and clinically relevant concepts about pediatric pathological fractures, emphasizing the interplay between bone biology, structural instability, and personalized treatment approaches. Three guiding principles are highlighted: first, etiological stratification should precede definitive fracture management, with prompt differentiation between benign lesions and aggressive or malignant conditions; second, fracture risk assessment should integrate symptoms, lesion size, cortical destruction, location, and pediatric-specific modifiers rather than relying solely on adult-derived tools; third, treatment should focus not only on achieving fracture union but also on restoring future mechanical safety and preserving growth potential. Simple bone cyst is the most common cause; osteogenesis imperfecta and fibrous dysplasia demonstrate how systemic matrix abnormalities and disordered remodeling can lead to recurrent fractures and deformities. Malignant bone tumor-related fractures are rare, but improper initial management can negatively impact oncologic care. Therefore, a structured diagnostic pathway, judicious use of imaging and biopsy, and multidisciplinary long-term management are essential. This review clarifies literature scope and limitations, distinguishes pediatric evidence from adult extrapolation, and provides a practical diagnostic and treatment algorithm for clinical practice.

title: Open reduction of the femoral butterfly fragment in closed femoral shaft fractures is associated with a higher rate of reoperation to promote union: a retrospective clinical cohort.
authors: Schlauch AM, Zakusylo A, Ball G, Biedermann B, Onafowokan O, Kennerly V, Domashevich T, Hellwinkel JE, Mauffrey C, Schaffer NE.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate whether the presence of and/or open reduction of a butterfly fragment in closed femoral shaft fractures was associated with reoperation to promote union. Methods Design: Retrospective cohort. Setting Single Level I Trauma Center. Patient selection criteria Included were patients who underwent surgical fixation of an acute OTA/AO 32A-C femoral shaft fracture between January 2017 and January 2024. Patients younger than 18 years, nonunion surgeries, Outcome measures and comparisons Patient demographics were retrospectively collected. A butterfly fragment was defined as a singular, wedge-shaped segment of comminution from the diaphysis of the femur. Groups were stratified based on the presence or absence of a butterfly fragment. The primary outcome was reoperation to promote union. Secondary outcomes included fracture-related infection (FRI) and presence of post-operative cortical step sign (CSS). Comparisons of primary and secondary outcomes were made between patients with and without a femoral butterfly fragment. A subgroup analysis was performed within the butterfly fragment group comparing open versus closed reduction of the butterfly fragment. Results 139 patients were included: 99 (71.2%) without a butterfly fragment (mean age 38.5years, range 18-92years; 62.6% male) and 40 (28.8%) with a butterfly fragment (mean age 35.5years, range 18-96years; 75.0% male). 10 (10.1%) patients without a butterfly fragment and 8 (20.0%) patients with a butterfly fragment underwent reoperation to promote union (p=0.2). Of the 40 patients with a butterfly fragment, 9 (22.5%) had open reduction of the butterfly fragment with cable fixation and 31 (77.5%) did not. The mean proximal and distal displacement of the butterfly fragment did not differ significantly between those managed with open versus closed reduction (38.8mm vs 35.4mm and 20.3mm vs 18.9mm, respectively, p>0.05). Open reduction to the butterfly fragment compared to closed reduction was associated with a higher rate of reoperation to promote union (66.7% vs 6.5%, p Conclusions Open reduction of the butterfly fragment in closed femoral shaft fractures was associated with a higher rate of reoperation to promote union compared to closed reduction. These findings emphasize biologic preservation. Level of evidence III.

title: Most National Football League Players Return to Play After Achilles Tendon Repair, Yet Only One-Half Regain Preinjury Performance With Persistent Pass-Rush Decline at Year 2.
authors: Skaik K, Hayes E, Macciacchera M, Meulenkamp B, Matache B, Pickell M.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate National Football League (NFL) player performance using advanced statistics after Achilles tendon (AT) repair. Methods NFL players who underwent AT repair between 2017 and 2023 were identified from a publicly available injury database. Demographic and performance data were collected preinjury and up to 2 seasons postinjury, with a minimum follow-up of 1 regular-season game required to assess return to play (RTP). RTP was defined as being active for a regular-season game and return to performance as achieving ≥90% of preinjury performance. Performance was assessed using Sports Information Solutions' points above replacement (PAR). Factors associated with RTP and return to performance were analyzed using binary logistic regression, with pre- and postinjury performance compared using paired t tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, as appropriate. Results Seventy-seven NFL players with AT repairs were identified. Ten were excluded for no prior regular-season play, leaving 67 included. Overall, 77.6% (n = 52) returned to play. Increasing age reduced the odds of RTP (odds ratio 0.75, 95% confidence interval [0.60-0.95], P = .02). Index games preinjury increased the odds of RTP (odds ratio 1.12, 95% confidence interval [1.01-1.24], P = .04). Body mass index, position, index games played, and index PAR were not significant. Among returnees, 50% (n = 26) achieved at least 90% of preinjury performance. Higher index PAR predicted lower odds of meeting this threshold (odds ratio 0.77, 95% confidence interval [0.66-0.90], P = .00). Pass-rush PAR declined at year 2 after injury from 1.17 (±5.19) preinjury to -0.66 (±2.15), P = .02. Conclusions In this study using publicly available data, 77.6% of NFL players returned to play after AT repair; however, only one-half of these players regained ≥90% of their preinjury performance. Older age reduced the likelihood of RTP, whereas more preinjury games started increased it. Higher preinjury PAR reduced the likelihood of performance recovery. Pass-rush performance declined by the second postinjury season. Level of evidence Level IV, retrospective therapeutic case series.

title: Long-Term Outcomes in NF1 Scoliosis Without Apparent Dystrophic Features After Posterior Spinal Fusion: A Minimum 5-Year Retrospective Cohort Study.
authors: Shao X, Deng Y, Zhou Y, Chen J, Yang J, Wang L, Zhang X, Sui W.
abstract: Study DesignRetrospective Cohort Study.ObjectivesTo evaluate 5-year complication rates, risk factors, and patient-reported outcomes (PROs) after posterior spinal fusion (PSF) for NF1 scoliosis without apparent dystrophic features.MethodsWe analyzed 72 patients (8-18 years) with Cobb ≥40° and no apparent dystrophic features who underwent PSF (2014-2017) with ≥5-year follow-up. Distal fusion levels were classified as stable vertebra (SV) or non-SV. Outcomes included dystrophic transformation, adding-on, implant failure, revision, and composite adverse events. Subtle dystrophic changes were assessed. LASSO regression with bootstrap validation was performed.ResultsAt 5 years, composite adverse outcome occurred in 30.6% (22/72). LASSO regression identified two independent risk factors: preoperative subtle dystrophic changes (OR 6.23, 95%CI 2.35-16.52, P<0.001) and fusion to non-SV (OR 3.76, 95%CI 1.48-9.54, P=0.005). Age <12 years was associated with higher complications in univariate analysis (P=0.017) but was not retained in the multivariable model. Mean Cobb angle improved from 51.8±8.5° to 18.2±6.0° (P<0.001). All SRS-22 domains improved significantly (all P<0.001). Patients with complications had lower pain and self-image scores (both P<0.001).ConclusionsNF1 scoliosis without apparent dystrophic features carries substantial long-term complication risks, which are associated with worse pain and self-image outcomes. Preoperative subtle dystrophic change is a poor risk factor and fusion to the SRS-defined stable vertebra contributes to better outcomes in this observational cohort. Long-term multidisciplinary surveillance with annual radiographic and SRS-22 domain assessment is essential for patient-centered care in this high-risk population.

title: Intrinsic capacity and hip fracture: A multinational analysis across 15 countries.
authors: Huang X, Ye M, Li X, Xu J, Wu J, Wu Q, Cai H, Qi L, Guo J, Chen J.
abstract: Background Managing hip fracture (HF) risk in older adults remains a major clinical challenge, with current prevention strategies heavily reliant on pharmacological agents that carry serious adverse events. The World Health Organization's intrinsic capacity (IC) framework offers a function-centred alternative, but robust cross-population evidence is limited. Methods We harmonized data from four longitudinal ageing cohorts across 15 countries (n = 33,452). IC was assessed across five domains, with higher scores indicating greater capacity. The primary outcome was incident HF. We employed Cox proportional hazards models, random-effects meta-analyses, bidirectional cross-lagged panel networks, and sensitivity analyses to examine baseline IC, its domains, and changes in IC over time. Results Higher baseline IC was associated with lower incident HF risk in the fully adjusted pooled individual-level analysis (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.975, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.966-0.985; p 2 = 89.43%), indicating that the association was not uniform across settings. Higher cognitive, locomotor, and psychological capacities were associated with lower HF risk, whereas sensory capacity showed a small positive association and vitality was not significantly associated with HF. Evidence for IC changes was mixed: trajectory associations varied with score weighting, and continuous IC change was not significantly associated with HF in the pooled analysis. Sensitivity analyses generally supported the baseline IC association. Conclusions Higher baseline IC was associated with lower incident HF risk overall, but the HRS finding and substantial heterogeneity do not support a uniform association across national or cultural settings. Its value for HF risk prediction requires further evaluation.

title: Immediate versus delayed MRI following medial open reduction for developmental dysplasia of the hip: Re-intervention rates and resource utilisation.
authors: Mil M, Hyde N, Moorhead R, Loh B, Donnan L.
abstract: Purpose The aim was to understand re-intervention rates and the cost differential between intraoperative and postoperative MRI groups, following medial open reduction for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), to evaluate the suitability of these two surgical care models. Methods Our single-centre retrospective study included patients Results We included 170 patients (197 hips): 128 patients underwent intraoperative MRI, while 42 underwent postoperative MRI. The overall re-intervention rate was 1.8% (3/170 patients). Re-intervention occurred in 0.8% (1/128) of cases with intraoperative MRI compared to 4.7% (2/42) with postoperative MRI (p=0.09). Intraoperative MRI was associated with a significantly longer theatre duration (169.3±48.0 vs 132.0±49.4 minutes, p Conclusion Given the low re-intervention rates in medial open reduction for DDH, the added costs of longer theatre duration for intraoperative MRI, combined with lost opportunity, may outweigh its benefits. Significance of study Instead of routine intraoperative MRI, next-day postoperative MRI can be utilised, based on individual cases taking into account surgical complexity and patient needs.

title: High-Tensile-Strength Suture Tape Provides Higher Load to Failure Than Conventional Suture for Glenoid Labral Repair in a Cadaveric Model.
authors: Drake CM, Karwandyar A, Uppuganti S, LeClere LE.
abstract: Purpose To compare the biomechanical pull-through strength of high-tensile-strength suture tape versus high-tensile-strength conventional suture in anterior and posterior glenoid labral repairs assessed by load-to-failure (N) testing in a cadaveric model. Methods Anterior labral tears were created in 10 matched pairs of fresh-frozen cadaveric scapulae, and posterior labral tears were made in 10 additional matched pairs. For each pair, 1 scapula was randomly assigned to be repaired with a suture tape, whereas the contralateral scapula was repaired with a conventional suture. Transosseous tunnels were drilled, and the suture tails were passed through the tunnels. The specimens were then loaded to failure at a positive displacement rate of 6.5 mm/min. The force at which the suture pulled through the labral tissue (measured in Newtons) and the mode of repair failure were recorded. Results Seven specimens were included in the final analysis for anterior repairs. In anterior labral repairs, suture tape exhibited a higher load to failure (312.4 ± 100.1 N) than conventional suture (250.1 ± 87.5 N), although the difference did not reach significance ( P = .054). Ten specimens were included in the final analysis for posterior repairs. In posterior labral repairs, suture tape had a significantly higher load to failure (303.0 ± 82.6 N) than conventional suture (237.0 ± 69.3 N), with a 65.9-N difference ( P = .046). All 14 repairs failed at the level of the tissue in anterior repairs. In posterior repairs, all 10 suture tapes and 6 conventional sutures failed at the tissue. Four posterior repairs using conventional suture failed at the level of the suture. Conclusions In this study, suture tape showed higher pull-through strength than conventional suture in posterior glenoid labral repairs in this time-zero cadaveric biomechanical model using transosseous tunnel repair with tied knots. Clinical relevance Understanding the differences in strength can allow surgeons to optimize the suture selection in glenoid labral repair and potentially reduce the incidence of repair failures at the suture-labrum interface.

title: Functional performance and 12-month change in effusion-synovitis in knees at risk of osteoarthritis: A longitudinal analysis using the osteoarthritis initiative.
authors: Wang Y, Liu H, Zhang H, Zhao W, Miao X, Tao Q, Wang T, Jiang J, Wang X, Yang X, Qiu X, Chen L, Chen L, Liao R, Yang Y, Liu D, Liu S, Yu B, Yang S, Wang T, Li S.
abstract: Background Effusion-synovitis is a key marker of synovial inflammation and is linked to the progression of knee osteoarthritis (KOA). However, the determinants of short-term changes in synovial inflammation remain unclear. This study examined the associations of baseline demographic, clinical, functional, and cardiometabolic factors with 12-month changes in effusion-synovitis volume in knees at risk of osteoarthritis (OA). Methods We performed a longitudinal analysis using data from the POMA incident OA cohort of the Osteoarthritis Initiative. Effusion-synovitis volume was quantified on magnetic resonance imaging at baseline and 12 months. The primary outcome was the 12-month change in effusion-synovitis volume. Linear mixed-effects models were used to evaluate associations between baseline factors and the outcome, adjusting for demographic and clinical covariates, including baseline effusion-synovitis volume and case/control status. Results Among 680 knees, female sex (β = 0.18, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.33; P = 0.019), older age (β = 0.03, 95% CI: 0.02 to 0.04; P Conclusions Baseline demographic and symptom-related factors, but not structural, metabolic, or functional measures, were associated with short-term changes in effusion-synovitis in knees at risk of OA. These findings highlight the importance of symptom-related processes in the progression of synovial inflammation.

title: Finite element analysis of different subtrochanteric osteotomy techniques in total hip arthroplasty for high hip dislocation.
authors: Diwu W, Xu H, Wu Q, Hong Y, Xia B, Han Y, Bi L, Wang Z, Yang M.
abstract: Aims Subtrochanteric shortening osteotomy in total hip arthroplasty (THA) for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) has variable outcomes. This study evaluated the initial stability of seven different osteotomy techniques. Methods A 3D finite element model of a femur with a stem was created. Seven models simulating osteotomies with different angles (0°, 45°, 90°, -90°, 120°, -120°, z-shaped) were analyzed. Outcomes included range of motion (ROM), bone/implant stress, and osteotomy surface separation. Results The 0° model had the greatest ROM (lowest stiffness). The z-shaped and -90° designs provided the best rotational stability. Analysis of the centre of rotation showed single-symmetric models (45°, z-shaped) shifted laterally, suggesting a 'windshield wiper' effect, while double-symmetric models (90°, -90°, 120°, -120°) stayed aligned with the prosthesis axis. Stress patterns differed: single-symmetric models concentrated stress on the lesser trochanter, while double-symmetric models stressed the greater trochanter, with a notable ring in the -90° design. Implant stresses were similar, except in the horizontal model. The -90° and 90° models had the least osteotomy separation, unlike the 45° model. Conclusion No single osteotomy technique outperformed others in all metrics. The z-shaped and -90° designs offered the best rotational stability; the -90° and 90° designs minimized axial separation; the 45° model showed the worst 'windshield wiper' effect. The 120° technique provided a balanced profile with moderate rotational stability, acceptable separation, and less pronounced stress rings, representing a reasonable compromise. The choice should be guided by clinical priorities.

title: Evolving Management of Hip Fracture Patients on Anticoagulant and Antiplatelet Medications: A 22-Year Cohort Study.
authors: House HE, Schwartz A, Shimizu M, Hong I, Cohen JB, Summers HD, Levack AE.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate temporal trends in anticoagulant (AC) and antiplatelet (AP) use among patients undergoing operative treatment of hip fractures and to assess the association of antithrombotic regimen with time to surgery and postoperative outcomes. Methods Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting Single North American Level I trauma center. Patient selection criteria Patients aged 55 years or older who underwent operative treatment for a hip fracture (AO/OTA types 31-A, 31-B, and 31-C) between 2000 and 2022 while receiving anticoagulant and/or antiplatelet therapy at admission were included. Outcome measures and comparisons Temporal trends in antithrombotic prescribing, time to surgery, perioperative transfusion, readmission, 90-day medical and surgical postoperative complications, and 90-day mortality were assessed. The odds of warfarin versus direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) prescription were compared across study years, and time to surgery from admission and each outcome were compared across study years and across antithrombotic regimens (warfarin, DOAC, DOAC or warfarin plus antiplatelet, and antiplatelet alone). Results 476 patients were included (mean age 81.2 years [range, 60-103]; 288 [60.4%] female). Anticoagulant therapy was used by 155 (32.7%) and antiplatelet therapy by 385 (80.7%); 64 (13.4%) received both. The odds of warfarin prescription relative to a DOAC decreased by an estimated 37% per year (odds ratio [OR] 0.63, 95% CI 0.53-0.74; P Conclusions In this 22-year single-center cohort of hip-fracture patients receiving anticoagulant (AC) or antiplatelet (AP) therapy, antithrombotic regimen was not associated with time to surgery, 90-day complications, or mortality. Perioperative transfusion and 1-year readmission rates declined over the study period independent of medication class. These findings supported expedited operative management of hip fractures in patients receiving AC or AP therapy. Level of evidence III.

title: Association Between Baseline Anemia and Nonunion After Proximal Humerus Fracture Across the Adult Lifespan.
authors: Nakken ER, Mamonov A, Garcia-Canga B, Whitney DG, Lang A, Aibinder WR.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the association between preexisting anemia and proximal humerus fracture (PHF) nonunion and to determine whether risk varies by anemia type and associated co-occurring conditions. Methods Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting Administrative claims database study using commercial and Medicare fee-for-service data from 2016 to 2023. Patient selection criteria Adults aged ≥19 years who sustained a PHF (OTA/AO 11) and had continuous insurance enrollment for ≥6 months after PHF were included, allowing entry into the at-risk period for nonunion. Anemia diagnosed during the 1-year period before the fracture was the primary exposure and was evaluated in three ways: (1) presence or absence of any anemia, (2) number of different co-occurring anemia conditions (range, 0-14), and (3) clinically relevant anemia categories, including nutritional, hemolytic, and aplastic/other anemias. Outcome measures The incidence rate (IR), IR ratio (IRR), and hazard ratio (HR) was estimated for the primary outcome of nonunion of the PHF from 6 to 18 months post-fracture, before and after accounting for potential confounders. Additionally, sub-group estimates were generated for patients 40, 50, 60, 70, and 80 years of age. Results There were 25,109 adults with a PHF and any type of anemia (mean [SD] age=76.0 [12.8] years; 78.2% women; 6.8% commercially-insured) and 64,389 with a PHF without anemia (68.3 [17.0] years; 74.6% women; 26.7% commercially-insured). The crude IR and IRR of PHF nonunion was significantly higher for the full anemia cohort (IR=6.0 [95%CI=5.1-6.8]; IRR=1.37 [95%CI=1.15-1.62) and for each anemia sub-cohort (IR [IRR] for 1, 2, and ≥3 co-occurring anemic conditions was 5.5 [1.25], 6.2 [1.42], and 8.1 [1.85], respectively) than the non-anemia cohort. Compared to the non-anemia cohort, the adjusted HR was not significantly different for the full anemia cohort (HR=0.97; 95%CI=0.80-1.17) or anemia sub-cohorts (HR range, 0.85-1.00). However, age strongly modified all associations (P for interaction, all ≤0.001). For all three types of anemia exposure (yes/no, count of co-occurring, clinically distinct groups), the HR of nonunion was elevated at the younger ages (age 40: HR=2.06 [95% CI=1.33-3.18]; age 50: HR=1.63 [95% CI=1.18-2.27]; age 60: HR=1.30 [95% CI=1.02-1.65]) and declined with older age, close to 1.00 by 70 years old and below 1.00 by 80 years old. Conclusions Anemia was associated with a higher rate of nonunion of the proximal humerus fracture among younger and middle-aged adults (HR=2.06, 1.63, and 1.30 for 40, 50, and 60 year old patients, respectively), but not for older adults. Level of evidence Prognostic Level III.

title: Arthroscopic Glenoid Fracture Repair With Dual Suture-Button Construct.
authors: Cahoy K, Guareschi ME, Guareschi ME, Rogalski BL, Friedman RJ, Eichinger JK.
abstract: Many glenoid fractures involving the glenoid rim are associated with shoulder instability; however, larger intra-articular glenoid fossa fractures creating substantial articular incongruity can be more challenging to manage because they involve the load-bearing articular surface of the glenohumeral joint. Open reduction and internal fixation is the current standard of care for displaced glenoid fossa fractures; however, operative management of glenoid fossa fractures remains challenging. Arthroscopic-assisted reduction and internal fixation has emerged as a minimally invasive alternative, but most arthroscopic techniques described in the literature focus on glenoid rim fractures or rely on intra-articular screws or anchors, which may be suboptimal for glenoid fossa fractures because of limited bone stock and the risk of articular cartilage violation. The arthroscopic technique described in this report is a viable alternative for select displaced glenoid fossa fractures that would otherwise be treated with open reduction and internal fixation or nonoperatively.

title: Age Over 50 Years Does Not Increase Failure Rates After Transosseous Medial Meniscus Root Tear Repair With a Minimum 2-Year Follow-Up.
authors: Stevens AC, Cavendish P, Milliron E, Kirven J, Mallory N, van der List JP, Barker T, Magnussen RA, Flanigan DC.
abstract: Purpose To determine whether outcomes of medial meniscus posterior root tear repair differ between patients younger and older than 50 years of age. Methods A retrospective review was performed of patients ≥18 years who underwent medial meniscus posterior root tear repair by 4 surgeons at 1 tertiary academic institution between 2012 and 2019. Patients were excluded if they did not undergo transosseous root repair or if they lacked a minimum 2-year follow-up. Demographics and surgical data were collected. Patients were contacted to identify failures and additional knee surgeries and to obtain patient-reported outcome measures. Failure rate and patient-reported outcome measures were compared between those Results Sixty-three patients were identified (66.7% female, 51.1 ± 10.4 years of age [range 20.8-68.9 years]), with a mean follow-up of 5.1 ± 1.6 years (range 2.0-8.0 years). Repair failure rates were similar for patients P = .71), with average time to repair failure of 0.5 ± 0.3 and 2.1 ± 1.7 years, respectively ( P = .08). Rates of progression to arthroplasty were 9.5% for both groups ( P = .99). Kellgren-Lawrence grade was higher in subjects that experienced failure with a median grade of 2 (interquartile range [IQR]: 1.5-2) compared with 1 (IQR: 1-2) in the no-failure group ( P = .03). International Knee Documentation Committee (69.7 ± 18.2 vs 73.2 ± 22.0 [ P = .68]) and Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (79.2 ± 13.5 vs 82.3 ± 18.1 [ P = .64]) were also similar between the 2 groups. Median Tegner Activity Scale and Marx Activity Rating Scale scores were 4 (IQR: 3-5) and 0 (IQR: 0-4) for the group P = .50 and .45, respectively). Conclusions In this study, we found similar rates of repair failure, conversion to arthroplasty, and patient-reported outcome measures between patients older and younger than 50 years of age undergoing transosseous medial meniscus posterior root tear repair at a minimum 2-year follow-up. Level of evidence Level III, therapeutic retrospective comparative study.

title: After-hours hip fracture surgery-influence on reoperation risk, mortality, and surgical complications: a cohort study of 98,607 patients from the Norwegian Hip Fracture Register.
authors: Boutera AT, Dybvik E, Engesæter LB, Guy P, Kristensen TB, Leer-Salvesen S, Hallan G, Sundet M, Gjertsen JE.
abstract: Background and purpose Previous studies have shown that timing of hip fracture surgery is important for outcomes. We aimed to determine whether hip fracture surgeries performed after regular working hours were associated with increased 1-year reoperation risk, 30-day mortality, or intraoperative complications. Methods Data from 98,607 patients ≥ 65 years with hip fracture reported to the Norwegian Hip Fracture Register between 2005 and 2023 were analyzed. Absolute risk estimates were calculated with Kaplan-Meier, and Cox regression models were used to estimate hazard rate rations (HRRs) for 1-year reoperation risk and 30-day mortality for surgeries performed in the evening (16:00-22:00) and nighttime (22:00-08:00) compared with daytime surgery (08:00-16:00). Analyses were adjusted for age groups, sex, the American Society of Anesthesiology (ASA) physical status class, cognitive impairment, type of fracture, type of surgery, waiting time to surgery, and duration of surgery. Surgeons self-reported intraoperative complications to the registry. Results 46,655 patients (47%) underwent daytime surgery, 40,916 (42%) evening surgery, and 11,036 (11%) nighttime surgery. The mean age was 83 years, 69% were females. Patients operated on during nighttime had overall shorter waiting time to surgery than the other groups. 1-year reoperation risk was 4.9% (n = 2,290) for daytime surgery, 5.2% (n = 2,151) for evening, and 6.0% (n = 673) for nighttime, with no statistically significant differences between the groups. Nighttime surgery was associated with a slightly lower 30-day mortality (7.8%, n = 870) compared with daytime surgery (9.6%, n = 4,494), HRR 0.91 (95% confidence interval 0.84-0.98). No statistically significant differences in intraoperative complications were observed across the 3 surgical time periods: daytime (2.9%), evening (2.9%), and nighttime (2.9%). Conclusion Evening and nighttime hip fracture surgery were not associated with increased risk for 1-year reoperation, 30-day mortality, or intraoperative complications compared with daytime surgery.

title: Regional Variations in Epidemiology, Diagnosis, and Surgical Management of Discoid Meniscus in Pediatric Populations Across Asia-Pacific and North American Regions: A Systematic Review.
authors: Chua CXK, Wang E, Tan CQ, Lim AKS, Hui JHP, Tan SHS.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate regional variations in clinical presentation, diagnostic approaches, and treatment algorithms for pediatric discoid meniscus between Asia-Pacific and North American regions. Methods A systematic review was conducted following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, searching PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure databases from inception to August 2025. Study characteristics, population details, imaging modality (sensitivity and specificity), study objective, incidence of bilateral involvement, surgical technique, and complications were recorded. Because of heterogeneity and predominantly low-level evidence, a qualitative synthesis was performed. Results Thirty-nine studies were included in the systematic review, predominantly Level III evidence. Epidemiological data suggested a higher reported incidence of bilateral discoid meniscus in Asia-Pacific (7%-33%) compared with North America (2%-21%), although findings were heterogeneous. Twelve radiological studies were evaluated and found Asia-Pacific studies reporting the use of alternative diagnostic technique (radiography and ultrasound), whereas North America relied exclusively on magnetic resonance imaging. Twenty-four surgical studies were included (13 Asia-Pacific, 11 North America), comprising 671 and 1442 knees, respectively. Partial meniscectomy/saucerization was the predominant surgical approach in both regions (89.7% vs 94.5%, P = .08), with low rates of subtotal or total meniscectomy. However, adjunctive procedures differed significantly; Asia-Pacific studies more commonly reported concurrent repair or stabilization procedures (47.7% vs 26.6%, P = .0001), whereas North American studies more frequently performed partial meniscectomy alone. Conclusions This systematic review suggests a higher incidence of bilateral discoid meniscus in Asia-Pacific, but findings were limited by heterogeneity. Although demographics and clinical presentation were similar between regions, imaging approaches differed, with radiographic and ultrasound studies reported exclusively in Asia-Pacific and North American studies relying solely on magnetic resonance imaging. Surgically, both regions primarily performed partial meniscectomy; however, adjunct procedures (stabilization and/or repair) were more common in Asia-Pacific. These findings underscore distinct regional treatment strategies and the need for standardized diagnostic and treatment frameworks. Level of evidence Level IV, systematic review of Level II to IV studies.

title: Osteomyelitis after open supracondylar fracture in a child: a case report and review of the literature.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Stubenböck E, Mindler G, Öhner T, Moser V, Beer T, Quadlbauer S.
abstract: The management of open fractures in children relies on several critical strategies to minimize the risk of infection, including the timing of surgical debridement, appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis, and the choice of osteosynthesis technique. Despite these considerations, the overall rate of postoperative infection in children remains relatively low. Consequently, clinical experience with deep postoperative infections in pediatric patients is limited. Furthermore, the highly variable and often subtle clinical presentation can make early diagnosis challenging. We present the case of an 8-year-old child who developed osteomyelitis following a Gustilo-Anderson grade III open supracondylar humerus fracture.

title: Ninja Warrior Athletes Have Diverse Athletic Backgrounds, High Fitness Levels, and Are Prone to Upper Extremity and Ankle Injuries.
authors: Gardner CH, DiStefano JG.
abstract: Purpose To characterize Ninja Warrior athletes' level and frequency of participation, exercise habits and capabilities, prior sports participation, injuries frequently sustained, and management of those injuries. Methods A survey was available to Ninja athletes at 5 gyms and competitions between July 2023 and February 2026. Athletes were included if they were over 18 years old and competed or trained on Ninja obstacles. The survey evaluated athletic background, injury data, and injury management data. Statistical significance was determined between men and women, and a regression analysis was performed. Results A total of 101 surveys were completed (64 men, 37 women). The mean age of respondents was 33.8 years (range 18-57 years). Men were more likely to sustain injuries than women (incidence rate ratio 2.5). Athletes had an average body mass index of 23.2 and averaged 20.9 pull-ups, a 195.5-s dead hang, and an 11.0-ft lache. The most common traumatic injury sites were hand (skin tears, 67.3%), ankle (48.5%), and shoulder (40.6%). The shoulder and elbow were the most common sites of overuse injuries. The rate of return to full preinjury level of participation was 70.7% in this study. Conclusions Ninja Warrior athletes have broad athletic backgrounds and display high reported levels of physical fitness. Unique traumatic injury mechanisms include static and dynamic stress on the fingertips as well as eccentric loading of joints. Men, on average, sustained more injuries than women. Overuse injuries most commonly occur in the shoulder and elbow regions. Clinical relevance This study provides useful data about the common phenotype of Ninja Warrior athletes and the injuries they sustain, which helps to guide diagnosis and treatment of these athletes.

title: Influence of ballistic and conventional resistance training on bone properties in postmenopausal women: A randomised controlled trial.
authors: Caliskan O, Marques EA, Breasail MÓ, Duckham RL, Folland JP, Brooke-Wavell K.
abstract: High-load conventional resistance training (CRT) is recommended for osteoporosis prevention. Ballistic resistance training (BRT) involves high velocity and impact forces with lower loads. The Resistance Exercise Programme on Risk of Osteoporosis and Osteoarthritis in Females (REPROOF) study examined effects of BRT and CRT, relative to control (CON) on proximal femur BMD. Healthy postmenopausal women aged 50-70 years were randomised into BRT, CRT or CON groups. BRT and CRT conducted supervised resistance training twice weekly for eight months. In CRT, concentric and eccentric phases each lasted ~2 s at 55-80% of one-repetition maximum (1RM). BRT involved explosive (maximum velocity) concentric movements at 20-50% of 1RM. Proximal femur and lumbar spine BMD were measured by DXA; tibia structure by peripheral QCT. Groups were compared using ANCOVA, adjusting for baseline values. Of 109 women randomised, 82 (63.1 ± 3.7 years; 24.5 ± 3.5 kgm -2 ; femoral neck T-score -1.1 ± 0.8) completed the study, with 98% adherence. BRT improved total hip BMD (+0.008 [0.001, 0.014] g/cm 2 ; P = 0.02) versus CON. CRT did not affect hip BMD but tibial shaft cortical BMD increased (+4.141 [1.007, 7.274] g/cm 2 ; P = 0.01) and cortical thickness declined relative to CON (-0.07 [-0.13, -0.01] mm; P = 0.03), accompanied by tibial shaft widening. BRT increased total hip and trochanter BMD (P ≤ 0.03) in the subgroup with low BMD. BRT benefitted proximal femur BMD relative to CON, including in the subgroup with low BMD. CRT did not affect hip BMD but caused tibial shaft structural adaptation that may affect strength in bending. BRT based interventions should be further developed and evaluated for osteoporosis prevention.

title: Hip Preservation Surgery for Isolated Labral Tears in Patients with Femoral Acetabular Impingement and Dysplasia Provides Comparable Patient-Reported Outcomes as Surgery but Slower Recovery and Higher Reoperation Rate for Dysplasia.
authors: Ricard MA, Poitras S, Juric M, Parisien A, Pacheco-Brousseau L, Carsen S, Grammatopoulos G, Beaulé PE.
abstract: Purpose To assess clinical outcomes after hip preservation surgery for patients grouped into the 3 following conditions: dysplasia, femoroacetabular impingement (FAI), or isolated labral tears. Methods Patients who underwent hip preservation surgery at our center between January 2018 and December 2021 were identified. Patients with dysplasia, FAI, or isolated labral tears were included. Clinical outcomes of the 3 condition groups were compared using the International Hip Outcome Tool-12 and Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System, which were collected preoperatively and at 3 months and 1 and 2 years postoperatively. Results A total of 378 patients were included: 80 (22.4%) with dysplasia, 173 (48.6%) with FAI, and 103 (28.9%) with isolated labral tears. Arthroscopy (n = 269, 75.6%) was the most common procedure, followed by periacetabular osteotomy (n = 82, 23.0.4%) and surgical dislocation (n = 7, 2.0%). All groups had significant improvements in their International Hip Outcome Tool-12 and Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System physical ( P P = .018). The percentages of patients attaining minimal clinically important difference on the International Hip Outcome Tool-12 at 1 year showed a significant difference between the 3 groups: 35.9% (FAI), 63.2% (dysplasia), and 48.6% (labral tears), P = .028. Reoperation rates, according to condition groups, were higher for dysplasia mainly because of the removal of internal fixation and similar between FAI and labral tear. Conclusions In this study, we observed significant improvements in the patient-reported outcome measures after hip preservation surgery for dysplasia, FAI, and isolated labral tears.
