Although dysplasia patients showed slower recovery and a higher reoperation rate, both the dysplasia and isolated labral tear groups were comparable in achieving minimal clinically important difference and substantial clinical benefit, whereas the FAI group had significantly lower percentages of patients achieving them. Level of evidence Level III, therapeutic retrospective comparative study.

title: Higher Opioid Consumption and Pain in the Early Postoperative Period After Rotator Cuff Repair Compared With Shoulder Arthroplasty.
authors: Johnson D, Shah KP, Longa AD, Walsh J, Masterson N, Pontes M, McMillan S.
abstract: Purpose To compare postoperative pain and opioid consumption between patients undergoing rotator cuff repair (RCR) and those undergoing elective shoulder arthroplasty (SA). Methods Fifty patients who underwent RCR (n = 25) and SA (n = 25), anatomic and reverse, were retrospectively reviewed until their 12-week postoperative appointment. Within the RCR cohort, most received concomitant acromioplasty and distal clavicle excision, whereas any biceps tearing was addressed by tenodesis. Pain was assessed by visual analog scale preoperatively, as well as 2 and 6 weeks postoperatively. Opioid consumption was also monitored by pill count at 2-, 6-, and 12-week postoperative visits. Results The SA group had significantly lower average opioid consumption at 2 weeks (8.7 vs 13.3 morphine milligram equivalents, P = .039) and lower pain on the visual analog scale at both 2 (3.0 vs 3.9, P = .007) and 6 weeks (1.3 vs 2.4, P P P = .022) timepoints was significantly greater for the SA group. Demographically, the SA cohort was older (71.0 ± 7.7 vs 60.9 ± 10.8 years of age, P P = .021), and stayed overnight more often than the RCR group (47% vs 0%, P = .011). Conclusions Patients undergoing RCR experienced greater postoperative pain and opioid consumption during the early postoperative period than those undergoing elective SA. These differences were statistically significant and exceeded the predefined minimal clinically important difference. Level of evidence Level III, retrospective comparative case series.

title: Five-year outcomes after brace-free versus brace-based rehabilitation following isolated anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with hamstring tendon autograft: long-term follow-up of a randomized controlled trial.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Schoepp C, Praetorius A, Tennler J, Raeder C, Schroeder M, Hax J, Seelmann C, Ohmann T, Efe T, Dudda M, Neidlein C.
abstract: Introduction Postoperative knee bracing following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) remains common practice despite growing evidence questioning its clinical benefit. Previous studies demonstrated that brace-free rehabilitation was noninferior to brace-based rehabilitation one year after isolated ACLR using hamstring tendon autograft; however, its long-term effects remain unknown. The purpose of this study was to evaluate long-term effects five years after surgery. Materials and methods Patients enrolled in a prospective randomized controlled trial conducted between 2016 and 2019 were recontacted approximately five years after isolated primary ACLR with hamstring tendon autograft for a long-term follow-up. In the original trial, 139 patients had been randomized to postoperative rehabilitation without a brace (n = 71) or with a functional knee brace (n = 68). Participants completed several patient-reported outcome measures. Furthermore, a standardized telephone interview was performed. Changes between the one-year and five-year follow-up were analyzed. Results Ninety-seven patients participated in the long-term follow-up (n = 45 brace-free group, n = 52 brace group). Mean follow-up was 5.2 ± 1.0 years. No significant differences were observed between groups regarding subjective knee function, activity level, quality of life, rerupture rate, revision surgery, or persistent knee-related complaints at final follow-up. However, there was a significant interaction between treatment group and time for the subjective IKDC score. Patients treated without postoperative bracing showed stable or slightly improved subjective knee function, whereas patients treated with a brace demonstrated a significant decline between one and five years. Discussion Brace-free rehabilitation after isolated ACL reconstruction with hamstring tendon autograft remains safe and effective more than five years after surgery. Postoperative bracing did not reduce rerupture rates, revision surgery, or long-term functional impairment. Instead, brace-free rehabilitation demonstrated a more favorable longitudinal development of subjective knee function. These findings further question the routine postoperative prescription of rehabilitative knee braces following isolated ACL reconstruction.

title: Erdheim-Chester Disease Mimicking a Benign Cystic Femoral Lesion: A Diagnostic Pitfall.
authors: Kum A, Güler S, Ordu M.
abstract: Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is a rare clonal non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis that usually shows characteristic long-bone involvement and may affect multiple organ systems. Localized skeletal presentations can be diagnostically challenging when imaging resembles a benign bone lesion. A 50-year-old man presented with progressive right distal femoral/knee pain for approximately 6 months, with difficulty bearing weight and walking. Radiographs demonstrated bilateral distal femoral lesions, initially considered possibly benign cystic bone lesions. Because the symptomatic right-sided lesion extended to the articular cartilage surface, curettage and right knee arthroplasty were performed during the same operative session. Histopathology showed fibrosis and numerous lipid-laden foamy histiocytes, prompting investigation for a histiocytic disorder. Lesional cells expressed CD68, Factor XIIIa, and CD163 but not CD1a or S100. VE1 immunohistochemistry showed no BRAF V600E protein expression; molecular testing was not performed. Subsequent 18F-FDG PET/CT identified multiple non-FDG-avid lytic-appearing osseous abnormalities of uncertain etiology, without skeletal or marrow FDG uptake considered significant for malignancy. Systemic treatment was deferred and clinical surveillance continued. This case illustrates a practical diagnostic pitfall: ECD may mimic a benign cystic femoral lesion despite an atypical initial radiological presentation. Recognition of the histopathological pattern, appropriate immunophenotyping, expert review when needed, and systemic staging are important for accurate classification and management.

title: Endoscopic Resection of Plantar Ganglion of the Great Toe via the Midline Plantar Portals.
authors: Pan X, Lui TH, Pan Y, Li CCH, Slocum AMY, Su W, Sun Y.
abstract: Toe ganglion cysts can be painful because of shoe compression or pressure during walking. Moreover, they can present as repeated rupture, infection, and continuous discharge. Surgery is recommended for symptomatic ganglion recalcitrant to conservative treatment. Open ganglionectomy has potential risk of wound complications, formation of painful scar, and high recurrence rate. The purpose of this technical note is to describe the details of endoscopic resection of plantar ganglion of the great toe via the midline plantar portals. This is a combination of both resection and internal drainage of the ganglion. This minimal invasive approach may help to reduce the risk of recurrence and the risk of injury to the digital neurovascular bundle.

title: Development and external validation of an explainable machine-learning model for the prediction of unfavourable clinical-radiological outcome at three months in thoracolumbar osteoporotic vertebral fractures.
authors: Gutiérrez-González R, Martínez-Núñez P.
abstract: No externally validated tools stratify three-month prognosis after thoracolumbar osteoporotic vertebral fracture. An explainable logistic-regression model with nine predictors achieved an external AUC-ROC of 0.744 (sensitivity 90.7%). The counterfactual analysis of vertebral augmentation, the only modifiable predictor, is hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as a treatment recommendation. Purpose Thoracolumbar osteoporotic vertebral fractures (OVF) carry substantial morbidity and mortality, yet no externally validated tool stratifies three-month prognosis. We developed and externally validated an explainable machine-learning model for the three-month unfavourable clinical-radiological outcome. Methods Retrospective observational study reported according to TRIPOD. Unfavourable outcome was defined as persistent pain, progression of vertebral height loss and/or worsening of independence in daily activities. A derivation cohort of 482 patients aged ≥50 years with acute thoracolumbar OVF treated at a tertiary centre (2017-2021) was used to train and internally validate seven algorithms with hyperparameter optimisation and stratified fivefold cross-validation. An independent two-centre cohort (n = 74) was used for external validation without retraining. Interpretability was based on SHAP values. Results The unfavourable outcome occurred in 53.9% of the derivation cohort and 58.1% of the external cohort. A nine-variable logistic-regression model with Platt calibration was selected (cross-validated AUC-ROC 0.675, 95% CI 0.622-0.728; external AUC-ROC 0.744, 95% CI 0.628-0.844). At the pre-specified internal Youden threshold (0.556), external sensitivity was 60.5% and specificity 71.0%; at a post-hoc external threshold (0.432), 90.7% and 54.8% (Brier 0.211, expected calibration error 0.096). Vertebral augmentation was the strongest and only modifiable predictor (mean |SHAP | = 0.278); counterfactual analysis showed an absolute risk reduction of 17.1-26.6 percentage points (median 25.3). Conclusion The model predicts the three-month outcome of thoracolumbar OVF with an external AUC-ROC of 0.744 and preserved calibration. The counterfactual analysis of vertebral augmentation is hypothesis-generating and not a treatment recommendation; larger external validation, long-term outcomes and harm assessment are required before clinical use.

title: Arthroscopic Double EndoButton Adjustable-Loop Plate Fixation for Acute Acromioclavicular Joint Dislocation.
authors: Huang S, Zheng Z, Qian C, Yuan H, Bao H.
abstract: Acute acromioclavicular joint dislocation is a shoulder injury. Surgical intervention is typically recommended for Rockwood type IV to VI injuries with significant displacement. Both traditional open surgery and existing arthroscopic techniques have limitations in terms of trauma, stability, and procedural complexity. This article introduces an arthroscopic fixation technique using a double EndoButton adjustable-loop plate. It aims to achieve anatomical reduction and sustained compressive fixation of the acromioclavicular joint through a dual-EndoButton structure and an adjustable-loop design. This method is relatively straightforward to perform, minimally invasive, and biomechanically sound, offering a reliable new option for the minimally invasive treatment of acute acromioclavicular joint dislocations. Preliminary clinical practice has shown favorable reduction outcomes, stable fixation performance, and potential for early rehabilitation.

title: Application of Extraperitoneal Laparo-Endoscopic Single-Site Surgery in the Treatment of Lumbosacral Trunk Entrapment: A Cadaveric Study and Clinical Case Series.
authors: Chen S, Miao J, Ma G, Wang Y, Zhang Z, Yang X, Fan S.
abstract: Objective Management of pelvic fracture with lumbosacral trunk entrapment remains controversial. Open surgery (OS) carries significant technical challenges and risks. Our team innovatively proposed extraperitoneal laparo-endoscopic single-site surgery (ELESS) to explore and release the lumbosacral trunk. This study aimed to identify the key anatomical parameters of the lumbosacral trunk, to introduce ELESS techniques for exploration and release of lumbosacral trunk entrapment, and to evaluate its safety, feasibility, and clinical efficacy compared to OS. Methods This study measured lumbosacral trunk parameters in 12 cadavers, and retrospectively analyzed clinical data of 36 patients with lumbosacral trunk entrapment from May 2022 to September 2024. Combined with anatomical data, preoperative enhanced CT and MRN tests, the lumbosacral trunk decompression surgery was performed precisely via ELESS (n = 16) and OS (n = 20). Demographic, surgical technique details, and clinical outcomes were obtained from patient records. Independent samples t-tests, Mann-Whitney U test, or the Chi-square test were used to perform comparisons. Results The distance from the start of lumbosacral trunk to the sacroiliac joint was 14.85 ± 1.43 mm. The total length of the lumbosacral trunk was 34.95 ± 2.13 mm, and its width was 7.92 ± 1.11 mm. The patients were followed up for at least 16 months. The ELESS group demonstrated a significantly shorter operative time (131.5 ± 13.6 min) and reduced intraoperative blood loss (119.1 ± 28.1 mL) compared to the OS group (151.7 ± 27.9 min and 1010.5 ± 118.6 mL, p Conclusions Anatomical data is essential to identify and locate the lumbosacral trunk during surgery. The ELESS for lumbosacral trunk decompression offers the advantages of precision, minimal invasiveness, and safety. Compared to traditional OS, the ELESS is associated with less bleeding and shorter operative time, representing a reliable option for managing pelvic fractures with lumbosacral trunk entrapment.

title: Anatomical Risk Factors for Patellofemoral Instability Vary by Dejour Type of Trochlear Dysplasia.
authors: Hartmann M, Caliskan B, Vlachopoulos L, Ackermann J, Fucentese SF.
abstract: Purpose To assess whether Dejour trochlear dysplasia (TD) types differ in their association with other patellofemoral anatomical variables in patients with patellar instability. Methods All patients with TD undergoing evaluation for patellar instability between January 2010 and December 2020 were included if a true lateral radiograph and a preoperative magnetic resonance imaging were available. Two reviewers independently assessed TD type (Dejour classification), femorotibial rotation, tibial tubercle-trochlear groove (TTTG) distance, sagittal TTTG, tibial tubercle-to-posterior cruciate ligament distance, supratrochlear spur height, sulcus depth, Merchant's congruence angle, trochlear sulcus angle, Caton-Deschamps index, patellotrochlear index, patellar tilt, angle, thickness, and width. Results The study included 330 patients (363 knees, 66.7% women, mean age 22.5 ± 7.9 years, body mass index 24.9 ± 5.4). TD distribution was type A (17.1%), B (33.6%), C (25.9%), and D (23.4%). Types B and D showed significantly increased Merchant's congruence angle ( P = .019), patellar tilt ( P P = .035), TTTG ( P P P Conclusions Patients with Dejour type B and D TD had significantly increased values in other patellofemoral instability risk factors compared with those presenting with type A and C dysplasia. Level of evidence Level IV, diagnostic retrospective case series.

title: State-space dynamics of joint coordination reveal preserved directional structure across running speeds.
authors: Garofolini A, Sparrow WA, Begg R.
abstract: Understanding whether locomotor demands are accommodated by reorganising inter-joint coordination or by scaling an existing coordination pattern is a fundamental question in biomechanics and motor control. We examined whether the directional organisation of ankle-knee moment coordination is preserved across running speeds using a state-space representation of their continuous interaction. Sagittal-plane ankle and knee moments were analysed in 31 experienced runners (30 male, 1 female; 28 competitive and 3 elite) running at 2.5, 3.5, and 4.5 m·s -1 . Trajectory geometry was characterised by loop area, path length, major-axis orientation, and anisotropy, while trajectory-attached vectors quantified the magnitude and direction of progression through four intrinsically defined coordination segments: Loading, Transfer, Propulsion, and Release. Increasing speed markedly expanded the coordination trajectory, increasing loop area and path length (both p < 0.001), with smaller changes in major-axis orientation (p = 0.003) and anisotropy (p = 0.005). Progression magnitude also increased with speed (p < 0.001), with a Speed × Segment interaction showing that the magnitude of this increase differed across coordination segments (p = 0.006). In contrast, although vector direction showed a significant effect of speed (p = 0.0016), reflecting modest overall directional shifts, but no significant Speed × Segment interaction (p = 0.084): the characteristic directional sequence through Loading, Transfer, Propulsion, and Release was preserved. Thus, running faster scales ankle-knee mechanical coordination while the segment-dependent directional structure was largely preserved. These findings distinguish increased mechanical demand from a clear reorganisation of inter-joint mechanical coordination across running speeds.

title: Serum P1NP is associated with hip bone mineral density gains after romosozumab readministration following bisphosphonate therapy in women with osteoporosis.
authors: Kobayashi T, Kobayakawa T, Morimoto T, Nakamura Y.
abstract: The association between baseline total P1NP and BMD response to romosozumab readministration following bisphosphonate therapy in women with osteoporosis remains unclear. This multicenter study found that higher baseline total P1NP was independently associated with greater 12-month hip BMD gains, although these findings require further validation. Purpose To investigate the association between baseline serum total procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide (P1NP) levels and subsequent changes in bone mineral density (BMD) after romosozumab readministration following bisphosphonate therapy in women with osteoporosis. Methods This multicenter study included 22 women (mean age, 76.7 years) with osteoporosis who received a second 12-month course of romosozumab following bisphosphonate therapy. Total P1NP was assessed (mean, 18.6 μg/L) at baseline. Lumbar spine (LS), total hip (TH), and femoral neck (FN) BMD were assessed at baseline and 12 months, and percent changes were calculated. Multivariable linear regression analyses evaluated associations between baseline total P1NP and BMD changes, adjusting for potential confounders. Receiver operating characteristic analysis evaluated the ability of baseline total P1NP to identify patients achieving a ≥ 3% increase in BMD at 12 months. Results BMD increased by ≥3% in 68.2%, 27.3%, and 36.4% of patients at the LS, TH, and FN, respectively. Higher baseline total P1NP levels were independently associated with greater 12-month increases in TH BMD (adjusted β, 0.31; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.03-0.59) and FN BMD (adjusted β, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.12-0.72), but not LS BMD (adjusted β, 0.18; 95% CI, -0.28 to 0.64). The optimal baseline total P1NP cutoff for identifying hip BMD responders was 14.8 μg/L, with an area under the curve of 0.714. Conclusion Higher baseline total P1NP levels were independently associated with greater 12-month hip BMD gains. Baseline total P1NP may help identify potential hip BMD responders, but these exploratory findings require validation.

title: Radiographic changes in disc height index and 12-month segmental motion following single-level microsurgical sequestrectomy for lumbar disc herniation.
authors: Jäckle K, Meier MP, Hawellek T, Roch PJ, Roch FE, Höller LF, Klockner FS, Awan Malik H, Weiser L, Lehmann W.
abstract: Objectives Longitudinal radiographic changes after microsurgical sequestrectomy for lumbar disc herniation remain incompletely characterized, particularly regarding disc height and segmental motion. This study aimed to quantify changes in Disc Height Index (DHI) from the preoperative assessment to 12-month follow-up, to describe radiographic segmental motion and the prevalence of prespecified radiographic instability criteria at 12 months, and to identify factors associated with these radiographic findings. Methods This retrospective single-center observational study included 250 patients who underwent single-level microsurgical sequestrectomy for lumbar disc herniation between January 2018 and December 2024 and had complete imaging required for the present analysis. Disc height and DHI were assessed using standardized radiographic measurements. Segmental motion and radiographic instability status were assessed on 12-month flexion-extension radiographs; corresponding preoperative functional radiographs were not systematically available. Recurrent disc herniation was assessed on postoperative MRI. Multivariable regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with DHI reduction and 12-month radiographic instability status. Because no nonoperative or alternative-surgery comparison group was available, the study was not designed to determine whether observed changes were caused by sequestrectomy or reflected the natural history of underlying degeneration. Results Mean disc height significantly decreased from 9.14 ± 1.48 mm preoperatively to 7.65 ± 1.89 mm at 12-month follow-up (p Conclusion Significant reductions in disc height and DHI were observed between the preoperative assessment and 12-month follow-up in this cohort treated with microsurgical sequestrectomy. Prespecified radiographic instability criteria were met by 24.4% of patients at 12 months. Because baseline functional radiographs were not systematically available, the study cannot determine whether radiographic instability developed after surgery. In the absence of a comparison group and patient-reported clinical outcomes, these findings should be interpreted as longitudinal disc-height observations and cross-sectional 12-month radiographic associations; they cannot establish a causal effect of sequestrectomy or the clinical relevance of the observed motion findings. Trial registration Registration of trial 2026-06-30 - Retrospectively registered. Trial registration number DRKS00040457.

title: Occipital pressure injury in the beach-chair position: a report of two cases and a review of the literature.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Alshanqiti B, Imam M, Gokaraju K, Gulihar A.
abstract: Pressure-related occipital complications of the beach-chair position have been attributed to headrest compression, prolonged immobilisation or systemic hypoperfusion. We present two patients who developed postoperative pressure alopecia and lesser occipital neuropraxia after shoulder arthroscopy on a T-MAX (Smith & Nephew, Andover, MA) beach-chair, used in its standard articulating-cradle and foam-mask configuration. Both remained normotensive throughout, with continuous cerebral oximetry showing no desaturation, and both were positioned in neutral alignment without rotation. One developed a well-demarcated patch of occipital alopecia after 92 min; the other developed lesser occipital neuropraxia after a 180-minute procedure. Both recovered fully, at four and five months respectively. Building on earlier reports implicating the retention straps alongside rotation and duration, we propose that in the near-upright position used here, at a trunk inclination of approximately 80 degrees, the load pressing on the occiput is supplied in part by the straps rather than by gravity alone. Because interface pressures were not measured, this remains a hypothesis requiring direct testing. We describe the layered padding and repositioning protocol subsequently adopted in our unit, emphasising pressure redistribution and repeated intraoperative checks of head position. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level V, Case Report.

title: Modified Autologous Biceps Acromioclavicular and Horizontal Neutralization (AutoBAHN) Technique Using a Free Biceps Tendon Autograft for Acromioclavicular Joint Stabilization.
authors: Gruber T, Van Eecke E, Lance L, Leschinger T, Scheibel M.
abstract: We present a modification to the autologous biceps acromioclavicular stabilization and horizontal neutralization technique. In contrast to the original technique, we propose releasing the long head of the biceps tendon (LHB) at the origin and securing the proximal portion to the scapular neck in either an inlay or onlay fashion. Similar to the original technique, the distal portion of the LHB is routed through the clavicle and secured with an interference screw. Next, the LHB is passed over the acromioclavicular joint and anchored in the lateral acromion, providing vertical and horizontal stabilization. This modification aims to preserve the fundamental biomechanical principles and advantages of the original technique, using a local, strong, and autologous graft that avoids donor site morbidity and allograft-related concerns. This technique expands the indication, offering a practical and versatile alternative for acromioclavicular joint reconstruction when preservation of the native LHB insertion is not feasible or desirable.

title: Delayed Implantation of a Maxillary Central Incisor Using a Modified Anatomic Healing Abutment and Transmembrane-Fixation Guided Bone Regeneration: A Case Report.
authors: Ma J, Li W.
abstract: Maxillary anterior bone loss complicates implant surgery. We adopted a modified abutment plus transmembrane-fixed GBR for delayed implantation in a 21-year-old patient. In this single case, the combined protocol was clinically feasible and associated with favorable short-term esthetic and functional outcomes.

title: Connecting Ligament Tears of the Lateral Meniscus in the Popliteal Hiatus Region: An Arthroscopic Classification Including 4 Types.
authors: Sun LN, Yan S, Shu H, Wei W.
abstract: Purpose To describe an arthroscopic classification system for connecting ligament tears in the popliteal hiatus of the lateral meniscus and describe their repair technique. Methods We retrospectively reviewed the data of patients who underwent lateral meniscus repair between 2019 and 2023. Inclusion criteria included isolated or combined tears of the connecting ligaments in the popliteal hiatus. All patients underwent arthroscopic examination and/or repair and were followed up for a minimum of 1 year. Tears were classified arthroscopically into 4 types: type 1, isolated radial tear of the meniscofibular ligament; type 2, isolated longitudinal tear of the meniscofibular ligament; type 3, isolated longitudinal tear of the posterior popliteomeniscal fascicle; and type 4, combined longitudinal tear of meniscofibular ligament and posterior popliteomeniscal fascicle. Clinical outcomes were assessed using Lysholm, Tegner, and International Knee Documentation Committee scores. Knee magnetic resonance imaging was performed at 1 year postoperatively. Results Among 188 patients with lateral meniscus tears, 24 (12.8%) had connecting ligament tears in the popliteal hiatus. These included 3 type 1 (12.5%), 4 type 2 (16.7%), 8 type 3 (33.3%), and 9 type 4 (37.5%) lesions. Mean postoperative Lysholm, Tegner, and International Knee Documentation Committee scores significantly improved compared with preoperative values (all P Conclusions This study describes an arthroscopic classification of popliteal hiatus-lateral meniscus tears. Additionally, all-inside suture arthroscopic repair of the popliteal hiatus ligament-lateral meniscus complex led to favorable patient-reported outcomes at short-term follow-up. Level of evidence Level IV, retrospective therapeutic case series.

title: Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes of Arthroscopic Free Bone Grafts Versus Latarjet Procedures for Anterior Shoulder Instability with Glenoid Bone Loss: A Systematic Review.
authors: Nguyen CD, Farquharson R, Wang E, Romero MR, Marks LA, Marigi EM, Tokish JM, Hassebrock JD.
abstract: Purpose of review Arthroscopic free bone grafts have emerged as an alternative bone augmentation technique for the management of anterior shoulder instability with glenoid bone loss. While coracoid transfer procedures remain widely used, free bone graft techniques have gained interest because of their anatomic restoration and avoidance of coracoid-related morbidity. The purpose of this systematic review is to synthesize the current available literature on arthroscopic reconstruction of the glenoid arc, evaluating its efficacy, safety, and clinical outcomes relative to arthroscopic and open Latarjet procedures. Recent findings A total of 37 studies (43 cohorts; 2,073 patients) met inclusion criteria: 18 arthroscopic free bone graft, 15 arthroscopic Latarjet, and 10 open Latarjet cohorts. Most of the studies were Level IV evidence, and consisted primarily of small, retrospective case series. Across all three procedures, postoperative pain improved to 1.1-1.2 on the VAS, and more than 90% of patients returned to sport. Recurrence or instability rates were 2.3%, 2.8%, and 2.2%, respectively (p = 0.791), and graft nonunion 3.0%, 6.0%, and 3.7% (p = 0.051). Within arthroscopic free bone graft cohorts, nonunion was 1.2% for iliac crest autograft, 22.5% for iliac crest allograft, and none for distal tibial allograft or scapular spine autograft (p < 0.001). Graft resorption was 6.7%, 3.4%, and 4.1% (p = 0.259), reaching 13.7% with distal tibial allograft. Other complications were more frequent after arthroscopic free bone graft (8.4%) than arthroscopic (4.7%) or open Latarjet (5.0%; p = 0.017). Arthroscopic free bone graft demonstrates favorable short- to mid-term clinical outcomes, with improvements in pain, return to sport, and recurrence rates that fall within the range reported for coracoid transfer procedures. Graft nonunion and resorption were low overall, although nonunion clustered in iliac crest allograft cohorts and other complications were more frequent after arthroscopic free bone graft. Interpretation is limited by the predominance of small, retrospective case series and heterogeneous outcome reporting. Higher-level prospective and comparative studies are warranted to better define the indications, radiographic healing characteristics, and long-term durability of arthroscopic free bone graft in the management of anterior shoulder instability.

title: Beyond chronological age: uncovering disease-dependent variability in AI-driven pediatric bone age assessment.
authors: Schön F, Meißner C, Spieth S, Pätzold K, Blum SFU, Hoffmann RT, Kühn JP, Kromrey ML.
abstract: Objectives To assess performance and agreement of a commercial artificial intelligence (AI) tool relative to routine pediatric radiologists' bone age assessments in a large pediatric cohort, with focus on different groups of growth disorders. Materials and methods One thousand five hundred sixteen anterior-posterior hand radiographs of pediatric patients (50.6% boys, mean age 10.84 ± 3.66 years) were retrospectively analyzed using the AI tool BoneAge. AI results were compared with board-certified pediatric radiologists' reports using Bland-Altman plots, Spearman correlations, and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Subgroup analyses were performed for three major indications: genetic/neuroendocrine (n = 1179), orthopedic (n = 152), and oncologic disorders (n = 185). Results Mean absolute difference (MAD) in estimated bone age by radiologists and AI was 6.4 ± 7.0 months for the whole cohort, with complete concordance in 45.1% of cases. Best results were achieved in orthopedic questions with an MAD of 4.1 ± 5.6 months (genetic/neuroendocrine: 6.6 ± 7.2, oncologic: 6.7 ± 6.3 months). There was significant correlation between AI and radiologists for the whole study population (ρ = 0.980), and the three main groups: genetic/neuroendocrine (ρ = 0.974), orthopedic (ρ = 0.952), and oncologic indications (ρ = 0.988). ICCs for the entire cohort and the main indication groups were > 0.9, indicating excellent agreement between radiologist and AI. Conclusion The investigated algorithm showed good agreement with bone age assessments performed by pediatric radiologists in a large pediatric cohort. Novel to previous studies, the indication for imaging was considered, demonstrating that agreement between algorithm output and radiologists' assessments varied across disease groups, with highest agreement observed in orthopedic indications. Key points Question The performance of artificial intelligence tools for bone age assessment among different subgroups of pediatric patients according to underlying diseases has not yet been investigated. Findings Automated bone age assessment reliably correlates with estimation by pediatric radiologists. Software output differs according to disease groups, with best results for orthopedic indications. Critical relevance statement In a real-world scenario, the commercial software showed good agreement with routine bone age assessments in a large cohort of pediatric patients. The observed disease-dependent variation suggests that radiologists should consider disease-specific differences when using additional automated tools.

title: Arthroscopic Targeted Anchor Placement During Broström Repair: A Minimally Invasive Technique Guide.
authors: Halpern R, Spadafora P, Martin KD, Efremov K.
abstract: Ankle sprains are among the most common orthopaedic injuries, with 20% to 30% of patients progressing to chronic lateral ankle instability despite conservative management. Arthroscopic lateral ankle ligament repair has shown outcomes comparable with open Broström repair while allowing treatment of concomitant intra-articular pathology. However, standard arthroscopic techniques may limit accurate anchor placement on the fibular footprint or require an accessory anterolateral portal, increasing incision burden, technical complexity, and risk to the superficial peroneal nerve. We describe an easily reproducible, arthroscopic targeted anchor placement technique for Broström repair using a 1.9-mm needlescope without the need for an accessory viewing portal. The procedure uses standard anteromedial and anterolateral portals, with the needlescope advanced directly to the anterior talofibular ligament fibular footprint for visualization. Knotless suture anchors are placed through the needlescope cannula, eliminating the need for an accessory anterolateral portal and the need for multiple assistants. This minimally invasive technique reduces incision burden while maintaining precise anchor placement. By avoiding an accessory lateral portal, it may decrease the risk of superficial peroneal nerve injury while preserving the benefits of arthroscopic lateral ankle ligament repair.

title: Arthroscopic Stabilization Reduces Recurrence but May Delay Return to Sport After First-Time Traumatic Anterior Shoulder Dislocation in Elite Male Athletes: A Systematic Review.
authors: Fraser C, Sedlacek D, Letts J, Brown D, Talbot W, Ralph-Wilkie J, Sattler L.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative management for first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation in adult athletes, with a focus on recurrent instability, return-to-play rates, and time to return to play. Methods Five databases were searched from inception to July 2025. Studies comparing arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative management in adult athletes (≥18 years) with first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation were included. The primary outcome was recurrent instability. Secondary outcomes included return-to-play rates and time to return to play. A narrative synthesis was performed given the nonrandomized and heterogeneous nature of included studies. Evidence certainty was assessed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation. Results Five studies (232 participants: 111 operative, 121 nonoperative) were included. Recurrent instability rates ranged from 3% to 14% in the operative group and 24% to 80% in the nonoperative group. Return-to-play rates were high for both approaches (operative: 93%-100%; nonoperative: 97%-100%). Nonoperative management was associated with earlier return to sport (2.3-5.7 weeks vs 18.7-39.3 weeks for operative management in studies reporting this outcome). All studies involved elite athletes, with female athletes substantially under-represented. Conclusions Arthroscopic stabilization was consistently associated with lower rates of recurrent instability than nonoperative management after first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation but required a longer time to return to play. Nonoperative management enabled an earlier return to play but was associated with higher recurrence. The evidence is limited primarily to male military, collegiate, and professional athletes, restricting generalizability to female, recreational, and broader adult athletic populations. Level of evidence Level III, systematic review of Level II and III studies.

title: Arthroscopic Physeal-Sparing Suture-Anchor Fixation for Pediatric Femoral-Side Posterior Cruciate Ligament Avulsion.
authors: Li Q, Yu R, Zhang Y, Jiang Q, Chen D.
abstract: Femoral-side posterior cruciate ligament injuries are rare in skeletally immature patients, and reconstruction using transphyseal tunnels carries the risk of growth disturbance. Primary repair, when feasible, provides a physeal-sparing and tissue-preserving alternative. Arthroscopic suture-anchor repair offers a safe and effective treatment option for pediatric femoral-side posterior cruciate ligament avulsions, preserving the native ligament and avoiding the potential complications associated with tunnel-based reconstruction.

title: All-Inside Double-Bundle Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction With Hamstring Autograft.
authors: Yang Z, Liu Y, Lin Y, Ji M, Lu J.
abstract: This technical report describes a reproducible all-inside double-bundle anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction technique performed through standard arthroscopic portals. The technique integrates the anatomical rationale of double-bundle reconstruction with the bone-preserving advantages of the all-inside approach. Independent preparation of the anteromedial and posterolateral grafts allows bundle-specific sizing and tensioning. Femoral and tibial closed-socket tunnels are created with preservation of adequate bone bridges to minimize the risk of tunnel convergence. Adjustable-loop cortical suspension devices are used on both the femoral and tibial sides, enabling independent bundle fixation at different knee flexion angles to better approximate native anterior cruciate ligament biomechanics. This technique aims to enhance anatomical restoration and rotational stability while reducing bone loss and graft length requirements. Technical pearls, potential pitfalls, and patient selection considerations are discussed. Although the technique is anatomically oriented and technically feasible, its clinical advantages over established reconstruction methods remain to be determined and warrant further investigation.

title: All-Arthroscopic Repair of Partial-Thickness Upper Border Subscapularis Tear With a Resorbable Bioinductive Bovine Collagen Implant.
authors: Winzenried AE, Allahabadi S.
abstract: Partial-thickness subscapularis tears are frequently underdiagnosed, and optimal management remains controversial. Bioinductive collagen implants have shown promising results in partial-thickness superior rotator cuff tears but have not been described for partial subscapularis pathology. This Technical Note describes a simple arthroscopic technique for bioinductive collagen implant repair or augmentation of partial-thickness subscapularis tears. This approach provides a reproducible biologic option for managing partial-thickness subscapularis tears while minimizing technical complexity.

title: Weight loss at a cost: Semaglutide and PYY3-36 aggravate pre-existing metabolic osteoporosis in female Wistar rats.
authors: Kloock S, Zytner P, Geiger N, Sequeira V, Schmitt-Böhrer AG, Felker J, Sarwar H, Weich A, Ignatius A, Fassnacht M, Haffner-Luntzer M, Dischinger U.
abstract: Incretin mimetics like semaglutide and peptide YY3-36 (PYY3-36) reduce appetite and body weight, however their individual and combined effects on bone in the setting of metabolic disease and associated osteoporosis (MetOP) lack mechanistic insights. Here, female Wistar rats were randomized to: [1] Healthy control, [2] MetOP-Saline, [3] MetOP-Sema, [4] MetOP-PYY, [5] MetOP-Sema+PYY. Animals in group 2-5 received a "Western diet" in combination with nitric oxide synthase inhibitor L-NAME to induce MetOP as previously described. Randomization to treatments occurred in week 9. After 16 weeks, femora were collected for micro-computed-tomography, histological analysis, RNA-seq, and qPCR. Serum was analyzed for bone turnover markers and steroid profiles (LC-MS/MS). Semaglutide alone and in combination with PYY3-36 significantly reduced body weight. Semaglutide induced a modest reduction in trabecular bone volume fraction (BV/TV), whereas PYY3-36 alone and in combination with semaglutide caused more pronounced trabecular deterioration, with the combination group exhibiting increased trabecular separation. Cortical bone parameters were unaffected. Osteoclast numbers were increased in the semaglutide and PYY3-36 groups. Gene expression analysis demonstrated only mild changes in femora of semaglutide-treated rats, while PYY3-36 treatment significantly upregulated angiogenesis- and extracellular matrix-associated genes. Collectively, these findings suggest that semaglutide modestly impairs bone health. PYY3-36 treatment led to deteriorated bone markers and increased resorption, potentially limiting its clinical application. Semaglutide and PYY3-36 in combination further aggravate bone loss in MetOP. These findings highlight the need to evaluate gut hormone-based weight loss strategies for long-term skeletal safety, especially in the vulnerable setting of pre-existing osteoporosis.

title: Two-year functional outcomes of kinematic versus mechanical alignment in primary total knee arthroplasty: a single-surgeon propensity-matched study in an Asian population.
authors: Neo BXB, Patil VV, Tay KD, Pang HN, Yeo SJ, Liow MHL.
abstract: Background Optimal coronal alignment in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains controversial, with kinematic alignment (KA) emerging as a patient-specific alternative to conventional mechanical alignment (MA). This study compared 2-year functional outcomes, patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) and complication rates between KA-TKA and MA-TKA in a propensity score-matched cohort. Methods This retrospective single-surgeon study included 1978 consecutive primary TKAs (KA: n = 921, 2018-2023; MA: n = 1057, 2010-2014). After excluding 76 revision TKAs, 1902 primary TKAs were eligible. A further 441 patients with incomplete follow-up were excluded (KA: n = 293, 33.1%; MA: n = 148, 14.6%), leaving 1461 patients who underwent propensity score matching. Following 1:1 nearest-neighbour propensity score matching for age, sex, body mass index (BMI) and baseline PROMs, 536 matched pairs (n = 1,072) were analysed. Outcomes included range of motion, Knee Society Knee and Function Scores (KSKS, KSFS), Oxford Knee Score (OKS), SF-36, MCID attainment, satisfaction, complications and revision rates at 6 months and 2 years. Results Both groups showed substantial postoperative improvement across all outcomes. At 6 months, KA achieved higher postoperative KSKS (86.7 versus 85.3, p Conclusions KA-TKA was associated with statistically higher scores in selected functional domains and comparable MCID attainment, patient satisfaction and revision-free survival at 2 years. These findings suggest KA is a feasible alignment strategy for primary TKA in the short term, although longer-term prospective data are required to confirm these associations.

title: The Clinical Outcome of a Fluoroscopy-Free "4-Step Cam Resection" Technique Compared With the Traditional Technique for Arthroscopic Treatment of Cam-Type Femoroacetabular Impingement.
authors: Li Y, Feng Z, Wang X.
abstract: Purpose To compare the clinical outcomes of the novel fluoroscopy-free "4-step cam resection" technique with the traditional cam resection method for treating cam-type FAI during hip arthroscopy. No established consensus exists on a standardized, reproducible technique that ensures complete cam resection without intraoperative fluoroscopy, and residual anterolateral cam deformity remains a leading cause of persistent impingement and revision surgery. The present study was therefore performed to determine whether the 4-step technique improves the completeness of cam resection compared with the conventional single-position technique. Methods Patients with symptomatic femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) who underwent the "4-step cam resection" technique between January 2021 and January 2022 were included. The 4-step intervention consisted of femoral head-neck osteoplasty performed sequentially with the hip placed in four positions: (i) 10° of flexion in maximal internal rotation; (ii) 10° of flexion in neutral rotation; (iii) 30° of flexion with rotation from internal to external; and (iv) 45° of flexion with rotation from internal to external. In the traditional technique, the cam lesion was resected with the hip in a single position of approximately 45° of flexion. No intraoperative fluoroscopy was used in either group. A historical control group extracted from our database was matched in a 1:1 ratio based on demographic and preoperative clinical variables. Outcomes were assessed using the Harris Hip Score (HHS), Hip Outcome Score (HOS), and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain. Radiographic measurements, including the lateral center-edge angle (LCEA) and alpha angle and gamma angle, were evaluated pre- and postoperatively. Results A total of 36 patients (36/40, 90.0%) in the study group (Group A, "4-step cam resection" technique) completed the final follow-up and 36 patients were matched as the control group (Group B, traditional technique). At a mean follow-up of 29 months, both groups demonstrated significant improvements in HOS, HHS, and VAS scores postoperatively (p Conclusion The "4-step cam resection" technique achieves comparable subjective outcomes compared with the traditional technique and is associated with a greater decrease of gamma angle, lower VAS score, and better HOS-Sports outcome.

title: Risk Factors for Diabetic Foot-Related Lower Extremity Amputation in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review.
authors: Eteuati J, Ntiamoah ME, Pitesa R, Mahadevan G, Hill AG.
abstract: Background Diabetic foot disease is a major cause of lower limb amputation (LLA) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where evidence on adjusted risk factors remains limited. This systematic review evaluates the risk factors for LLA and amputation-related mortality in diabetic foot disease across LMICs. Methods Embase, MEDLINE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (via Ovid), PubMed, and Scopus were searched from inception to March 2026. Studies of adults with diabetes in LMICs reporting LLA with adjusted effect estimates were included. Pooling of effect estimates was prespecified to require at least three comparable studies per domain. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale or AXIS. Results Sixteen studies (19,529 participants; 1604 amputation events) provided usable effect estimates; 12 reported adjusted estimates from multivariable models. No domain contained three or more comparable estimates, so quantitative synthesis was not undertaken. Osteomyelitis was independently associated with amputation in both studies assessing it (aOR 5.60, 95% CI 2.93-10.78; aOR 11.8, 95% CI 5.1-27.5). Peripheral arterial disease was associated with LLA in two of three studies using objective vascular assessment (aOR 2.80, 95% CI 1.52-5.11; aOR 3.23 per grade, 95% CI 2.68-3.89). Prior amputation was associated with LLA in two DFU cohorts reporting concordant estimates (aOR 2.86 and 3.08). Ulcer severity was associated with amputation in every study assessing it, using five different classification systems. Prolonged ulcer duration carried an adjusted odds ratio of 10.3 (95% CI 4.06-26.13), and each additional preoperative day was associated with a 9.3% increase in the odds of major amputation. Neuropathy showed no independent association of meaningful size in any adjusted analysis, and HbA1c was not associated in the largest adjusted DFU cohort analysis, although a smaller study with 10 outcome events reported a positive association. Conclusion Peripheral arterial disease, ulcer severity, osteomyelitis, prior amputation, and delayed access to care were associated with LLA in LMIC settings. Neither neuropathy nor HbA1c showed an independent association of meaningful size in adjusted analyses of established DFU cohorts. Prospective LMIC cohorts using standardized definitions are needed.

title: Radiographic Accuracy of Identifying Anterolateral Tibial Plafond Involvement in Pronation External Rotation Ankle Fractures.
authors: Lee CM, Oosten J, Allahverdian A, O'Hara S, Rockov ZA, Audet M, Earhart JS, Ewing BA, Weatherford BM, Garlich JM, Marecek GS.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the rate of anterolateral tibial plafond involvement in pronation-external rotation (PER) ankle fractures and analyze the accuracy of radiographs, using CT as the reference standard among fractures with paired imaging, in detecting anterolateral tibial plafond involvement, impaction, and predicting surgeons' stated intent to pursue direct visualization and articular reduction, as determined by surgeon assessment of the imaging findings. Methods Design: Multi-institutional retrospective chart review. Setting Two level 1 trauma centers in the United States. Patient selection criteria Adult patients operative treated PER ankle fractures (AO/OTA 44C) from 2020-2022 and adequate preoperative radiographs, defined as an AP, mortise and lateral view of the injured ankle were included. A subset of these patients also had preoperative CT imaging of the injured ankle and were therefore evaluated with both imaging modalities. Outcome measurements and comparisons All images were reviewed by 4 fellowship-trained orthopaedic trauma surgeons. For this study, anterolateral tibial plafond involvement was defined as the presence of any fracture line or impaction involving the anterolateral plafond, and impaction (a subset of involvement) as where the anterolateral plafond was crushed and depressed. A finding was considered present if at least 3 of the 4 reviewers indicated its presents on first-round responses. The rates of involvement and impaction were determined among all fractures based on radiographs alone, and separately among the subset of patients with paired radiographs and CT. Using CT as the gold standard, we determined the accuracy of radiographs and compared surgeons' stated intent to pursue direct visualization and articular reduction of the anterolateral plafond fracture before versus after review of CT imaging. Results Eighty-three PER ankle fractures were included (mean age 43.3 years [range, 17-89]; 63.9% male), of which 37 also had CT scans (mean age 39.2 years [range, 17-83]; 73.0% male). Among all 83 fractures, anterolateral tibial plafond involvement and impaction were identified on radiographs in 14.5% and 4.8% of cases, respectively. Among the 37 PER ankle fractures with both plain radiographs and CT scans, anterolateral plafond involvement was identified in 13.5% of radiographs versus 37.8% of CT scans (p=0.346) and impaction in 5.4% of radiographs versus 8.1% of CT scans (p=0.005). The diagnosis of impaction using plain radiographs was correct in 66.7% of fractures compared with CT, resulting in a sensitivity of 67%, specificity of 100%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 100%, and negative predictive value (NPV) of 97%. The diagnosis of anterolateral plafond involvement using plain radiographs had a sensitivity of 21%, specificity of 91%, PPV of 60%, and NPV of 66% compared with CT. Plain radiographs predicted surgeons' stated intent to pursue direct visualization and articular reduction in 66.7% of cases and had a PPV of 100% and NPV of 97%. Conclusions In PER ankle fractures, the rates of anterolateral tibial plafond involvement and impaction were 37.8% and 8.1% on CT, respectively. Plain radiographs demonstrated high specificity but limited sensitivity for identifying both impaction (67%) and involvement (21%). Because anterolateral plafond impaction was relatively uncommon in PER fractures, a CT obtained for this purpose alone would yield a positive finding in only a minority of cases; nonetheless, CT should be considered for PER ankle fractures more broadly, given that plain radiographs miss a meaningful proportion of both involvement and impaction and interobserver reliability of radiograph-based assessment was poor. Level of evidence Prognostic level III.

title: Promise or folly? Targeting the joint or the brain: evidence of peripheral and central treatments for osteoarthritis pain.
authors: Barroso J, Schnitzer TJ.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) pain emerges from the interaction between peripheral signals generated within and around the affected joint and the central neural systems that transform those signals into the experience of pain. We propose that the relative contribution of these components varies across patients and over time, placing OA pain along a mechanistic continuum rather than within a simple peripheral-central dichotomy. This continuum is reflected in treatment response. Interventions that reduce joint pathology or nociceptive signaling can produce substantial analgesia, and joint replacement relieves pain in most patients even after years of symptoms. Yet pain may persist despite technically successful surgery, while pharmacological, psychological, and neuromodulatory treatments benefit some patients but not others. These observations suggest that treatment effects cannot be understood solely by assigning therapies to peripheral or central categories. Rather, treatments perturb different elements of an interconnected pain system, and their effects may propagate beyond their immediate targets. Reducing joint-derived nociceptive input may reverse central adaptations, whereas interventions acting on neural, psychological, or modulatory processes may alter the amplification, salience, modulation, and experience of signals arising from the joint. OA is unusually informative among chronic pain conditions; because its principal peripheral source can often be treated directly-and, through arthroplasty, substantially removed-it provides a natural model for examining when chronic pain remains dependent on ongoing nociception and when additional mechanisms limit recovery. Variation in treatment response may consequently reveal not only whether an intervention works, but which processes are sustaining pain in a particular patient. In this review, we examine established and emerging treatments for OA pain as probes of an interconnected pain system. We consider how their mechanisms and clinical effects inform OA pain biology, explain treatment success and failure, and support more precise phenotyping, treatment selection, and therapeutic development.

title: Preserved tendon reflexes in a clinically suspected sensory-predominant GBS-spectrum disorder: a case report.
authors: Min X, Liu W, Wang R, Yang X, Ke T, Zhang W, Zhang G, Guo X, Xiao Y.
abstract: Background Guillain-Barré syndrome usually comes to clinical attention because of progressive weakness and reduced or absent tendon reflexes. Some patients, however, present mainly with sensory symptoms and still have preserved reflexes, making early diagnosis more difficult. Case presentation A 71-year-old Han Chinese man presented with distal paresthesia after an episode of diarrhea, and the symptoms became noticeably worse over the next 2 days. The sensory disturbance spread in a glove-and-sock pattern and was accompanied by heaviness in the legs, difficulty walking, and mild distal weakness. Neurological examination showed reduced distal superficial sensation, preserved tendon reflexes, and no pathological reflexes. Brain MRI showed no clinically relevant abnormality, and spinal MRI showed degenerative changes without a definite central lesion explaining the symptoms. Cerebrospinal fluid showed protein of 590 mg/L with a reported white blood cell count of 0.001 × 10 6 /L, a pattern compatible with albuminocytologic dissociation. Because nerve conduction studies and electromyography were not completed during hospitalization, the diagnosis remained a clinically suspected sensory-predominant disorder within the GBS spectrum rather than electrophysiologically confirmed classic GBS. Clinical notes recorded improvement during hospitalization, and the patient regained independent ambulation after receiving intravenous immunoglobulin alongside supportive and adjunctive therapies. At a telephone follow-up approximately 12 months later, he reported no recurrence; no objective follow-up examination was available. Conclusions In patients with acute symmetric distal sensory symptoms after a gastrointestinal illness, preserved tendon reflexes do not by themselves exclude a GBS-spectrum disorder. In this patient, the clinical course and cerebrospinal fluid findings supported consideration of that diagnosis, but the absence of electrophysiological testing precluded confirmation. This case emphasizes the diagnostic challenge posed by atypical sensory-predominant presentations and also highlights that, without electrophysiological confirmation, both subtype assignment and overall diagnostic certainty remain constrained.

title: Paired DXA and pQCT of bone parameters in a clinical paediatric population: A cluster analysis.
authors: Tan J, Hart NH, Chivers P, Rantalainen T, Barrat N, Beeson B, Siafarikas A.
abstract: Accurate assessment of bone health in paediatric clinical populations is needed for the prevention of both non-specific and condition-specific bone deficits. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), particularly "total body less head" (TBLH), is the preferred clinical measurement. However, peripheral quantitative computed tomography (pQCT) provides additional structural insights of value to a paediatric population. Criteria are needed to establish the value of pQCT beyond use in research settings. To determine the contributions of pQCT and DXA, we analysed data from 457 individuals from a Western Australian paediatric centre routinely employing joint DXA-pQCT imaging. Sex-specific cluster analysis was performed utilising DXA-TBLH BMD, pQCT (4% and 66% arm and leg volumetric density), age and height to define clinical phenotypes and guide decision making on adding pQCT to BMD analyses. Results showed DXA and pQCT measurements were positively correlated, particularly at the 4% site. Cluster analysis showed two clusters with lower bone density and higher fracture frequency characterised by malabsorption and bone mineral metabolism conditions in females, and bone mineral metabolism and neuromuscular conditions in males. DXA and pQCT variation was greatest in these clusters, with DXA being lower. Females showed greater variability between DXA and pQCT, with height as an influencing factor. These findings reinforce the utility of combined DXA and pQCT in paediatric bone health assessment particularly in high-risk groups.

title: One-Stage Posterior-to-Anterior Ankle Arthroscopy Using a Single Operative Setup and Patient Repositioning Technique: A Technical Note.
authors: Paquot J, Roche D, Lopes R.
abstract: This technical note describes a 1-stage arthroscopic technique for the management of combined posterior and anterior ankle pathology that preserves standard patient positioning while reducing operative time and material costs. The procedure begins with posterior ankle arthroscopy performed in the prone position using standard posterior portals. After treatment of the posterior lesions, the patient is carefully repositioned to the supine position without redraping or changing instrumentation. The same sterile surgical field, operating table, and arthroscopic instruments are maintained throughout the procedure. Anterior ankle arthroscopy is then performed using standard anterior portals. Strict coordination between the surgical and anesthesia teams ensures safe patient repositioning while preserving sterility. This 1-stage technique allows arthroscopic treatment of combined anterior and posterior ankle pathology using familiar prone and supine positioning. By avoiding redraping and the use of duplicate sterile instrumentation, it optimizes surgical workflow, reduces operative time, and decreases material costs while providing a reproducible approach.

title: Modeling bone abnormalities in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Skeletal phenotypes, glucocorticoid responses, and translational considerations.
authors: Barroso E, Li J, Wang L, Li H.
abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is increasingly recognized as a multisystem disorder in which skeletal fragility is one of the major sources of morbidity. Bone deficits arise before loss of ambulation and in glucocorticoid-naïve patients, indicating that reduced mechanical loading and steroid toxicity are important but incomplete explanations. Animal models provide an opportunity to study the skeletal consequences of dystrophin deficiency, muscle degeneration, altered muscle-bone signaling, impaired growth, and glucocorticoid exposure. However, the bone phenotype varies markedly among models. The widely used C57BL/10-mdx mouse has a mild muscle phenotype and may exhibit preserved or increased cortical indices during growth, whereas DBA/2 J-mdx mice show more consistent growth and skeletal impairment. Compound murine models can intensify muscle disease but do not necessarily recapitulate human skeletal development. Dystrophin-deficient rats develop age-related trabecular deterioration, and golden retriever muscular dystrophy dogs show bone changes that track muscle structure and function, although skeletal characterization in large-animal models remains sparse. Glucocorticoid-treated mdx mice reproduce clinically relevant growth suppression, cortical thinning, suppressed bone formation, and reduced mechanical quality while retaining treatment-related gains in muscle performance. These models have supported proof-of-concept studies of bisphosphonates, intermittent parathyroid hormone, growth hormone, and mitochondrial peptides. This review summarizes and compares skeletal phenotypes across DMD models, evaluates responses to glucocorticoids, identifies methodological factors that explain discordant findings, and proposes a translational framework for incorporating bone outcomes into DMD therapeutic development.

title: Mobile radiation shielding device for scatter dose reduction during portable radiography in an orthopedic ward.
authors: Cheewakul J, Ina N, Marshall SK, Chaichulee S.
abstract: Portable radiography in orthopedic wards exposes healthcare professionals and adjacent patients to scatter radiation in open, shared clinical environments. In crowded wards, maintaining an optimal distance or clearing the area during exposure is often impractical. This study designed, constructed, and evaluated a foldable mobile radiation shielding system comprising two three-panel units, each with a chromed steel frame (210 × 180 cm) with 0.6-mm nominal lead sheets covered by a vinyl outer layer (66 × 100 cm) per panel, mounted on wheeled castors for bedside deployment. The two units were deployed together, one along each lateral side of the bed. Scatter dose rates were measured using an radiation survey meter and a portable X-ray unit during phantom radiography across common orthopedic projections at eight angular positions (0°-315° in 45° increments) and five distances (50-250 cm). The two-unit configuration achieved a median scatter dose reduction of 94.1% (IQR: 88.0%-97.7%; Wilcoxon W = 51,360, N = 320, p < 0.001). Reductions were broadly consistent across tube voltages (65-85 kVp) and remained substantial across all measurement distances (84.3%-89.6% across 50-250 cm), but varied significantly by angular position, with the highest reduction at 90° (mean 96.91%) and the lowest reductions recorded at 0° (mean 54.02%) and 180° (mean 75.69%). These two directions represented the open axial ends of the setup and were not directly covered by the side-mounted shielding panels. Under a representative high-workload scenario, the two-unit configuration reduced estimated annual occupational doses across all projections, with all post-shielding means remaining well below the average annual occupational dose limit of 20 mSv/year. User feedback was more favorable among radiologic technologists (mean 4.80/5) than among orthopedic ward nurses (mean 3.67/5). The two-unit configuration showed substantial scatter reduction and may serve as an additional protective measure during portable radiography in orthopedic ward settings, with positioning guidance required to maximize protection at clinically relevant angular locations.

title: Longitudinal changes in infrapatellar fat pad fibrosis following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a retrospective cohort study.
authors: Takei S, Imoo Y, Onuma H, Mammoto T, Kobayashi H.
abstract: Background Infrapatellar fat pad (IFP) fibrosis is implicated in anterior knee pain, limited range of motion (ROM), and posttraumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). However, its precise longitudinal progression remains unclear. This study aimed to elucidate the dynamic changes in IFP fibrosis from preoperative to 12 months post-ACLR using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Methods We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients who underwent anatomic double-bundle ACLR using autologous hamstring tendon grafts. IFP fibrosis was semiquantitatively graded (grades 0-5) using proton density-weighted (PDW) sagittal MR images obtained preoperatively and at 6 and 12 months postoperatively. Patients were categorized into mild (grades 0-3) and severe (grades 4-5) IFP fibrosis groups. Temporal changes in the proportion of the severe group across the three time points were evaluated using Cochran's Q test, followed by the Bonferroni-corrected McNemar test for pairwise comparisons. Results Of 558 consecutive cases screened, 169 patients (mean age, 23.9 years) were included in the final analysis. The proportion of patients classified into the severe fibrosis group significantly changed over time (Cochran's Q test, χ 2 (2) = 24.0, p Conclusions IFP fibrosis is an early and persistent pathological event following ACLR and is established primarily within the first 6 postoperative months. This early onset suggests a critical time window for targeted interventions to mitigate inflammation and prevent the irreversible establishment of IFP fibrosis, providing a basis to investigate the long-term PTOA risk.

title: Locking-compression plate (LCP) or angled blade plates (ABP) for femoral osteotomies in children with spastic cerebral palsy (CP) gross motor function classification system (GMFCS) III, IV, and V.
authors: Zaldivar B, Ramirez-Schneider LC, Balcázar-Muñoz EI, Arango-Piedrahita N, Macallister-Diaz JN, Mafla-Gómez M, Garcia-Rueda MF.
abstract: Purpose To compare hardware-related complications and intraoperative variables between locking compression plates (LCP) and angled blade plates (ABP) used for proximal and/or distal femoral osteotomies in patients with spastic cerebral palsy (CP) classified as Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) III-V. Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted, including patients younger than 18 years with spastic CP (GMFCS III-V) who underwent proximal and/or distal femoral osteotomies between 2015 and 2022. Demographic variables, plate type, operative time, blood loss, and hardware-related complications (implant failure, peri-implant fracture, and non-union) were recorded. Comparisons between groups were performed using generalized linear mixed-effects models to account for patients with multiple procedures. Results A total of 285 patients were included, with a mean follow-up of 23 months. Twenty-six complications occurred in 24 patients: 12 in the LCP group (4.9%) and 14 in the ABP group (3.6%). No significant differences were observed in overall complication rates between plate types for femoral osteotomies. All peri-implant fractures, implant failures, and non-unions at the distal femur were with ABP. LCP fixation was associated with longer operative time and greater blood loss. Conclusions LCP and ABP demonstrate comparable hardware-related complication rates in children with CP undergoing femoral osteotomies. Recommendations on hardware selection for distal femoral osteotomy warrant larger studies in non-ambulatory patients. Significance of findings Proximal femoral osteotomies in patients with CP can be performed with either hardware, with comparable complication rates; however, the focus of future studies should be on plate types for the distal femur.

title: Juvenile Paget disease due to osteoprotegerin deficiency: clinical, biochemical, and radiographic findings during zoledronate therapy in four children.
authors: Canoruc Emet D, Celık NB, Oguz B, Unsal Y, Simsek Kiper PO, Ozon A, Gonc N.
abstract: We report extended pediatric follow-up outcomes of zoledronic acid therapy in four children with TNFRSF11B related juvenile Paget disease. In the context of limited pediatric long-term data, our observations indicate favorable growth, mobility, and skeletal outcomes when therapy is initiated early and adjusted according to clinical course. Background Juvenile Paget's Disease (JPD) is an ultra-rare metabolic bone disorder associated with accelerated bone turnover, skeletal deformities, fractures, bone pain, sensorineural hearing loss and growth impairment. Although bisphosphonates are the main therapeutic option, there are no established guidelines regarding drug choice, dosage, and dosing frequency. Objective To describe the clinical, biochemical, and radiological findings observed during extended pediatric follow-up of children with TNFRSF11B related JPD treated with zoledronate (ZOL), and to provide observational evidence that may contribute to treatment strategies. Methods The study included four children: three siblings with severe JPD, carrying homozygous exon 2-5 TNFRSF11B deletion; and one child with intermediate JPD, carrying homozygous frameshift variant. All received bisphosphonates from diagnosis, initially Pamidronate (PMD) with a switch to ZOL when response was inadequate. Follow-up durations ranged from 6 to 14 years. Clinical findings, bone pain, growth and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity were evaluated every three months, and imaging was performed annually. Results Following PMD treatment, bone pain and ALP activity improved partially, however ALP normalized only after ZOL treatment. Despite normal ALP activity, some patients had recurrent bone pain and fractures during ZOL treatment, leading to treatment intensification. Early initiation of ZOL, with increased dose and frequency, especially during rapid growth, resulted in marked clinical improvement and improvement in growth parameters. Nevertheless, definitive adult height outcomes remain unavailable and profound sensorineural hearing loss was not prevented. ZOL also produced significant radiological improvements, including better trabecular structure, corticomedullary differentiation, diaphyseal modeling, and reduced femoral bowing. In contrast, delayed treatment and poor adherence were associated with worse skeletal outcomes. Conclusion Children with JPD experienced marked clinical, skeletal and linear growth improvement with early and adequate ZOL therapy. ZOL dosing should be guided not only by ALP activity but also by growth monitoring, skeletal findings, bone pain, fracture occurrence, and mobility.

title: Hypertension dissociates radiographic and symptomatic progression in a male rat model of post-traumatic osteoarthritis.
authors: Yip SL, Zhang Y, Zhang L, Lu X, Yau SY, Dong C, Au MT, Wen C.
abstract: Objective This study investigated the impact of hypertension on the relationship between structural damage and pain sensitivity in a post-traumatic osteoarthritis (OA) rat model, and explored possible neurovascular factor underlying radiographic-symptomatic dissociation in OA. Method The 6-month-old male rats underwent anterior cruciate ligament transection (ACLT) to induce post-traumatic OA in spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) and normotensive Wistar Kyoto (WKY) inbred strains. Joint structural changes were assessed via micro-CT and histology at 8 weeks post-surgery. Mechanical sensitivity and motor function were longitudinally monitored at baseline, 4-week and 8-week post-surgery. Based on lumbar dorsal root ganglia (DRG) RNA sequencing results, in vivo calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) replenishment experiment was performed for proof-of-concept. Results SHR exhibited comparable articular cartilage degradation and subchondral bone loss to WKY following ACLT surgery. Strain-specific differences in surgical responses were confined specifically to mechanical pain processing, where WKY developed marked post-traumatic mechanical hypersensitivity (ACLT week 0 vs 8: 41.48 ± 15.76 gf vs 26.14 ± 9.404 gf; 95% CI: 0.3918-30.27, p = 0.0436), whereas SHR maintained hypoalgesia (ACLT week 0 vs 8: 31.88 ± 6.482 gf vs 42.73 ± 7.056 gf; 95% CI: -18.94 to -2.766, p = 0.0092), indicating a dissociation between the severity of joint damage and pain sensitivity. DRG transcriptomic analysis revealed the downregulation of CGRP-mediated nociceptive signalling in hypertensive rats. Exogenous CGRP replenishment partially restored mechanical sensitivity in SHR without affecting joint structural integrity or affective and cognitive behaviour. Conclusion Hypertension decouples structural damage from mechanical sensitivity in male rats with post-traumatic OA. While joint degradation progresses to a comparable extent in both strains, hypertensive rats maintain higher pain thresholds despite severe structural breakdown, with CGRP as a plausible neurovascular factor underlying this phenomenon.

title: Feasibility of patient-reported outcomes measurement information system (PROMIS) computerized adaptive tests in patients receiving physical therapy: A mixed-methods study.
authors: Haan EA, Doomen A, Wittink H, Kiers H, Arensman RM, Terwee CB.
abstract: Introduction Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) are widely used in physical therapy, but both clinicians and patients report respondent burden due to the number and the length of existing instruments. PROMIS® Computerized Adaptive Tests (CATs) may reduce this burden, yet their feasibility in primary care physical therapy is unknown. This study examined the feasibility of Dutch-Flemish PROMIS CATs in patients with musculoskeletal (MSK) disorders of the spine and upper extremity. Methods We conducted a mixed-methods concurrent triangulation study in 14 physical therapy practices where PROMIS CATs were integrated into the electronic health record system and administered during routine care. A survey assessed physical therapists' experiences and opinions regarding acceptability, demand, practicality, and implementation. Semi-structured interviews with physical therapists and patients further explored these domains. Survey data were analyzed descriptively, and interview transcripts were thematically analyzed by two independent researchers. Results Twenty-five physical therapists completed the survey. Ten physical therapists and nine patients participated in interviews. Most physical therapists reported that PROMIS CATs were easy to use and facilitated focused discussions about symptoms and functioning. Patients described CATs as quick to complete and relevant to their condition and were willing to complete PROMs if results were used in consultations. Reported barriers included the simultaneous use of legacy PROMs (patients), difficulties using the online portal, and uncertainty about interpreting CAT scores (therapists). Some participants reported that certain CAT items felt less relevant and expressed a desire to view individual item responses. Conclusions PROMIS CATs are considered feasible to implement in physical therapy practice and are generally experienced as acceptable, efficient, and clinically useful. Future implementation should focus on phasing out legacy PROMs to reduce respondent burden, improving skills in score interpretation, ensuring financial reimbursement for use, incorporating PROMIS into clinical guidelines, and evaluating additional PROMIS domains relevant to primary care physical therapy.

title: Explainable deep learning localizes age-discriminative candidate regions on hand radiographs of adult women.
authors: Jang HS, Cho J, Kim DH, Kim MG, Choi D, Lee SH, Park C, Kim YK, Kang HJ, Ye JC.
abstract: Objective To determine whether deep learning can distinguish younger from older adult women on hand radiographs and to identify candidate anatomical regions for age-group discrimination using explainable artificial intelligence and quantitative cortical measurements. Materials and methods This retrospective, single-center, exploratory study included 2,221 women sampled consecutively within each age group during 2020-2023 (1,134 aged 20-45 and 1,087 aged 55-80 years at radiography). Patients contributed one posteroanterior radiograph and were assigned to mutually exclusive training, validation, or test sets. Five architectures were evaluated on the same 334 held-out test radiographs (171 younger; 163 older), with performance averaged across five random-seed runs. DenseNet121 was selected by descriptive comparison for gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) and ray-based analyses with retraining. Manual cortical measurements of test radiographs yielded metacarpal and proximal phalangeal indices for candidate rays identified by Grad-CAM. Results DenseNet121 achieved the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC, 0.996; 95% CI, 0.992-0.999). Grad-CAM showed prominent activation around the third proximal phalanx, with additional activation in the second and fourth rays. Performance remained high after ray masking; the third-ray-only model achieved the highest mean accuracy among single-ray models. The third proximal phalangeal index had the highest AUC among the six indices (0.956; 95% CI, 0.937-0.976). Conclusion Grad-CAM, ray-based analyses, and quantitative cortical measurements support the third proximal phalanx as an anatomically interpretable candidate region for age-group discrimination in adult women. Integrating explainable artificial intelligence with quantitative radiographic assessment provides an exploratory workflow for investigating hand skeletal aging, with potential relevance to broader musculoskeletal imaging research.

title: Does Perineural Dexamethasone Prolong the Time to First Rescue Opioid Analgesia Compared With Intravenous Dexamethasone in Pediatric Hip Surgery? A Randomized Blinded Trial.
authors: Reysner T, Shadi M, Janusz P, Musielak B, Idzior M, Wieczorowska-Tobis K, Reysner M.
abstract: Background The pericapsular nerve group (PENG) block is an increasingly utilized regional anesthesia technique for pediatric hip surgery.
