Dexamethasone prolongs the duration of peripheral nerve blocks and can be administered either intravenously or perineurally; however, the comparative pediatric evidence on postoperative analgesia and metabolic effects with these two routes is limited. Questions/purposes (1) Does perineural dexamethasone prolong the time to first rescue opioid analgesia compared with intravenous dexamethasone when used as an adjunct to PENG block in pediatric hip surgery? (2) Does perineural dexamethasone reduce postoperative opioid consumption and pain intensity? (3) Does the route of dexamethasone administration influence postoperative inflammatory markers and blood glucose levels? (4) Is perineural dexamethasone associated with an increased risk of neurologic complications? Methods This randomized, blinded trial was conducted at a single urban tertiary university referral center in Poznań, Poland, providing subspecialty pediatric orthopaedic care. Parents and caregivers, treating anesthesiologists, surgeons, and outcome assessors were unaware of group allocation. Between February 2025 and March 2026, we assessed 72 children scheduled for elective reconstructive hip surgery. Children age 3 months to 6 years with developmental dysplasia of the hip or neurogenic hip displacement associated with cerebral palsy were considered potentially eligible. Of the 72 children assessed, 92% (66) met the eligibility criteria. Nine percent (6 of 66) of these children were not enrolled because four families declined participation and two declined regional anesthesia. The remaining 83% (60 of 72) were randomized. No participants were lost during the 48-hour in-hospital follow-up or had incomplete outcome data, and all 60 were included in the analysis. The perineural and intravenous groups had mean ± SD ages of 4.8 ± 1.2 and 5.2 ± 1.1 years, respectively; 47% (14 of 30) and 50% (15 of 30) were boys, and 70% (21 of 30) and 73% (22 of 30) had developmental dysplasia of the hip. The remaining children had neurogenic hip displacement associated with cerebral palsy. There were no clinically important between-group differences in these baseline characteristics. All patients received standardized spinal anesthesia and multimodal postoperative analgesia consisting of paracetamol 15 mg/kg and metamizole 15 mg/kg every 6 hours, ibuprofen 10 mg/kg every 8 hours, and rescue nalbuphine 0.1 mg/kg for Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability (FLACC) scores of ≥ 4. The primary endpoint was time to first rescue opioid analgesia within 48 hours. Secondary endpoints included total opioid consumption, postoperative pain scores, inflammatory markers (neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio [NLR] and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio [PLR]), blood glucose levels, and peripheral nerve injury assessed at 12, 24, and 48 hours. Results We found no difference between the perineural and intravenous dexamethasone groups in time to first rescue opioid analgesia after adjustment for age, body weight, and duration of surgery (HR 0.56 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.28 to 1.08]; p = 0.08). Perineural dexamethasone reduced total opioid consumption during the first 48 postoperative hours (mean ± SD 0.131 ± 0.048 versus 0.225 ± 0.053 mg/kg morphine milligram equivalents (MMEs), mean difference -0.095 mg/kg [95% CI -0.121 to -0.068]; p Conclusion After adjustment for age, body weight, and duration of surgery, we found no difference between perineural and intravenous dexamethasone in time to first rescue opioid analgesia. Perineural dexamethasone was associated with lower opioid consumption and lower early postoperative blood glucose levels. Larger multicenter studies are needed to evaluate these findings in pediatric regional anesthesia. Level of evidence Level I, therapeutic study.

title: CORR Insights®: What Are the Oncologic Outcomes of Patients With Osteosarcoma and Venous Tumor Thrombi Managed by an Aggressive Multidisciplinary Approach of Chemotherapy and Surgical Resection?
authors: Smolle MA.

title: Arthroscopic Double-Bundle Posterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using Superficial Quadriceps and Hamstring Autografts With All-Suspensory Fixation.
authors: Chou HI, Wu SC, Liu LL, Lee KT.
abstract: Double-bundle posterior cruciate ligament reconstruction provides superior posterior stability and knee kinematics compared with single-bundle techniques but remains technically challenging regarding graft management and fixation. Several strategies can be implemented to obtain improved outcomes while mitigating complications, including techniques for optimizing arthroscopic visualization, graft preparation, fixation methods, tensioning, and tunnel positioning. In this technical note, we present a double-bundle posterior cruciate ligament reconstruction technique using a 4-stranded superficial quadriceps tendon autograft for the anterolateral bundle and a 4-stranded hamstring tendon autograft for the posteromedial bundle with all-suspensory fixation and internal brace augmentation. The objective of this technique is to provide robust biomechanical stability to accurately restore native knee kinematics.

title: Arthroscopic Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using Iliotibial Band Autograft With Bone Block.
authors: Huang D, Weng W, Wang J, Ye Z, Wang G, Chen X, Huang J.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction is the first-line treatment for ACL injury, whereas existing autologous grafts each have inherent limitations. This study describes the use of an iliotibial band (ITB) graft with a bone block for ACL reconstruction, designed as a femoral bone block combined with tibial tendon configuration, which precisely matches the anatomical attachment and biomechanical loading characteristics of the native ACL. The surgery is performed through arthroscopic evaluation, harvesting and weaving of the ITB with a bone block, creation of femoral and tibial bone tunnels, and graft introduction and fixation. This graft features the advantage of easy harvesting of the ITB, whereas the femoral bone column allows for rapid bone-to-bone healing, enhances stability within the femoral tunnel, and reduces the risk of tunnel widening and femoral-sided rerupture. Tibial-sided tendon fixation avoids excessive tibial tunnel enlargement and simplifies surgical steps. Arthroscopic ACL reconstruction using the ITB with bone block is technically straightforward and provides high initial stability. It offers another graft option for both primary treatment of ACL injury and revision surgery after failed reconstructions and is particularly suitable for patients with multiple previous tendon harvests from the same knee or those requiring large-diameter grafts because of bone tunnel enlargement.

title: Alcohol Consumption as a Predictor of Outcomes in Open Carpal Tunnel Release Surgery: A Systematic Review.
authors: He E, Mikhael MAS, Videon L, Crispin MD.
abstract: Background Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is a common peripheral nerve entrapment; open carpal tunnel release (OCTR) surgery is the gold standard surgical technique. Pre-operative alcohol consumption is a known predictive factor of polyneuropathy and post-operative outcomes. The aim is to investigate the influence of alcohol consumption on OCTR surgery outcomes. Methods A systematic review registered with PROSPERO was performed using PRISMA guidelines. Study selection included English language randomised controlled trials, cohort longitudinal studies and case series on adults published within a 10-year period (2015-2025). ROBINS-I was utilised for a risk of bias assessment. Results Eight studies were eligible as per the criteria. There is little to no evidence which suggests pre-operative alcohol consumption impacts OCTR post-operative outcomes (p = 0.60); depression (p = 0.46), Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire (BCTQ) (p = 0.16), palmar pain (p = 0.27), wound healing disturbance (p = 0.85), numbness (p = 1.00), pain (p = 0.50), Kelly Score (p = 1.00) and return to work (p = 0.67). There is varying evidence associating pre-operative alcohol consumption with post-operative infection; one study reported little to no evidence (p = 0.39) and another reported very strong evidence (p Conclusion There is little to no evidence that alcohol consumption impacts outcomes in patients undergoing OCTR surgery. Further studies should investigate the impact of pre-operative alcohol consumption on post-operative infection risk and revision surgery outcomes.

title: What Are the Oncologic Outcomes of Patients With Osteosarcoma and Venous Tumor Thrombi Managed by an Aggressive Multidisciplinary Approach of Chemotherapy and Surgical Resection?
authors: Liang H, Qi F, Liu K, Du Z, Sun X, Guo W, Wang J, Yang Y.
abstract: Background Macroscopic venous tumor thrombus (VTT) is a rare but aggressive manifestation of osteosarcoma that poses substantial challenges for both surgical management and systemic disease control. Our previous work characterized its frequency, radiographic features, and adverse prognostic association, particularly in pelvic osteosarcoma; however, surgical management was heterogeneous. The patient-level outcomes achieved after a standardized multidisciplinary treatment approach and the association between VTT resection strategy and postoperative oncologic outcomes remain unclear. Questions/purposes (1) What were the oncologic outcomes of patients with osteosarcoma with macroscopic VTT treated under a standardized treatment algorithm incorporating aggressive surgical resection? (2) Did the choice of VTT resection strategy affect oncologic outcomes? Methods We screened the records of 39 patients with treatment-naive osteosarcoma and macroscopic VTT identified on imaging who were treated according to a standardized multimodal treatment algorithm between 2019 and 2024. This algorithm consisted of standardized multimodal imaging at diagnosis to detect and characterize VTT. After biopsy confirmation, patients received four-agent neoadjuvant chemotherapy, preoperative inferior vena cava filter placement when technically feasible, and repeat imaging to reassess the resectability of both the primary tumor and VTT. Surgery was undertaken only when both lesions were considered resectable. VTT involving peripheral venous branches or completely occluded and enlarged major veins was managed with en bloc venous resection, whereas thrombectomy was performed for VTT involving patent or partially patent major veins. Postoperative chemotherapy was initiated 2 to 3 weeks after surgery. After excluding one patient without pathologic confirmation of the macroscopic VTT, two patients in whom en bloc resection of the primary tumor was not achieved, and seven patients who did not receive postoperative chemotherapy, 29 patients were included in this retrospective analysis. The study population was young (mean ± SD age 16 ± 7 years), with a slight male predominance (17 of 29 patients), and primary tumors were distributed between the extremities (16 of 29) and pelvis (13 of 29). More than half of the patients presented with metastatic disease (16 of 29), most VTTs involved major venous trunks (22 of 29), and 20 of 29 patients had Results Patients treated under the standardized algorithm had limited durable disease control, with disease progression in 26 of 29 patients, a median PFS of 7 months (95% confidence interval [CI] 0 to 16), and an estimated 2-year OS of 60%. Patients with localized disease had longer PFS (median 13 months [95% CI 8 to 19] versus 5 months [95% CI 4 to 5]; p = 0.046) and MPFS (median 13 months [95% CI 8 to 19] versus 4.6 months [95% CI 4 to 5]; p = 0.04) than those with metastatic disease. There were no differences in OS (not reached versus median 32 months [95% CI 10 to 54]; p = 0.52), PFS (median 11 months [95% CI 0 to 31] versus 6 months [95% CI 3 to 9]; p = 0.62), LRFS (median 21 months [95% CI 9 to 34] versus 61 months [95% CI 2 to 120]; p = 0.54), and MPFS (median 13 months [95% CI 0.3 to 25] versus 8 months [95% CI 3 to 13]; p = 0.24) between patients who had thrombectomy versus en bloc venous resection. Conclusion Despite a standardized multidisciplinary approach incorporating perioperative chemotherapy and aggressive resection of both the primary tumor and macroscopic VTT, progression remained frequent, and durable disease control was uncommon. Among these 29 selected patients, VTT resection strategy-thrombectomy versus en bloc venous resection-was not detectably associated with oncologic outcomes, although the two groups were not directly comparable. Surgeons should recognize that osteosarcoma with macroscopic VTT is a rare, highly aggressive condition for which current treatment modalities seldom achieve a cure and should carefully balance the potential oncologic benefit of aggressive surgery against its morbidity. Future prospective multicenter studies should refine patient-level selection criteria and directly evaluate the incorporation of adjuvant radiotherapy into this standardized treatment algorithm. Novel systemic therapies should also be investigated to improve control of metastatic and rapidly progressive disease. Level of evidence Level III, therapeutic study.

title: Updates on Low Energy Availability in Athletes: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and the Female or Male Athlete Triad.
authors: Kussman A, Leonard N, Fahy K.
abstract: Purpose of review This paper evaluates the latest literature on low energy availability (LEA) in athletes, which is the basis for the clinical conditions known as the Female Athlete Triad, Male Athlete Triad, and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). It explores how these different conditions are related, and how the clinician can approach screening, diagnosis, and management of LEA in athletes. Recent findings Within the past five years the Male Athlete Triad Consensus Statements were published in 2021, expanding upon knowledge regarding LEA in the Female Athlete Triad and applying this to the male population. Additionally, there has been an important update to the REDs model and a new clinical assessment tool (CAT2) published in 2023. This is based on new research into the different physiologic and psychologic sequelae of LEA. This has sparked additional discussion regarding the diagnosis, management, and prevention of LEA. The consequences of LEA can be severe, and can affect multiple different organ systems. Treatment should ideally involve a multidisciplinary team consisting of a physician, dietitian, and mental health provider, but may also include additional professionals such as athletic trainers, physical therapists, physiologists, other medical specialists, or other members of the athlete support system (including family and coaches). The mainstay of management remains optimizing energy availability (EA) through improving macro and micronutrient intake, and also requires addressing some of the more common sequelae of LEA. Prevention largely focuses on educational efforts and fostering healthy environments, particularly when discussing weight, body composition, and performance.

title: Translation and cultural adaptation of the Oxford Shoulder Score to Swedish and validation of a new 7-day recall version in patients with a proximal humerus fracture.
authors: Lundin PC, Sundh TFD, Adolfsson LE, Björnsson Hallgren HC.
abstract: Background and purpose The Oxford Shoulder Score (OSS) is a widely applied patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) designed to assess function and pain in individuals with shoulder disorders. We primarily aimed to evaluate a translated and culturally adapted Swedish version of the original OSS and secondarily to evaluate a version with a 7-day recall period, intended for rapidly changing conditions such as the early phase following fractures and surgeries. Methods The OSS was translated according to Beaton's guidelines for cross-cultural adaptation. 246 patients with a nonoperatively treated proximal humerus fracture completed the Swedish OSS and the QuickDASH at 1 week (T1, 7-day recall period), 3 months (T2, 7-day recall period), and 12 months (T3, 4-week recall period). Results Convergent validity between OSS and QuickDASH (Spearmans's rho) was rs -0.75 (95% confidence interval [CI] -0.80 to -0.68) at T1, -0.88 (CI -0.91 to -0.84) at T2, and -0.86 (CI -0.90 to -0.81) at T3. Responsiveness for change scores (T2-T1) was -0.77 (CI -0.82 to -0.70) and (T3-T2) -0.80 (CI -0.85 to -0.74). Internal consistency for the respective domains was for pain at T1 0.73 (CI 0.68-0.78), at T2 0.84 (CI 0.80-0.87), at T3 0.87 (CI 0.84-0.89), and for function at T1 0.74 (CI 0.68-0.78), at T2 0.88 (CI 0.86-0.90), at T3 0.91 (CI 0.89-0.92). Intra-rater reliability was ICC = 0.94 (CI 0.90-0.96) between T3 and 2 weeks later. Conclusion The Swedish translation of the OSS demonstrated excellent measurement properties. The 7-day recall version demonstrated equivalent good validity, responsiveness, and reliability and seems valuable for monitoring fresh injuries such as proximal humerus fractures.

title: The relationship between ankle dorsiflexion range of motion and reactive postural control mechanisms in response to anterior perturbations.
authors: Pashaei M, Ramezanloo H, Hatefi M.
abstract: Adequate ankle dorsiflexion range of motion (DF-ROM) is essential for generating sufficient corrective torque during an ankle strategy; however, limitations in dorsiflexion may mechanically constrain this response, potentially leading to earlier reliance on hip or stepping strategies. Although indirect evidence links dorsiflexion capacity to dynamic balance performance, it remains unclear whether restricted dorsiflexion influences the selection of reactive postural control strategies in healthy young adults. Twenty active male participants were recruited for this study. Ankle DF-ROM was measured via the weight-bearing lunge test and categorized as either normal (≥20°) or restricted (<20°). Reactive postural control was assessed in response to a single unexpected anterior perturbation administered by a custom-engineered movable platform, with the perturbation load normalized to participants' body mass. Sagittal-plane kinematics were recorded at 60 Hz and independently evaluated by two blinded raters to classify the initial balance recovery response into ankle, hip, or stepping strategies based on established criteria. Statistical analysis revealed no significant association between ankle DF-ROM category and the type of reactive postural control strategy employed following anterior perturbations. Pearson's chi-square test indicated no significant relationship between dorsiflexion status and balance strategy selection (χ2(2) = 0.826, p = 0.662). Due to low expected cell counts, Fisher's exact test was also conducted, corroborating the absence of a significant association (two-sided p = 0.835). The distribution of postural strategies did not differ substantially between participants with normal and restricted dorsiflexion. In healthy young adults exposed to a standardized anterior perturbation, ankle DF-ROM was not independently associated with reactive postural strategy selection. These findings suggest that the postural demands imposed by the perturbation may have contributed to the predominance of stepping responses and may have reduced the sensitivity to detect an influence of ankle mobility on strategy selection.

title: The impact of functional sagittal pelvic tilt on CT-based hip dysplasia diagnostics in adults: a cross-sectional 3D simulation study.
authors: Hüsken MFT, Lissendorp F, Magré J, Willemsen K, Weinans H, Sakkers R, Nasrabadi J, Arbabi V, Bekkers J, Ten Ham AM, Schlösser TPC, Van der Wal BCH.
abstract: Background and purpose Accurate acetabular coverage assessment is essential for diagnosing adult hip dysplasia. Computed tomography (CT) best evaluates 3-dimensional acetabular morphology but is typically acquired supine, while symptoms arise during weightbearing. This study evaluates how sagittal pelvic tilt affects CT-based acetabular parameters in adults with hip dysplasia and whether pelvic tilt causes clinically relevant measurement changes. Methods 3D-models from supine CT of 29 adults with hip dysplasia (lateral center-edge angle (LCEA) ≤ 25°) yielded 39 affected hips. LCEA, inclination (AI), anterior/posterior/horizontal acetabular sector angles (AASA, PASA, HASA), acetabular version (AV), extrusion index (EI), and total and loadbearing coverage were measured. Pelvic tilt was simulated in 5° increments from 30° anterior to 30° posterior around the hip centers and parameters were remeasured in each position. Differences Results Median supine LCEA was 21°, AI 50°, AASA 43°. Across -30° to +30° tilt, AASA/loadbearing coverage decreased, PASA/AV increased, LCEA/EI showed parabolic patterns, and HASA/total coverage remained stable. From supine to simulated upright, paired mean differences were: LCEA -1° (95% confidence interval [CI] -2 to 0), AASA -4° (CI -5 to -3), PASA +4° (CI 4 to 5), HASA 0° (CI -1 to 1), AV +4° (CI 3 to 4), AI +1° (CI -1 to 3), EI +2% (CI 0 to 4), total coverage 0% (CI 0 to 0), and loadbearing coverage -2% (CI -2 to -2). Conclusion Functional sagittal pelvic tilt resulted in generally small changes in CT-based acetabular measurements in dysplastic hips, which may be clinically relevant in borderline cases, particularly for AASA, PASA, acetabular version, and EI, whereas LCEA and AI were not significantly affected.

title: Task-specific gait biomechanics following unilateral iliosacral screw fixation for posterior pelvic ring injury.
authors: Jäckle K, Kramer M, Meier MP, Hawellek T, Roch PJ, Homann C, Castro WHM, Wagner H, Boström K, Lehmann W, Weiser L.
abstract: Background Patients treated with unilateral iliosacral screw fixation for posterior pelvic ring injury may experience residual functional limitations. It remains unclear how these limitations manifest during tasks with different biomechanical demands. This exploratory study compared task-specific gait biomechanics between patients after fixation and healthy controls. Methods In this prospective cross-sectional observational study, 11 patients after unilateral iliosacral screw fixation (mean age 68.73 ± 9.89 years; 10 women) were compared with 21 healthy controls (52.48 ± 20.36 years; 11 women). Participants performed level walking, stair climbing, and step crossing using an Xsens MVN inertial motion capture system. Pelvic kinematics and model-estimated muscle activation and joint contact forces were evaluated using Computed MyoGraphy. Repeated trials were analyzed using participant-level random-intercept mixed models adjusted for age and sex. Pelvic rotation during stair climbing was the primary outcome; other outcomes were secondary or exploratory. Results Pelvic rotation during stair climbing was lower in patients (adjusted difference -5.45°, 95% CI -7.98 to -2.92°; within-family FDR-adjusted q = 0.0003). Contralateral pelvic tilt during step crossing was greater (adjusted difference 1.44°, 95% CI 0.46-2.41°; q = 0.011). No statistically significant group differences were detected in the analyzed level-walking parameters, thoracic counter-rotation, lower-limb muscle activation, or hip joint contact-force asymmetry. Model-estimated peak L5-S1 joint contact force during stair climbing was lower in patients (adjusted difference -0.70 × body weight; q = 0.001). Conclusions Patients after posterior pelvic ring injury treated with unilateral iliosacral screw fixation showed task-specific differences in pelvic movement during demanding locomotor activities. The findings support including stair and step tasks in functional assessment, but do not establish that fixation caused the observed differences. Small sample size, demographic imbalance, and the absence of patient-reported outcomes limit clinical interpretation.

title: Task-specific effects of noisy galvanic vestibular stimulation on gait symmetry in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
authors: Li Y, Zhang Z, Yasen A, Peng X, Miao Y, Qian S, Xie H.
abstract: Background Vestibular dysfunction has been identified as a potential contributor to postural instability and gait asymmetry in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). Noisy galvanic vestibular stimulation (nGVS) enhances gait performance by optimizing vestibular signal processing via stochastic resonance. However, how nGVS modulates gait symmetry in AIS and whether its efficacy depends on locomotor tasks or spinal deformity severity remain to be elucidated. This study aimed to investigate the effects of nGVS on medial-lateral gait symmetry in patients with AIS during level walking and single-step stair negotiation. Methods This single-group crossover study recruited 30 patients with AIS to perform level walking, stair ascent, and stair descent under nGVS, sham-stimulation, and no-stimulation conditions. Primary dependent measures included medial-lateral gait symmetry across kinematic (lateral trunk displacement (T), lateral trunk lean (α), lateral pelvic displacement (P), pelvic obliquity (β), and hip adduction (θ)) and kinetic domains (first (ML1) and second (ML2) medial-lateral ground reaction force peaks), quantified by the symmetry index (SI) and normalized cross-correlation coefficient (Xcorr). Post-hoc comparisons prioritized the (nGVS vs. sham) contrast to isolate true nGVS efficacy. Correlations between the sham-controlled net efficacy (Δ) and Cobb angle were also examined. Results Compared to sham stimulation, nGVS significantly increased Xcorr_α (descent: p = 0.017; ascent: p = 0.033), Xcorr_β (descent: p = 0.006), Xcorr_θ (ascent: p = 0.008), and Xcorr_ML (descent: p p = 0.015; ascent: p = 0.022) during single-step stair negotiation. Correlation analyses revealed that greater Cobb angle was significantly correlated with Δ Xcorr_ML (descent: ρ = 0.583, p = 0.001; ascent: r = 0.575, p = 0.001), Δ Xcorr_α (descent: r = 0.539, p = 0.002; ascent: ρ = 0.427, p = 0.019), Δ Xcorr_β (descent: ρ = 0.394, p = 0.031), Δ Xcorr_θ (ascent: r = 0.398, p = 0.030), and Δ SI_ML1 (descent: ρ = - 0.444, p = 0.014). However, this state-dependent relationship did not reach statistical significance across Δ SI_α ( r = - 0.394, p = 0.137) and Δ SI_β ( r = - 0.423, p = 0.108). Conclusions These findings demonstrated that nGVS ameliorated medial-lateral gait symmetry in AIS by refining multi-segmental control under heightened biomechanical demands, indicating a task-specific pattern. Furthermore, nGVS-induced enhancements in medial-lateral gait symmetry were state-dependent, wherein patients exhibiting larger Cobb angles within the mild-to-moderate range (10°-30°) derived greater biomechanical gains.

title: Real-world treatment patterns following denosumab discontinuation: a descriptive epidemiological study.
authors: Yoshiyama T, Fukasawa T, Masuda S, Matsuda S, Kawakami K.
abstract: This descriptive epidemiological study suggests that sequential osteoporosis therapy after denosumab discontinuation is underutilized in real-world practice. Within 1 year after discontinuation, approximately 30% of patients restarted denosumab, approximately half had no subsequent osteoporosis treatment, and only 16% initiated sequential osteoporosis therapy. Purpose To describe real-world treatment patterns following denosumab discontinuation, including delayed reinitiation, no subsequent osteoporosis treatment, and sequential osteoporosis therapy. Methods This descriptive epidemiological study used a Japanese claims database (April 2014-March 2024). We included adults aged ≥40 years who newly initiated denosumab and discontinued it after ≥2 doses. Discontinuation was defined as the last administration before a gap of >240 days or final observed administration followed by ≥240 days without another administration. The primary outcomes within 1 year after discontinuation were delayed denosumab reinitiation, no subsequent osteoporosis treatment, and sequential osteoporosis therapy. We also described the type and timing of sequential therapy and estimated the 1-year cumulative incidence of fragility fractures. Results Among 37,526 eligible patients, the 1-year cumulative incidence of delayed denosumab reinitiation was 29.6%, the probability of no subsequent osteoporosis treatment was 50.9%, and the cumulative incidence of sequential osteoporosis therapy was 16.3%. Oral bisphosphonates were the most frequently used sequential therapy (26.7%), followed by romosozumab (22.2%), selective estrogen receptor modulators (21.3%), intravenous bisphosphonates (15.1%), teriparatide (14.6%), and abaloparatide (0.1%). Sequential therapy was most often initiated 180-209 days after discontinuation, particularly for romosozumab (45.7%), whereas selective estrogen receptor modulators were frequently initiated 0-29 days after discontinuation (39.8%). The 1-year cumulative incidence of fragility fractures was 5.4%. Conclusions Within 1 year after discontinuation, approximately 30% of patients restarted denosumab, half received no subsequent osteoporosis treatment, and one in six initiated sequential therapy. These findings suggest a substantial gap in the continuity of osteoporosis care.

title: Psychometric validation of the European Portuguese version of Quality of Life Questionnaire of the European Foundation for Osteoporosis (QUALEFFO-41) in the Portuguese population.
authors: Azevedo SF, Barbosa AP, Cunha A, Melim D, Augusto D, Pimentel G, Oliveira M, Vieira R, Barcelos A.
abstract: The European Portuguese version of the QUALEFFO-41 showed good reliability, validity, and excellent discriminatory ability between patients with vertebral fragility fractures and controls. These findings support its use as a disease-specific quality-of-life instrument in Portuguese clinical practice and research. Purpose Vertebral fragility fractures substantially impair quality of life (QoL). The Quality of Life Questionnaire of the European Foundation for Osteoporosis (QUALEFFO-41) is a disease-specific instrument widely used to assess QoL in patients with vertebral fractures; however, its psychometric properties have not yet been validated for use in Portugal. This study aimed to perform the psychometric validation of the European Portuguese version of the QUALEFFO-41. Materials and methods A multicentric prospective validation study was conducted in Portuguese patients with vertebral fragility fractures and age- and sex-matched controls. Following cognitive debriefing and cultural adaptation, participants completed the QUALEFFO-41 and the SF-36, with a 2-week retest interval. Internal consistency (Cronbach's α), test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient, ICC), construct validity (convergent and discriminant validity), criterion validity (correlations with SF-36), and discriminatory ability were assessed. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed to determine optimal cut-off points. Results Seventy-five participants were included (55 patients with vertebral fragility fractures and 20 controls). Internal consistency was adequate across domains (Cronbach's α 0.70-0.98) and excellent for the total score (α = 0.90). Test-retest reliability was high, with ICCs ranging from 0.75 to 0.98. Multitrait analysis demonstrated satisfactory convergent (71.4-100%) and discriminant validity (70.6-100%). Significant correlations were observed between QUALEFFO-41 domains and corresponding SF-36 domains, particularly for general health perception (r = -0.85). Patients with vertebral fragility fractures reported significantly worse QoL than controls across all domains and the total score (p Conclusions The European Portuguese version of the QUALEFFO-41 demonstrates robust reliability, validity, and strong discriminatory capacity. It is a valid and reliable instrument for assessing quality of life in Portuguese patients with vertebral fragility fractures in both clinical practice and research settings.

title: Practice Patterns in Femoral Rotational Decision-Making During Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Cross-Sectional Survey Among Brazilian Knee Surgeons.
authors: Gonçalves Filho GM, Pallone LV, Mandarino M, Rocha de Faria JL, Monteiro da Palma I, Salim R.
abstract: Background Surgeons use different references, balancing strategies, and technology to determine femoral component rotation in total knee arthroplasty. This survey described reported practice patterns among Brazilian knee surgeons. Methods A cross-sectional electronic survey was conducted among knee surgeons practicing in Brazil in February 2026. The questionnaire assessed alignment approach, strategy for femoral rotation and ligament balance, main rotational reference, frequency of use of individual references, scenarios avoiding isolated posterior condylar referencing, and availability and routine use of technology-assisted tools. Associations with routine robotic and navigation use were assessed using Fisher's exact test with odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals. Results Seventy-nine surgeons responded. Mechanical alignment was most common (64.6%). Hybrid technique (48.1%) and gap balancing (36.7%) were more frequent than measured resection alone (13.9%). The most frequent single method was combining references (34.2%), and respondents routinely used a median of 4 individual references (interquartile range, 3-5); only 6 (7.6%) routinely used 1 reference. Isolated posterior condylar referencing was avoided in lateral condylar hypoplasia (86.1%) and severe valgus (70.9%). Robotic instrumentation was available to 64.6% and used routinely by 25.3%; its association with volume attenuated among surgeons with access, whereas its association with named nonmechanical alignment responses persisted after individualized case-by-case responses were excluded. Conclusions Reported femoral rotational decision-making most commonly involved several references and balance-oriented strategies rather than a single landmark. Technology adoption reflected both access and use. These findings describe reported practice rather than measured rotational outcomes or evidence of superiority.

title: Posterior Tibial Slope Is Not Associated With Failure After Medial Meniscus Posterior Root Tear Repair at a Minimum 2-Year Follow-Up.
authors: Rock C, Myers RJ, Agner KE, Al Janabi H, Abdelshahid M, Nowell J, Barker T, Kaeding CC, Magnussen RA, Flanigan DC, Apseloff NA.
abstract: Purpose To examine the relation between posterior tibial slope (PTS) and failure after medial meniscus posterior root tear (MMPRT) repair. Methods Patients who underwent isolated primary arthroscopic transtibial pullout MMPRT repair between 2012 and 2022 at a single institution and with a minimum 2-year follow-up were retrospectively identified. Patients were grouped into high (PTS ≥ 12°), intermediate (PTS 8°-11°), and low (PTS ≤ 7°) categories. Failure was defined as repeat ipsilateral knee arthroscopy or conversion to knee arthroplasty. A Kaplan-Meier curve and log-rank test were employed to analyze the relation between PTS and MMPRT repair failure. Results A total of 74 patients (77% women) with a mean age of 52.3 ± 9.3 years (range 23.5-73.3 years) with a minimum 2-year follow-up were identified. The mean follow-up time was 4.8 years (range 2.4-7.8 years) in the failure group and 6.2 years (range 3.4-9.2 years) in the nonfailure group ( P = .004). The mean follow-up was 6.21 ± 1.74 years in the high PTS group, 5.91 ± 1.64 years in the intermediate group, and 5.50 ± 1.81 years in the low group ( P = .478). The overall failure rate was 15/74 (20.3%) at a median (interquartile range) of 2.70 (0.80-5.19) years. No significant differences in time to failure were observed among PTS groups. The median (interquartile range) surgery-free survival time was 6.2 (4.6-7.8) years in the high PTS group (n = 22; 5 failures), 6.2 (4.7-7.8) years in the intermediate PTS group (n = 38; 8 failures), and 5.5 (3.9-7.2) years in the low PTS group (n = 14; 2 failures) ( P = .91). There were also no significant differences in coronal alignment among PTS groups. Conclusions In this study, PTS was not significantly associated with failure rates or time to failure after isolated MMPRT repair. Level of evidence Level III, therapeutic retrospective comparative study.

title: Osteoarthritis year in review 2026: Epidemiology and therapy.
authors: Duong V, Kobayashi S, Fu K, King LK.
abstract: Aim The aim of this review was to summarise the key epidemiological and therapeutic research on osteoarthritis (OA) published between April 2025 and March 2026. Methods We conducted a narrative review drawing on a search of the MEDLINE database and an informal survey to OA experts. Studies were eligible if they were published between April 1, 2025, and March 31, 2026, conducted on humans, and published in English. From our search, total of 1305 papers were screened by pairs of two authors, resulting in 97 papers considered for potential inclusion and twenty-nine included. Twenty-one studies were identified by OA experts, of which three additional papers were included. A total of 32 papers were included in the review based on their novelty, quality and relevance to OA epidemiology and therapy (n=18 for epidemiology and n=14 for therapy). We prioritised longitudinal cohort studies for epidemiological papers and randomised controlled trials for therapeutic papers. Results Findings from epidemiological studies confirmed the role of metabolism and physical inactivity in development and progression of OA, as well as identified potential emerging risk factors of air pollution exposure and the role of endogenous and exogenous hormones. Therapeutic interventions for OA focused on pharmacotherapy interventions, including the repurposing of drugs, methotrexate and metformin. There was new evidence for potential mechanisms of glucagon-like peptide-1 therapies in OA and their cost-effectiveness, in addition to ongoing critical research into new disease-modifying therapies and pain-targeted interventions. One surgical study found that high tibial osteotomy provided structural and symptomatic benefits in selected people. Conclusion Research published during 2025 to 2026 reinforces the multifactorial nature of OA. Most new epidemiological findings require verification before inferring causality, and few new therapies studied are ready for routine adoption. There is still a need for disease-modifying OA drugs in addition to highly effective symptomatic treatments. Meanwhile, implementation of existing first-line OA care and prevention strategies should be prioritised.

title: Nipple reconstruction using banked autologous costal cartilage with modified Hammond flap technique.
authors: Park SK, Bernal IC, Brito EM, Daza S, Weiss ES.

title: Navigated robotic guidance for minimally invasive bertolotti resection technical feasibility and workflow evaluation.
authors: Good ZR, Good CR.
abstract: Bertolotti syndrome is characterized by symptomatic lumbosacral transitional vertebral anatomy in which an enlarged transverse process articulates or fuses with the sacrum or ilium. Diagnosis can be difficult because transitional anatomy is common, symptoms may overlap with other spinal disorders, and the pain generator may arise from the pseudoarticulation, adjacent disc or facet, instability, or nerve compression. When targeted nonoperative treatment fails, surgical options include resection, nerve decompression, or fusion depending on anatomy and the dominant pain mechanism. Published evidence supports image guidance for localization and confirmation of resection and describes early robotic assistance for incision planning; however, evidence specific to robotic Bertolotti resection remains limited. This original article evaluates the technical feasibility and workflow of a preoperatively planned, navigated robotic workflow to perform minimally invasive Bertolotti resection. A technical framework is presented for preoperative computerized computed-tomography planning, convergent access through a minimally invasive incision, and navigated robotic trajectory-controlled drilling of bone-cut trajectories across the transverse processes and pseudoarticulations, osteotomy, fragment removal and verification of complete decompression or resection. Feasibility was assessed by completion of the planned navigated robotic steps, intraoperative confirmation of registration and resection, and review of technical, perioperative, and imaging outcomes. These concepts may improve reproducibility and reduce challenges related to limited visualization and complex three-dimensional anatomy, but they should not be interpreted as proof of superior outcomes. This initial paper outlines a novel technique, however; further comparative studies using standardized measures of pain, disability, operative time, blood loss, radiation exposure, navigation accuracy, resection quality, and reoperation rate are needed before the clinical value of robotic guidance can be established.

title: Musical Feedback to Reduce the Knee Adduction Moment Via Center of Pressure Medialization: A Proof-of-Concept Study in Healthy Adults for Knee Osteoarthritis Gait Retraining.
authors: Cedin L, Antognini C, Knowlton C, Ferrigno C, Wimmer MA.
abstract: Elevated knee adduction moment (KAM) is a primary contributor to medial knee osteoarthritis (OA) progression. Medialization of center of pressure (CoP) can reduce KAM, but sustaining engagement and a consistent walking pattern remains a challenge. We investigated whether concurrent plantar pressure-modulated musical feedback would cue a medial CoP shift to reduce KAM without producing detrimental lower limb compensations in healthy adults. Twelve participants (6F/6M; age: 31.5 ± 5.3 years) walked while a marker-based motion analysis system (Qualisys) and wireless pressure-sensing insoles (Moticon) recorded gait. Real-time insole data drove auditory feedback: self-selected music was progressively muffled whenever the participant failed to shift their CoP medially beyond their threshold (25 % reduction in peak lateral CoP from baseline). Gait was assessed at baseline, post-instructions, and post-training. Repeated-measures ANOVA was used for kinetics and spatiotemporal outcomes, and statistical parametric mapping, as a secondary analysis, for kinematic waveforms. All participants medialized their CoP based on instructions and musical feedback. Musical feedback significantly reduced the second KAM peak (post-training: -13.7 %; p = 0.002) and the knee adduction angular impulse (post-training: -9.4 %; p < 0.001), but with a borderline increase in peak knee flexion moment (p = 0.050) that may reflect compensation. Gait adaptations were executed without a change in walking speed. Also, foot progression angle and stride width remained unchanged. CoP medialization was achieved mainly through ankle inversion, ankle external rotation, and hip internal rotation. These preliminary findings support concurrent sonified biofeedback for gait retraining, warranting evaluation in medial knee OA patients.

title: Minimally Invasive Biological Gracilis Augmentation of Fascia Lata for Intra- and Extra-articular Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: XO FAST Technique.
authors: Denis-Aubrée P, Herman S, Hardy A, Bohu Y.
abstract: The fascia lata (FL) is a long-established and proven graft for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, allowing intra- and extra-articular reconstruction to be combined with a single graft and a single femoral tunnel, without femoral fixation. Despite its biomechanical and clinical advantages, its use has been limited by the morbidity of the donor site and the size of the incision. We describe a minimally invasive technique for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction using a pedicled FL strip reinforced with the gracilis tendon, which reduces donor-site morbidity while maintaining the benefits of combined reconstruction. This technique is based on reproducible anatomical landmarks for harvesting the FL, a limited lateral, and simplified graft preparation. The graft allows optimal control of anterior and rotational stability of the knee while preserving the extensor apparatus and the semitendinosus tendon. The absence of femoral fixation, the use of a single femoral tunnel, and a single tibial interference screw make this technique particularly suitable for pediatric surgery, revision surgery, and situations with a high risk of rerupture. This technical note presents a reliable and reproducible alternative to conventional techniques for reconstructing the anterior cruciate ligament using the FL, limiting morbidity while optimizing stability and functional outcomes.

title: Medial Patellofemoral Ligament Reconstruction With Transverse Reefing (Tubing) of Medial Patellar Retinaculum and Biological Fixation.
authors: Makhmalbaf H, Hoseinzadeh Moghaddam S, Vatankhah A, Ebrahimzadeh MH, Samei M, Ganji R.
abstract: The medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) is regarded as one of the main stabilizers of the knee. Its importance is underscored by the fact that in most cases of acute lateral patellar dislocation, rupture of the MPFL occurs. It is also a key factor in recurrent patellar dislocations. Therefore, MPFL reconstruction surgery is the current approach to managing such cases. Numerous techniques have been practiced by surgeons, with some being more prevalent than others. Although there is extensive literature comparing the efficacy and safety of different techniques, no clear consensus has been reached. Furthermore, recurrent postoperative complications, such as knee pain, have prompted surgeons to seek new and less invasive techniques. In this technical note, we describe an implant-free MPFL reconstruction method leveraging the medial patellar retinaculum. Through horizontal suturing, a reinforced tubular reef is created to mimic the native MPFL and is secured via a subperiosteal femoral pouch with minimal invasiveness. This approach avoids bone tunnels, and it is expected to reduce fracture risk, eliminate donor-site morbidity, and enhance reproducibility for surgeons.

title: Maintenance of periarticular joint angles after varization double-level osteotomy for severe valgus deformity: a technical and radiographic mid-term case series.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Herbst M, Schröter S, Ateschrang A, Histing T, Ahrend MD.
abstract: Purpose To assess the restoration and mid-term course of mechanical alignment and periarticular femoral and tibial joint angles after varization double-level osteotomy (DLO) in patients with severe valgus malalignment. Methods This retrospective case series included 13 knees treated with medial closing-wedge distal femoral and high tibial osteotomy between 2011 and 2015. Eight knees were available at a minimum follow-up of five years. Mechanical alignment and periarticular joint angles were assessed preoperatively, six weeks postoperatively, and at final follow-up. Individual radiographic trajectories, conversion to total knee arthroplasty, complications, and postoperative patient-reported outcomes were evaluated descriptively. Results Seven patients with eight knees were assessed after a mean follow-up of 7.5 ± 1.2 years. Mean mTFA changed from 9.6 ± 2.6° valgus preoperatively to - 1.4 ± 1.5° six weeks postoperatively and 0.1 ± 4.7° at final follow-up. Mean mLDFA changed from 86.1 ± 2.2° to 90.5 ± 2.5° postoperatively and 90.2 ± 2.4° at final follow-up; mean mMPTA changed from 92.4 ± 1.6° to 86.4 ± 1.5° and 87.3 ± 2.1°, respectively. Individual trajectories were heterogeneous; one knee developed recurrent valgus alignment with a marked increase in JLCA. None of the eight knees underwent conversion to total knee arthroplasty. Three complications occurred, and implant removal was performed in all knees. Conclusion Within the limitations of this small retrospective case series, varization DLO restored mechanical alignment and periarticular femoral and tibial joint angles in selected patients with severe valgus malalignment. Group-level periarticular bony angles remained close to the early postoperative values at mid-term follow-up, although individual radiographic trajectories were heterogeneous. Larger prospective comparative studies are required to determine clinical effectiveness, complication rates, survivorship, and valgus-specific indication criteria.

title: Influence of stem undersizing during direct anterior approach for total hip arthroplasty on periprosthetic bone biomechanics : a finite element analysis.
authors: Liskay J, Marcián P, Apostolopoulos V, Nachtnebl L, Tomáš T.
abstract: Aims Stem undersizing during cementless total hip arthroplasty (THA) may occur more frequently when the procedure is performed through the direct anterior approach (DAA) because of limited femoral exposure. Insufficient stem-bone contact may compromise primary stability and alter load transfer in the proximal femur. The aim was to investigate the biomechanical effects of femoral stem undersizing on periprosthetic bone using finite element analysis. A secondary objective was to evaluate whether the presence of a femoral stem collar modifies these biomechanical effects. Methods Patient-specific finite element models of the full femur were generated from CT data. Eight finite element models were analyzed, combining four implantation configurations of the AMIStem-P designs (Adequate Fit, Adequate Fit-Collared, Undersized, and Undersized-Collared) with two cancellous bone density conditions, representing 100% and 90% cancellous bone density. A hip joint force representing the peak loading phase during normal walking/single-leg support was applied. Strain intensity in periprosthetic trabecular bone was assessed according to Frost's mechanostat theory, and von Mises stress distribution in the femoral stem was evaluated. Results Stem undersizing markedly increased strain intensity in the periprosthetic trabecular bone and enlarged regions exceeding the mechanostat overload threshold (> 3,000 µε). Adequate stem-bone fit with cortical support substantially reduced the volume of overloaded bone tissue. The presence of a collar reduced strain levels, particularly in undersized configurations, indicating improved proximal load transfer. Reduced cancellous bone density resulted in a moderate additional increase in strain. Simulated load reduction markedly decreased periprosthetic strain levels. Implant stresses remained well below material limits. Conclusion Femoral stem undersizing may substantially increase strain within the periprosthetic trabecular bone and enlarge regions exposed to overload conditions. Achieving adequate stem-bone fit with cortical support was associated with a marked reduction in periprosthetic bone strain. The presence of a collar appeared to partially mitigate the adverse mechanical effects of undersizing by improving proximal load transfer.

title: Graft selection in combined PCL and PLC reconstruction: a scoping review of current evidence and knowledge gaps.
authors: Rinaldi VG, Fogacci A, Sassoli I, Morri M, Cimatti P, Dallari D, Zaffagnini S, Marcheggiani Muccioli GM.
abstract: Graft selection is a key component of combined posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) and posterolateral corner (PLC) reconstruction, yet the factors guiding graft choice remain poorly defined. The purpose of this scoping review was to map current graft utilization patterns, examine how graft selection is reported in relation to injury characteristics and reconstructive strategy, summarize the available graft-related clinical evidence, and identify methodological and reporting gaps that currently preclude evidence-based recommendations. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Studies published between January 2005 and January 2025 reporting graft selection in adult patients undergoing combined PCL and PLC reconstruction were included. Data regarding study characteristics, graft utilization, surgical techniques, clinical and radiological outcomes, and factors influencing graft selection were extracted and descriptively synthesized. Fourteen studies involving 365 patients met the inclusion criteria. Most studies were retrospective case series with moderate methodological quality. Allografts, particularly Achilles and tibialis tendon allografts, were more frequently used for PCL reconstruction, whereas hamstring autografts predominated in PLC reconstruction. However, no single graft strategy emerged as standard practice. The rationale underlying graft selection was explicitly reported in only 3 of 14 studies (21.4%), while fixed institutional protocols predominated and no study described a patient-specific graft selection algorithm. Furthermore, no study directly compared alternative graft sources or reported graft-specific clinical outcomes. Despite substantial heterogeneity in graft utilization, reconstruction techniques, and outcome assessment, satisfactory clinical and radiological outcomes were consistently reported. Current literature describes which grafts are used for combined PCL and PLC reconstruction but provides limited information on how or why graft selection is performed. The absence of standardized reporting, comparative studies, and graft-specific outcome analyses currently prevents evidence-based recommendations. Future prospective studies should evaluate graft selection as a dedicated research question and incorporate standardized reporting of decision-making criteria and graft-specific outcomes.

title: Fundamentals of osteoarthritis prevention: progress and future directions in treatment targets and trial design.
authors: Losciale JM, Dell'Isola A, Roos EM, Bierma-Zeinstra S, Runhaar J, Whittaker JL.
abstract: Objective To summarize recent advances, current concepts, and future directions in osteoarthritis (OA) prevention. Design This narrative review is presented in four sections: recent initiatives that have advanced OA prevention, OA risk factors and prevention targets, considerations for OA prevention clinical trials, and future directions. Recent trials, protocols and examples from OA and other health conditions are used to illustrate common challenges, trade-offs, and emerging approaches to prevention research and trial design. Results Recent initiatives have advanced approaches for identifying populations at increased risk of OA, defining early-stage symptomatic OA, and informing prevention trial design. Current approaches to studying OA risk factors highlight important distinctions between factors that define OA at-risk populations and those that represent meaningful prevention targets, emphasizing the need to move beyond associations toward understanding causal mechanisms and modifiable pathways. Designing OA prevention trials remains challenging because of heterogeneity within at-risk populations, uncertainty about optimal outcomes and endpoints, and the long-time horizons often required to observe meaningful changes in disease and illness trajectories. Future progress may be accelerated through the application of prognostic approaches, surrogate outcomes, and innovative trial designs that improve study feasibility and support more efficient evaluation of OA prevention strategies. Conclusion Continued progress towards OA prevention will require moving beyond simply identifying who is at risk towards understanding how, when, and for whom interventions may alter disease and/or illness trajectories. Achieving this will require stronger integration of causal thinking, prognostic approaches, and flexible study designs that reflect the heterogeneity of OA populations and interventions. Together, these approaches can help generate more informative, feasible, and actionable evidence to advance the field toward effective, scalable prevention strategies to reduce the growing burden of OA.

title: Fracture risk in 85-year-old women: associations with volumetric bone mineral density, physical performance and falls.
authors: Wihlborg A, Åkesson KE, Gerdhem P.
abstract: This prospective study demonstrates associations of volumetric BMD (vBMD) by pQCT, areal BMD (aBMD) by DXA, physical performance (one-leg balance, gait speed, and knee extension force), and fall history with fracture risk in 85-year-old women. A failed one-leg balance test was associated with both hip and any fracture independent of femoral neck aBMD. Total radial vBMD was associated with any fracture. Gait speed and previous falls showed associations with fracture risk of similar magnitude as femoral neck aBMD. These findings suggest that functional performance measures may enhance fracture risk assessment in older women. Purpose This prospective study evaluates associations between fracture risk and volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) by peripheral quantitative computed tomography (pQCT), physical performance tests, and fall history, in comparison with femoral neck areal BMD (aBMD) by DXA, in 85-year-old women. Methods In the Osteoporosis Prospective Risk Assessment (OPRA) study, 382 women aged 85 years were followed for a mean of 4.3 years. Participants underwent pQCT of the radius and tibia and DXA of the hip and lumbar spine, performed physical performance tests (one-leg standing balance, considered failed if balance could not be maintained for 5 s; gait speed, analyzed continuously; and knee extension force, measured by isometric dynamometry), and reported fall history. Cox proportional hazards models estimated fracture risk, adjusting for BMI, previous fracture, smoking, and use of vitamin D, glucocorticoids, and bisphosphonates. Results During a mean follow-up of 4.3 years, 116 women (30%) sustained a fracture. Trabecular vBMD at the radius and tibia was associated with lower risk of any fracture (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.55-0.85 and HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.55-0.86, respectively). Radial trabecular vBMD was also associated with lower hip fracture risk (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.42-0.98). Femoral neck aBMD was associated with lower risk of any fracture (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.62-0.90), but not hip fracture (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.50-1.00). A failed balance test and low gait speed was associated with higher risk of any fracture (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.04-2.29 and HR 1.22, 95% CI 1.01-1.48, respectively). In multivariate analyses, a failed balance test remained associated with any fracture (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.12-2.56) and hip fracture (HR 2.30, 95% CI 1.05-5.02). Total radial vBMD remained associated with any fracture (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.63-0.996). Conclusion Volumetric BMD by pQCT was associated with fracture risk independent of commonly recognized clinical risk factors in 85-year-old women. Physical performance tests were associated with fracture risk in unadjusted analyses, and the one-leg balance test additionally remained associated after adjustment for clinical risk factors and femoral neck aBMD.

title: Controlled Tensioning Medial Patellofemoral Ligament Augmentation Using Double-Tape Suture and Arthroscopic Lateral Soft-Tissue Release for Patellar Instability.
authors: Tan HY, Luo YF, Zeng JH, Huang P, Jin S, Deng XH, Zhang ZZ, Lin NH, Zhou AY, Chen Z.
abstract: Overtensioning the medial patellofemoral ligament during reconstruction is a key cause of patellofemoral overload, anterior knee pain, and limited flexion. We present a reproducible, tension-calibrated augmentation technique using a single 4.75-mm SwiveLock anchor preloaded with double FiberTape and sutures-eliminating graft harvest. This technique is intended as an augmentation rather than a full ligament substitution. The staged fixation strategy, combined with arthroscopic evaluation and selective lateral release, serves to minimize the risk of medial overconstraint. The anchor is placed at the Schöttle point, and sutures are passed subcapsularly to the medial patella, exiting through two 2.5-mm transverse bone tunnels. Initial lateral knot fixation is performed, followed by stepwise lateral release and vastus lateralis detachment to relieve residual lateral tension. Final FiberTape fixation is completed under arthroscopic visualization, allowing real-time adjustment to avoid overtightening. Final fixation was performed at approximately 30° of knee flexion, with the patella centered within the trochlear groove. This technique restores patellar tracking, permits full flexion, and may help reduce the risk of recurrence in recurrent patellar instability.

title: Clinical outcomes and safety reporting after image-guided and non-image-guided subtalar joint injections: a systematic review.
authors: Gibson J, Agrawal N, Maleyko I, Thompson B, Saran S, Labidi M, Botchu R.
abstract: Background Subtalar joint (STJ) injections are used for chronic hindfoot pain but evidence comparing guidance methods remains limited. Methods This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020. PubMed, Embase (via Ovid), Scopus and Web of Science were searched from inception to December 2025, and the searches were re-run in a broadened form in July 2026. Eligible studies included comparative studies, single-arm cohort or case-series studies with 10 or more procedures and technical/cadaveric accuracy studies reporting subtalar-specific outcomes. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data and assessed risk of bias. Heterogeneity and scarce direct comparison precluded meta-analysis. Results Seventeen studies were eligible: 12 reported clinical data and five reported cadaveric technical accuracy data only (one clinical study also contributed a cadaveric control arm). Denominators are reported in their own units and are not combined: the clinical studies contributed 129 patients (six studies), 100 injected joints (four studies) and 779 injections (two studies). Ultrasound, fluoroscopy and landmark-guided injection were each reported in five studies. No study of CT or SPECT-CT guidance provided a subtalar-specific outcome. Needle placement accuracy ranged from 68 to 100%, but difference in design, populations and confirmation methods prevented comparison between modalities. Conclusion STJ injections are associated with clinical improvement but evidence is predominantly observational and heterogeneous. Differences in reporting technical accuracy, injectate, clinical response and adverse events prevent comparison of guidance methods. No modality's superiority is established. Prospective comparative studies using standardised outcomes and consistent safety reporting are needed.

title: BMI and Varus Malalignment Compound to Define a High-Risk Phenotype for Compartment-Specific Knee Osteoarthritis Progression.
authors: White MS, Kogan F, Delp SL, Chu CR, Sherman SL, Pai S A, Gold GE, Chaudhari AS, Gatti AA.
abstract: Objective Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of disability, yet which patients will experience structural decline remains unclear. Body mass index (BMI) and lower limb alignment are established risk factors for KOA, but their independent and interactive effects on compartment-specific cartilage loss and total knee replacement (TKR) have not been characterized at scale. Design We analyzed 5,930 limbs from 3,191 participants in the Osteoarthritis Initiative followed over 0-60 months. Cartilage thickness in the weight-bearing medial and lateral femur and tibia was quantified, and lower limb alignment was measured using hip-knee-ankle (HKA) angle obtained from full-limb radiographs. Linear mixed-effects models estimated the associations of BMI and lower limb alignment with longitudinal changes in cartilage thickness, modeled as interactions with time and with each other and adjusted for age, sex, and baseline Kellgren-Lawrence grade. Logistic regression with participant-clustered standard errors modeled TKR odds within five and ten years after each limb's baseline. Results In the medial compartment, BMI and varus alignment interacted, with their combined effect exceeding the sum of independent effects (femur: β = 0.0016 mm/year per 1-SD BMI x 1-SD HKA, 95% CI [0.0001, 0.0031]; tibia: β = 0.0018, 95% CI [0.0008, 0.0028]). In the lateral compartment, alignment, but not BMI, was associated with faster cartilage loss, and its association was nonlinear (time x HKA 2 : femur β = -0.0032 mm/year, 95% CI [-0.0038, -0.0027]; tibia β = -0.0033, 95% CI [-0.0040, -0.0026]). TKR odds increased 1.11-fold at five years (95% CI [1.04, 1.18]) and 1.14-fold at ten years (95% CI [1.08, 1.21]) per 1-degree greater absolute HKA deviation from the radiographically healthy reference angle (-1.0°). BMI did not modify the association between HKA deviation and TKR. Conclusion BMI and lower limb alignment influence structural KOA progression through compartment-specific pathways. The compounding interaction in the medial compartment identifies high BMI combined with varus malalignment as a high-risk phenotype for medial structural progression.

title: Arthroscopic Anatomic Rotator Cable Reconstruction Using Palmaris Longus Autograft: Surgical Technique.
authors: Lim TK, Park HS.
abstract: This technical note describes an arthroscopic anatomic rotator cable reconstruction technique using a palmaris longus tendon autograft for selected large U-shaped posterosuperior rotator cuff tears with limited tendon mobility. After thorough stepwise release and mobilization, the graft is introduced into the subacromial space and fixed to the anatomic anterior and posterior cable insertion sites and woven through the residual rotator cuff near the musculotendinous junction. The graft is tensioned to recreate the native semilunar cable arc, whereas the rotator cuff is simultaneously reduced to the medial footprint, followed by combined cuff-to-bone repair over the reconstructed cable. By recreating the native anterior-posterior cable architecture and integrating the autologous graft with the repaired cuff, this technique aims to restore biomechanical load-sharing and force coupling while permitting long-term biologic incorporation. As such, arthroscopic rotator cable reconstruction using a palmaris longus autograft may provide a valuable anatomic surgical option for rotator cable-deficient shoulders in which anatomic tendon repair alone is not feasible.

title: A randomized study on migration of the Spectron EF and the Charnley flanged 40 cemented femoral stems: secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial using radiostereometric analysis (RSA) with 10 years' follow-up.
authors: Johannessen HG, Hallan G, Furnes O, Fenstad AM, Lygre SH, Haugan K, Kadar T, Badawy M, Indrekvam K, Aamodt A, Høl PJ.
abstract: Background and purpose Our primary aim was to compare the 10-year migration of the proximally roughened Spectron EF stem with the Charnley flanged 40 stems in cemented THA. Secondary aims were to assess the influence of polyethylene type on Spectron EF migration, and clinical outcomes. Methods In this randomized trial (NCT00698672), 150 patients (70% women; mean age 70 years) underwent cemented THA with either a Charnley stem (n = 30) or a Spectron EF stem (n = 120, 4 groups with different articulating surfaces). The articulations utilized conventional polyethylene (CPE) or highly crosslinked polyethylene (XLPE) cup liners combined with either cobalt-chromium (CoCr) or Oxinium (OxZr) femoral heads. RSA was performed postoperatively and up to 10 years. Migration was analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Clinical outcome was assessed with the Harris Hip Score (HHS). Results After 10 years, 48 patients (14 Charnley, 34 Spectron EF) had evaluable RSA data. Both stems showed posterior translation, subsidence, and retroversion. Retroversion was greater for the Charnley stem than the Spectron EF stem at 3.2° (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.7-3.8) and 1.5° (CI 1.2-1.8), respectively, with a mean difference of 1.7° (CI 1.1- 2.4). The Spectron EF stem had more subsidence at 0.72 mm (CI 0.56-0.88) vs 0.32 mm (CI 0.06-0.57) for the Charnley stem, with a difference of 0.41 mm (CI 0.11-0.71). Spectron EF stems articulating with XLPE had 0.44 mm (CI 0.12-0.76) more subsidence than stems articulating with CPE. HHS improved from 41 (SD 15) to 86 (SD 19) for the Charnley stem and 45 (SD 13) to 86 (SD 15) for the Spectron EF stem with no statistically significant difference between the groups. Conclusion After 10 years, the Spectron EF stem showed less retroversion, but more subsidence than the Charnley stem, with otherwise similar migration and clinical outcomes. XLPE articulating stems had more subsidence than CPE with the Spectron EF stem.

title: A primary study of inverted right-angle configuration cannulated screws fixation of femoral neck fracture based on elaborated 3-dimensional features of the femoral head and neck region.
authors: Liu C, Zhang H, Liu Y, Liu P, Hou Y.
abstract: Background CT-based three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction was used to analyze the detailed anatomical morphology of the femoral head-neck region, and a modified inverted right-angle cannulated screw configuration was proposed to reduce the risk of posterosuperior screw in-out-in (IOI) placement during femoral neck fracture fixation. Methods Imaging data from 22 patients (12 males and 10 females; mean age, 52.5 ± 16.8 years) were retrospectively analyzed. CT data of both hips were imported into Mimics to construct 3D digital femoral models for morphologic analysis and screw trajectory simulation. Based on the observed anterior offset of the femoral head-neck canal and the sloped posterosuperior cortex of the femoral neck, a modified inverted right-angle screw configuration and a negative anteversion fluoroscopic view were proposed. Technical feasibility was preliminarily illustrated in two patients with femoral neck fractures. Results The femoral head-neck axis showed an anterior offset relative to the proximal femoral axis, which may increase the risk of posterosuperior IOI screw trajectory with the traditional inverted triangle configuration. In the 3D simulation, the modified inverted right-angle configuration placed the posterosuperior screw within the proposed safety zone. The negative anteversion fluoroscopic view appeared useful for identifying potential IOI screw trajectory. Technical feasibility of the proposed configuration was illustrated in two patients with femoral neck fractures, in whom no postoperative IOI screw displacement was observed on CT. Conclusion The anatomical features of the femoral head-neck region may contribute to the risk of posterosuperior IOI screw trajectory with the traditional inverted triangle configuration. In this CT-based morphologic and simulation study, the modified inverted right-angle configuration showed a more favorable simulated position of the posterosuperior screw within the proposed safety zone, while negative anteversion fluoroscopy may help identify potential IOI screw trajectory. These preliminary findings require further validation through biomechanical studies and larger comparative clinical investigations.

title: Ultrasound-Assisted Endoscopic Lesser Trochanter Resection for Ischiofemoral Impingement.
authors: Mitsuya Y, Miyatake K, Kusaba Y, Arakawa H, Tsujiku S, Inaba Y.
abstract: Ischiofemoral impingement is a rare cause of buttock pain resulting from narrowing of the space between the ischial tuberosity and the femoral lesser trochanter. Although most cases improve with conservative treatment, refractory cases may require surgical treatment. One such treatment option includes endoscopic resection of the lesser trochanter, which is an uncommon, extra-articular, endoscopic surgery that carries several complication risks, such as injury of important neurovascular structures. By marking the sciatic nerve preoperatively and making a portal under ultrasound guidance, this surgery can be performed safely and easily.

title: The Role of the AO Spine Primary Infection Classification in Evaluating Medical and Surgical Management: A Narrative Review.
authors: Kweh BTS, Vaccaro AR, Schroeder GD, Aly MM, El-Sharkawi M, Dandurand C, Neuhoff J, Karamian BA, Xiong GX, Chhabra HS, Bransford R, Joaquim AF, Tee JW.
abstract: Study DesignNarrative review.ObjectivesTo clarify definitions and classifications regarding the diagnosis, medical managementand role of spinal surgery in the treatment of primary pyogenic spinal infections.MethodsA comprehensive review of the MEDLINE, OVID, Embase, Google Scholar and Cochrane Database of Systematic reviews was conducted to characterize historical means of diagnosing spondylodiscitis and explore current controversies in the management of primary pyogenic spinal infections. This includes evaluating the role of aggressive early surgical intervention versus conservative maximal medical management. The AO Spine Primary Infection Classification System is introduced and framed against this historical backdrop.ResultsSurgical intervention in the treatment of pyogenic spinal infection is traditionally reserved for cases of neurological deficit, mechanical instability, or to facilitate microbiological diagnosis. Contemporary studies contend that early surgical debridement leads to superior source control and improved functional as well as neurological outcomes. We note that the majority of these studies are retrospective in nature and that there is a consistent lack of a clear definition of spondylodiscitis or stage of pyogenic primary spinal infection, variation in antibiotic regimens and lack of clear definitions as to what constitutes early or late surgery.ConclusionsPatients who suffer from pyogenic primary spinal infections present at different time courses along their illness and therefore existing studies examining early or late surgical interventions are confounded by this heterogeneity. Existing studies remain disparate due to the absence of a reliable classification. The AO Spine Primary Infection Classification System presents a universal and standardized means of communicating severity of spinal infections.

title: The "osteostat": A theory of bone mechanosensing and setpoint adaptation based on osteocytes.
authors: Pauchard Y, Buenzli PR.
abstract: The osteocyte network in bone is believed to play an important role for how bone tissues sense and respond to mechanical stimulation. Yet, bone adaptation to mechanical loads is often conceptualised as a simple response to mechanical stimuli, such as Wolff's law, which is based on mechanical variables only and takes no account of the cellular basis of mechanosensation. Wolff's law presumes the existence of a reference mechanical stimulus, the mechanical setpoint, above which bone is added , and under which bone is removed. In this paper, we develop a theory of bone tissue sensing and adaptation based on osteocytes to provide new understanding of the role played by osteocyte signals in mechanical adaptation. In this theory, the mechanical setpoint of Frost's mechanostat is explicitly embodied as osteocyte properties involved in mechanotransduction. The mechanical setpoint is allowed to adapt due to the replacement of osteocytes during remodelling, making the setpoint space and time dependent. We propose a mathematical model to implement this new theory of bone adaptation and present numerical simulations of this model to explore how mechanobiological response curves (effective Wolff's laws) are modulated by setpoint adaptation during remodelling. By accounting for varying osteocyte populations within bone tissue, we explore bone adaptation under osteocyte disruptions, which is particularly relevant to age-related bone loss. Our model suggests that biological disruptions of remodelling balance cannot always be compensated by mechanical feedback, and that setpoint adaptation during remodelling may have significant observable consequences, such as hysteresis in bone response signatures that resemble lazy zones.

title: Subchondral bone marrow lesions in osteoarthritis: From pathogenic mechanism to clinical treatment.
authors: Ni HY, Zhang LZ, Yang YY, Yang X, Jin KX.
abstract: Subchondral bone lesions play a significant role in the initiation and progression of osteoarthritis (OA). Bone marrow lesions (BMLs) are one of the key pathological features of OA subchondral bone. Since BMLs are mainly detected through MRI with clinical insidious characteristics, they are not given sufficient attention during the initial inspection. In fact, some BMLs can be detected prior to visible cartilage lesions, osteophytes and joint space narrowing, etc. Further research indicated that BMLs are related to cartilage damage, subchondral cysts, and late-stage joint replacement. They may be one important factor causing OA patient pain with functional impairment and reduced quality of life. Clinically, BMLs are proposed for early OA diagnosis and have potential to be a marker of OA progression. Currently, with the wide application of high spatial resolution MRI and related progress of histological studies, our understanding of OA related BMLs (OABMLs) continues to evolve. Therefore, this paper summarizes research views on BMLs, including the possible etiological factors, imaging and histological pathological features, and methods of conservative and surgical treatments. After analyzing the relation between the pathogenesis mechanism and corresponding therapeutic methods, it further proposed that the core principle of treatment behind the underlying mechanisms would be reducing stress and improving bone remodeling, which is expected to provide practicality evidence and reference for basic research and clinical treatment of OABMLs. The translational potential of this article Osteoarthritis-related bone marrow lesions (OABMLs) represent a critical yet underutilized target for early diagnosis and mechanism-guided treatment in osteoarthritis. This work systematically synthesizes the current research landscape of BMLs-from basic science to clinical management-and proposes a translational framework that directly links pathogenic mechanisms to therapeutic approaches. Core mechanisms and corresponding treatments are summarized from both mechanical and biological perspectives, with the aim of facilitating mechanism-based treatment selection. The principles of reducing excessive mechanical stress and improving bone remodeling should be considered across all treatment modalities and integrated throughout the entire therapeutic process, encompassing both conservative and surgical interventions. By elucidating the relationship between pathogenic mechanisms and therapeutic strategies, this work is expected to provide practical guidance for basic research, inform the development of more effective treatment algorithms, and improve clinical outcomes for OABMLs with substantial translational potential.

title: Statistically Fragile Evidence Underlies Comparative Trials of Arthroscopic Meniscectomy Versus Nonoperative Management for Degenerative Meniscus Tears.
authors: Bosco AP, Rasquinha RD, Voyer E, Rosenberg AE, Quinn M, Marcaccio S.
abstract: Purpose To assess the statistical robustness of comparative studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing arthroscopic meniscal debridement or meniscectomy with nonoperative or sham interventions. Methods Comparative studies and RCTs of meniscus debridement or meniscectomy versus nonoperative or sham interventions were identified through a comprehensive literature search in June 2025 following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Study characteristics, dichotomous outcomes, and continuous outcomes were extracted. The fragility index and continuous fragility index were calculated as the number of event reversals required to change significance; these metrics were normalized by sample size to calculate the fragility quotient (FQ) and continuous FQ.
