The distal interphalangeal joints of the index and little fingers were most commonly involved, with the index finger affected in 71%, the little finger in 30%, and 18% reporting lesions on both fingers. Rotator cuff reconstruction was the procedure most frequently associated with laceration occurrence; however, no significant correlation was found between laceration frequency and the number of reconstructions performed per year ( r = 0.091, P = .371). Similarly, no association was observed between handedness and the affected side, with 43% reporting bilateral involvement ( χ 2 = 2.464, P = .292). Hyperkeratosis was observed in 54.4% of affected surgeons, suggesting a potential adaptive response to repetitive skin trauma. Conclusions Finger lacerations are a common problem among shoulder surgeons. Seventy-nine percent of respondents reported being regularly affected, particularly at the distal interphalangeal joint of the index and little fingers. Surgeons performing rotator cuff repairs showed a significantly higher incidence of finger lacerations at present. Clinical relevance Finger lacerations and glove microlesions during knot tying are common among shoulder surgeons and may compromise barrier integrity. The lack of widely effective preventive measures underscores the need for improved strategies to protect both surgeons and patients.

title: Evaluation of articular cartilage of the glenohumeral joint in patients with labral tears using T2 mapping technique on MRI: Is there a correlation between cartilage T2 values and labral tear location or frequency of shoulder dislocation?
authors: Kim AY, Antony CD, Choi JA, Lee SA.
abstract: Objectives The purpose of this study was to evaluate glenohumeral cartilage using T2 mapping and to investigate whether cartilage T2 values were associated with labral tear location and frequency of shoulder dislocation. Methods In this prospective study, 30 shoulder MRIs with T2 mapping were performed at a 3.0 T scanner. T2 values of cartilage were measured twice by two radiologists after dividing the glenoid and humeral side into 9 areas as: anterosuperior, anterior_middle, anteroinferior, central_superior, central_middle, central_inferior, posterosuperior, posterior_middle, posteroinferior. Intra- and interobserver agreements were calculated using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Labral tears were classified according to location into following groups: superior labral tear group (10-2 o'clock), anterior labral tear group (2-6 o'clock), posterior labral tear group (6-10 o'clock), inferior labral tear group (5-7 o'clock), MDI group (multidirectional instability, involving 3 quadrants or more). Correlations were analyzed using independent student T and ANOVA tests. Results Overall interobserver agreement was moderate (glenoid, 0.612; humeral head, 0.530), whereas intraobserver agreement was good (glenoid, 0.763; humeral head, 0.866). Glenoid cartilage T2 values differed significantly between tear-location groups in the anterosuperior and posteroinferior regions. Cartilage T2 values were not significantly associated with the frequency of shoulder dislocation. Conclusion Interobserver agreement was moderate overall but varied by region, whereas intraobserver agreement was good. Labral tear location was associated with significant differences in T2 values in the anterosuperior and posteroinferior glenoid cartilage regions. No significant association was observed between cartilage T2 values and the frequency of shoulder dislocation.

title: Enhancing return to daily life activities after total and unicompartmental knee arthroplasty with a personalized ehealth program - Results of the multicentre ACTIVE randomized controlled trial.
authors: Straat AC, Coenen P, Maarleveld JM, Huirne JAF, Kerkhoffs GMMJ, Anema JR, Kuijer PPFM, ACTIVE trial group.
abstract: Objective After knee arthroplasty, there is little guidance regarding return to daily life activities including work and sport, despite the importance of these outcomes for patients. Personal eHealth programs provide peri-operative guidance to patients, facilitating earlier recovery. The objective was to assess whether our eHealth program enhances resumption of daily life activities for knee arthroplasty patients compared to usual care. Design A multicentre, single-blind randomized controlled trial across eleven Dutch medical centres was performed. Eligible patients were of working-age, on the waiting list for a primary total- or unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, employed ≥8 h a week, and willing to return to work. The intervention included the personalized eHealth program 'iRecover' with an activity tracker providing personalized advice regarding return to self-chosen daily life activities, a one-time case-manager consultation, and goal attainment scaling. The primary outcome was the time from surgery to return to self-selected daily life activities using PROMIS-PF. The control group received usual care including an eHealth component. Effectiveness was tested using cox proportional hazard models. Results From October 2020-January 2023, 145 patients (58 years, female: 54%) were randomized in the intervention and 142 (59 years, female: 51%) in the control group. Median time to resume self-selected daily life activities was 52 days [32-84] in the intervention group, compared to 75 days [36-137] in the control group (Hazard Ratio: 1.6 (1.3-2.0)). Conclusions Compared to care as usual, our personalized eHealth program reduced time to return to self-selected daily life activities with a median of 23 days. Trial registration Dutch CCMO register (NL67692.029.18), reference date version 1 14-04-2020.

title: Effect of pelvic floor reconstruction on postoperative urinary continence after robot-assisted radical prostatectomy: a meta-analysis.
authors: Wu X, Lu H, Huang W, Shao Z.
abstract: Urinary incontinence after robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) remains a common and burdensome complication. Whether pelvic floor reconstruction (PR) helps restore continence is still debated. We searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science from database inception to October 8, 2026, for controlled studies comparing PR with no reconstruction (nPR) during RARP. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots, Begg's, and Egger's tests. The certainty of evidence was rated using the GRADE approach. Twenty-two studies (5 RCTs and 17 non-RCTs) with 6425 patients (4134 PR and 2291 nPR) were included. At postoperative weeks 1, 2, 4, 12, 24, and 52, continence rates were significantly higher in the PR group than in the nPR group (pooled ORs ranged from 2.58 at 24 weeks to 2.82 at 12 weeks; all 95% CIs excluded 1). Significant heterogeneity was found at all time points except week 2 (I² = 74.3%-87.5%); the 2-week analysis showed minimal heterogeneity (I² = 0.0%). No obvious publication bias was detected. The GRADE assessment indicated that the certainty of evidence was moderate at 2 weeks and low at all other time points, primarily due to the predominance of observational studies and high heterogeneity. Pelvic floor reconstruction during RARP may improve early urinary continence recovery. However, given the low certainty of evidence, considerable heterogeneity, and the predominance of observational data, the magnitude and durability of this benefit remain uncertain. PR should be considered a reasonable option rather than a standardized intraoperative adjunct. Further high-quality, multicenter RCTs with uniform endpoints are warranted.

title: Effect of Mechanical Alignment on Clinically Significant Outcomes, Reoperation, and Failure After Osteochondral Allograft Transplantation of the Knee.
journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
authors: Sardesai KS, Ackermann J, Vega T, Kunze KN, Jesse JE, Alfonsi S, Caplan BE, Morgan JT, Friedman LR, Gilat R, Yanke A, Chahla J, Cole BJ.
abstract: Background Identifying and addressing mechanical malalignment is an important component of treating symptomatic osteochondral defects with osteochondral allograft (OCA) transplantation. However, little is known about how malalignment influences short- to midterm outcomes after OCA transplantation. Purpose To evaluate whether mechanical alignment measurements including the hip-knee-ankle (HKA) angle, lateral distal femoral angle (LDFA), medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA), and joint line convergence angle (JLCA) predict clinically significant outcome achievement, graft failure, and reoperation after OCA transplantation with or without concomitant realignment. Study design Case series; Level of evidence, 4. Methods Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) were collected preoperatively and at a minimum 2-year follow-up in patients receiving OCA from 2005 to 2023. PROMs included the International Knee Documentation Committee score and Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score subscales. Clinically significant outcome thresholds were the minimal clinically important difference (MCID), substantial clinical benefit (SCB), and Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS). Preoperative full-length, weightbearing radiographs were used to measure the HKA angle, LDFA, MPTA, and JLCA. Multivariable logistic regression was used for clinically significant outcome achievement and all-cause reoperation; failure and arthroplasty were summarized descriptively because of the low number of events. Results A total of 66 patients (mean age, 34.1 ± 11.5 years; mean body mass index, 27.8 ± 4.8 kg/m 2 ; 50% female) met inclusion criteria. Mean alignment measurements were 1.8°± 4.0° for the HKA angle, 86.8°± 2.3° for the LDFA, 86.3°± 2.3° for the MPTA, and 1.7°± 1.0° for the JLCA. Although PROMs improved at the final follow-up, no preoperative alignment measure was statistically associated with MCID, PASS, or SCB achievement or with all-cause reoperation ( P > .05). In total, 25 (37.9%) patients underwent reoperation; graft survivorship was 93.9%, with 4 failures and 3 arthroplasty conversions. In an exploratory subanalysis, 16 patients with an HKA angle >5° of varus or valgus (13 with concomitant realignment) did not have significantly different rates of reoperation (43.8% vs 36.0%; P = .768) or graft failure (6.3% vs 6.0%; P > .999) compared to their remaining counterparts. Conclusion In this small, heterogeneous cohort, preoperative mechanical alignment measures were not statistically associated with clinically significant outcome achievement or all-cause reoperation after OCA transplantation. These hypothesis-generating findings do not establish the absence of an alignment effect or define a threshold for realignment because most patients with severe preoperative malalignment underwent concomitant realignment, which may have contributed to the favorable overall outcomes, and failure events were infrequent.

title: Does the Timing of Surgical Debridement Affect Outcomes in Septic Arthritis of the Native Hip and Knee? A Propensity-weighted Analysis.
authors: Randall ZD, Barber HF, McAndrew CM, Berkes MB.
abstract: Background Septic arthritis of the native hip and knee can cause irreversible cartilage damage and systemic illness. Because operative debridement provides source control, delaying it may permit infection to progress, potentially increasing the need for repeat surgery and the risk of death; however, evidence examining these associations remains limited. Questions/purposes Is delayed debridement associated with increased risk of (1) repeat debridement or (2) 1-year mortality in septic arthritis of the native hip and/or knee? Methods We performed a retrospective cohort study using the Florida State Inpatient Database, a statewide, all-payer database that records procedures by hospital day and includes longitudinal patient identifiers. Between October 2015 and December 2022, we identified 3587 adult admissions involving septic arthritis of the native hip (n = 1014) or knee (n = 2573) treated with surgical debridement. We excluded 1% (42 of 3587) of admitted patients in whom the first debridement occurred after hospital day 10, leaving 99% (3545 of 3587) for analysis (hip n = 1001; knee n = 2544). No included outcome or covariate data were missing. In the screened hip and knee cohorts, the mean ± SD ages were 55 ± 17 years and 60 ± 16 years, respectively, and 46% (462 of 1014) and 34% (879 of 2573) were female. Debridement occurred on hospital days 0 to 1 in 51% (506 of 1001) of hip admissions and 59% (1510 of 2544) of knee admissions; the remaining 49% (495 of 1001) and 41% (1034 of 2544), respectively, underwent debridement on day 2 or later. Stabilized inverse probability-of-treatment weighting was used to balance measured baseline covariates. Weighted log-binomial regression was used to estimate adjusted relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Among patients with septic knee arthritis, debridement on day 2 or later was associated with a higher risk of repeat debridement than debridement on days 0 to 1 (13% [133 of 1034] versus 5% [72 of 1510], adjusted RR 2.40 [95% CI 1.81 to 3.19]; p Conclusion Surgeons should prioritize prompt debridement of septic knee arthritis, and hospitals should implement coordinated pathways to avoid preventable delays. No timing-specific recommendation can be made for septic hip arthritis based on our findings. Larger multicenter studies with granular data on presentation, diagnostic aspiration, antibiotic administration, and debridement are needed to clarify whether debridement timing influences outcomes in septic hip arthritis and to distinguish preventable delays from those related to diagnostic uncertainty or the management of medical comorbidities. Level of evidence Level III, therapeutic study.

title: Distal Humerus Nonunion Following Failed Internal Fixation: How do the Outcomes of Internal Fixation and Total Elbow Arthroplasty Compare?
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Nieboer M, Yu K, Tangtiphaiboontana J, Barlow J, Morrey M, Sanchez-Sotelo J, O'Driscoll S.
abstract: Background Distal humerus nonunions are difficult to treat. The supracondylar ostectomy and shortening (S.O.S.) technique, which combines humeral shortening, parallel plating, and bone grafting, maximizes the success of internal fixation. The purpose of this study was to compare the outcomes of the S.O.S. technique with the outcomes of total elbow arthroplasty (TEA) for distal humerus nonunions. Materials and methods This retrospective review identified 25 distal humerus nonunions treated with the S.O.S. procedure and 45 TEA's performed specifically for distal humerus nonunion at a single institution between 1995 and 2019. All elbows had undergone at least 1 prior fixation attempt. The S.O.S. cohort had a younger mean age and less common intra-articular nonunion compared to the TEA cohort. Sex, mean number of prior surgeries, history of open fracture, and history of infection were similar between groups. Outcomes included complications, reoperations, range of motion, and Mayo Elbow Performance Scores (MEPS). Results In the SOS cohort, 2 elbows were lost to follow-up, 21 elbows achieved union, and 2 elbows failed to heal and subsequently underwent conversion to a TEA. Complications occurred in 9 elbows (36%) following S.O.S. compared to 18 elbows (40%) following TEA (OR 0.8, p=0.7). The rates of all-cause reoperation were 48% (12 elbows) after S.O.S vs 27% (12) after TEA (OR 2.5, p=0.08). The S.O.S. cohort had a 100° mean flexion-extension arc compared to 115° for TEA (p=0.06) with similar mean pronation-supination arcs (S.O.S. 155° vs TEA 145°, p=0.2). MEPS scores were similar between groups (S.O.S 79 points, TEA 82 points, p=0.6). When stratifying by location of nonunion, elbows with intra-articular nonunion undergoing S.O.S had a 75% reoperation rate compared to 35% for extra-articular nonunions (OR 5.5, p=0.08). Intra-articular nonunions achieved higher MEPS with TEA compared to S.O.S. (85 vs. 51 points, p Conclusion Despite achieving a high union rate, the S.O.S. procedure presented similar results compared to TEA in terms of MEPS, motion, complications, and reoperations. Elbows with an intra-articular nonunion had better outcomes with TEA while elbows with an extra-articular nonunion fared better with the S.O.S. Procedure

title: Concomitant pelvic ring injury compromises acetabular reduction quality: A propensity score-matched analysis with surgical sequence subgroup study.
authors: Lee CY, Jung WC, Lee JH, Yoon TR, Park KS.
abstract: Background Concomitant pelvic ring injury is reported to compromise acetabular fracture reduction, yet matched comparisons are scarce and the optimal surgical sequence remains debated. We assessed whether pelvic ring injury compromises anatomical acetabular reduction, and whether fixation sequence influences reduction quality and complications. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 119 consecutive patients with isolated displaced acetabular fractures and 20 patients with combined pelvic ring and acetabular injuries treated at a tertiary trauma center (2004-2023). One-to-one propensity score matching using age, sex, and Letournel classification yielded 20 matched pairs (n = 40). Within the combined group, eight patients underwent acetabulum-first and 12 underwent pelvic ring-first fixation. The primary outcome was anatomical acetabular reduction (modified Matta criteria, 0-1 mm) graded by two independent reviewers. Secondary outcomes were pelvic ring reduction and postoperative complications. Results Anatomical acetabular reduction was achieved in 14 of 20 isolated patients (70.0%) versus four of 20 combined patients (20.0%; p = 0.004). Within combined injuries, acetabulum-first showed a numerical trend toward better reduction (37.5% vs 8.3% anatomical; p = 0.132). Pelvic ring reduction did not differ between sequence subgroups (75.0% vs 83.3%; p = 0.450). Excluding pre-existing sciatic palsies, any complication occurred in two of eight acetabulum-first (25.0%) versus eight of 12 pelvic ring-first patients (66.7%; p = 0.170), driven by post-traumatic osteoarthritis (12.5% vs 41.7%). Conclusion Concomitant pelvic ring injury significantly compromises anatomical acetabular reduction. Where precise pelvic ring reduction is achievable, pelvic ring-first fixation remains appropriate; where it is not, acetabulum-first or temporary pelvic stabilization followed by definitive fixation should be considered to avoid fixing the acetabulum onto a malreduced pelvic ring.

title: Combined Arthroscopic Anterior Cruciate Ligament and Oblique Popliteal Ligament Reconstruction of the Knee.
authors: Amouzadeh Omrani F, Sarzaeem MM, Manafi Rasi A, Omidian MM, Alahgholiei A, Dolikhani M, Pourmojarab A.
abstract: The oblique popliteal ligament is the largest ligamentous structure of the posterior knee capsule and serves as a primary restraint to genu recurvatum and a contributor to rotatory stability. This technical note describes an arthroscopic-assisted method for oblique popliteal ligament reconstruction, performed as an isolated procedure or in combination with anterior cruciate ligament, posterior cruciate ligament, or multiligament knee reconstructions. Indications include symptomatic post-traumatic genu recurvatum, posterior capsular laxity, recurrent or high-risk anterior cruciate ligament failure associated with hyperextension, persistent posterior or rotational instability, and complex multiligament injuries. The technique uses standardized femoral and tibial tunnels; controlled posterior graft passage through posteromedial, trans-septal, and posterolateral portals; and fixation in slight knee flexion to optimize posterior capsular tension in full extension. The procedure is designed to restore native posterior knee biomechanics while minimizing neurovascular risk. Oblique popliteal ligament reconstruction may represent a valuable adjunct in managing selected cases of knee instability characterized by hyperextension and posterior capsular deficiency.

title: CORR Insights®: How Does the Achievement of Minimum Clinically Important Difference, Substantial Clinical Benefit, and Patient Acceptable Symptom State Change Over Time After Periacetabular Osteotomy?
authors: Allen M.

title: Beyond accuracy: is reproducibility the case for robotics in spinal trauma surgery?
authors: Soni A, Vidyadhara S, Iyer RD, Thirugnanam B, Rao SK.
abstract: The accuracy of robot-assisted pedicle screw placement is well established, largely from elective surgery for degenerative disease. Spinal trauma presents a different problem: surface landmarks are distorted, patients are often multiply injured or frail, bone quality is poor, and surgery is frequently performed out of hours by whoever is available. This narrative review proposes that the main potential contribution of robotics in spinal trauma is reproducibility, defined as low variation in the technical result across operators, cases and operating conditions, and examines how far the evidence supports this. Available data suggest that robotic accuracy depends less on surgeon experience and case difficulty than conventional techniques do, but experience still matters, and no study has tested equivalence across surgeons or conditions. Evidence for consistent performance at night or in emergencies is limited. Most of the data come from elective or mixed cohorts with technical endpoints, and reported reductions in blood loss and hospital stay often reflect percutaneous surgery rather than robotic guidance alone. We describe 202 consecutive operations for traumatic, osteoporotic and pathological spinal fractures from a single centre; these data illustrate the range of cases managed within one robotic workflow and do not test the proposal. Registration drift in unstable segments, device failure, radiation, set-up time and cost remain important limitations. The robot does not replace expertise in trauma surgery. It may move part of the expertise that governs screw placement from the individual surgeon to a trained team, but this remains to be demonstrated.

title: Age-associated alterations in morphometry, intra-cortical canals, lacunar architecture, and mineral density in Type 2 diabetes: Implications for vertebral bone fragility in ZDF rats.
authors: Ali W, Monahan G, McNamara L, Vaughan T.
abstract: Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) is associated with elevated bone fracture risk despite normal or higher bone mineral density (BMD), yet the mechanisms underlying vertebral fragility remain poorly understood. We investigated age-related changes in (1) growth, (2) microarchitecture, (3) microporosity (4) mineralization and (5) mechanical properties of vertebral bone from control and diabetic male ZDF rats at 12-weeks and 46 weeks of age. We report that vertebral growth and microarchitecture were compromised in diabetic rats at late-stage diabetes (46-weeks), as compared to control rats, evident from lower vertebral height and depth, thin cortical bone, and deteriorated trabecular architecture. While control rats maintained stable mineral density distribution with ageing, diabetic rats exhibited increased heterogeneity in cortical and trabecular bone in late-stage diabetes, despite unaffected mean BMD. In central cortical bone, diabetic rats had accelerated loss of intra-cortical canals as compared to controls with an unaffected age-driven lacunae density. In the central trabecular bone, T2D induced enlarged lacunae and altered mineral density distribution at early-stage diabetes (12 weeks), while as disease progressed, lacunae became rounder whilst maintaining lacunar density. Furthermore, age-matched differences in peri-lacunar mineralization were not found between control and diabetic rats. These multifactorial changes may contribute to the reduced failure load of vertebral body in diabetic rats (35% lower than age-matched control rats) at 46-weeks of age. Our findings underscore that fracture risk assessment and therapeutic strategies must look beyond BMD in T2D patients.

title: Adalimumab Does Not Improve Clinical Outcomes After Needle Fasciotomy for Dupuytren Contracture: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Trial.
authors: Brouwers J, Claessens F, Mergaerts L, Vandezande L, Degreef I.
abstract: Background Dupuytren disease is a fibroproliferative disorder in which tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-driven myofibroblast activity contributes to progressive digital flexion contractures by causing collagen deposition. Needle fasciotomy mechanically releases established collagen cords but does not target the underlying fibroproliferative process. Adalimumab, an anti-TNF agent, has been shown to reduce nodule hardness in early-stage Dupuytren disease, but it remains unknown whether it has additional impact combined with needle fasciotomy in more established contractures. Questions/purposes (1) Does a single perioperative intralesional injection of adalimumab immediately after needle fasciotomy increase the proportion of patients achieving at least 10° improvement in total passive extension deficit (TPED)? (2) Does adalimumab improve the change in TPED at 3 and 12 months? (3) Does adalimumab improve VAS pain and QuickDASH scores at 3 and 12 months? (4) What complications occurred in the adalimumab and placebo groups? Methods We conducted a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled pilot trial at a hand surgery department in a single academic center in adults with Dupuytren disease and an indication for needle fasciotomy. Eligible patients had a Dupuytren diathesis score greater than 4 and a nonfixed compound metacarpophalangeal and/or proximal interphalangeal contracture. Thirty patients were randomized 1:1 to receive a single 40-mg intralesional injection of adalimumab or matching saline placebo immediately after needle fasciotomy. One patient was excluded after randomization, leaving 29 patients for analysis (14 in the adalimumab group and 15 in the placebo). Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney U tests were used for categorical and continuous outcomes, respectively. Results Adalimumab did not improve the proportion of patients achieving at least a 10° improvement in TPED. At 3 months, 86% (12 of 14) of patients in the adalimumab group and 87% (13 of 15) in the placebo group achieved this improvement level, with a between-group difference in proportions of -1% (95% confidence interval [CI] -31% to 29%; p > 0.99). At 12 months, 71% (10 of 14) and 80% (12 of 15) of patients, respectively, achieved the endpoint, with a between-group difference of -9% (95% CI -41% to 24%; p = 0.68). Both groups showed no difference in change in TPED at 3 months; the median (IQR) change was -30° (-60° to -10°) versus -26° (-86° to -14°) at 3 months (Hodges-Lehmann estimate of between-group difference -4°; p = 0.76) and -32° (-60° to -5°) versus -24° (-80° to 5°) at 12 months (Hodges-Lehmann estimate of between-group difference 7°; p = 0.75). Pain and QuickDASH scores improved over time in both groups, with no between-group difference at 3 or 12 months (p > 0.05 for all). One procedure-related complication occurred; no adverse events related to either study injection were reported or observed. Conclusion A single 40-mg intralesional injection of adalimumab added to needle fasciotomy did not improve extension, TPED, pain, or QuickDASH outcomes compared with placebo at 3 or 12 months. Given the absence of detected benefit in this pilot trial, adalimumab should not be used routinely as an adjunct to needle fasciotomy outside a clinical trial. Further studies investigating repeated or higher-dose regimens, treatment at earlier disease stages, and potential combination approaches are needed to better define the therapeutic role of anti-TNF treatment and determine whether it may have a clinical application before its use in routine practice can be considered. Level of evidence Level II, therapeutic study.

title: 18-years Follow-up after Mosaicplasty in Adolescent Athletes with Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Elbow.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Toftdahl L, Ovesen J, Thillemann TM.
abstract: Background Autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty is an established surgical treatment of unstable osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) lesions of the elbow. However, the information on the long-term outcomes is lacking. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the long-term clinical and radiographic results after autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty in the treatment of OCD of the elbow. Methods This prospective long-term follow-up study is an extension of previously published data on 10 patients treated with autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty due to advanced, unstable OCD at the capitellum from 2003-2007. Objective and patient-reported outcomes were evaluated including Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Oxford Elbow Score, Quick-Disability of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (Quick-DASH), Timmerman-Andrews Score, a Subjective Elbow Value, and Range of Motion (ROM). Radiographic signs of osteoarthritis were graded according to the Kellgren-Lawrence classification. Results At mean 18 years (range 16.0-19.7) five patients were available for follow-up. Mean age at follow-up was 34.4, and all five patients were women. MEPS was a median 100 (range 85-100). Activities of daily life were mildly affected in two patients. Two patients had non-symptomatic osteoarthritis grade 1 and 2. Patients experienced a functioning and near-normal elbow. Conclusion The long-term results after mosaicplasty are encouraging, and we find it reasonable to recommend mosaicplasty as the surgical treatment in this group of female patients with advanced, unstable OCD lesions of the elbow. However, it is of concern that two out of five patients had non-symptomatic early radiographic signs of osteoarthritis at an early age. As this study has an inclusion rate of 50 % of the original cohort, attrition bias must be taken into consideration. Level of evidence Level IV, case series, treatment study.

title: Upper body posture affects three-dimensional scapula orientation: Clinically applicable models may quantify patient-specific scapula orientation in an upright standing patient.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Ritter D, Dampier K, Olmsted AD, Poltaretskyi S, Raiss P, Bachmaier S, Moroder P.
abstract: Background Scapulothoracic orientation is a key determinant of shoulder function and influences implant positioning and clinical outcomes in shoulder arthroplasty. However, current preoperative planning relies on supine CT scans, which does not represent the patient's upright scapular orientation. Clinically viable methods to quantify upright scapula orientation are lacking. The aim of this study was to quantify upper-body posture obtained from simple lateral photographs. We hypothesized that these photographs can be used to predict three-dimensional (3D) scapular orientation in an upright position. Methods A database of 123 lateral photographs was used in this study to extract clinical assessment parameters (CAPs): forward head posture (FHP), forward shoulder posture (FSP), thoracic kyphosis index (TKI), and forward elbow-humerus ratio (EHF). A validated 3D skeletal upper-body model was used to simulate nine sagittal posture variations, generating corresponding scapular orientations: internal rotation (SIR), anterior tilt (SAT), and upward rotation (SUR). Each CAP was correlated with the 3D model outputs. Weighted correlation models were developed to predict continuous upright scapular orientations for each patient photograph. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering (Ward's method) identified objective upper body posture subgroups. Results All CAPs demonstrated normal distributions. Clustering revealed three distinct sagittal posture groups. Strong correlations were found between CAPs and scapular orientation in the 3D model, particularly between TKI and all scapular angles (R 2 ≥ 0.94). Applying these correlations enabled continuous prediction of upright scapular orientation in all subjects. Predicted SIR, SAT, and SUR differed significantly between posture clusters (P Conclusion Upper body posture in the standing position correlates with upright scapular orientation. Quantifying posture through simple lateral photographs and applying prediction models provides a clinically feasible method to estimate patient-specific upright scapula orientation. This posture-informed approach offers a practical adjunct to supine CT-based preoperative planning and may improve accuracy in implant positioning and range-of-motion simulation. Level of evidence Basic Science Study, Computational Modeling.

title: Subtotal cricoid cartilage resection and crico-tracheal reconstruction for papillary thyroid carcinoma involving cricoid.
authors: Pang F, Ma G, Shi Z, Liu D, Guo Y, Xie L, Zhuang S, Xie M, Wu L, Liu T.
abstract: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) invading laryngotracheal structures is challenging. When most of the cricoid is involved, total laryngectomy is often recommended. We describe a function-preserving alternative using subtotal cricoid resection and crico-tracheal reconstruction. A 51-year-old man with recurrent PTC after thyroidectomy, neck dissections, and radioactive iodine presented with dyspnea. The tumor involved ~75% of the cricoid cartilage and the first to fourth tracheal rings. Subtotal cricoid excision preserved the left one-quarter, followed by tracheal rotation and anastomosis to the residual cricoid. Recovery was uneventful. Oral feeding began on day 15 and decannulation occurred on day 21. Bronchoscopy on day 25 showed a patent airway and a well-healed anastomosis. Margins were negative. At 1.5 years, voice was satisfactory without dyspnea or recurrence. In selected PTC with major cricoid involvement, subtotal cricoid resection with crico-tracheal reconstruction can preserve laryngeal function.

title: Stemless Anatomic Total Shoulder Arthroplasty is Associated with Less Opioid Use at Initial Follow-up.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Krumm ZR, Denard PJ, Brockmeier SF, Petre D, Kissenberth M, Shah A, Lederman E, Werner BC.
abstract: Background As the rates of total shoulder arthroplasty (TSA) rise, surgeons are tasked with the need to manage initial postoperative pain to facilitate outpatient surgeries and increase functional and patient reported outcomes while minimizing avoidable complications and revision. Of particular interest is the effect of anatomic TSA (aTSA) design on postoperative pain and opioid use, especially in light of the national effort to reduce opioid prescriptions following orthopedic surgery. Methods A multi-center retrospective cohort study was performed on patients who underwent either short-stem or stemless aTSA between 2013 and 2023. Two cohorts were established and baseline data on demographics, preoperative Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain, and preoperative opioid use were obtained. The primary endpoint of this study was the postoperative VAS pain at the initial (10-14 day) postoperative follow-up, with the reported opioid use and the need for opioid medication refill as secondary endpoints. Student's t-test was performed on continuous variables, and chi-square or Fisher's exact test was performed on categorical variables as appropriate. Multivariable linear regression was performed to determine predictors of postoperative VAS. Results 817 patients were included in this study; 366 patients in the short-stem cohort and 451 in the stemless cohort. No difference was observed between groups for the preoperative VAS pain (p=0.102), postoperative VAS pain (p=0.838), and change in VAS pain (p=0.117). The prevalence of opioid use was lower at the initial follow-up visit in the stemless cohort (35.4% vs 48.9% in short-stem, p Conclusion Patients undergoing stemless aTSA may not demonstrate different postoperative pain scores at initial follow-up than patients undergoing short-stem aTSA; however, use of a stemless aTSA has a weak to moderate association with less opioid medication use at initial follow-up. Although there was no statistically significant difference in postoperative VAS pain scores, patients who underwent stemless aTSA used less opioid medication by their initial 10-14 day postoperative visit than their short-stemmed aTSA comparison cohort. Level of evidence Level III; Retrospective Cohort Comparison; Treatment Study.

title: Robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty: a narrative review of resection accuracy and individualized soft-tissue balance.
authors: Shen L, Zhai C, Jiang T, Wang Y.
abstract: Robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (RA-TKA) was introduced to reduce variability in bone resection and component positioning. Contemporary platforms do much more than that: they combine three-dimensional planning, intraoperative registration, objective gap assessment and virtual component adjustment. As a result, the question has shifted from whether a robot can reproduce a planned resection to whether robotic data can be used to individualize alignment and soft-tissue balance. This review follows that shift and examines the clinical evidence behind it. This narrative review examined the relationship between robotic resection accuracy, individualized soft-tissue balancing, and clinical outcomes. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched for English-language peer-reviewed studies published between January 2010 and September 2026, using combinations of the terms ("robotics" OR "robotic" OR "robot-assisted" OR "robotic-assisted" OR "robot arm" OR "robotic arm") AND ("arthroplasty, replacement, knee" OR "total knee arthroplasty" OR "total knee replacement" OR "knee arthroplasty" OR "knee replacement"). Reference lists of key reviews and primary studies were hand-searched. Priority was given to randomized trials, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, large comparative cohorts, long-term studies, and studies that quantified intraoperative gap or laxity behavior. The most reproducible advantage of RA-TKA is still execution accuracy, with fewer limb- and component-alignment outliers than conventional instrumentation. The newer value proposition is more complex. Depending on the platform and workflow, robotic systems can quantify compartment gaps and support virtual component adjustments, while force-controlled assessment is available in selected systems. These capabilities may reduce soft-tissue releases, but their clinical value depends on the balancing strategy and target definitions. Contemporary functional and patient-specific workflows often achieve high rates of predefined gap balance while keeping joint-line orientation within guardrails. Clinical superiority, however, is inconsistent. In recent randomized trials, functional alignment markedly reduced soft-tissue release, but patient-reported outcomes were not consistently superior to mechanical alignment at 2 years. Long-term survivorship data remain limited and conflicting, and economic value depends heavily on procedural volume, platform costs and downstream resource use. RA-TKA improves execution accuracy and can facilitate quantitative soft-tissue assessment and individualized planning. These capabilities have not established consistent superiority in patient-reported outcomes or survivorship. Further evidence is needed to validate alignment and laxity targets and determine the long-term clinical and economic value of specific workflows.

title: Relative Real-time Arthroscopic Evaluation of Glenohumeral Structural Failure during Manipulation under Anesthesia for Primary Frozen Shoulder.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Abdel-Mordy Kandeel A, Lasheen MM, Ali Elsayed AF, Morsi E.
abstract: Background Patterns of glenohumeral structural failure during manipulation under anesthesia (MUA) for management of frozen shoulder (FS) have not yet been thoroughly examined. This study investigated the necessity of macroscopic glenohumeral capsular failure/tearing during MUA for motion restoration in patients with primary FS. Methods This prospective case-series study (conducted between November 2023 and May 2025) included 31 patients with primary FS. Patients were managed with 1 st -look arthroscopy (evaluating the integrity of the different glenohumeral structures) followed by MUA, 2 nd -look arthroscopy (documenting the primary outcome of the study; i.e., post-manipulation glenohumeral structural disruptions/failure, especially the capsular tears), and then combined anterior and posterior arthroscopic glenohumeral release. Secondary outcome measurements included immediate post-MUA passive range of motion (ROM), as well as 6-month postoperative (post-MUA and arthroscopic release) ROM and Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) scores. Results The mean age of included patients was (52.41±11.31) years. 2 nd -look arthroscopy revealed post-manipulation disruption of the intra-articular adhesions and the superior glenohumeral ligament in all (100%) patients; however, no capsular tear was detected in any patient. Otherwise, different glenohumeral structures showed post-manipulation minor failure (not necessitating repair), including superior labrum from anterior to posterior (SLAP) lesion in 4 (12.8%), antero-inferior labral detachment in 4 (12.8%), middle gleno-humeral tear in 3 (9.7%), inferior glenohumeral ligament tear in 1 (3.2%), partial articular-sided supraspinatus tendon avulsion (PASTA) lesion in 4 (12. 8%), and partial subscapularis tear in 3 (9.7%) patients. Major structural failure (necessitating repair) was encountered in 6.4% of the study group, including a full-thickness rotator cuff tear in 1 (3.2%) patient and an avulsion fracture of the greater tuberosity in another (3.2%) patient. There was an immediate post-manipulation significant improvement in passive ROM with further significant improvement on 6-month postoperative evaluation (P-value ˂0.05). In addition, the final postoperative evaluation revealed significant improvement in VAS and ASES scores (P-value ˂0.05). Conclusion Immediate post-MUA motion restoration in middle-aged patients with primary FS might be attributed to the MUA-induced disruption of the intra-articular adhesions (a consistently encountered finding in this study) and/or capsular stretching out/micro-tears (rather than capsular macro-tears). However, currently reported conclusions should be validated via further larger-volume cohort clinical studies.

title: Recurrence After Primary Lumbar Discectomy: Rate, Reoperation, and Risk Factors in A Single-Center Cohort Over A 10-Year Study Period.
authors: Yıldızhan S, Rakip U, Canbek İ, Gazi Boyacı M, Korkmaz S, Aslan A.
abstract: Objective Recurrent lumbar disc herniation after primary discectomy is a clinically important complication whose temporal pattern, revision surgical profile, and associated comorbidities remain incompletely characterized in long-term cohorts. We aimed to define the rate and timing of reoperation-confirmed recurrence, characterize the revision profile, and examine associated risk factors. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 432 consecutive patients who underwent primary lumbar discectomy between January 2015 and December 2024, with a median follow-up of 85 months (interquartile range 50-103). Recurrence was defined as reoperation-confirmed, same-level ipsilateral reherniation after an initial pain-free interval. Follow-up status and external reoperations were verified through the national electronic health record system up to the study end date (6 March 2026), with no loss to follow-up. Associations were examined using multivariable logistic regression (with Firth penalization) and Cox proportional hazards modeling. Results Reoperation-confirmed recurrence occurred in 28 patients (6.5%); this represents the reoperation-confirmed recurrence rate rather than the overall incidence of recurrent herniation, since conservatively managed recurrences were not counted. Recurrence was predominantly late, with 68% of events beyond the first postoperative year (median 18.5 months). At reoperation, 21 patients (75%) required instrumented posterolateral fusion for objective segmental instability, with a mean segmental translation of 4.2 ± 1.1 mm and a mean angulation of 12.2° ± 2.1° on dynamic flexion-extension radiographs, both exceeding the predefined instability thresholds. The remaining 7 patients (25%) underwent revision discectomy alone. No second recurrence occurred over a median post-revision follow-up of 61.5 months. In the primary logistic model, hypertension was associated with recurrence (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 3.42, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.04-11.21; p = 0.043), whereas the association of diabetes mellitus was of similar magnitude but did not reach statistical significance (OR 3.17, 95% CI 0.97-10.35; p = 0.056). Diabetes mellitus reached significance only in the secondary Firth penalized and time-to-event analyses. Active smoking was not associated with recurrence (OR 0.64; p = 0.321). Given the limited number of events (n = 28), these findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory; in particular, the study was not powered to overturn existing evidence linking smoking with recurrence, and the 10-year survival estimate is exploratory given few patients at risk beyond 5 years. Conclusion In this 10-year single-center cohort, reoperation-confirmed recurrence occurred in 6.5% of patients and was predominantly late (median 18.5 months), indicating that postoperative surveillance should extend beyond the first year. Three quarters of revisions required instrumented fusion for objective instability. No second recurrence was observed. Hypertension was associated with recurrence in the primary analysis, whereas the association of diabetes mellitus did not reach significance in the primary model and was supported only by secondary analyses. Both comorbidities should be investigated further in adequately powered multicenter studies.

title: Precision in achieving planned HKA alignment using a hybrid method of resection in imageless robot assisted total knee arthroplasty: a retroprospective study of 103 knees.
authors: Rathod PM, Raju S, Nehru AP, Vasudevan V, Naik R, Singhi PK, Chandrasekaran N.
abstract: Evidence on hybrid robotic-resection workflows in robotic-assisted TKA is limited. This study quantified agreement between planned, intraoperatively achieved, and early postoperative standing hip-knee-ankle (HKA) alignment using a hybrid resection workflow with the CORI system. We retrospectively reviewed 85 patients (103 knees) from 264 consecutive primary TKAs performed with the imageless hand-held robot (CORI) system at a single center between September 2024 and August 2025. The distal femur was resected and the proximal tibia refined with the burr, and the remaining femoral cuts were made with a conventional 4-in-1 jig. HKA was measured preoperatively, as planned, and as achieved intraoperatively after resections with trials and on full-length weight-bearing radiographs at 3 weeks. Forgotten joint score (FJS 12) was recorded at 6 months. Agreement was assessed using mean signed error, RMSE, and 95% confidence intervals, and measurement reliability using ICC for inter and intra-observer variations. The cohort comprised 85 patients (103 knees; 67 unilateral, 18 bilateral). Mean preoperative HKA was 166.1° ± 6.7° and improved to 177.8° ± 1.9° on early postoperative standing radiographs. Planned HKA was 178.8° ± 0.8° and intraoperatively achieved HKA was 178.0° ± 1.6°, a mean signed error of - 0.8° ± 1.3° (95% CI), indicating slight under-correction relative to plan. RMSE was 1.50° (planned vs achieved), 2.17° (planned vs postoperative), and 1.98° (achieved vs postoperative). Mean FJS 12 at 6 months was 76.0 ± 11.8 (range 54-95) Measurement reliability (inter and intra observer) was good to excellent (ICC 0.89-0.98).In this retrospective series, the hybrid CORI workflow showed close agreement between planned, intraoperatively achieved, and early postoperative standing HKA, with a small mean under-correction of 0.8° relative to plan. These findings are descriptive; without a comparator or long-term clinical outcomes, they cannot establish equivalence to fully robotic or conventional TKA. Prospective comparative studies are needed to evaluate the comparisons.

title: Postoperative prophylactic and delayed oral antibiotics after total shoulder arthroplasty: a multi-institutional database analysis.
authors: Shehadeh TH, Singh A, Chaudhry J, Lanham N.
abstract: Background To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of prophylactic and delayed postoperative oral antibiotics following total shoulder arthroplasty (TSA). Methods The TriNetX database was queried for primary TSA patients. Those with prior pathologic fracture, upper extremity malignancy, infection, prosthetic joint infection (PJI), or revision surgery within 6 months were excluded. After 1:1 propensity score matching, two comparisons were performed: (1) prophylactic oral antibiotics within 1 postoperative day versus controls (n=5,891 per cohort) and (2) delayed oral antibiotics on postoperative days 7-30 versus controls (n=3,087 per cohort). Outcomes at 30 and 90 days included acute kidney injury (AKI), emergency department (ED) visits, readmission, PJI, and revision surgery. Results At 30 days, prophylactic antibiotics were associated with fewer readmissions (2.78% vs. 3.73%; P=0.004), with no differences in AKI, ED visits, PJI, or revision surgery. At 90 days, they were associated with higher PJI (0.92% vs. 0.48%; P=0.004) and a trend toward lower ED visits (5.25% vs. 6.16%; P=0.032) and readmissions (3.70% vs. 4.67%; P=0.009), but higher revision surgery (1.17% vs. 0.73%; P=0.014). Delayed antibiotics were associated with higher rates of AKI, ED visits, readmissions, and revision surgery at both 30 and 90 days (all P Conclusions Although residual confounding cannot be excluded, postoperative prophylactic or delayed oral antibiotics were not associated with reduced PJI or revision surgery and may be associated with antibiotic-related adverse effects. Level of evidence: III.

title: Patients Use Google to Ask Questions About the Structure, Function, and Risks of Peptide Use in Orthopaedic Surgery.
authors: Obana KK, Weiss DL, Chen JY, Levine SB, Chen AZ, Luzzi AJ, Trofa DP.
abstract: Purpose To identify the common patient questions and to evaluate the quality of online resources regarding peptide therapy, namely, body protection compound-157, in orthopaedic surgery. Methods Three orthopaedic peptide searches were entered into a clean Google Web Search on June 30, 2025. Questions under the "People also ask" tab were expanded sequentially. The first 100 consecutive results meeting inclusion criteria for each query were included (300 total). Questions or websites unrelated to orthopaedic peptides and repeat verbatim questions within each query were excluded. Questions were categorized into 1 of 3 Rothwell Classifications and subcategorized by topic. Websites were categorized based on source. The Journal of the American Medical Association Benchmark Criteria was used to evaluate the quality of each website. Results Most questions fell into the Rothwell Fact category (61.0%). Most common question topics were Structure/Function (31.7%), Risks/Complications (20.7%), and Treatment Comparisons (9.7%). The least common question topics were Specific Activities (0%), Pain (0.3%), Longevity of Treatment (0.7%), and Management (0.7%). The most common websites were Commercial (28.0%), Academic (18.0%), and Government (18.0%). PubMed articles consisted of 98.1% of Government websites. The overall average Journal of the American Medical Association score was 2.0 ± 1.5. Government websites had the highest score (3.6 ± 0.7) and constituted 48.6% of websites with a score of 4/4. Medical Practice and Single Surgeon websites had the lowest Journal of the American Medical Association score of 0.7 ± 1.0 and 0.7 ± 0.9, respectively. Conclusions The most common online patient questions pertain to the structure, function, and risks associated with peptide therapy. The quality of the information is heterogeneous. Clinical relevance Because of the increasing popularity and accessibility, improved technology, and limited research, physicians should be aware of the most common online patient questions pertaining to peptide therapy in orthopaedics. Care should be taken when presenting the impact of peptides without discussing the quality to avoid overvaluing its impact.

title: Operative versus nonoperative management of olecranon fractures in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Lima JPC, Morales Ribeiro V, Segatti R, Butturi Varone B, Dos Santos Cardoso F, Giordano V.
abstract: Introduction Displaced olecranon fractures in the frail geriatric patient represent a therapeutic challenge, involving the decision between operating to achieve anatomical reduction of the articular surface or not operating due to the high risks associated with poor bone quality and failure of mechanical fixation. Materials and methods PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane were systematically searched for studies published from inception through February 2026 comparing tension band wiring, plate fixation, or cerclage wiring with nonoperative treatment for displaced olecranon fractures in geriatric patients. Risk ratio (RR) was used to evaluate binary outcomes, and standard mean difference (SMD) for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Of 459 articles, eight studies were included. A total of 723 older adults were included. Most patients had Mayo type IIA or IIB fractures. Tension band wiring was the most frequently performed surgical technique, followed by plate fixation and cerclage wiring. Operative treatment was associated with a lower risk of radiographic nonunion (RR 0.19; 95% CI 0.04, 0.8) but increased the risk of overall complications (RR 3.21; 95% CI 1.63, 6.35) and reoperation (RR 4.85; 95% CI 1.72, 13.65) compared to nonoperative treatment. Physical function showed a non-significant trend toward improvement with operative treatment (SMD -0.29; 95% CI -0.72, 0.14). At final follow-up, pain intensity was low and comparable between the two treatment groups across the majority of studies. Approximately half of the reoperation excess comprised elective or symptomatic implant removal, and the overall certainty of the evidence is low. Conclusion In older adults with displaced olecranon fractures, operative management was associated with a reduced risk of radiographic nonunion and with a higher risk of complications and reoperation compared to nonoperative management. Level of evidence Level III Systematic Review/MetaAnalysis Treatment Study.

title: Long-term clinical outcomes of distal biceps tendon reconstruction using fascia lata allograft.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Fawzy H, Hilgersom NFJ, Nijs A, Oost IK, Eygendaal D, The B.
abstract: Background Distal biceps tendon reconstruction using graft augmentation is indicated when primary repair is not feasible. Long-term outcome data on fascia lata allograft reconstruction remain limited. The purpose of this study was to evaluate long-term functional outcomes, complications, and patient satisfaction following distal biceps tendon reconstruction using fascia lata allograft. Methods This retrospective case series included adult patients who underwent distal biceps tendon reconstruction using fascia lata allograft between June 2008 and June 2023. Thirty-nine eligible patients were identified, of whom 27 were included in the final analysis after providing informed consent. Baseline characteristics, surgical details, and complications were obtained from medical records. Long-term outcomes were assessed at a single follow-up time point using patient-reported outcome measures, including the Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (QuickDASH) and the Oxford Elbow Score (OES), as well as additional questions regarding satisfaction and return to work and sports participation. Results Twenty-seven male patients were included with a median age of 49 years (range, 36-64) and a median follow-up of 78 months (range, 15-190). Sixteen complications occurred in 12 patients (44%), of which 11 (69%) were minor. The most common complication was lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve neuropraxia (56%), which resolved in most cases. The mean QuickDASH score was 10 and the mean OES was 88. Among patients employed prior to injury, 77% returned to work. Among those participating in sports before injury, 52% resumed their previous sport level and frequency. Overall satisfaction and satisfaction with arm function were high (mean, 4.3/5), whereas satisfaction with arm appearance was lower (mean, 3.1/5). Conclusion Fascia lata allograft reconstruction for chronic distal biceps tendon ruptures provides good long-term functional outcomes and high overall patient satisfaction. Although complication rates were notable, most events were minor and transient. Occupational demands and cosmetic expectations should be considered during preoperative counseling.

title: Large Language Models Aligned With Medical Experts on Established Topics but Were Less Aligned on Emerging or Debated Topics in Posterolateral Corner Treatment: An Artificial Intelligence-Augmented Delphi Study.
authors: Yu Y, Tollefson LV, LaPrade RF, Chahla J, Oettl FC, Samuelsson K, Feldt R.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate how Large Language Models (LLMs) align with a concurrently performed human medical expert-modified Delphi study on the posterolateral corner and to qualitatively analyze LLM behavior. Methods Four commercially available and current LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Pro. GPT-4o, o4-mini, and o3) were tasked with rating posterolateral corner consensus statements on a 5-point Likert scale and estimating the level of expert consensus for each statement, mirroring a human expert Delphi process. LLM performance was evaluated based on alignment with expert majority opinion, accuracy in predicting expert consensus, and self-consistency across multiple LLM invocations. Deep research to improve LLM performance was also explored. Results LLM-generated ratings showed moderate correlation with average expert ratings, with some models exhibiting tendencies toward overly positive ratings. Consensus derived from LLM self-consistency did not reliably approximate expert consensus. LLM estimates of consensus were informative, with some models showing improved alignment with actual expert consensus. Qualitative analysis revealed distinct behavioral patterns across different LLMs regarding justification generation, certainty expression, and handling of conflicting evidence. Preliminary findings suggest that deep research capabilities can enhance rating accuracy as well as consensus prediction. Evidence of hallucination in LLM reasoning is observed and requires further verification. Conclusions Although LLMs show potential in reflecting expert medical knowledge and estimating consensus, their direct ratings and self-consistency may not perfectly align with expert panels. Different LLMs display unique strengths and weaknesses, suggesting that model selection or a combination can be beneficial for applications like modified Delphi studies. Improved consensus estimation was seen by providing the models access to web search, enabling them to find recent, relevant research articles. Level of evidence Level V, expert opinion.

title: Knotless Suture Anchors Reduce Repair Time in Arthroscopic Hip Labral Repair Compared With Knotted Anchors.
authors: Kahana-Rojkind AH, McCarroll T, Quesada-Jimenez R, Reyes-Cordova A, Sandler D, Sugarman EP, Domb BG.
abstract: Purpose To compare procedure time between knotless and knotted all-suture anchors during arthroscopic acetabular labral repair in a cadaveric model and to evaluate implications for surgical training and workflow efficiency. Methods Ten fresh-frozen cadaveric hemipelvis specimens underwent arthroscopic labral repair. Five specimens (20 anchors) were repaired using knotted all-suture anchors, and 5 specimens (20 anchors) were repaired using tensionable knotless all-suture anchors. A standardized simple-loop suture configuration was used in all repairs. Repair time per anchor was recorded and subdivided into "Pass," "Tie/Convert," and "Cut" phases. Comparisons between groups were performed using independent t tests or Mann-Whitney U tests, with α = 0.05. Results Mean total repair time per anchor was significantly shorter in the knotless group (79.36 ± 18.07 seconds) compared with the knotted group (142.48 ± 27.96 seconds; P = .007). Tie/Convert phase was also significantly shorter in the knotless group (15.92 ± 4.50 seconds vs 73.11 ± 18.44 seconds; P P = .050). Cut phase was shorter with knotless anchors (11.35 ± 4.93 seconds vs 25.70 ± 27.06 seconds; P = .191) although not statistically significant. Conclusions Knotless suture anchors significantly reduced acetabular labral repair time compared with knotted anchors in this cadaveric model, primarily because of a shorter Tie/Convert phase required for suture fixation. Clinical relevance Knotless suture anchors may streamline labral repair by eliminating arthroscopic knot tying. Their technical simplicity and efficiency may benefit surgical training and enhance consistency among less experienced surgeons.

title: Infliximab for Refractory Diffuse Sclerosing Osteomyelitis of the Mandible Associated With Ulcerative Colitis: A Case Report.
authors: Yao M, Obata K, Takei K, Miyake Y, Fujishima M, Kishimoto K.
abstract: Diffuse sclerosing osteomyelitis (DSO) of the mandible is a chronic nonbacterial inflammatory bone disease. We report a 65-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis who presented with swelling and pain of the left mandible. The lesion was refractory to tooth extraction, prolonged antibiotics, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. CT showed widespread loss of trabecular structure and osteosclerosis, and bone scintigraphy demonstrated abnormal uptake confined to the mandible, without findings suggestive of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome. DSO was diagnosed based on the overall clinical course, progressive radiological findings, persistence despite treatment of the suspected odontogenic foci and repeated antibiotic therapy, and supportive histopathological findings. Anti-tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) therapy was considered for the refractory DSO, and infliximab was selected because it is also effective for ulcerative colitis; her symptoms resolved promptly, and imaging showed marked improvement with restoration of trabecular bone. No relapse or treatment-related adverse events occurred during 3 years of follow-up. The clinical and radiographic improvement observed following infliximab treatment in this older adult raises the possibility that TNF-α-mediated inflammatory pathways may be involved in refractory DSO associated with ulcerative colitis and supports further investigation of anti-TNF-α therapy in this setting.

title: Glycerin suppositories as inexpensive multi-sequence MRI skin markers.
authors: Blum A, Clara M, Taihi A, Noureddine R, Teixeira PG, Boubaker F, Gillet R.
abstract: Objective To assess MRI conspicuity and clinical usability of a commercially available glycerin suppository as a low-cost skin marker for musculoskeletal MRI across routine sequences. Materials and methods A glycerin suppository was compared in vivo with vitamin E, water, olive oil, and diluted gadoteric acid solution across routine musculoskeletal MRI sequences. Conspicuity was scored independently by two musculoskeletal radiologists on a 4-point ordinal scale. Clinical usability was retrospectively assessed in 130 examinations at 1.5 and 3 T. One fat-sensitive image set (conventional T1-weighted or Dixon fat-only) and one fluid-sensitive set were scored independently by two readers. Scores of 2 or higher defined usability. Inter-reader agreement was assessed with Cohen kappa. Results Experimentally, the glycerin suppository showed the most consistent multi-sequence visibility among the tested markers. Unlike vitamin E markers, it remained highly conspicuous on fat-suppressed T1-weighted, fat-suppressed T2-weighted, and Dixon water-only images; it remained visible on STIR but showed lower conspicuity on Dixon fat-only images. Packaging did not affect visibility. Clinically, the marker was usable on both image sets in 123/130 examinations (94.6%) for reader 1 and 120/130 (92.3%) for reader 2. Usability on conventional T1-weighted images was 100% for both readers but decreased on Dixon fat-only reconstructions to 80.0% and 66.7%, respectively. Weighted kappa was 0.90 for fat-sensitive and 0.88 for fluid-sensitive scores. No marker-related image-quality degradation occurred. Conclusion Glycerin suppositories are inexpensive, disposable MRI skin markers with broad sequence visibility. Their limitation is reduced conspicuity on Dixon fat-only reconstructions.

title: Functional Outcomes After Total Ankle Replacement: A Forgotten Joint Score-12 Analysis With Up to 10-Year Follow-up.
authors: Shetty CB, Wales K, Shah K, Ramanathan AK.
abstract: BackgroundTotal ankle replacement (TAR) offers pain relief and preservation of motion in patients with end-stage ankle arthritis. The Forgotten Joint Score-12 (FJS-12) is a validated patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) designed to assess joint awareness, but data in TAR remain limited.MethodsA retrospective study of all TARs performed at our institution between 2014 and 2023 was conducted. Patients with a minimum of 2 years of follow-up were contacted by telephone, and the FJS-12 was administered. Mean follow-up was 4.83 ± 2.48 years (range 2-10). Demographics, surgical details, and complications were recorded. Statistical analyses explored factors associated with FJS-12 scores. At the end of FJS-12 administration, patients graded their satisfaction on a 4-point Likert scale.ResultsOf 102 ankles screened, 81 patients were eligible (mean age 69.7 years; mean body mass index [BMI] 31.3). Female sex (P = .008), right-sided TAR (P = .004), and additional tendo-Achilles lengthening (P = .004) were associated with lower FJS-12 scores. Scores declined at 3 years post-surgery (P = .011). Other factors, including BMI, smoking, and hypertension, had no significant impact. Based on the score distribution and satisfaction analysis, the Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) threshold corresponded to an FJS-12 of 43, and the forgotten-joint threshold to 85.ConclusionTotal ankle replacement provided favorable short- to mid-term functional outcomes, as measured by the FJS-12. The FJS-12 is a sensitive PROM that detects subtle differences in patient-reported outcomes and may be a useful adjunct in routine TAR follow-up. We propose preliminary TAR-specific PASS and forgotten-joint thresholds that closely match those reported for knee replacement and are lower than those for hip replacement. These thresholds provide clinically meaningful benchmarks for patient satisfaction and should be validated in larger, prospective, multicentre cohorts.Level of Evidence:Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Female Sex Is Independently Associated With Greater Sagittal Tibial Tubercle-Trochlear Groove Distance and Patellar Tilt in High-Grade Trochlear Dysplasia.
authors: Hartmann M, Caliskan B, Ackermann J, Fucentese SF.
abstract: Purpose To assess sex-related differences in patellofemoral (PF) anatomy among patients with PF instability and high-grade trochlear dysplasia (Dejour types B-D). Methods Consecutive patients with symptomatic PF instability and high-grade trochlear dysplasia (Dejour types B-D) who were scheduled for surgical treatment between January 2010 and December 2020 and had available preoperative radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging were retrospectively identified at a single center. Patients with normal trochlear morphology, type A dysplasia, missing preoperative magnetic resonance imaging, or prior osseous procedures were excluded. Standardized magnetic resonance imaging-based measurements were obtained for trochlear morphology, tibial tubercle position, and patellar geometry. Depending on data distribution, parametric or nonparametric tests were used to compare sexes. Multivariate linear mixed-effects models were performed to calculate regression coefficients ( B ) with 95% confidence intervals, adjusting for patient clustering, age, body height, supratrochlear spur height, Caton-Deschamps index, sulcus depth, and tibiofemoral rotation. Results A total of 301 knees from 278 patients were analyzed; 192 knees (63.8%) were from female patients. The mean age was 22.6 ± 8.1 years (range, 11-50 years), and the mean body mass index was 24.9 ± 5.5 (range, 16.4-48.1). Distribution according to the Dejour classification was 40.5% type B, 31.2% type C, and 28.2% type D. Female patients showed smaller patellar width (37.9 ± 3.4 mm vs 41.3 ± 4.1 mm; P P P = .001) and sagittal tibial tubercle-trochlear groove (sTTTG) distance (9.9 ± 5.2 mm vs 8.4 ± 6.0 mm; P = .005). After adjustment for age and body height, differences in patellar width, patellar thickness, patellar tilt, and sTTTG remained significant. After additional adjustment for supratrochlear spur height, Caton-Deschamps index, sulcus depth, and tibiofemoral rotation, patellar tilt ( B = 3.51°, P = .021) and sTTTG distance ( B = 2.36 mm, P = .004) remained greater in female patients. Conclusions Among patients with PF instability and high-grade trochlear dysplasia, female sex was associated with greater patellar tilt and sTTTG distance after adjustment for age, body height, and relevant anatomical covariates. Level of evidence Level III, prognostic retrospective comparative study.

title: Endoscopically Assisted Periacetabular Osteotomy for Treatment of Hip Dysplasia: The Orthopaedic Total Extraperitoneal Approach.
authors: Öztürk V, Çelik M, Çağdaşer S, Hürmeydan ÖM, Aslantaş FÇ, Kural C, Bilgili MG.
abstract: The orthopaedic total extraperitoneal (O-TEP) approach is an endoscopic technique that has recently emerged as an option, particularly for the surgical management of pelvic and acetabular fractures. Unlike conventional orthopaedic endoscopic procedures, O-TEP was developed by adapting the laparoscopic totally extraperitoneal approach, commonly used for inguinal hernia repair, to orthopaedic surgery. In technically demanding procedures such as periacetabular osteotomy (PAO), minimizing soft-tissue dissection and directly visualizing critical neurovascular structures are essential. Owing to its minimally invasive design, the O-TEP PAO technique is intended to limit soft-tissue dissection while enabling direct visualization of key vascular and neural structures at risk. This Technical Note provides a step-by-step description of O-TEP PAO technique for acetabular dysplasia and discusses its feasibility, potential advantages, and key limitations in the context of the current literature on endoscopy-assisted PAO techniques.

title: Diagnosis and Management of Quadrilateral Space Syndrome Using Arthroscopic, Extra-Capsular Axillary Nerve Release.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Whitelaw K, Vasquez D, Wiley N, Macksood J, Elhassan B, Lohre R.
abstract: Introduction Quadrilateral space syndrome (QSS) is an uncommon condition that can produce debilitating shoulder pain and dysfunction. Management has been mediated through various open and arthroscopic techniques, though cohort studies remain limited. Given the lack of literature covering QSS, the objective of this study is to characterize patient outcomes of arthroscopic axillary nerve release within the quadrilateral space. Our hypothesis is that quadrilateral space syndrome can be treated with an arthroscopic, all extra-capsular release to improve pain and measured patient reported outcome measures (PROMs). Materials & methods A retrospective chart review was performed of all patients diagnosed with quadrilateral space syndrome and receiving arthroscopic quadrilateral space release at a single institution performed by two surgeons between 2021 and 2024. Patient demographics, pre-and post-injection patient reported outcome measures (PROMs) and pre-and post-operative PROMs were collected. Results Sixty patients, each with one unique treated shoulder and no bilateral cases, were identified as receiving treatment for QSS. Of these, 40 (66.7%) underwent arthroscopic quadrilateral space release, while 20 (33.3%) received image-guided injection alone. The average follow-up of surgical patients was 29.5 +/- 15.6 months, with 17 patients completing greater than two-year follow-up. Forty patients (n=40/60; 66.7%) had prior ipsilateral shoulder surgery with an average of 2 +/- 3.5; range: 1-20) prior surgeries. Following arthroscopic release, VAS pain scores (7.0 +/- 2.1 vs 3.3 +/- 2.4; p Conclusion Arthroscopic, extracapsular axillary nerve release is effective at improving measurable pain and PROM measures with a low complication profile in short-term follow-up. Surgical pain relief was comparable to diagnostic injection.

title: Cost-Effectiveness of Open Reduction Internal Fixation Versus Radial Head Arthroplasty for Mason III/IV Radial Head Fractures: A Decision Analytic Markov Model.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Kumar R, Salman SG, Bouras A, Rice SW, Shen O, Cheng C, Bhashyam AR.
abstract: Background Mason type III and IV comminuted radial head fractures present a treatment dilemma between open reduction internal fixation (ORIF) and radial head arthroplasty (RHA). Functional outcomes, implant complications, and later treatment options vary across patients. We evaluated the cost-effectiveness of these strategies under explicit clinical and economic assumptions. Methods We constructed a 5-state Markov cost-utility model for a Mason III/IV fracture, using a 10-year horizon, 3% annual discounting, and US Medicare payment benchmarks. An illustrative base case used good outcome probabilities of 15/23 for ORIF and 20/22 for RHA. Time-zero allocation of follow-up outcomes, state utilities, and later transitions were assumptions. Index costs used verified 2025 Physician Fee Schedule and Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System rates. We performed one-way, probabilistic (10,000 iterations), breakeven, and structural sensitivity analyses. Results ORIF accrued $16,795 and 7.045 quality-adjusted life years (QALYs); RHA accrued $19,242 and 7.299 QALYs. RHA's incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) was $9,627/QALY, with incremental net monetary benefit of $22,970 at $100,000/QALY. Allocating outcomes at year 2 yielded $14,880/QALY, assuming zero unmeasured early differential secondary-care costs. RHA was cost-effective in 94.6% of probabilistic iterations at $100,000/QALY. The breakeven ORIF good outcome probability was 85.7%. When initial clinical outcomes were equal, ORIF was less costly with equal QALYs. Conclusion The illustrative base case favored RHA under the assumed functional difference and utilities. Higher ORIF success, early convergence, or a treatment-specific utility burden could remove that preference. These conditional findings require validation with contemporary fracture-specific utility and treatment-pathway data. Level of evidence Level III; Economic and Decision Analysis.

title: Continuation of Clopidogrel in Total Knee Arthroplasty: Perioperative Bleeding and Cardiovascular Outcomes in a Consecutive Case Series.
authors: Abbaszadeh A, Mortazavi SMJ, Sahebi M, Ayati Firoozabadi M.
abstract: Background Perioperative clopidogrel management in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is challenging because interruption may increase thrombotic risk, whereas continuation may increase bleeding. Evidence remains limited. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 31 consecutive patients (35 knees) undergoing primary TKA while continuing clopidogrel 75 mg daily (April 2018-September 2019). A multidisciplinary team involving orthopaedic surgery, cardiology, and anesthesiology determined continuation. One senior surgeon performed all procedures using a tourniquet-free technique with intravenous and intra-articular tranexamic acid. All patients also received low-dose aspirin for at least 2 weeks postoperatively as venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Outcomes through 90 days included bleeding, transfusion, wound complications, infection, major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events, symptomatic venous thromboembolism, and anesthesia-related complications. Results Mean age was 69 ± 6.4 years; mean estimated blood loss was 285 ± 95 mL, and mean hemoglobin decrease was 1.8 ± 0.6 g/dL. No transfusions or major bleeding occurred. Minor wound drainage followed 3 procedures (8.6%), and superficial cellulitis occurred in 1 knee (2.9%); no deep infections occurred. Four patients (12.9%) reported mild, nonspecific headaches; none met criteria for post-dural puncture headache. No clinical signs or symptoms suggestive of spinal hematoma or persistent neurologic deficit, and no myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death, were observed. Conclusions Clopidogrel continuation during primary TKA may be feasible in carefully selected patients receiving multidisciplinary assessment and multimodal blood management. The small sample, retrospective design, and absence of a control group preclude conclusions about comparative safety.

title: Clinical Outcomes, Implant Survival, and Complications of Expandable Endoprostheses for Lower Limb Reconstruction in Skeletally Immature Patients with Bone Sarcoma: A Systematic Review and Single-Cohort Meta-Analysis.
authors: Piezzo M, Tinelli O, Malfi P, Garofalo R, Fazioli F, Pezzella R.
abstract: Background The management of malignant bone sarcomas in the lower extremities of skeletally immature children and adolescents remains a major challenge in orthopedic oncology. Expandable endoprostheses have become more popular over the last decades, but scientific data are limited. Methods To provide reliable data on functional outcomes, complications, and survival rates after this procedure, we conducted a systematic literature review and meta-analysis of prospective and retrospective studies. The primary objective was Musculoskeletal Tumor Society functional score. Secondary objectives included complications and survival rates. Risk of bias was assessed using the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies (MINORS) tool. Results A total of 1055 patients from 27 studies met the eligibility criteria. Overall methodological quality was moderate, with a mean MINORS score of 10.44. The mean age at surgery was 10.0 years (range 2.0-16.0), and the median follow-up was 5.44 years (range 1.7-24.0). Osteosarcoma accounted for 88.0% of cases and Ewing sarcoma for 10.4%. The pooled estimate of Musculoskeletal Tumor Society score was 82.9 (95% confidence interval [CI] 80.5-85.3). The pooled complication rate was 58.0% (95% CI 48.0-67.0), with no significant difference between minimally invasive and non-invasive expansion mechanisms. According to the Henderson/International Society of Limb Salvage classification, type III structural failures were the most frequent failure mode in both minimally invasive and non-invasive cohorts. The pooled 5-year overall survival rate was 76.0% (95% CI 54.7-89.2).
