Stress distributions in the labrum and elongation of the articular capsule were analyzed using ANSYS Workbench®. The model represents the changes present in the corresponding bone and cartilage. Therefore, the reported outcomes are limited to the biomechanical parameters of stress and elongation of the soft tissues derived from the numerical simulation. The healthy model served as the baseline for comparison. In the labrum, models with bone defects showed lower stress values than the healthy model, indicating reduced functional disruption of the suction-cup effect. Regional analysis revealed localized compression in the superior labrum, suggesting tissue pinching, and areas close to zero stress indicated a loss of uniform distribution. For the articular capsule, elongation remained stable up to a 31% bone defect; beyond this threshold, elongation increased, which was interpreted as capsular laxity. The values presented correspond to a trend seen exclusively in the numerical simulation. This study establishes a foundation for patient-specific simulations to predict the risk of instability and guide surgical decision-making. From Bankart repair to remplissage or bone augmentation procedures, this approach supports a more personalized method for managing shoulder instability.

title: Comparative mortality of pelvic ring fractures vs. hip fractures in adults ≥55 years: A propensity-matched cohort study.
authors: Sabat L, Johnson M, Pasha M, Perdue P, Zuelzer D.
abstract: Background Hip and pelvic fragility fractures are associated with substantial mortality in older adults. While standardized care pathways are established for hip fractures, management of pelvic fragility fractures remains less defined. This study compared mortality between matched hip and pelvic ring fracture patients managed operatively or nonoperatively. Hypothesis Pelvic and hip fractures would demonstrate comparable mortality within operative and nonoperative treatment groups. Patients and methods This retrospective cohort study used the TriNetX network to identify adults aged ≥ 55 years with hip or pelvic ring fractures. Patients were stratified by operative or nonoperative management, and cohorts were propensity score matched 1:1 based on demographic and clinical characteristics. The primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes were mortality at 30 days, 90 days, and 2 years. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated 1-year mortality. Results After matching, 255,202 patients per cohort were included in the nonoperative subgroup and 11,448 per cohort in the operative subgroup. Among nonoperative patients, 1-year mortality was higher after hip than pelvic fracture (11.13% vs 10.68%; HR 1.123, 95% CI 1.105-1.141). Among operative patients, 1-year mortality was also higher after hip fracture (8.84% vs 5.94%; HR 1.424, 95% CI 1.314-1.545). However, 30-day mortality was higher after operative pelvic fracture (3.11% vs 2.49%; p = 0.004). Male sex, older age, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease were associated with increased mortality. Discussion Hip fractures were associated with greater 1-year mortality across management strategies; however, operative pelvic fractures demonstrated greater early mortality. These findings highlight pelvic fragility fractures as high-risk injuries warranting further evaluation of standardized geriatric care pathways. Level of evidence III.

title: A bedside score using arrival data to identify major hemorrhage after blunt pelvic ring fracture: Development and validation.
authors: Salman SG, Phadke RA, Carlin T, Rosenfelt T, Ramirez J, Mendez-Reyes JE, Hoffman MK, Leonard J, Davis RW, Ward JL, Vera RM, Silberfein EJ, Rana A, Atassi OH, Perkins CH, Dawson JR, Wilson C, Fitzgerald CA, Seger CP, Zielinski MD, Mattox KL, Dumas RP.
abstract: Background Early recognition of major hemorrhage after blunt pelvic ring injury could guide mobilization of transfusion and hemorrhage-control resources. We developed an arrival-based bedside score and compared its performance with shock index. Methods We studied 239,736 adults with documented blunt pelvic ring fractures in the 2019-2024 National Trauma Data Bank. Major hemorrhage was defined as a hemorrhage-control procedure, hemorrhagic death, or transfusion of ≥ 1000 mL or ≥ 4 units of red blood cells within 4 h. Penalized logistic regression selected arrival variables for an integer score. We assessed performance in a held-out test set (n = 79,912) and at approximately matched alert volume. A model refitted on 2019-2022 admissions was evaluated in 2023-2024. Subgroup analyses were post hoc. Results Major hemorrhage occurred in 26,479 patients (11.0%); 31.0% were aged ≥ 75 years, and 45.9% had fallen. In the test set, the score achieved an AUROC of 0.882 (95% CI, 0.879-0.886), exceeding shock index by 0.060 (95% CI, 0.055-0.064; P Conclusions In patients with documented blunt pelvic ring fractures, an arrival-based score identified major hemorrhage more accurately than shock index at a similar alert burden. Reduced performance after falls and uncertain applicability to suspected fractures warrant caution. External validation and prospective impact assessment are needed before clinical use.

title: What is the most critical secondary stabilizer in preventing scapholunate dissociation? : a cadaveric biomechanical study during simulated wrist motion.
authors: Park IJ, Kang SH, Lee JY, Roh YT, Park HY, Wang CJ, Kwak DS.
abstract: Aims Isolated injury of the scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL) will not produce static instability of the scapholunate joint. For this, secondary stabilizers must also be compromised. There is no consensus on which secondary stabilizer is the most important in preventing static scapholunate instability (SLI), but many studies have reported the importance of dorsal intercarpal (DIC), scaphotrapeziotrapezoid (STT), and long radiolunate (LRL) ligaments. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the roles of the SLIL, DIC, STT, and LRL ligaments in preventing scapholunate dissociation. Methods A total of 36 fresh-frozen upper limb cadaveric specimens were prepared. A wrist motion simulator with a linear guide rail system (tendon load/motion-controlled system) and five motion capture systems were used. The experimental groups were as follows: 1) intact wrist and ligaments, 2) SLIL transection, 3) DIC transection, 4) STT transection, and 5) LRL transection. The DIC, STT, and LRL ligament transections were randomly assigned. The scapholunate distance, radioscaphoid angle (RSA), radiolunate angle (RLA), and scapholunate angle (SLA) were measured during continuous extension-flexion and ulnar deviation-radial deviation movements. Results Isolated transection of the SLIL was not sufficient to alter the normal kinematics of the SL joint. However, when the DIC ligament was transected in the first stages, a significant increase in the scapholunate distance was observed, and significant changes were observed in the RSA and SLA. Furthermore, when the DIC was transected in the second and third stages, the increase in scapholunate distance was significantly greater than that with transection of the other ligaments. Conclusion The DIC ligament demonstrated the greatest influence on both distraction and rotational stability of the scapholunate joint.

title: Traumatic hip dislocation: Clinical and epidemiological features, management and prognostic factors in a series of 44 cases from a tertiary centre.
authors: Mencía González JP, Sánchez Cózar L, Martínez Alfaro A, Maes ASM, Eckardt Haag ME, Huguet Carmona JL, Marco Sabater A, Alcázar Pérez Á, González Rojo P.
abstract: Introduction Traumatic hip dislocation is an uncommon but potentially severe injury requiring emergency management. We aimed to describe the clinical and epidemiological features and associated injuries of patients with traumatic hip dislocation treated at a tertiary centre, and to analyse the factors related to complications and to the need for salvage surgery. Patients and methods Retrospective observational study of 44 patients aged 15 years or older treated between 2010 and 2024. Demographic variables, injury mechanism, direction of the dislocation, associated fractures (Judet-Letournel and Pipkin classifications), management and complications were recorded. Bivariate analysis used Fisher's exact test for categorical variables and the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables; a p value Results Mean age was 37.4 years (SD 19.3) and 70.5% of patients were men. The commonest mechanism was a road traffic accident (52.3%) and the posterior direction was the most frequent (72.7%). A complex dislocation (with an associated fracture) was present in 72.7% of patients, and 36.4% occurred in the context of polytrauma. Closed reduction was performed in 88.6% of cases, with a median time to reduction of 2 h. The most frequent complication was sciatic nerve injury (20.5%). Femoral head osteonecrosis occurred in 2 patients (4.5%). Male sex was associated with more late complications (p = 0.043), and a prolonged hospital stay was associated with both early (p = 0.002) and late (p = 0.017) complications. Complex dislocations showed a consistent trend towards greater morbidity. Conclusions Traumatic hip dislocation predominantly affects young men after high-energy trauma. Prompt reduction was associated with a low rate of osteonecrosis. The presence of associated fractures and a prolonged hospital stay identify patients with a worse course.

title: The surgical outcome among children with congenital pseudoarthrosis of Tibia: Our 12 years of experience.
authors: RajBhandari T, Pokharel S, Gurung YP, Bhusal R, Banskota B, Banskota AK.
abstract: Background Congenital Pseudoarthrosis of the Tibia (CPT) is a rare condition characterized by poorly perfused, invasive hamartomatous fibrous tissue that leads to fracture and pseudoarthrosis of the tibia. Management challenges include achieving union and preventing refractures. This study aims to evaluate surgical interventions and their outcomes in managing congenital pseudoarthrosis of the tibia in children. Materials and methods This retrospective study reviewed 70 CPT cases treated between 2010 and 2022 at Nepal's only specialized center for children with physical disabilities. It assessed demographics, surgical procedures, and outcomes, with techniques including periosteal grafting and the Masquelet method. Union was defined radiologically, and analyses were conducted using MS Excel and SPSS. Results This study included 70 CPT patients; 40 male (57.1%) and 30 female (42.9%). The mean age at presentation was 3.84 years, with the first surgery at 5.38 years. Most cases were Boyd type 5 (71.43%) and Crawford type 4 (71.43%). Of 35 patients who underwent surgery, the union rate was 41.93% (13/31), with a refracture rate of 23.08% among unions. Periosteal grafting had a 50% union rate, while the Masquelet technique achieved 41.67%. Conclusions This study highlights the challenges in managing Congenital Pseudoarthrosis of the Tibia (CPT), emphasizing the need for personalized surgical approaches based on patient age, limb length discrepancy, and classification. Effective patient counseling on risks and benefits is crucial for informed decisions.

title: Surgical anatomy of the Over-the-Rectus Extrapelvic (OREX) approach defines safe zones for W-plate fixation of the anterior pelvic ring.
authors: Da Cunha Q, Hellwinkel JE, Mauffrey C, David G.
abstract: Objectives To define the procedure-specific surgical anatomy of the pre-symphyseal region relevant to W-plate fixation by characterizing the soft-tissue layers, identifying critical neurovascular structures, and defining quantitative safe zones for dissection and plate placement. Methods Fresh-frozen adult cadavers underwent standardized low Pfannenstiel dissections reproducing the Over-the-Rectus Extrapelvic (OREX) exposure required for W-plate fixation. Pre-symphyseal soft-tissue layers were sequentially dissected from the skin to the anterior pubic symphysis. The locations of critical neurovascular structures relative to the pubic midline and pubic tubercles were recorded, together with anatomical layers, dimensions of the prepubic ligamentous-aponeurotic complex, soft-tissue thickness, sex-related anatomical differences, and surgical safe zones. Results Three reproducible anatomical layers were identified in ten specimens. The superficial layer contained the pre-symphyseal fat pad and superficial epigastric vessels. The intermediate layer contained the spermatic cord or round ligament, ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves, and suprapubic artery, with these critical structures located at a mean distance of approximately 3.2 cm from the midline. The deep layer was consistently formed by the Pyramidalis-anterior pubic Ligament-Adductor longus Complex (PLAC), which covered the anterior pubic symphysis and measured a mean of 4.6 × 3.1 cm. No critical neurovascular structure crossed the central trajectory corresponding to W-plate placement. Female specimens demonstrated greater preperitoneal soft-tissue thickness, whereas lateral surgical safe zones were narrower in male specimens. Conclusion The pre-symphyseal region demonstrated a reproducible three-layer surgical anatomy with a predictable distribution of critical neurovascular structures. Quantitative anatomic mapping defined procedure-specific safe zones for extrapelvic W-plate fixation and provided practical guidancefor surgical exposure, implant positioning, and avoidance of iatrogenic injury. Level of evidence Level IV, therapeutic study.

title: Software-based concordance analysis of a predictive surgical planning model for target gap achievement in robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty.
authors: Hu M, Yu M, Meng F, Luo Z, Xia Y, Weng X, Zhai D, Feng B.
abstract: Background In robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA), achieving soft-tissue balance requires repeated intraoperative plan adjustment and remains experience-dependent. Predictive models may support planning, but their clinical value depends on whether model-generated plans approximate predefined target gaps within the robotic workflow. This study assessed the software-based concordance between model-generated plans and predefined target gaps in robotic-assisted TKA. The predefined target gaps were planning set points established within the robotic software rather than measured intraoperative gaps. Methods This retrospective software-based concordance study included 209 complete-case knees undergoing robotic-assisted TKA. A machine-learning-based predictive model generated a bone-resection plan, which was imported into the robotic planning software to calculate software-derived medial and lateral gaps in extension and flexion. These software-derived gaps were compared with predefined target gaps, which were planning set points rather than measured values and were 18 mm in 819 of 836 gap-level observations (98.0%). The primary analysis focused on target gap deviation, defined as the software-derived gap minus the predefined target gap. As a benchmark, the deviation of the preadjustment gaps from the same targets was used as a preadjustment reference. Results A total of 836 gap-level observations were analyzed. The overall mean target gap deviation was -0.142 mm (SD, 1.411 mm), with a mean absolute error of 1.016 mm. Overall, 77.6% of software-derived gaps were within ±1 mm of target, and 93.4% were within ±2 mm. Bland-Altman analysis showed a small overall bias of -0.142 mm, with 95% limits of agreement from -2.91 to +2.62 mm. At the knee level, only 43.1% of knees had all software-derived gaps within ±1 mm of target. Gap-level deviations ranged from -7 mm to +5 mm, and 16.3% of knees (34/209) had at least one gap with an absolute deviation > 2 mm. Compared with the preadjustment reference (MAE 2.002 mm, 49.4% within ±1 mm), the model substantially reduced deviation (MAE 1.016 mm, 77.6% within ±1 mm, p Conclusions In this software-based concordance analysis, the predictive planning model generated surgical plans whose robotic software-derived gaps approximated predefined target gaps with a mean absolute deviation of approximately 1 mm. The model-generated plan reduced target-gap deviation relative to the initial preadjustment plan within this target-conditioned workflow. However, because the targets were near-uniform (98.0% at 18 mm) and all measurements were software-derived, compartment-specific bias, moderate whole-knee consistency (43.1%), and occasional outlier deviations indicate that the model should be used as a surgeon-supervised decision support tool rather than as an autonomous planner. Prospective validation against measured intraoperative and postoperative gaps is required before clinical effectiveness can be claimed.

title: Risk factors for complications following surgical fixation of pelvic ring fractures: a retrospective cohort study.
authors: Kojima KE, Argotte PLP, Esteves DS, Guimarães MGV, Medina R, Abe Puccetti VLY, de Camargo Leonhardt M, Santos Silva JD.
abstract: Background Surgical fixation of pelvic ring fractures carries a substantial risk of postoperative complications, particularly surgical site infection, yet the relative contribution of fracture pattern and associated soft tissue injury to this risk remains incompletely defined. Objective To describe the rate and spectrum of complications following surgical fixation of pelvic ring fractures and to identify factors independently associated with these complications, with particular attention to acute surgical site infection. Methods Retrospective, single-center cohort study of 126 patients who underwent surgical fixation of pelvic ring fractures between December 2014 and November 2024, reported in accordance with the STROBE statement. Candidate demographic, injury-related, and treatment-related exposures were compared against a composite primary outcome (any postoperative complication) and against acute infection using Fisher's exact test, Pearson chi-square test, the Mann-Whitney U test, and multivariable logistic regression. Results Overall, 39 of 126 patients (31.0%) experienced at least one postoperative complication; chronic pain (22.2%) and acute surgical site infection (16.7%) were the most frequent individual components. In bivariate analysis, the presence of a Morel-Lavallée lesion at baseline was significantly associated with both the composite outcome (OR 12.65, 95% CI 1.42-112.27, p = 0.011) and acute infection (OR 12.12, 95% CI 2.06-71.37, p = 0.007); Young-Burgess fracture pattern was also associated with infection (p = 0.018). After multivariable adjustment for infection, a Morel-Lavallée lesion (adjusted OR 17.69, 95% CI 2.46-126.95, p = 0.004) and combined-mechanism fracture pattern (adjusted OR 8.25 versus anteroposterior compression, 95% CI 1.91-35.58, p = 0.005) remained independently associated with infection. Neither the presence, technique, nor surgical approach of posterior ring fixation was associated with any complication type, and time from injury to definitive fixation (median 13 days) showed no significant association with either outcome. Conclusion A Morel-Lavallée lesion identified at initial evaluation was associated with postoperative complications in bivariate analysis and, together with a combined-mechanism fracture pattern, remained an independent predictor of surgical site infection after multivariable adjustment. No statistically significant association was identified between posterior fixation technique and complication risk. Level of evidence III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Proximal Versus Joint Line Medial Collateral Ligament Trephination (Pie-Crusting): Effects on Meniscal Extrusion and Tibiofemoral Contact Mechanics in a Cadaveric Model.
journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
authors: Abbasian M, Partan M, Korabelnikov T, Patel RR, Chen KM, Moteshakereh SM, Zarei H, Arciero RA.
abstract: Background Medial collateral ligament (MCL) trephination (ie, "pie-crusting") is used to improve visualization and working space within the medial compartment during knee arthroscopy, but the variability in techniques raises concern for meniscotibial ligament injuries, meniscal extrusion (ME), and altered joint contact mechanics. Purpose To evaluate the effects of proximal versus joint line MCL trephination on ME and knee contact mechanics. Study design Controlled laboratory study. Methods A total of 10 fresh-frozen cadaveric knees (5 matched pairs) were allocated to 2 groups: proximal trephination and joint line trephination (n = 5 each). Measurements were obtained in the intact condition and repeated after percutaneous MCL trephination. The medial joint opening was assessed arthroscopically and radiographically. Under a 1000-N axial load applied for 30 seconds at 0° and 30° of knee flexion, ME was measured radiographically, and tibiofemoral contact pressure and contact area were recorded using an intra-articular pressure sensor. All statistical analyses were performed using commercial software. Results The cadaveric specimens had a mean age of 61.4 years. The joint line group required more needle pokes to achieve adequate release. Both techniques increased the medial joint opening and ME relative to baseline (all P ≤ .05), while no significant changes in contact pressure or area were noted. Contact pressure was higher after joint line trephination at full extension ( P = .018) and 30° of flexion ( P = .035), although after adjusting for the number of needle pokes, a significant difference was only noted at full extension ( P = .024). Compared with proximal trephination, joint line trephination produced greater increases in ME at full extension ( P = .026) and 30° of flexion ( P P = .021). Conclusion When comparing joint line and proximal MCL trephination in a cadaveric model, both techniques increased the medial joint opening and ME; however, joint line trephination caused greater extrusion and less favorable contact mechanics than proximal trephination. Further in vivo studies are needed to determine the clinical relevance of these findings. Clinical relevance This research characterized the biomechanical effects of MCL trephination location on ME and joint contact mechanics. This knowledge supports favoring proximal trephination to limit iatrogenic disruption of the medial compartment.

title: Proceedings from the 2025 International Consensus Meeting on Orthopedic Infections: Diagnosis of Periprosthetic Shoulder Infection.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Namdari S, Zmistowski B, Fiandeiro M, Gupta S, Nicholson T, ICM Shoulder Group.
abstract: Background Prosthetic joint infection (PJI) following shoulder arthroplasty is difficult to diagnose because clinical findings are often nonspecific, conventional diagnostic tests have variable sensitivity, and Cutibacterium acnes (C. acnes) may cause indolent infection with limited systemic inflammatory response. Diagnostic criteria have also largely been adapted from hip and knee arthroplasty with limited shoulder-specific validation. This International Consensus Meeting (ICM) reviewed the available evidence and developed consensus recommendations for the diagnosis of shoulder PJI. Methods The Shoulder Group of the 2025 ICM on Orthopedic Infections included international shoulder surgeons, infectious disease physicians, and microbiology experts experienced in shoulder arthroplasty and PJI. Thirty-two diagnostic questions underwent question-specific literature review, presentation to the consensus group, discussion, and voting. A modified Delphi process was used to establish consensus. Delegates voted to agree, disagree, or abstain. Consensus was categorized by percentage agreement, while strength of recommendation was assessed separately based on evidence quality, consistency, and directness. Results Consensus was achieved for 31 analyzed questions, with agreement ranging from 72% to 100%; 29 resulted in recommendations for clinical practice and 2 were identified as requiring further research. Question 47, which addressed the definition of PJI, was reported separately. Humeral component loosening, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) were supported as components of the diagnostic criteria, whereas cloudy fluid, postoperative stiffness, serum WBC count, and D-dimer were not supported as independent criteria. Arthroscopic tissue biopsy, frozen section, and selective ultrasound-guided aspiration or synovial biopsy were supported as adjuncts to diagnosis. Five intraoperative tissue specimens, prolonged aerobic and anaerobic culture incubation, and routine perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis were supported. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) and synovial neutrophil testing were supported as adjuncts; alpha-defensin was considered potentially useful but insufficiently validated for formal inclusion; and leukocyte esterase inclusion was not recommended. Routine use of bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), or positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) was not supported. Evidence remained insufficient to determine the clinical significance of polymicrobial molecular results or routine negative control samples. Conclusion The 2025 ICM provides a consensus framework for the diagnosis of shoulder PJI, identifying several measures that can be incorporated into current clinical practice. However, substantial uncertainty remains because most recommendations are supported by limited evidence and several diagnostic tests lack sufficient sensitivity. Prospective, shoulder-specific studies are needed to define diagnostic thresholds and determine the role of emerging molecular, biomarker, and imaging modalities.

title: Posterior Capsular Release in Soft-Tissue Balancing to Correct Valgus Deformity and Flexion Contracture During Total Knee Arthroplasty.
authors: Sugita T, Sogi Y, Miyatake N, Sasaki A, Kodajima S, Hashimoto K, Aizawa T.
abstract: Total knee arthroplasty for valgus knee deformities presents many challenging problems, especially in soft-tissue handling, although many soft-tissue balancing techniques have been described to date. Posterior capsular release, a soft-tissue balancing technique used to correct both valgus deformity and flexion contracture during total knee arthroplasty, is described in this technical note. Because this procedure does not sacrifice important lateral stabilizers, varus instability in knee flexion can be avoided. Furthermore, the release is performed just posterior to the femoral condyle without the risk of damaging the lateral collateral ligament and peroneal nerve associated with the posterior capsular division technique. We recommend this procedure as the first-choice strategy because additional procedures are required in some cases.

title: Platelet-Rich Plasma versus Corticosteroid Injections for Subacromial Impingement Syndrome: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Liu L, Roemer J, Gerges PE, Lugo E, John DQ, Lima DJL, Routman HD.
abstract: Background Subacromial impingement syndrome (SAI) is a common cause of shoulder pain. Corticosteroid injection (CS) provides short-term relief, but concerns about tendon health and durability have increased interest in platelet-rich plasma (PRP) as an alternative. This meta-analysis compared pain and functional outcomes after PRP versus CS for SAI. Methods A systematic review was performed per PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for randomized controlled trials comparing PRP and CS for SAI. VAS pain scores and shoulder-specific functional outcomes were extracted, and random-effects meta-analyses were performed at baseline, short-term, and mid-term follow-up. Results Eight studies (518 patients; 7 RCTs and 1 non-randomized comparative study) were included, with 259 patients per group. Baseline VAS scores were comparable (MD 0.03, 95% CI -0.09 to 0.15; I 2 = 0%). Short- and mid-term VAS scores showed no significant difference between groups (short-term MD 0.47, 95% CI -0.35 to 1.29; mid-term MD 0.50, 95% CI -1.80 to 2.80), though heterogeneity was substantial (I 2 = 93.6% and 98.0%), falling to 49.2% and 80.2% after excluding the non-randomized study. Functional outcomes were inconsistently reported; at 6 months, Constant score differences ranged from -13.0 to +17.2, and UCLA differences ranged from -0.6 to +0.3. Conclusion PRP and CS showed no significant difference in short- or mid-term pain relief for SAI, but heterogeneity between trials was substantial. Functional outcomes were inconsistently reported across studies. Current evidence does not show it is clinically superior to CS for pain relief, and treatment choice should still weigh cost, availability, and patient preference. Level of evidence Level II, Systematic Review.

title: Non-linear associations between parity and long-term risk of osteoporosis.
authors: Yuan W, Liao J, Tao L, Song H, Wang H, Huang J, He J, Liu H, Wu T, Zhou H, Zhang Y, Song C.
abstract: Our findings suggest that although pregnancy and lactation are periods of physiological calcium loss, higher parity is not associated with an increased risk of postmenopausal osteoporosis; rather, it appears to confer a long-term protective effect. Purpose Osteoporosis is a significant public health burden. While parity induces transient bone loss, their long-term skeletal impact remains poorly understood. This study aimed to clarify the associations between parity, defined as the number of live births, and the risk of osteoporosis, osteoporotic fractures, and bone mineral density (BMD). Methods We analyzed data from 119,969 women in the UK Biobank. Associations between parity and incident osteoporosis or fractures were evaluated using unweighted and inverse probability of treatment weighting Cox proportional hazards models. Generalized linear models assessed associations with femoral neck and lumbar spine BMD. Models were adjusted for sociodemographic, genetic, lifestyle, and clinical factors. Results Compared with nulliparous women, those with a parity of 2 or 3 exhibited a significantly reduced risk of osteoporosis in the weighted fully adjusted model. In addition, parity of 3 exhibited a significantly reduced risk of osteoporotic fracture compared with the nulliparous group. This protection was evident in women ≥ 60 years and those with normal body mass index. Parity was not significantly associated with areal BMD changes after full covariate adjustment. Conclusion In women aged 40-69 years at baseline, a parity of 2 or 3 confers long-term protection against osteoporosis and osteoporotic fracture (a arity of 3), occurring independently of BMD changes. These findings support the integration of parity into clinical risk assessment tools, ultimately contributing to more effective osteoporosis prevention and a reduced fracture burden across women's lifespan.

title: Morbid Obesity May be Associated With Increased Odds of Prosthetic Joint Infection After Anterior-Based Total Hip Arthroplasty.
authors: Byrne AR, Buchalter WH, Dash AS, Neuwirth AL, Geller JA, Shah RP, Cooper HJ, Herndon CL, Sarpong NO.
abstract: Background Obesity increases perioperative risk after total hip arthroplasty (THA), particularly with anterior-based approaches. However, outcomes among patients with class II versus class III obesity remain poorly defined. This study compared early complications and patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) between these obesity classes. Methods We retrospectively reviewed patients with BMI ≥35 kg/m² undergoing elective anterior-based primary THA from January 2022 to January 2025. Patients were stratified into BMI 35-39.9 kg/m² (Class II) and BMI ≥40 kg/m² (Class III) cohorts. Firth penalized logistic regression evaluated the association between BMI group and prosthetic joint infection (PJI) requiring operative irrigation and debridement (I&D). Results 193 patients were included (BMI ≥40: n = 53; BMI 35-39.9: n = 140). The BMI ≥40 kg/m² cohort had a greater proportion of females (77.4% vs 57.1%; P = .015) and higher ASA classification ( P = .02). PJI occurred more frequently in the BMI ≥40 cohort (7.5% vs 1.4%; P = .049). Unadjusted odds of PJI were higher with BMI ≥40 kg/m² (OR 5.03, 95% CI 1.08-29.6), but the association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for age, sex, and surgical approach. Both cohorts demonstrated significant improvement in WOMAC and SF-12 Physical scores at 3 months without between-group differences. Conclusions Patients with BMI ≥40 kg/m² demonstrated higher observed PJI rates after anterior-based THA while achieving comparable early functional improvement. These findings suggest a clinically important risk signal warranting confirmation in larger studies rather than establishing BMI ≥40 kg/m² as an independent risk threshold.

title: Milwaukee shoulder syndrome: a neglected and underrecognized basic calcium phosphate crystal arthropathy.
authors: Kougkas N, Avgerou P, Karantanas AH.
abstract: Milwaukee Shoulder Syndrome (MSS) is a rare but extremely aggressive form of destructive arthropathy, primarily affecting elderly women. Despite its distinct clinical profile, it remains an under-recognized and frequently misdiagnosed entity. This review synthesizes current knowledge on pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and diagnostic nuances of MSS to improve clinical recognition. The condition is defined by the intra-articular deposition of basic calcium phosphate (BCP) crystals, such as hydroxyapatite. These crystals trigger the release of proteolytic enzymes, leading to massive rotator cuff tears, superior migration of the humeral head, and rapid joint destruction. A hallmark of MSS is the "inflammatory paradox": a striking dissociation between severe structural damage and a non-inflammatory or minimally inflammatory synovial fluid profile (typically < 2,000 cells/mm3), which often is hemorrhagic. Diagnosis is challenged by the nanocrystalline nature of BCP crystals, which are non-birefringent and invisible under standard polarized light microscopy, requiring specialized staining (Alizarin Red) or advanced analytics for confirmation. Multimodal imaging is essential, with plain radiography showing advanced degeneration and MRI or CT delineating the extent of soft tissue and bony destruction. Treatment is currently limited to supportive measures, including recurrent joint aspiration, analgesia, and physical therapy. In advanced cases, reverse total shoulder arthroplasty remains the primary surgical intervention for functional restoration. As the aging population grows, increasing clinician awareness of MSS-particularly its unique synovial fluid characteristics-is vital for reducing diagnostic delay and optimizing patient care.

title: Microfracture at the Acetabular Rim as Biological Augmentation of Labral Reconstruction Improves Autograft Vascularization and Integration: A Porcine Model.
journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
authors: Jun H, Yiling T, Yonglie Z, Ying Z, Yang P, Lingchuan G, Ran X, Chenjun H, Yao T, Gang C, Tiao S, Guangxing C.
abstract: Background Labral reconstruction is used for irreparable acetabular labral tears, but graft incorporation is often limited by insufficient vascular ingrowth. Bone marrow stimulation at the acetabular rim may enhance revascularization and promote biological healing. Purpose To determine whether acetabular rim microfracture improves vascularization and tissue integration of labral autografts compared with reconstruction alone in a porcine model. Study design Controlled laboratory study. Methods A total of 36 skeletally mature pigs were randomized to labral reconstruction with acetabular rim microfracture (RCMC) or reconstruction alone (RC). A 10-mm segment of the acetabular labrum was resected to create a standardized defect. In the RCMC group, the acetabular rim was microfractured with multiple 2-mm holes, followed by autograft reconstruction with an Achilles tendon graft fixed to the rim. In the RC group, the same reconstruction was performed without microfracture. Hips were harvested at 6, 12, and 24 weeks for macroscopic and histological analysis. Results At 12 and 24 weeks, RCMC hips more often showed complete defect filling and smoother articular surfaces than RC hips. Histologically, RCMC grafts showed more mature fibrocartilaginous remodeling, whereas RC grafts remained predominantly fibrous on the articular side with a persistent gap from adjacent cartilage. At 6 weeks, vascular distribution was more uniform in RCMC, whereas in RC it was mainly confined to the capsular side; by 24 weeks, both groups showed a native labrum-like peripheral vascular pattern. Compared with RC, RCMC showed a progressive increase in type 2 collagen, indicating more advanced fibrocartilaginous matrix remodeling. Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick-end labeling staining showed that apoptosis was higher early in RCMC and then gradually declined, whereas RC showed delayed increases. Conclusion Acetabular rim microfracture enhanced early and uniform revascularization of labral autografts and was associated with more advanced fibrocartilaginous remodeling and more labrum-like integration than reconstruction alone. Clinical relevance In this porcine segmental labral reconstruction model, acetabular rim microfracture was associated with enhanced histological vascularization, matrix remodeling, and interface integration. These preclinical findings support further investigation of rim microfracture as a potential biological adjunct to labral reconstruction; however, biomechanical and clinical studies are required before its functional effectiveness or clinical applicability can be established.

title: Low-dose CT of the sacroiliac joints in suspected axial spondyloarthritis: Agreement with the rheumatologist's clinical diagnosis at baseline and two-year follow-up.
authors: Korteweg MA, Wessels MI, van der Heijden WRP, Koetser ICJ, Bartels B, van der Laken CJ.
abstract: Objective To assess agreement between baseline low-dose CT (ldCT) findings of the sacroiliac joints (SIJs) and the treating rheumatologist's clinical diagnosis, at baseline and after at least two years of follow-up, in patients clinically suspected of axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA). Materials and methods In this prospective observational study, adults suspected of sacroiliitis underwent ldCT of the SIJs between June 2023 and February 2024 at baseline. Two musculoskeletal radiologists independently evaluated examinations while blinded to clinical data. The rheumatologist's diagnosis at baseline and after at least two years, made with access to ldCT findings, served as comparator; no independent reference standard was available. Agreement with the clinical diagnosis, interobserver agreement and radiation dose were assessed. Results Seventy-nine patients (53 women, 26 men; mean age 43 years) were included; 25 (32 %) had a clinical axSpA diagnosis at 2 year follow-up. Both comparisons were subject to incorporation bias. Against the baseline clinical diagnosis, ldCT sensitivity was 81 % (95 % CI 57-93) and specificity 83 % (71-90); against the 2-year diagnosis, sensitivity was 80 % (61-91) and specificity 93 % (82-97), with positive and negative predictive values of 83 % and 91 %. Of 11 patients reclassified as axSpA during follow-up, 9 had a positive baseline ldCT. Interobserver agreement was substantial (kappa 0.68). Mean effective dose was 0.45 mSv. Conclusion ldCT of the SIJs was feasible at radiation doses comparable to conventional radiography and structural lesions were interpreted reproducibly. Agreement with the rheumatologist's diagnosis is likely inflated by incorporation bias. Independent validation is required before changing imaging pathways.

title: Long-Term Efficacy of Restricted Quantitative Superior Placement Technique in Total Hip Arthroplasty for Severe Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: An 8- to 10-Year Follow-Up of a Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial.
authors: Li S, Yang Z, Jiang D, Xie Y, Lu X, Zhao X, Gu M, Li Z, Liao W, Zhang Z.
abstract: Objective Total hip arthroplasty (THA) in patients with developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), particularly those with Crowe II or III dysplasia, is challenging because of abnormal acetabular morphology and deficient bone stock. This study aims to compare the long-term outcomes of true anatomic versus restricted quantitative superior placement of the acetabular component. Methods This prospective, patient- and assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial was conducted from August 1, 2013, to July 31, 2024. Forty-four hips were allocated 1:1 to true anatomic center placement or restricted quantitative superior placement. Restricted quantitative superior placement was defined as positioning the cup center no more than 15 mm superior to the true anatomic center. Harris Hip Score (HHS), 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36), complications, perioperative outcomes, and radiographic parameters were assessed. The mean final follow-up was 8.94 years. Independent-samples t-test, Mann-Whitney U test, Chi-square test, and Fisher's exact test were used for statistical analysis. Results No statistically significant between-group difference was observed in prosthetic complications. No revisions were recorded among the 36 hips that completed the 8-10-year follow-up. At the 8-10-year follow-up, the restricted quantitative superior placement group had a higher HHS than the true anatomic center group (93.70 ± 5.20 vs. 86.73 ± 11.62, p = 0.024); multiple imputation analysis showed a mean difference of 5.79 points (95% CI, 0.46-11.13; p = 0.034). Significant between-group differences were also observed at 2 and 7 years. SF-36 scores did not differ significantly between groups. Morselized bone grafting was required in 45.5% of the anatomic center group and 40.9% of the restricted quantitative superior center group. Structural grafting was used in 18.2% and 9.1%, respectively. Radiographic analysis showed higher center of rotation height and less limb lengthening in the restricted quantitative superior center group. Conclusions Restricted quantitative superior placement within 15 mm above the true anatomic center was associated with higher long-term HHS, with no significant difference in prosthetic complications and no revisions recorded among the 36 hips that completed the 8-10-year follow-up. It may represent a potential reconstructive option for patients with DDH. Trial registration Chictr.org, ChiCTR-TRC-1404388; https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=5182.

title: Less Can Be as Effective as More: Two WOSI Items Capture Clinical Outcomes After Surgical Stabilization for Shoulder Instability.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Sawicka-Garbarek E, Kaszyński J, Cisowski P, Kaczmarek P, Ślęzak M, Soroko E, Lubiatowski P.
abstract: Background WOSI is one of the most popular and detailed questionnaires in both rating of the current patient status as well as measuring patients' recovery after treatment of shoulder instability. It includes questions about both psychological and somatic aspects of the patient's functioning. Our aim was to test whether the psychological items of the WOSI questionnaire, regarding beliefs and emotions, can be an indicator of recovery. Methods WOSI items with the highest psychological load (PSYCHE-WOSI) were identified through expert rating and assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient and hierarchical cluster analysis (Ward's method, tree diagram). Data from 78 patients (mean follow-up, 4.3 months) after surgical stabilization for shoulder instability, including WOSI, UCLA, Constant, ASES, and SST scores, were used to assess their utility as recovery indicators. Correlation, regression, and canonical correlation analyses were performed to identify PSYCHE-WOSI items most strongly associated with pain, function, range of motion, and overall PROMs. Results The PSYCHE-WOSI factor comprised items 13, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, and 21. Items 15 and 17 showed the strongest associations with function, range of motion, and overall PROMs, whereas items 16 and 21 were most strongly associated with pain outcomes. Conclusion A distinct psychological factor can be identified within WOSI. PSYCHE-WOSI items are strongly associated with PROMs and may provide a simple, rapid, and cost-effective tool for assessing recovery, supporting a more holistic, patient-centered approach to postoperative rehabilitation. Level of evidence Basic Science Study, Validation of Outcome Instrument.

title: Intra-articular Extender Button Deployment Without a Secondary Incision for Salvage of Compromised Femoral Cortical Fixation in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
authors: Singh P, Boyd B, Marsh D, Chan FJ.
abstract: As suspensory fixation techniques for anterior cruciate ligament grafts gain popularity, so does the need to troubleshoot when intraoperative complications arise. A compromised lateral femoral cortex that cannot support the suspensory fixation is a complex intraoperative complication that can lead to graft failure. During these situations, an extender button is often used via a secondary incision. The technique described in this article allows for intra-articular passage of the extender button without the need for a secondary incision using 2-0 Vicryl sutures to attach the extender button to the suspensory button prior to graft passage. This cost-effective method can decrease operative time and potentially decrease postoperative pain and wound complications by foregoing the need for a second incision.

title: Incidence, Temporal Trends, and Associated Characteristics of Hip Fracture in Long-Term Care Residents: A Population-Based Cohort Study in British Columbia.
journal: Journal of the American Medical Directors Association
authors: Muhammad O, Whiting SJ, Rostami M, Feng C.
abstract: Objectives To examine temporal trends in hip fracture incidence and determine whether resident-level or facility-level characteristics were associated with hip fracture occurrence among long-term care residents in British Columbia, Canada. Design Population-based retrospective cohort study. Setting and participants A total of 33,739 adults aged ≥65 years newly admitted to 305 licensed long-term care facilities in British Columbia between 2010 and 2014. Methods Linked Canadian administrative health data integrated hospital discharge records with resident- and facility-level assessment data. Residents were followed from admission until first hip fracture, death, discharge, transfer, or administrative censoring. Hip fracture incidence rates were calculated per 100,000 person-years. Multivariable logistic regression examined resident-level and facility-level characteristics associated with hip fracture occurrence. Results Among 33,739 residents, 1914 (5.7%) sustained a first hip fracture, corresponding to an overall incidence rate of 3418 per 100,000 person-years. Annual incidence declined from 3830.5 per 100,000 person-years in 2010 to 3146.4 per 100,000 person-years in 2014, representing an 18% relative reduction. Independent characteristics associated with fracture occurrence included lower body mass index categories compared with obesity (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.36-1.82), female sex (aOR, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.45-1.78), dementia (aOR, 1.46; 95% CI, 1.33-1.62), age 90 years and older (aOR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.18-1.51), and recent falls (aOR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.03-1.29). In contrast, facility size, rurality, and health region were not independently associated with fracture occurrence after adjustment for resident-level characteristics. Conclusions and implications Hip fracture incidence declined modestly but remained substantial. Fracture occurrence was associated primarily with resident-level clinical characteristics rather than broad facility-level structural indicators. These findings support systematic identification of high-risk residents and suggest that fracture prevention efforts may be most effective when targeted toward low body mass index, dementia, advanced age, and recent falls.

title: Fracture-related infection after operative fixation of acetabular fractures: Incidence and factors independently associated with infection.
authors: Ramesh P, Imran A, Devendra A, M S S, Mogan K, Sp S, Dheenadhayalan J, Rajasekaran S.
abstract: Background The purpose of this study was to determine the incidence of fracture-related infection following acetabular fracture fixation and to identify factors independently associated with its occurrence. Methods A retrospective single-center cohort study was conducted at a Level I trauma center. Patients aged ≥ 18 years who underwent operative fixation of an acetabular fracture between January 2021 and July 2025 were included. Fracture-related infection was defined according to the AO/EBJIS consensus definition. Patients were followed for a minimum of 12 months. Multivariable analysis was performed using Firth penalized logistic regression. Results Of 359 patients, 27 (7.5%) developed fracture-related infection. All 27 met at least 1 confirmatory criterion. The median time to diagnosis was 9 days (IQR, 7-14), with 20 infections (74.1%) diagnosed within 14 days of fixation. Sixteen infections (59.3%) were culture-positive, with gram-negative organisms more common than Staphylococcus aureus. Eleven infections (40.7%) were culture-negative, including 6 patients who had received empirical linezolid before tissue sampling. All infected patients underwent infection-related reoperation; 23 (85.2%) were managed with debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention, and 4 (14.8%) underwent implant removal. On Firth penalized multivariable analysis, higher body mass index (adjusted OR, 1.33; 95% CI, 1.15-1.55), longer operative duration (1.63; 1.11-2.36), diabetes mellitus (2.55; 1.09-6.05), and a longer admission-to-surgery interval (1.08; 1.00-1.16) were independently associated with infection. Polytrauma was not independently associated with infection (2.10; 0.89-5.09). At final follow-up, fracture union was achieved in 20 patients (74.1%). Conclusions Fracture-related infection after acetabular fracture fixation appears to reflect a combination of patient-related and operative factors. Recognizing these factors may help identify patients at higher risk and allow closer postoperative surveillance. Level of evidence Prognostic Level III.

title: Forequarter Lateral Implosion Injury: A Review of Recognition and Multidisciplinary Management.
authors: Muldiiarov V, Weatherby DJ, White TW, Ayzenberg M, Bauman ZM.
abstract: Background Forequarter lateral implosion injury (LII) is a severe combined injury of the chest wall and ipsilateral shoulder girdle after high-energy trauma. This review summarizes current evidence and provides a practical framework for recognition, multidisciplinary assessment, and management. Methods Published literature on combined ipsilateral chest wall and shoulder-girdle injuries was reviewed and synthesized by a clinical topic. This evidence was integrated with the authors' clinical perspectives on recognition, multidisciplinary assessment, treatment selection, and operative planning. Results LII is characterized by combined disruption of the chest wall and shoulder girdle, often including displaced or segmental rib fractures with clavicular and/or scapular injury. Computed tomography (CT) is central to identifying chest wall instability, shoulder-girdle displacement, and global forequarter malalignment. Available evidence supports multidisciplinary assessment but does not justify routine fixation of every injured component. Operative management should be selective and based on established chest wall and orthopedic indications, respiratory physiology, injury severity, functional demands, and surgical expertise. Conclusions LII should be recognized and assessed as an integrated chest wall-shoulder girdle injury rather than a collection of isolated fractures. Combined or staged reconstruction may be appropriate when operative indications coexist, whereas nonoperative management remains appropriate in selected patients. Further studies are needed to define treatment selection and long-term functional outcomes.

title: Factors Associated with Functional Improvement After Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty: A Comprehensive Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Xiong R, Li W, Wang S, Jiang C, Zhu Y.
abstract: Background Reverse total shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA) is now widely used across diverse indications. Existing meta-analyses usually evaluate single factors and rely solely on postoperative functional scores, without accounting for baseline status. A comprehensive quantitative synthesis of determinants of functional improvement, using change in validated scores from pre- to postoperative, is therefore needed. Objective This study aims to systematically evaluate patient- and surgery-related determinants of functional enhancement after rTSA, based on changes in ASES score and Constant-Murley score, through a systematic review and meta-analysis, and provide an evidence-based reference for clinical decision-making. Methods PubMed, EMBASE and Cochrane Library were searched from inception to November 2025. Randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies of reverse shoulder arthroplasty reporting relevant ASES or Constant outcomes by patient- or surgery-related exposures were included, with analyses primarily focused on preoperative-to-postoperative changes. Effect sizes were extracted and pooled using Review Manager 5.3, applying fixed- or random-effects models according to heterogeneity, with publication bias evaluation, and study quality assessment. Results Sixty-five studies were included, with overall methodological quality judged to be high. Meta-analyses showed that prior shoulder surgery was the only consistent patient determinant of smaller gains in ASES and Constant scores, whereas age and obesity had no meaningful impact, and lower socioeconomic status predicted worse postoperative ASES. Among surgical factors, humeral cemented fixation and subscapularis repair were associated with greater functional improvement. Funnel plots supported the robustness of these findings. Conclusion This meta-analysis is the first to prioritize pre- to postoperative change in function after rTSA. Prior shoulder surgery was associated with less improvement in ASES and Constant scores, whereas cemented humeral fixation was associated with greater improvement in Constant scores and subscapularis repair with greater improvement in ASES scores. Level of evidence Level IV, systematic review and meta-analysis.

title: Enhanced visualization and quantitative evaluation of traumatic vertebral bone marrow edema using multiparameter fusion imaging with spectral CT.
authors: Zhang Y, Luo S, He A, Sun Y, Wen J, Liu H.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the diagnostic performance of calcium-suppressed (CaSupp), electron density-weighted (EDW), and fused CaSupp + EDW images from dual-layer detector spectral CT for traumatic vertebral bone marrow edema (BME), with MRI as the reference standard. Methods Seventy-one patients with lumbar traumatic fractures (355 vertebral bodies) underwent spectral CT and 3.0 T MRI within 72 h. Conventional CT, CaSupp, EDW, and fused images were reconstructed. Three radiologists of different seniority assessed image quality and qualitatively diagnosed BME; one radiologist measured virtual Hounsfield units (vHU) and percentage electron density (%EDW). Friedman, Fleiss' kappa, ROC, GEE, and McNemar analyses were applied (α = 0.05). Results Fusion imaging achieved the highest accuracy (94.7 %, 95 % CI 92.1-97.1 %), sensitivity (88.7 %, 95 % CI 81.7-95.8 %) and NPV (97.0 %), outperforming conventional CT (sensitivity 63.4 %) at comparable specificity (96.3 %). Inter-reader agreement was excellent for fusion (κ = 0.810) but poor to slight for CaSupp (0.027) and EDW (0.171). vHU and %EDW were higher in BME-affected than normal vertebrae (both P Conclusion Multiparameter fusion of CaSupp and EDW enables simultaneous visualization and quantification of vertebral BME with superior diagnostic performance and inter-reader consistency. It may serve as a useful supplementary tool for patients with MRI contraindications or in the emergency setting.

title: Endoscope-assisted vs. conventional anterior cervical discectomy and fusion for single-level degenerative cervical disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Wang ZY, Dai YX, Ma ZJ, Yu PF, Liu JT, Li HW.
abstract: Background Endoscope-assisted anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (EA-ACDF) has been introduced as a modified technique for the treatment of degenerative cervical disease, but its comparative efficacy and safety relative to conventional ACDF (CA-ACDF) remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to compare EA-ACDF with CA-ACDF for single-level degenerative cervical disease. Methods PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, CNKI, WanFang, VIP, and SinoMed were searched from inception through September 7, 2026. Comparative studies of EA-ACDF vs. CA-ACDF were included. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Results Eleven retrospective comparative studies involving 755 patients were included. Compared with CA-ACDF, EA-ACDF was associated with longer operative time (MD = 17.31 min, 95% CI 11.38-23.23), but lower intraoperative blood loss (MD = -17.31 mL, 95% CI -24.38 to -10.25), postoperative drainage volume (MD = -10.97 mL, 95% CI -16.98 to -4.96), length of hospital stay (MD = -0.67 days, 95% CI -1.16 to -0.17), and overall complication rate (RR = 0.44, 95% CI 0.25-0.78). No significant between-group differences were observed in final Japanese Orthopaedic Association score, Neck Disability Index, visual analogue scale score, cervical lordosis, or fusion rate. The certainty of evidence ranged from low to very low. Conclusion EA-ACDF may offer modest perioperative advantages at the cost of longer operative time, while short- to mid-term clinical, radiographic, and fusion outcomes appear broadly similar. Current evidence does not establish clinical superiority. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251123475, identifier CRD420251123475.

title: Decoding transcriptional, metabolic, and cell death signatures in osteoarthritis and endemic osteoarthritis at single-cell resolution.
authors: Bian X, Fan Y, Zhang D, Zhang Y, Wen Y, Cheng S, Yang X, Gao D, Lammi MJ, Zhang F, Guo X, Sun S.
abstract: Aims This study aims to investigate the molecular differences of cellular heterogeneity, metabolic, and cell death signatures between osteoarthritis (OA) and Kashin-Beck disease (KBD) at single-cell resolution. Methods Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on 139,943 chondrocytes isolated from 17 human cartilage samples, comparising three healthy controls, eight patients with OA, and six patients with KBD. Chondrocyte populations were identified using the Louvain algorithm and systematically compared across the three groups. Differentially expressed genes, functional enrichment, metabolic activity, and cell death-related signatures were analyzed. Key findings were further validated using immunohistochemistry staining and quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Results We found that pre-hypertrophic chondrocytes (preHTC), fibrocartilage chondrocytes (FC), pre-inflammatory chondrocytes (preInfC), and inflammatory chondrocytes (InfC) populations were enriched in OA, whereas proliferation chondrocytes (ProC) and homeostasis chondrocytes (HomC) predominated in KBD. In OA cartilage, OA-associated genes displayed upregulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling and immune activation pathways in preInfC and InfC populations. In contrast, KBD-associated genes exhibited marked activation of endoplasmic reticulum stress and oxidative stress responses in ProC-2, ProC-3, and HomC-2 subpopulations. OA was characterized by metabolic reprogramming with enhanced ECM remodelling and inflammation-related pathways, whereas KBD exhibited a globally suppressed metabolic profile. Additionally, ferroptosis activity was significantly higher in KBD cartilage compared with OA and control cartilage, with the strongest enrichment observed in ProC and HomC populations. Conclusion Although OA and KBD chondrocytes were broadly conserved across 11 identified populations, they exhibited distinct disease-specific transcriptional profiles, metabolic activities, and cell death signatures. These findings enhance our understanding of chondrocyte heterogeneity and identify the InfC population in OA, as well as the ProC and HomC populations in KBD, as potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

title: Comparative outcomes of endovascular versus synthetic bypass for isolated superficial femoral artery lesions: A 3-year single-center cohort study.
authors: Han C, Kim GM, Choi J, Tak YJ, Lee C, Lee CW, Bae M, Wang IJ, Huh U.
abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) ranges from intermittent claudication to critical limb‑threatening ischemia (CLTI), with <3% of intermittent claudication cases progressing to CLTI. This study aimed to compare the outcomes of percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with stenting (PTAS) and synthetic graft femoropopliteal bypass (FPB) in a homogeneous PAD cohort. A subgroup analysis of TransAtlantic Inter-Society Consensus (TASC) B and C lesions, which lack standardized treatment algorithms, was also performed. We retrospectively analyzed 88 patients with no prior history of vascular interventions in the same limb who were treated for isolated superficial femoral artery lesions between 2016 and 2020 (29 underwent PTAS and 59 underwent FPB). Primary outcomes were reintervention, limb amputation, mortality, and vessel patency (primary, assisted primary, and secondary) over a 3‑year follow‑up. Subgroup analysis was performed to assess differences in treatment outcomes. No statistically significant differences were detected in reintervention, limb amputation, mortality, or patency between the two treatments. For loss of primary patency, the hazard ratio (HR) for FPB versus PTAS was 1.89 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.76-4.69; log-rank p = 0.146) and 1.23 (95% CI, 0.45-3.38) after adjustment for lesion length and TASC grade. In the TASC B and C subgroup, no significant differences were observed in primary, assisted primary, or secondary patency (log-rank p = 0.809, 0.302, and 0.135, respectively). The study was underpowered to detect modest effects (post-hoc power for primary patency, 34.4%). In this small single-center cohort, no statistically significant difference in 3-year outcomes was detected between PTAS and FPB for isolated superficial femoral artery lesions; clinically meaningful differences cannot be excluded, and the findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating.

title: Clinical outcome of a modern patellofemoral arthroplasty prosthesis into the second decade - a cohort study with minimum 10-year follow-up.
authors: Tsikopoulos K, White P, Musawi HA, Newman J, Porteous A, Robinson J, Murray J, Bristol Knee Group.
abstract: Background A modern patello-femoral joint arthroplasty (PFA) prosthesis featuring a sided trochlea on-lay component produced in oxinium (i.e., oxidized zirconium) has been introduced recently to reduce wear and increase wettability. Good medium-term functional outcome and survivorship have been documented as of yet. The aim of this study was to explore the long-term outcomes in a consecutive series with 10-year follow-up. Methods Data were collected between September 2005 and November 2014 and a total of 161 modern PFJ replacements with a mean follow-up of 13.8 years (range 2 to 22 years) were considered. The primary outcome was the assessment of implant survivorship and revisions 10 years post-operatively and beyond. Secondary outcomes included the assessment of the Oxford Knee Score (OKS) preoperatively, one and five years post-operatively in addition to complications and all-cause mortality. Results The revision free survival of this modern implant was 92% at 5y, 81% at 10y, 78% at 15y and 75% at 20 years, and there was no effect for sex (P = 0.371), nor age (P = 0.902),nor side (P = 0.554).The mean preoperative and five-year postoperative OKSs were 18.83 (SD 7.51) and 30.00 (SD 12.77), respectively (mean difference was 11.17 [95% CI 8.17 to 14.17]; P Conclusions This study shows satisfactory implant survivorship 20 years post-operatively and good functional outcomes up to 5 years postoperatively.

title: Case Report: Combined anterior and posterior open synovectomy for recurrent primary synovial chondromatosis of the knee in a female young adult.
authors: Alaqeel M, Alsalloum A, Aldaijy M, Alqarni A, Aljammaz B.
abstract: Synovial chondromatosis is an uncommon, benign condition in which the synovium forms cartilage nodules that can break off and become loose bodies inside a joint. It usually affects a single large joint and often causes pain, swelling, mechanical symptoms, and loss of motion. The diagnosis is often suggested by history, physical examination, and imaging findings, but confirmation depends on histopathology. Due to disease rarity, it is often misdiagnosed or recognized late. We describe a 21-year-old woman with recurrent and progressive left knee primary synovial chondromatosis after incomplete open excision performed following functional limitation. She returned with worsening pain, stiffness, and knee arc of motion of only 30°-50°. Imaging showed diffuse synovial thickening and numerous ossified loose bodies filling both the anterior and posterior compartments of the knee. Given the extent of disease and failure of prior surgery, we performed open synovectomy using an anterior medial parapatellar approach and a posterior lazy-S approach, allowing compartment visualization and removal of loose bodies and diseased synovium. Histopathology confirmed synovial chondromatosis without malignant features. Her recovery was uneventful, with marked pain relief and improved gait and range of motion of 0°-115°. This case shows that recurrent, compartment-spanning disease may require a tailored open approach. Combined anterior and posterior synovectomy achieved symptomatic and functional improvement in selected cases. Posterior-compartment disease should be considered and addressed if present at the index operation; leaving it in situ led to recurrence and subsequent revision.

title: Balancing Iliac Crest Avoidance and Neural Safety in L5/S1 TELD: Quantitative Identification of a Candidate Balanced Trajectory Window Using AI-Assisted 3D MRI Reconstruction.
authors: Wang Y, Huang C, He Q, Lu J, Li M, Liu X, Zhou J, Bian C, Zhang G, Luo H, Zhang R, Liu F, Yang X, Su Z, Lu S.
abstract: Objective Transforaminal endoscopic lumbar discectomy (TELD) at L5/S1 is challenging due to the iliac crest barrier. Conventional planning relies on CT or 2D imaging, inherently lacking soft-tissue contrast to visualize neural structures. This study aimed to define a quantitative candidate balanced trajectory zone using AI-assisted 3D MRI reconstruction to simultaneously evaluate iliac crest obstruction and neural safety constraints. Methods A deep learning model was trained on 50 thin-slice lumbar MRIs to achieve precise segmentation and 3D reconstruction of neural, dural, and osseous structures. Thirty lumbar models were selected after image- and reconstruction-quality screening for surgical puncture simulation. Using a 5° increment as the angular increment, 49 virtual working trajectories (coronal plane angles, CPA 0°-30° and cross-sectional angles, CSA 0°-30°) were established for each bilateral intervertebral foramen, yielding a total of 2940 trajectories. Intersection volumes between each trajectory and the iliac crest, L5 nerve root, dural sac, and articular processes were quantitatively analyzed. Results The model achieved an 86.4% mean Dice coefficient (73.2%-92.4%). Among 2940 trajectories, 1207 (41.1%) completely avoided the iliac crest. Spatial analysis revealed a trade-off: increasing CSA reduced iliac and S1 superior articular process obstruction but increased L5 osseous removal, whereas steeper CPAs spared the L5 nerve root but risked the L5 inferior articular process. Quantitative analysis identified a candidate balanced trajectory window (CPA 20°-25°, CSA 25°-30°) that achieved a balance between iliac crest avoidance, neuro-osseous preservation, and facet integrity. Conclusions This candidate trajectory window (CPA 20°-25°/CSA 25°-30°) may provide a useful reference for balancing iliac crest avoidance with neuro-osseous safety. These findings provide quantitative constraints for manual planning and for the future development of computer-assisted trajectory-planning systems.

title: Avascular necrosis of the femur following COVID-19: an updated systematic review.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Azadvari M, Akbari N, Hatam S, Rastkar M, Razavi SZE.
abstract: Background One of the complications of COVID-19 infection is avascular necrosis of the femoral head. To date, various studies have reported a wide range of osteonecrosis of the femoral head in patients with COVID-19. The previous systematic review included only 14 studies. So, this systematic review aims to update the findings of these studies. Methods Databases such as PubMed, Scopus, EMBASE, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were systematically searched by two independent researchers on April 1st, 2024. Results A literature search revealed 1229 records, 161 full-texts were evaluated, and finally, 55 studies remained for systematic review. Fifty-five studies were included in this systematic review. Four studies were cross-sectional studies, six were retrospective studies, and the remaining (45studies) were case reports or case-series studies. Totally, 864 cases were included. Except for 12 studies, 43 studies reported the administration of steroid therapy in included cases. The most common underlying conditions were hypertension, followed by diabetes. In 274 (31.7%) of included cases, AVN was bilateral, and both hips were involved. In some studies, non-surgical treatments-including supplement therapy, anticoagulant therapy, physiotherapy, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy-were administered. Several studies reported symptomatic improvement in patients treated with the core decompression approach. Total hip arthroplasty (THA) was the most commonly used surgical treatment. Conclusions Avascular necrosis of the femoral head in cases that have survived COVID-19 should be considered carefully as early diagnosis helps to preserve the joint and its function.

title: Arthroscopic Fixation of Ulnar Coronoid Process Fracture With Suture and Button Stabilization.
authors: Jiang Z, Wei K, Li J, Ma Y, Jiang G, Chen B, Cui Z.
abstract: Ulnar coronoid fractures often cause elbow instability, whereas conservative treatment risks stiffness. Traditional open surgical approaches are frequently associated with challenges such as inadequate exposure, risks of neurovascular injury, and heterotopic ossification. Although arthroscopic transosseous fixation offers a less invasive alternative, it may still cause fragment comminution, particularly when the bone fragments are small. This technical note describes an arthroscopic fixation technique using the capsular-fragment continuity. The procedure involves placing high-strength sutures through the anterior capsule. A bony tunnel terminating at the fracture bed (without traversing the free fragment) is then created in the ulnar shaft using a posterior cruciate ligament reconstruction guide. A suture passer is advanced from the tunnel's posterior exit, through the capsular-fragment continuity, to retrieve the high-strength sutures, which are secured over an Endobutton plate for fixation. This technique provides a safe, effective, and minimally invasive option for coronoid fractures, especially with elbow instability.

title: Arthroscopic 3-Point Suture-Bridge Fixation for Posterior Cruciate Ligament Tibial Avulsion Fractures via Triple Bone Tunnels.
authors: Yao W, Liu P, Li Z, Xin X, Li Y, Jia H, Liu Z.
abstract: Posterior cruciate ligament tibial avulsion fractures are a distinct clinical entity. Although the optimal fixation strategy for these fractures remains debated, arthroscopic fixation emerges as a preferred surgical approach owing to its minimally invasive nature, superior intra-articular visualization, and effectiveness in restoring ligamentous tension and joint stability. In this technical note, we use a 3-point fixation technique involving 3 small-diameter tibial bone tunnels for the management of a posterior cruciate ligament tibial avulsion fracture. This approach facilitates precise fracture reduction and significantly enhances postoperative knee joint stability.

title: Anatomical Conoid Ligament Reconstruction Improves Posterior Stability in Neer Type IIB Distal Clavicle Fractures: A Cadaveric Biomechanical Study.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Kurata S, Inoue K, Tsujimura K, Imanaka A, Kawamura K, Sinthubua A, Mahakkanukrauh P.
abstract: Hypothesis This biomechanical study aimed to compare suture button tape (SBT) fixation techniques using different clavicular drill-hole positions in a Neer type IIB distal clavicle fracture (DCF) model. We hypothesized that anatomical conoid ligament reconstruction would provide greater posterior stability than that provided by anterior reconstruction without compromising superior stability. Methods A Neer type IIB DCF model was created using 12 fresh-frozen cadaver shoulders and tested using the following three groups: conoid group (intact conoid ligament); anatomical group (drill hole placed at the posterior aspect of the clavicle over the conoid tubercle); and anterior group (drill hole placed at the anterior one-third of the clavicular width). Reduction accuracy was assessed by measuring displacement rates (superior, anteroposterior, and combined) at the reduced positions. Mechanical stability was evaluated by applying 70-N superior and posterior loads to the proximal clavicle and measuring displacement relative to the reduced position. A statistical analysis using Friedman tests was performed; if the results were significant, then pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were subsequently performed. Bonferroni correction was applied across all 21 pairwise comparisons. An adjusted P Results No significant pairwise differences in reduction accuracy were detected after Bonferroni correction. Under superior loading, the median displacement rates were 33.2%, 4.2%, and 12.6% in the conoid, anatomical, and anterior groups, respectively. The displacement rate in the anatomical group was lower than that in the conoid group (adjusted P = .021). No significant difference between the two reconstruction groups was detected. Under posterior loading, median displacement rates were 48.1%, 16.5%, and 23.7% in the conoid, anatomical, and anterior groups, respectively. The displacement rate in the anatomical group was lower than that in the conoid and anterior groups (adjusted P = .010 and .031, respectively). The mean within-specimen difference in posterior displacement between the anterior and anatomical groups was 1.8 mm (95% confidence interval, 0.6-2.9 mm). Conclusion Anatomical reconstruction using SBT provided greater resistance to posterior displacement than that provided by anterior reconstruction, with a mean within-specimen reduction in posterior displacement of 1.8 mm under a 70-N posterior load. No statistically significant difference in superior displacement was detected between the two reconstruction groups. The clinical relevance of the observed posterior displacement difference has not yet been established. Level of evidence Basic Science Study, Biomechanics.

title: An accessible efficient intervertebral disc vision-language model training strategy with LLM-based retrieval method for spine MRI report generation.
authors: Chen X, Wang P, Wang Y, Han H, Ji X, Wang T, Wei B.
abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly important in healthcare, and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in understanding and integrating information from medical images and clinical text. This study explores a low-cost and effective MLLM-based approach for automated radiology report generation from lumbar spine MRI, aiming to improve reporting efficiency and consistency. Methods To mitigate the challenges of limited data availability and the high costs associated with applying MLLMs to spinal report generation, we proposed using the axial plane of a single lumbar intervertebral disc (IVD) and the adjacent vertebrae as the research subject. We constructed the pipeline of data processing to get disc-corresponding images and medical reports based on large language models (LLMs). Then, We fine-tuned presently mature MLLMs under conditions of 1125 patient samples and hardware limitations, achieving considerable results. Results In addition to performance evaluated using traditional natural language processing metrics, including BLEU (0.24), ROUGE-L (0.53), and CIDEr (1.28), we further validated the proposed strategy on clinical pathological classification tasks, achieving F1 scores of 0.93 for disc pathology, 0.81 for canal stenosis, and 0.91 for dehydrated disc. Notably, the model achieved diagnostic performance comparable to that of experienced radiologists for canal stenosis and dehydrated disc. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed strategy. Furthermore, our experiments show that the LLM-based data evaluation pipeline is stable and reliable. Conclusion This study offers a new perspective on the field of spinal reporting and outperforms existing methods on both performance and cost. Meanwhile, there is a considerable room for improvement in aspects of data volume and training scale.

title: All-Arthroscopic Muscle Advancement Technique for Repair of Massive Posterosuperior Rotator Cuff Tears in the Lateral Decubitus Position.
authors: Nakazawa K, Manaka T, Hirakawa Y, Ito Y, Nishiura R, Mori S, Terai H.
abstract: Massive posterosuperior rotator cuff tears remain challenging because of the high retear rate after arthroscopic repair. Muscle advancement has been reported as an effective technique for reducing repair tension and improving healing in severely retracted supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendons. Although all-arthroscopic muscle advancement has recently been reported, previously described techniques were performed in the beach-chair position. We describe an all-arthroscopic muscle advancement technique in the lateral decubitus position. This technical note describes the indications, technique, and technical aspects of this procedure. Indications include massive posterosuperior rotator cuff tears in which the supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendons cannot be reduced to the greater tuberosity with conventional release alone, particularly in patients without severe fatty degeneration. The procedure is performed in the lateral decubitus position using a traction device and a 30° arthroscope.
