Stepwise release of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus from the scapula is performed arthroscopically, followed by rotator cuff repair after sufficient advancement to the greater tuberosity is confirmed. This technique may allow anatomic reduction and low-tension repair even in difficult-to-repair tears. The lateral decubitus position may provide a wider working space and improved visualization around the scapula; however, advanced arthroscopic skills and careful attention to the suprascapular nerve are required.

title: A Single Intra-articular Injection of Autologous Stromal Vascular Fraction for Moderate-to-Severe Knee Osteoarthritis: Results of a Multicenter Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial With 12-Month Follow-up.
journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
authors: Garza JR, Moorman CT, Baria M, Santa Maria D, Bowen J, Sparks N, Rubin JP.
abstract: Background This randomized controlled trial evaluated the 12-month outcomes of a single intra-articular injection of autologous adipose-derived stromal vascular fraction (SVF), prepared and administered during the same clinical encounter, for the treatment of moderate-to-severe knee osteoarthritis (OA). Purpose/hypothesis To evaluate the efficacy of a single intra-articular injection of 25 million autologous adipose-derived SVF cells for moderate-to-severe knee OA, compared with placebo, at 12 months. The authors hypothesized that SVF-treated patients would demonstrate a significantly greater responder rate based on prespecified clinically meaningful improvements in pain and function derived from composite outcomes of the index and contralateral knees. Study design Randomized controlled trial; Level of evidence, 1. Methods Adults aged 35 to 85 years with symptomatic unilateral or bilateral knee OA were eligible if the index knee demonstrated a Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index pain score of ≥8, an Outerbridge grade of 2 to 4 on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and a Kellgren-Lawrence grade of 2 to 4 on radiographs. Autologous adipose-derived SVF was prepared using a point-of-care isolation system during the same clinical encounter, assessed against predefined release criteria, and administered as a single intra-articular injection into the index knee. MRI of the index knee was obtained at baseline and at 12 months. Results A total of 618 participants were assessed for eligibility, of whom 114 were randomized (SVF, n = 83; placebo, n = 31). At 12 months, a single intra-articular injection of 25 million SVF cells demonstrated statistical superiority over placebo for the primary composite clinical endpoint. The responder rate was 51.8% (43/83) in the SVF group compared with 29% (9/31) in the placebo group (difference, 22.8% [95% CI, 3.5%-42%]; 1-sided P = .0149). No serious investigational device-related adverse events were reported. Conclusion A single intra-articular injection of 25 million autologous adipose-derived SVF cells resulted in statistically superior and clinically meaningful improvements in pain and function at 12 months compared with placebo, with no serious investigational device-related adverse events reported. Registration IDE 16734; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04440189.

title: Utilization of a Lifestyle Medicine Program for Presurgical Health Optimization: Impact on Early Postoperative Outcomes of Hip and Knee Arthroplasty.
authors: Prather H, Leupold O, Carli A, Gonzalez Della Valle A, Cushner F, Cheng J.
abstract: Background Chronic systemic inflammation is associated with osteoarthritis and chronic diseases that increase surgical risk before total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA). This study compares early postoperative outcomes between patients who did and did not complete an intensive lifestyle medicine (LSM) program to reduce chronic systemic inflammation. Methods Anthropometric variables, lifestyle measures, patient-reported outcome measures, and postoperative 90-day outcomes (ie, length of stay, infection, persistent pain, opioids) were obtained from an LSM repository. Comparisons were made between patients who completed the intensive LSM track (multiple visits, interprofessional providers) and those who declined behavior change preoperatively (selective track: single provider visit). A subanalysis evaluated glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) medication users. Results Among 292 patients (72% women; 62 ± 9 years; 76% White), 154 completed the intensive track and 138 participated in the selective track. Most (91%) had ≥2 chronic diseases. Baseline characteristics were similar between tracks, except for higher anxiety/depression scores in the intensive track (3.3 ± 3.0 vs 1.8 ± 2.4[ P P P = .001]), with no differences in other outcomes. Conclusions Postoperative persistent pain rates were significantly lower in patients who completed an intensive LSM program before THA or TKA, compared to patients who did not engage in health improvement. GLP-1RA users showed no health benefits and required more opioid refills.

title: Triggers of Gout Flares from Local to Systemic Perspectives.
authors: Straton AR, Crisan TO, Joosten LAB.
abstract: Gout is the most common type of inflammatory arthritis, caused by MSU crystal deposition in the joint, resulting from chronic hyperuricemia. Typically, the first clinical presentation is a gout flare characterized by severe pain, redness, joint swelling, and limited mobility. Despite continuous exposure to increased serum urate concentration followed by MSU crystal formation, flares are unpredictable and intermittent when poorly managed. Acute gout flares follow a two-step model: firstly, MSU crystals build up and, secondly, an endogenous or exogenous triggering event is needed. Once both triggers are given, resident macrophages initiate an acute inflammatory response. However, these additional factors are still under debate and increased serum urate concentrations alone are insufficient to ignite gout flares. In this review, we aim to sharpen our understanding of the unique characteristics responsible for transitioning from an asymptomatic state to acute joint inflammation observed in gout patients. We focus on integrating joint mechanisms during a gout flare, such as NLRP3 inflammasome activation, macrophage heterogeneity changes, and local physicochemical conditions with systemic influences from immunometabolism and genetic variation to explain the interindividual variability in flare susceptibility.

title: The effect of three dimensional-printed guides on assisting rotational axis localization of hinged external fixator in the surgery for elbow terrible triad injury.
authors: Chen H, Zhao T, Gao H, Ma P.
abstract: Purpose This study evaluated the effect of 3D-printed guides on rotation-axis localization for hinged external fixation in terrible triad (TT) injury of the elbow. Methods We enrolled 55 patients with TT injuries treated with a hinged external fixator between January 2017 and January 2025, divided into a guide group (n = 29) and a freehand group (n = 26) according to the method of rotation-axis localization, with follow-up at six weeks and one year postoperatively. Pin insertion time, number of fluoroscopic exposures, elbow range of motion, functional elbow rate, Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), type and incidence of complications, and number and causes of reoperations were compared between groups. Results Compared with the freehand group, the guide group had a shorter mean pin insertion time (300.93 ± 21.97 s vs. 1392.5 ± 218.16 s) and fewer fluoroscopic exposures (2.31 ± 0.54 vs. 17.50 ± 2.93; both P 0.05). At the final follow-up, flexion-extension arc (134.36° ± 18.21° vs. 125.75° ± 26.44°), rotation arc (165.71° ± 20.34° vs. 157.04° ± 26.84°), MEPS (97.86 ± 7.26 vs. 95.21 ± 11.28), functional elbow rate (93% vs. 79%), and complication rate (11% vs. 21%) remained similar, without significant differences (P > 0.05). During follow-up, one patient in the guide group required reoperation for heterotopic ossification, whereas three patients in the freehand group required reoperation for heterotopic ossification or fixator loosening. Conclusion Compared with freehand localization of the rotation axis, guide-assisted localization reduced pin insertion time, fluoroscopic exposures, and pin adjustments. Furthermore, the guide group demonstrated non-inferiority in surgical outcomes compared to the freehand group.

title: Synthetic CT from biplanar radiographs for patellofemoral anatomical assessment: development and validation of an adapted X2CT-GAN model.
authors: Lu Q, Pan R, Qian J, Fang F, Hu H.
abstract: Objectives Accurate assessment of osseous morphology is essential for the diagnosis and surgical management of patellofemoral instability. Methods capable of providing CT-like anatomical information while reducing radiation exposure are therefore of considerable clinical interest. This study aimed to validate the accuracy of radiography-derived synthetic computed tomography (sCT) generated by a deep learning model for anatomical assessment of patellofemoral instability. Methods A total of 210 paired radiographs and CT scans were retrospectively collected and randomly divided into a training set (n = 170) and a validation set (n = 40). A deep learning model based on the X2CT-GAN framework was used to reconstruct sCT volumes from anteroposterior and lateral radiographs. Two blinded readers independently measured tibial tubercle-trochlear groove (TT-TG) distance, trochlear sulcus angle, and Caton-Deschamps index on both sCT and real CT images. Reliability, inter-modality agreement, and threshold-based classification agreement were evaluated. Results All intra- and inter-observer reliability values were excellent. Inter-modality agreement was excellent for TT-TG distance and good for trochlear sulcus angle. Agreement for patellar height was good. The mean absolute error for TT-TG distance ranged from 1.24 to 1.38 mm. Agreement for threshold-based classifications ranged from substantial to almost perfect, with high specificity observed across all evaluated cutoff values. Conclusions Radiography-derived sCT demonstrated good agreement with real CT for both quantitative measurements and threshold-based classifications relevant to clinical decision-making in patellofemoral instability. These findings suggest that radiography-derived synthetic CT may represent a promising lower-radiation alternative for anatomical assessment of patellofemoral instability in selected clinical scenarios.

title: Staged Revision Reverse Total Shoulder Arthroplasty to Functional Hemiarthroplasty With Retained Humeral Implant: A Salvage Technique.
authors: Aguirre T, DeFoor MT, Dickinson NJ, Unger FA, Vidal M, Blankenship M, Provencher MT.
abstract: With the increased incidence and indications for reverse total shoulder arthroplasty, the increased need for revision shoulder arthroplasty also continues to rise. Therefore, revision strategies and techniques are essential to optimize patient outcomes and preserve function, particularly in the challenges of glenoid failure, poor glenoid bone stock, and/or poor native bone quality. Because of the risk of intraoperative fracture, increased blood loss, prolonged operative time, excessive implant costs, and the high risk of complications of a humeral stem extraction and revision, extraction of a well-fixed humeral stem may be unnecessary and undesirable. When feasible, stem retention is preferred, which can lead to reduced surgical morbidity, cost-saving practice habits, and better patient outcomes, especially in systems lacking platform convertibility. This Technical Note expands the reconstructive salvage options in systems lacking platform convertibility through conversion of a reverse total shoulder arthroplasty to a functional hemiarthroplasty by cementing a glenosphere onto a retained, nonconvertible, stemmed humeral tray. This technique may serve as a definitive solution or, more likely, a temporary construct in select salvage and revision cases, offering joint stability and pain control while preserving articular congruency and avoiding the morbidity associated with full-component revision.

title: Spatial architecture of the synovium identifies clinically relevant phenotypes of osteoarthritis.
authors: Tsubaki T, Miyahara J, Arino Y, Naoi Y, Kawaguchi K, Kono K, Yamagami R, Taketomi S, Ishikura H, Kasai T, Ennishi D, Tanaka S, Saito T, Chijimatsu R.
abstract: Objectives Osteoarthritis (OA) is a heterogeneous joint disease characterized by marked variability in etiology and clinical symptoms. We aimed to determine whether spatial organization of synovial tissue underlies clinically relevant heterogeneity in knee OA. Methods We developed a deep learning-based semantic segmentation framework to analyze hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole-slide images of human synovium. Spatial entropy and inter-tissue connectivity metrics were incorporated to evaluate local pathology. We further applied graph neural network-based community modeling to classify tissue structures based on their microenvironment. Results The model identified key OA-associated histological features, including synovial lining hyperplasia, immune cell infiltration, angiogenesis, and fibrotic remodeling. Quantitative analysis of tissue composition revealed that enrichment of dense fibrous tissue was associated with poorer postoperative outcomes. However, tissue proportion alone did not adequately capture baseline disease status. Inter-tissue connectivity-based analysis showed that enrichment of Lining-Micro vessel interactions was associated with lower preoperative KOOS Symptom scores, indicating more severe symptoms, and elevated synovitis scores. Using features derived from graph neural network-based modeling, Micro vessels segregated into two distinct communities, one enriched in adjacent lining structures and another associated with immune-rich regions, and their relative abundances varied among knee OA patients. Integration with matched synovial single-cell RNA sequencing data showed increased predicted interactions between lining fibroblasts and endothelial cells in the Lining-Micro vessel-rich phenotype. These interactions were enriched for angiogenesis-related VEGF and ANGPTL signaling, providing supportive evidence for a distinct fibroblast-endothelial signaling state. Conclusions These findings indicate that the spatial organization of synovial architecture, beyond simple tissue composition, captures clinically relevant heterogeneity in knee OA and links histological microenvironments to cell-cell communication networks.

title: Significant Differences in the Presentation, Diagnosis, and Management of Juvenile Osteochondritis Dissecans Exist Among Asia-Pacific and European Surgeons.
authors: Hui SJ, Liew JJL, Chew KY, Loke RWK, Hui JHP, Malhotra R.
abstract: Purpose To compare diagnostic and treatment preferences for juvenile osteochondritis dissecans between Asia-Pacific and European surgeons. Methods Between January 2024 and July 2024, an electronic survey was distributed to orthopaedic surgeons affiliated with Pediatric Research in Sports Medicine Asia-Pacific (n = 54 invited). Responses were compared with data from the 2023 European Society of Sports Traumatology, Knee Surgery and Arthroscopy survey. Domains included clinical presentation, imaging preferences, nonoperative strategies, operative techniques, and follow-up protocols. Proportions were compared using χ 2 or Fisher's exact tests ( P Results Fifty-four surgeons (100%) responded to our survey. A total of 104 surgeons were analyzed (54 Asia-Pacific, 50 Europe). Trauma was more frequently cited as a presenting factor in Asia-Pacific (knee: 100% vs 17%; ankle: 100% vs 21%; P P P P P P P P = .002), whereas Asia-Pacific surgeons favored osteochondral autograft (68% vs 33%; P = .001) and antegrade drilling (84% vs 48%; P Conclusions Significant regional differences exist between Asia-Pacific and European surgeons in the presentation, diagnostic evaluation, and management strategies for juvenile osteochondritis dissecans. Clinical relevance Marked regional variation exits in the diagnostic and therapeutic management of juvenile osteochondritis dissecans. These differences influence imaging selection, operative thresholds, and surgical technique choice. Understanding such variability is essential for developing international consensus guidelines and ensuring consistent, evidence-based care across various health care systems.

title: Rotator Cuff Repair with Concomitant Biceps Tenodesis is Cost-Effective at Mid-Term Follow-up: A Systematic Review and Cost-Effective Analysis.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Berreta RS, Badin D, Koyejo LD, Chan D, Ashkar A, Siragusa J, Harris E, Fox H, Jain A, Srikumaran U.
abstract: Background There is limited evidence describing the cost-effectiveness of isolated rotator cuff repair (RCR) compared to rotator cuff repair with biceps tenodesis (BT) in the treatment of primary rotator cuff tears at mid-term follow-up. Purpose (1) To perform a cost utility analysis comparing RCR to RCR with BT in patients with rotator cuff tears over a 5-year time horizon. Methods A decision tree economic model was constructed to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of RCR vs RCR with BT across a 5-year time horizon. Model transition probabilities, costs, and health utility measures, based on EQ-5D (European Quality of Life-5 Dimension) scores, were derived from the literature. Health utility was measured in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and cost-effectiveness was based on the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) considering a willingness to pay (WTP) threshold of $50,000/QALY. Monte Carlo probabilistic and one-way sensitivity analysis was performed to assess for parameter uncertainty. Each cycle length was defined as 1 year, and 5-year costs and utilities were calculated with 3% annual discounting. Results Over a 5-year horizon, RCR with BT yielded 3.713 QALYs at a mean cost of $34,182 compared to 3.651 QALYs and $33,372 for RCR alone. RCR with BT was found to be cost-effective with an ICER of $13,064/QALY and a positive net monetary benefit of $2,289. RCR with BT was the preferred treatment in 88.51% of 1,000 simulations on probabilistic sensitivity analysis. One-way sensitivity analyses demonstrated cost-effectiveness for performing RCR with BT was maintained with tenodesis implant costs up to $3,048, revision rates up to 6.7%, and additional operative time up to 53.7 minutes. Conclusion Despite higher upfront costs, performing biceps tenodesis at the time of index rotator cuff repair provides greater quality-adjusted life years and is cost-effective compared to isolated rotator cuff repair at mid-term follow-up. Level of evidence Level III, Economic Study.

title: Robotic navigation-assisted versus conventional freehand placement of the infra-acetabular screw in acetabular fracture surgery: A retrospective comparative study.
authors: Cao W, Chen Z, Liu H, Zhan N, He J, Qi L, Li J, Zheng Y, Tang J, Li M, Chen H.
abstract: Background The infra-acetabular screw (IAS) is an important component of fixation constructs for complex acetabular fractures, but accurate freehand placement is technically demanding, and evidence on robotic navigation-assisted IAS placement remains limited. This study compared robotic navigation-assisted (RA) and conventional fluoroscopic freehand (CF) IAS placement in acetabular fracture surgery. Methods In this retrospective study, 53 patients with acetabular fractures who underwent IAS fixation between June 2022 and July 2024 were included, 28 underwent RA placement using the HoloSight robotic navigation system and 25 underwent CF placement. The primary outcome was screw-placement accuracy, graded on postoperative CT according to the Lonstein criteria. Secondary outcomes included the number of guide-wire adjustments, fluoroscopy frequency, IAS insertion time, total operative time, intraoperative blood loss, fracture reduction quality, hip function, and complications. Results The grade 0 (no cortical penetration) rate was higher in the RA group than in the CF group (96.4% [27/28] vs. 60.0% [15/25], p = 0.005). RA placement was associated with fewer guide-wire adjustments (0.07 ± 0.26 vs. 3.60 ± 1.15), fewer fluoroscopies (9.32 ± 1.66 vs. 21.28 ± 3.18), shorter IAS insertion time (10.36 ± 2.50 vs. 26.68 ± 4.11 min), shorter total operative time (134.54 ± 15.46 vs. 155.80 ± 18.48 min), and less intraoperative blood loss (468.21 ± 84.68 vs. 588.40 ± 80.76 mL) (all p Conclusions Robotic navigation-assisted IAS placement was associated with significantly higher screw-placement accuracy and greater procedural efficiency than the conventional freehand technique, without compromising fracture reduction quality, hip function, or safety.

title: Relationships between cam morphology and [<sup>18</sup>F]sodium fluoride PET uptake in asymptomatic hips.
authors: Watkins L, Datta S, Goyal A, Vainberg Y, Shalit R, Stevens KJ, Gold GE, Kogan F.
abstract: Objective Bone deformities are linked to femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) and increased risk of hip osteoarthritis (OA) but are also common in the general population. The purpose of this study is to examine relationships between FAI-linked morphology and resting bone metabolic activity in asymptomatic hips. Methods This exploratory secondary analysis of hip scans from a [ 18 F]NaF PET-MRI study on knee pain included 76 asymptomatic hips from 41 individuals (53 ± 13 years, body mass index 25.9 ± 5.1 kg/m2, 21 female/20 male). Hips were evaluated for cam, pincer, and additional morphology with the Hip Osteoarthritis MRI Scoring System. Mean and maximum PET standardized uptake values (SUV) were recorded for the femoral head-neck junction, center of the femoral head, and anterolateral acetabulum. The influence of morphology on SUV mean and SUV max was assessed with linear mixed effects models. Results Forty-two hips had isolated cam morphology, two had isolated pincer morphology, and four had mixed-type morphology. Cam morphology or alpha angles were not associated with increased bone metabolic activity. Hips with gluteal tendinitis/trochanteric bursitis had significantly higher SUV max in the center of the femoral head (p = 9.98e-5). No other morphological features were associated with bone metabolic activity, though the low prevalence of features such as pincer morphology limits interpretation of these findings. Conclusion In older asymptomatic hips without OA, no association was detected between cam morphology and elevated resting bone remodeling. Understanding structure-function relationships in asymptomatic hips with cam morphology may help contextualize findings associated with pain in patients with FAI or OA.

title: Procyanidin B2 ameliorates osteoporosis by modulating osteoclast precursor differentiation through activation of the PI3K/Akt/Nrf2 axis.
authors: Zou Y, Wang C, Zhang T, Huang Y, Xu H, Ma X, Li L, Lyu F, Zhang F.
abstract: Osteoporosis (OP) is a chronic, systemic skeletal disorder characterized by excessive osteoclast activation and bone resorption, for which effective therapies with minimal adverse effects remain limited. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated during oxidative stress promote osteoclast differentiation and are considered a primary contributor to OP pathogenesis. Procyanidin B2 is a natural flavonoid with potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties; however, its therapeutic efficacy and underlying mechanisms of action in OP remain unclear. In this study, we investigated the effects of procyanidin B2 on osteoclastogenesis using tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase staining, quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction, and pit formation assays. Our findings indicate that procyanidin B2 inhibits RANKL-induced osteoclastogenesis in a dose-dependent manner. Mechanistically, procyanidin B2 activates the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (Akt) signaling pathway, thereby upregulating nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) expression. This induction of Nrf2 enhances ROS clearance in osteoclast precursors (OCPs), leading to functional modulation of their differentiation trajectory rather than mere suppression of OCP proliferation. Moreover, micro-computed tomography and histological analyses reveal that procyanidin B2 alleviates ovariectomy-induced bone loss in mice and demonstrates favorable in vivo biocompatibility. Collectively, these findings indicate that procyanidin B2 mitigates OP by modulating OCP differentiation throughout activation of the PI3K/Akt/Nrf2 axis and highlight its potential as a novel natural therapeutic agent for the prevention and treatment of OP.

title: Patient safety competence in orthopaedic care: The interplay of education, orientation, and workplace learning.
journal: International Journal of Orthopaedic and Trauma Nursing
authors: Ketola S, Rauhala A, Eloranta S.
abstract: Patient safety competence is a fundamental prerequisite for safe, high-quality healthcare. However, less is known about how healthcare professionals perceive their competence and how it develops. This study examined self-assessed patient safety competence of healthcare professionals working in orthopaedic care, across the WHO patient safety competence domains, perceived sources of competence development, and views on future learning needs. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among healthcare professionals working in outpatient, ward, perioperative, anesthesia, rehabilitation, and managerial roles in a specialized orthopedic hospital in Finland. Self-assessed patient safety competence was relatively high across all domains. The highest ratings were observed in teamwork, infection prevention and control, and patient safety in invasive procedures, whereas systems thinking and understanding the impact of complexity on patient care received the lowest ratings. Significant differences were identified in patient, client, and family involvement, with the highest ratings reported by outpatient clinic nurses, and in infection prevention and control, where scrub nurses reported the highest competence. Practical clinical work and workplace orientation were perceived as the primary sources of competence, while formal continuing education played a less prominent role. Despite high competence ratings, respondents expressed substantial interest in further competence development, particularly through workplace-based learning and unit-level training. The findings suggest that patient safety competence develops primarily through experiential learning and workplace-based socialization rather than through formal education alone. Patient safety competence should therefore be understood not only as an individual capability but also as an organizational resource embedded in learning processes, knowledge sharing, and patient safety culture.

title: Pathogen-specific positron emission tomography for Enterobacterales bone infection.
authors: Gordon O, Napiorkowski A, Flavahan K, De Jesus P, Dikeman DA, Kronenberg A, Archer NK, Jain SK.
abstract: Aims Gram-negative bone infections involving Enterobacterales group of bacteria pose a growing concern, especially for orthopaedic surgeries and diabetic ulcers. Current imaging methods either identify morphological changes by CT and MRI, or inflammation, using white blood cell scans or 2-deoxy-2-[ 18 F]fluoro-d-glucose ([ 18 F]-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET). While valuable, these are not specific, resulting in delayed diagnoses. PET/CT using 2-deoxy-2-[ 18 F]fluoro-d-sorbitol ([ 18 F]-FDS) is a novel method for detecting living Enterobacterales bacteria in vivo, via a conserved sorbitol-specific bacterial pathway. In this study, we aim to evaluate [ 18 F]-FDS PET/CT for detection and monitoring of Enterobacterales bone infection in a mouse model. Methods We adapted a murine model of Gram-positive implant-associated spine infection to a Gram-negative infection model. We compared microbiological techniques to imaging with [ 18 F]-FDG and [ 18 F]-FDS. We determined the standardized uptake value (SUV) ratios for detection of bacterial infection and response to therapy, in 48 mice with surgical implants infected with either Escherichia coli or Staphylococcus aureus and compared them to controls with surgical implants but no infection. Results Both bacteria induced substantial bone pathology with reduced bone density. [ 18 F]-FDS PET could specifically detect implant-associated spinal infections due to E. coli with a mean SUV ratio of 2.2 (SD 1.3), which was substantially lower in S. aureus (0.7 (SD 0.2); p = 0.002) and uninfected mice (1.0 (SD 0.1)). In contrast, [ 18 F]-FDG could not differentiate between the two bacterial infections or the control (p = 0.497). Finally, [ 18 F]-FDS PET could determine antibiotic efficacy, and monitor infection over time. Conclusion We demonstrate that [ 18 F]-FDS affords a highly accurate and clinically translatable detection of Enterobacterales bone infection. This novel modality offers a rapid and specific method to diagnose and monitor bone infections, inform medical decisions, reduce the need for surgery, and limit unnecessary antibiotic use. Similar approaches may be implemented to develop tracers for other bacteria.

title: Paediatric chronic Monteggia Bado III fracture: how to avoid and treat.
authors: Vaz R, Alves C, Cabral J, Carvalho M.
abstract: Paediatric Monteggia fracture is misdiagnosed in 28% of cases, with possible functional impairment in delayed diagnosis. Assessment of the radiocapitellar alignment on both anteroposterior and lateral views of the elbow is imperative, especially when an apparently isolated ulnar fracture is present. Although Bado I injuries are the most common and diagnosed on lateral radiographs, type III injuries often go unnoticed due to inadequate examination of the anteroposterior view. We present a case of a 6-year-old female patient with a neglected Monteggia fracture (Bado III). The patient underwent surgery 10 months after initial trauma, involving open reduction of the radial head, repair of the annular ligament, and proximal ulnar osteotomy. At 1 year follow-up, the patient achieved a QuickDASH of 0. This case highlights the importance of early recognition and appropriate imaging evaluation, while demonstrating that satisfactory outcomes can be achieved in chronic cases with proper surgical management.

title: Open access route and citation impact in orthopaedic research: A comparison of Gold/hybrid, Green, and Bronze open access within ten high-impact subscription-based journals.
authors: Daniels WJ, Cruickshank M, Dejong T, Ghert M.
abstract: Open access (OA) publishing has expanded access to research, but citation patterns may differ across OA routes. We examined the association between OA route and citation rate within ten high-impact, predominantly subscription-based orthopaedic journals, analysing 24,115 articles published from 2014 to 2019. Journals in which more than 95% of articles were OA were excluded by design; fully OA journals were therefore not represented, and every Gold OA article in this corpus was published as hybrid OA within a subscription journal (hereafter Gold/hybrid OA). Articles were classified as Gold/hybrid OA, Green OA, Bronze OA, or Closed Access using Web of Science OA indicators. Results are reported in three layers: unadjusted descriptive comparisons, a primary adjusted analysis, andsensitivity analyses. The primary analysis used an entropy-balanced negative binomial generalized linear mixed model adjusting for publication year, document type, author count, and journal influence, with journal-level random effects. Most articles were Closed Access (78.5%), followed by Green OA (9.1%), Bronze OA (8.7%), and Gold/hybrid OA (3.8%). In the primary analysis, Gold/hybrid OA and Green OA had higher citation rates than Closed Access (rate ratio 1.41, 95% CI 1.30-1.54; and 1.35, 95% CI 1.28-1.43), and did not differ from each other (1.04, 95% CI 0.95-1.15). Citation rates varied by publication year: Gold/hybrid OA had the highest predicted rate in recent cohorts and Green OA in older cohorts with longer follow-up. Bronze OA had the lowest unadjusted citation counts, largely because it was enriched for lower-cited document types. The higher citation rates for Gold/hybrid and Green OA persisted across all sensitivity analyses. Within subscription-based orthopaedic journals, OA routes are not interchangeable; these findings do not extend to fully OA journals.

title: Musculoskeletal Health in Elite Athletes With Bilateral Lower Limb Loss: The ADVANCE Cohort Study.
authors: Watson F, O'Sullivan O, Bull A, Bennett A, Kemp H, Fear N, Boos C, Behan FP.
abstract: Context Lower limb (LL) loss can be detrimental to bone and joint health. Exercise improves musculoskeletal outcomes in individuals without LL loss, but with limited investigation after LL loss. The aim is to assess differences in bone and joint health between elite athletes and nonathletes with bilateral LL loss to assess associations between exercise and musculoskeletal health in this population. Design ADVANCE (Armed Services Trauma Rehabilitation Outcome) is a longitudinal cohort study involving UK military personnel and veterans who served in Afghanistan. Methods Sixty-four ambulatory participants with bilateral LL loss were included. Seven participants were elite athletes (athlete group; n = 7) and were compared with the remaining participants (nonathlete group, n = 57). The Kellgren-Lawrence score for knee and hip osteoarthritis (OA), femoral neck and lumbar spine bone mineral density (BMD), Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, Non-Arthritic Hip Score, International Physical Activity Questionnaire, and 6-minute walk test distance were compared. Outcomes were also compared between the Athlete group and Nonathlete group split by activity level. Results Participants were 33.1 ± 4.7 years old and 6.9 ± 1.5 years postinjury. No Athlete group participants had knee OA compared with 51.8% of Nonathlete participants. There was a weak trend for more prevalent hip OA in the Nonathlete group (P = .074); 7.1% Athlete group participants and 30.7% Nonathlete group participants had Kellgren-Lawrence score ≥ 1. Femoral neck BMD was not different between groups, but there was a trend for lower lumbar spine BMD in the Nonathlete group compared with the Athlete group (-0.41 vs 0.57; P = .06). More active nonathletes had better femoral neck t scores than less active nonathletes, P = .03. Neither Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score Pain, Symptoms, Non-Arthritic Hip Score, nor 6-minute walk test distance were different between groups. Conclusion Athletes and active nonathletes with LL loss may have favorable BMD profiles. Athletes with LL loss have lower prevalence of radiographic hip and knee OA. Although not conclusive due to our study design, this suggests that exercise may be associated with beneficial musculoskeletal health outcomes in this population.

title: Medial clavicle fracture with anterosuperior sternoclavicular joint dislocation: joint-sparing suture anchor imbrication and open reduction internal fixation.
authors: Light JJ, Chehade G, Czajka C.

title: Locking plate fixation with cerclage augmentation and bone grafting for Vancouver B2 periprosthetic femoral fractures around cementless stems: a surgical option in elderly high-risk patients unsuitable for revision arthroplasty (mid-term outcomes).
authors: Shan X, Tian Z, Wang H, Li H, Lu J, Feng Z, Xu R, Qiao Y, Zhou S, Zhang H.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the mid-term clinical and radiographic outcomes of open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with a locking plate, cerclage wires, and bone grafting for Vancouver B2 periprosthetic femoral fractures (PFF) in elderly, high-risk patients who are unsuitable for revision arthroplasty after primary cementless total hip arthroplasty (THA). Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 28 elderly patients with Vancouver B2 PFFs treated with locking plate fixation and cerclage wiring. Patient demographics, operative parameters (time, blood loss), and hospital stay were recorded. Fracture healing time, Harris Hip Score (HHS), and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) were evaluated preoperatively and at the final follow-up, with VAS also assessed postoperatively. Complications were documented. Results The mean follow-up was 63.86 months (range, 24-120). During the follow-up period, three patients died due to advanced age, and two patients were lost to follow-up because of changes in contact information or failure to attend scheduled visits. Mean operative time was 176.32 ± 20.46 min, and mean blood loss was 358.93 ± 188.59 mL. All fractures united, with a mean healing time of 3.89 months. HHS improved significantly from 43.93 preoperatively to 90.32 at final follow-up ( P P Conclusion For selected high-risk elderly patients with Vancouver B2 PFF who are unsuitable for revision arthroplasty, ORIF with locking plate, cerclage wires, and bone grafting appears to be a potentially viable treatment option. Its success depends on rigorous case selection and standardized perioperative management, and further long-term prospective studies are warranted to confirm its durability.

title: Knee flexion influences MRI-based static tibiofemoral rotation after ACL injury and reconstruction.
authors: Ackermann J, Jones M, Ball SV, Kabeer AS, Bamania P, Watura C, Lee JC, Williams A.
abstract: Purpose To determine the influence of knee flexion on MRI-based static TF rotation, and evaluate whether this relationship is modified by anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) state, posterior tibial slope asymmetry (ΔPTS), or lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET). Methods A retrospective review was conducted of professional soccer players who underwent primary ACL reconstruction between 2012 and 2024 with available MRI. Static TF rotation, medial and lateral PTS, and knee flexion were measured on MRI. ΔPTS was defined as the difference between lateral and medial PTS. Linear mixed-effects models assessed associations, including interactions for flexion, ΔPTS, ACL state, and LET, with adjustment for meniscal status. Results A total of 310 MRI examinations from 106 professional soccer players (mean age 23.3 ± 4.2 years) with ACL injury (n = 106) and after ACL reconstruction (n = 204) were retrospectively analyzed. Greater knee flexion during MRI acquisition was associated with increased internal TF rotation (β = 0.15° per 1° flexion; 95% CI, 0.02-0.27°; p = 0.020). ΔPTS was a strong independent predictor of TF rotation (β = 1.33° per 1° ΔPTS; 95% CI, 0.72-1.95°; p Conclusion Knee flexion during MRI acquisition significantly influences axial TF rotation. PTS asymmetry remains an independent determinant of rotational alignment, although its apparent effect decreases at greater flexion angles and after ACL reconstruction. Based on model estimates, a clinically plausible 10-20° difference in knee flexion during MRI acquisition may produce approximately 1.5-3° of apparent static TF rotation. In MRI studies of static TF rotation standardizing the flexion angle of knees is critical.

title: Is surgeon technique a modifiable risk factor for heterotopic ossification after posterior acetabular fracture fixation? A multi-surgeon study.
authors: Kumar DS, Luther L, Schaffer NE, Litten RM, Traven SA, Moore RS, Moreno-Diaz AF, Velasco-Castro J, Maxson R, Sumpter AE, Agarwal A, Boyce RH, Collinge CA, Evans JM, Jahangir AA, Johnson JP, Mir HR, Perdue AM, Quade JH, Sethi MK, Spitler C, Stinner DJ, Tatman LM, Mitchell PM.
abstract: Introduction Heterotopic ossification (HO) is a well-recognized complication following operative fixation of acetabular fractures through a posterior approach. Established risk factors largely reflect nonmodifiable patient and injury characteristics. Whether surgeon-controlled aspects of operative technique influence HO remains poorly defined. The purpose of this study was to determine if the individual surgeon and specific technique variables are associated with HO after accounting for established patient and injury factors. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 1292 patients who underwent acetabular fracture fixation through a Kocher-Langenbeck approach at two Level 1 trauma centers between 2010 and 2025 by 14 fellowship-trained orthopaedic traumatologists. Patients receiving any form of HO prophylaxis were excluded. Four surgeon-controlled variables were examined: aggressiveness of gluteus minimus debridement, trochanteric osteotomy, thrombin gel use, and closed suction drainage. HO was graded on final radiographs by two independent reviewers using the Brooker classification, with third-reader adjudication for disagreements, and categorized as little-to-no (grade 0-I), moderate (grade II), or severe (grade III-IV). Mixed-effects logistic regression models with surgeon as a random effect were used to assess the associations between patient, injury, and surgeon-controlled technique variables, as well as the individual surgeon, with severe and moderate HO formation. Results Little-to-no HO occurred in 1132 patients (87.6%), moderate HO in 96 (7.4%), and severe HO in 64 (5.0%). Aggressive gluteus minimus debridement was not associated with HO severity. For severe HO, the surgeon did not contribute meaningfully to model performance, and no surgeon-controlled technique variables were significant; severe head injury, mechanical ventilation beyond 72 h, African-American race, and dual surgical approaches were associated with severe HO. For moderate HO, the surgeon contributed moderately, and both trochanteric osteotomy (odds ratio [OR] 3.7, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.1-12) and closed suction drainage (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.0-3.1) were associated with increased odds of moderate HO. Conclusion Severe HO following posterior acetabular fracture fixation is predominantly driven by patient and injury characteristics rather than surgeon technique. Aggressive gluteus minimus debridement does not appear to reduce HO risk, and prevention efforts should prioritize patient-level risk stratification.

title: Intraoperative visualization with 3D fluoroscopy for posterior pelvic fixation is associated with lower cumulative imaging-related radiation exposure.
authors: Tse S, Chinweze RO, Velasco-Castro J, Andring N, Jbeily E, Robinson C, Saade A, Simister S, Campbell ST, Fitzpatrick E, Lee MA, Saiz AM, Soles GL.
abstract: Introduction Achieving optimal screw positioning in posterior pelvic ring (PR) fracture fixation is critical for fracture stability and safety. Formerly, our institution used intraoperative plain-film fluoroscopy followed by postoperative computed tomography (CT) to assess fracture reduction and screw placement. Introduction of the 3D mobile C-arm enables immediate volumetric intraoperative assessment, may improve intraoperative visualization, and may alter conventional imaging requirements. This study compared cumulative imaging-related radiation exposure between cases performed with intraoperative 3D fluoroscopy (3DF) against standard intraoperative plain-film fluoroscopy (2DF), including postoperative CT utilization. Methods A retrospective review was conducted on patients treated for posterior PR fractures at a level 1 trauma center between 2014 and 2023. Utilization of 3DF or plain-film fluoroscopy, and any intraoperative screw changes were documented. Rates and details of postoperative complications and subsequent reoperations were recorded for patients with > 3 months follow-up. Radiation doses for 3DF, 2DF, and postoperative CT were extracted from radiology reports. Results Among 245 patients (mean age 47.2, 52.2% male) undergoing fixation for posterior PR fractures, 89 (36.3%) had 3DF intraoperatively, while 156 (63.7%) had 2DF. 27 patients (8 3DF, 19 2DF, p = 0.443) had screws changed intraoperatively, primarily to modify screw path (n = 16, 59.3%), to achieve better purchase/reduction (n = 5, 18.5%), to modify screw size (n = 3, 11.1%), to change screw type (n = 2, 7.4%), and failure to advance screw (n = 1, 3.7%). Mean radiation dose for the 3DF group was significantly lower (179.2 mGy vs 526.1 mGy, p 3 months follow-up, reoperation was less frequent with 3DF (9.5% vs 31.2%, p = 0.012), predominantly for symptomatic implant removal. Discussion and conclusion Intraoperative 3DF was associated with lower cumulative radiation exposure compared to traditional fluoroscopy with routine postoperative CT, and intraoperative dose alone was also lower. Reoperation was less frequent in the 3DF group, but most reoperations were implant removals for symptomatic or planned indications. These findings highlight the potential of 3DF as a practical radiation efficient quality assurance tool in posterior pelvic fixation.

title: Intra-individual relationships between jump height and lower-limb joint kinetics in single-leg countermovement jumps in male athletes.
authors: Yamamoto S, Kubota H, Imai K, Miyazaki T.
abstract: Athletes show trial-to-trial intra-individual variability in performance outcomes during repeated maximal-effort motor tasks within a single competition. Although inter-individual relationships between performance outcomes and joint kinetics have been demonstrated, the trial-to-trial intra-individual relationships remain unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to clarify the intra-individual relationships between jump height and lower-limb joint kinetics during single-leg countermovement jumps (CMJs) in male athletes. Fifty-two male athletes performed 12 maximal-effort single-leg CMJs within a single session. Ground reaction forces and marker coordinates were recorded, from which jump height and lower-limb joint kinetics were calculated. Hierarchical linear modeling was used to examine the intra-individual relationships between jump height and each joint kinetic variable. Significant positive fixed effects on jump height were observed for hip (extension torque [γ 10 = 0.013], flexion-extension power [γ 10 = 0.005], and positive work [γ 10 = 0.018]) and ankle joint kinetics (plantarflexion torque [γ 10 = 0.035] and positive work [γ 10 = 0.045]), whereas no significant fixed effects were observed for knee joint kinetics (γ 10 ≤ 0.007). The inter-individual correlation analysis showed that greater values of hip and knee joint kinetics and ankle plantar-dorsiflexion power were associated with greater jump height. These results indicate that the intra- and inter-individual analyses showed different patterns of associations between jump height and lower-limb joint kinetics. Moreover, significant random effects were observed for all lower-limb joint kinetics, indicating that these intra-individual relationships differed among participants. Understanding joint kinetics associated with trial-to-trial intra-individual variability in jump height may contribute to identifying participant-specific biomechanical factors underlying jump height.

title: Impact of radiographic damage on health-related outcomes across rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and hand osteoarthritis: a comparative analysis of disease burden.
authors: Kökoğlu EO, Cengiz G, Kaplan H, Denizhan TK, Beke SK, Çalış M, Sofu N, Zararsız GE.
abstract: Introduction/objectives To evaluate the comparative impact of radiographic joint damage on hand functions, objective grip strength, and quality of life across patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), and hand osteoarthritis (OA). Method This cross-sectional study included patients with RA (n = 50), PsA (n = 40), and hand OA (n = 40). Objective grip strength was measured using a calibrated JAMAR hydraulic dynamometer. Radiographic damage was assessed using the modified Total Sharp Score (mTSS) for inflammatory cohorts and the Kellgren-Lawrence (K-L) scale for hand OA. Functional status and psychosocial impact were evaluated through Duruöz Hand Index (DHI), Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (QuickDASH) questionnaire, Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ), and the Short Form-36 (SF-36) Health Survey scales. Spearman correlation analyses and adjusted multivariable linear regression models were performed to evaluate the relationship between radiographic damage and functional outcomes. Results Despite marked differences in disease duration, radiographic damage, and treatment profiles, objectively measured grip strength and patient-reported hand disability did not differ significantly among the three disease groups (all p > 0.05). In unadjusted analyses, greater radiographic damage was associated with lower grip strength in PsA (r = - 0.405, 95% CI - 0.637 to - 0.107), but not with QuickDASH or DHI; no significant associations between radiographic damage and these functional outcomes were observed in RA or hand OA. After multivariable adjustment, high radiographic damage remained associated with lower grip strength in PsA (β = - 9.02, 95% CI - 17.19 to - 0.85), but was not associated with QuickDASH or DHI. Disease activity was most strongly associated with functional outcomes in RA, whereas radiographic severity was not independently associated with grip strength or patient-reported hand function in hand OA. Grip strength was inversely correlated with hand-specific patient-reported outcomes across all disease groups. Conclusion Although patients with RA, PsA, and hand OA experience comparable levels of hand dysfunction, the factors associated with functional impairment differ according to disease phenotype. Structural damage appears to have a greater influence on objective hand performance in PsA, whereas disease activity predominates in RA and radiographic severity alone does not explain disability in hand OA. These findings highlight the importance of disease-specific interpretation of structural damage and support comprehensive functional assessment in patients with inflammatory and degenerative hand arthritis. Key Points • Patients with RA, psoriatic arthritis, and hand OA exhibited comparable levels of objectively measured grip strength and patient-reported hand disability despite substantial differences in disease duration and radiographic severity. • Multivariable analyses demonstrated disease-specific determinants of functional impairment: radiographic damage was independently associated with reduced grip strength only in psoriatic arthritis, whereas disease activity was the principal factor associated with functional outcomes in RA and radiographic severity alone did not explain disability in hand OA. • Functional impairment in hand OA cannot be explained solely by structural radiographic changes, underscoring the need for comprehensive functional assessment beyond conventional imaging findings.

title: Horizontal and Multidirectional Single-Leg Hop Tests Predict Isokinetic Quadriceps and Hamstring Strengths After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
authors: Kırık ABT, Akdemir E, Karaduman E, Güzel N, Genç AS, Anıl B, Korkmaz Salkılıç E, Kehribar L, Önder Y, Yılmaz AK.
abstract: Background After anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), isokinetic strength and single-leg hop tests (SLHT) are used to assess return to sport readiness. This study examined the relationships and predictive effects of isokinetic knee extension (Ex) and flexion (Flx) strength with 5 SLHTs at 6 to 8 months post-ACLR. Hypothesis There would be significant correlation between knee Ex and Flx strengths on the operated side and 5 different SLHTs; SLHTs would significantly predict knee isokinetic Ex and Flx strength. Study design Cross-sectional study. Level of evidence Level 3. Methods Fifty-one male participants underwent unilateral ACLR. Lysholm, International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC), and Tegner scales were assessed preoperatively and 6 to 8 months postoperatively. At the same follow-up, isokinetic strength at 60°/s, 180°/s, and 240°/s and 5 SLHTs were tested on both limbs. Data were analyzed with paired t tests, Pearson correlations, Fisher's exact test, and simple linear regression; limb symmetry index (LSI) cut-off was ≥85%. Results Isokinetic strength and single-leg hop (SH), crossover hop, and medial side triple-hop (TH) distances did not differ significantly between limbs ( P > 0.05), whereas TH and 90° medial rotation hop distances were significantly shorter on the operated side ( P P P > 0.05). High correlation was found between Ex strength at 60°/s and SH and TH distances on the operated side, and high-moderate correlations were found at 180°/s and 240°/s. Flx strengths showed a similar but slightly lower degree of correlation. Simple linear regression models revealed that especially SH and TH distances significantly predicted both Ex and Flx strengths (adjusted R 2 0.26-0.52; P P = 0.01). Conclusion The findings show that SH and TH tests were highly predictive of isokinetic knee strength after ACLR. Clinical relevance SLHTs after ACLR can be used as a practical and accessible complement to isokinetic measurements.

title: Health resource utilization and direct procedural costs of arthroplasty surgery: a retrospective cost analysis.
authors: Albishi W, Albaroudi A, Aldaijy M, Alshaygy I, Alaqeel M, Alaseem A.
abstract: Background As osteoarthritis becomes more prevalent, demand for procedures such as total knee arthroplasty (TKA), total hip arthroplasty (THA), and other joint replacement procedures is rising. Understanding the cost drivers and patient demographics is important for maintaining financial sustainability while ensuring optimal patient care. This study aims to determine the costs associated with various arthroplasty procedures, analyze comparison of costs between different arthroplasty procedures, and fill the gap in the local literature regarding direct cost burden of arthroplasty surgery in Saudi Arabia. Methods This retrospective study included 1,833 patients who underwent arthroplasty procedures. The costs were converted into USD, and their trends over time were analyzed. Statistical analyses, including independent samples t tests and chi-square tests, were used to compare costs across procedures, age groups, and sex. The projection analysis was applied to project the number procedures and expected costs for 2030. Results The total expenditures for the study period exceeded $25 million, with TKA accounting for 65% of the total cost. Female patients composed 74.7% of the patient population, and male patients were generally older. TKA had the highest total cost at $16,632,000 and the greatest number of cases at 1,386. The highest average cost was for hip revision arthroplasty at $18,666.67, followed by shoulder arthroplasty at $16,533.33. By 2030, arthroplasty cases are projected to increase 3-fold, with the total cost rising to $20.87 million compared with 2021. Conclusion The total expenditures of arthroplasty procedures, particularly TKA, are significant, with the costs projected to increase by 2030. Strategic planning, including expanding infrastructure, optimizing resources, and adopting cost-saving measures such as bulk purchasing, will be crucial to maintaining high-quality patient care while addressing the increased demand.

title: Gender Experiences of Training and Practicing Orthopaedic Surgeons in Australia: A Mixed Methods Study.
authors: Freeman C, Evans R, Larkins S, Morrey C.
abstract: Introduction Orthopaedic surgery remains Australia's least gender-diverse medical specialty. Despite extensive global literature on barriers to gender equity, no prior study has applied an established gender bias instrument to assess gender bias in Australian orthopaedics. Methods A national mixed methods study was conducted comprising a cross-sectional survey and semi-structured interviews. Eligible participants included all practising orthopaedic surgeons and trainees in Australia. The survey utilised an adapted version of the 47-item Gender Bias Scale and was distributed via the Australian Orthopaedic Association and departmental mailing lists. Interviewees were recruited from survey volunteers and were undertaken to provide explanatory depth and contextualisation to the survey findings. Results 163 orthopaedic surgeons and trainees (85 male, 78 female) completed the survey. Female participants were significantly more likely to report barriers across the male culture and unequal standards domains. Twenty of the 47 GBS items showed significant gender differences (p Conclusion This study presents Australian data on key barriers to gender equity in orthopaedics, providing an evidence base for future policy. Achieving progress will require more than increasing representation. It will take thoughtful policy and continuous effort to address structural and attitudinal barriers.

title: From fluoroscopy to artificial intelligence: three decades of percutaneous pelvic ring fixation-a bibliometric and science-mapping analysis (1996-2026).
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Vicenti G, Ferorelli D, Loiodice M, Sirago G, Solarino G, Dell'Erba A.
abstract: Introduction Percutaneous pelvic-ring fixation requires implant placement within narrow osseous corridors. Navigation, robotics and artificial intelligence (AI) have successively been proposed to improve accuracy and reduce radiation exposure. This study mapped three decades of research on these technologies, characterising publication trends and the field's intellectual, conceptual and social structure. Materials and methods The Web of Science Core Collection (primary dataset, with parsed cited references) and Scopus (robustness comparison) were searched on 8 June 2026. Searches combined pelvic-fixation and technology terms and targeted articles, reviews and conference papers; degenerative-spine, deformity, arthroplasty and isolated acetabular records were excluded, while adjacent WoS categories retained by platform indexing were evaluated in sensitivity analysis. Bibliometrix analyses comprised performance indicators, collaboration patterns, co-citation, keyword co-occurrence, thematic mapping and trend analysis on a harmonised keyword field. Results The primary corpus comprised 271 documents from 97 sources, with 1311 authors and 16.3 mean citations per document. Output rose from low single digits before 2010 to 25-29 documents per year in 2022-2023; an exploratory logistic model indicated continued rapid growth. The Journal of Orthopaedic Trauma and Injury dominated the source landscape, while Germany, China, Switzerland and the United States led production. Foundational percutaneous-fixation studies and the subsequent navigation literature structured the intellectual base. Navigation, fluoroscopy and screw insertion formed the conceptual backbone, whereas explicit AI terminology appeared in only 1 of 271 documents at the author-keyword level. Conclusions Percutaneous pelvic-ring fixation research is in sustained growth around a mature navigation backbone, while robotics, augmented reality and AI form a thin but identifiable emerging frontier. The findings support research prioritisation, cross-border collaboration and transparent reporting of new technologies in trauma orthopaedics.

title: Forearm Pronation Mechanics and Prior Upper Extremity Injury History in Professional Baseball Pitchers: A Biomechanical Analysis.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Eskew J, Manzi J, Dowling B, Hingorani A, Mack V, Kew M, Brusalis C, Kremchek T, Gulotta LV, Carr JB, Dines JS.
abstract: Background Forearm pronation during baseball pitching has received increasing attention because of its potential relationship with upper extremity loading. Purpose To evaluate the association between forearm pronation mechanics and prior upper extremity injury history in professional baseball pitchers. Methods Biomechanical data from 304 professional baseball pitchers were analyzed. Forearm pronation at foot contact, maximum pronation velocity, and pronation excursion were evaluated. Logistic regression analyses controlling for age, leg length, elbow varus torque, and handedness assessed associations with pitchers self-reported prior injuries across 24 injury subcategories. Univariate comparisons were performed for Superior Labrum Anterior to Posterior (SLAP)-injured versus pitchers with no prior injury and all pitchers without SLAP/labral injury history. Results 263 (86.5%) pitchers demonstrated forearm pronation at foot contact (mean 36° ± 19°), while 41 (13.5%) exhibited forearm supination (mean -12° ± 11°). No statistically significant associations were identified between forearm pronation mechanics and upper extremity injuries overall (n = 107), elbow injuries (n = 65), UCL sprains/tears (n = 39), or the majority of other injury categories. An exploratory analysis of SLAP/labral injury (n = 16) identified a significant inverse association with forearm pronation excursion (OR 0.597 per 10° increase, 95% CI 0.310-0.978, p = 0.039). This association did not remain significant after FDR correction for multiple comparisons (adjusted p=0.976) but remains directionally consistent across multiple covariate specifications. Univariate analysis confirmed that pitchers with prior SLAP injury had significantly reduced pronation excursion (13° vs 22°, p = 0.017), reduced shoulder external rotation at maximum external rotation (162° vs 166°, p = 0.044), and were older (22.7 vs 21.6 years, p = 0.007) compared to uninjured controls. These differences remained significant when compared against all pitchers without SLAP/labral injury history, regardless of other injury history: pronation excursion (13° vs 21°, p=0.016), SER at MER (162° vs 166°, p=0.042), and age (22.7 vs 21.9 years, p=0.033). Conclusion Forearm pronation mechanics were not significantly associated with prior injury history across the majority of injury categories including the elbow, challenging theoretical concerns regarding flexor-pronator overload. In an exploratory analysis, pitchers with prior labral/SLAP injury demonstrated reduced forearm pronation excursion; however, this association did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons and was based on a limited number of injury events. Because biomechanical assessment occurred after the reported injuries, the temporal relationship between reduced pronation excursion and SLAP/labral injury cannot be determined. This finding should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating and requires prospective validation.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of the Resisted Anterior Drawer (RAD) Test for Lateral Elbow Instability in Lateral Epicondylitis.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Caekebeke P, van Riet R.
abstract: Background Lateral epicondylitis (LE) is increasingly recognized as a multifactorial condition in which subtle lateral elbow instability may contribute to persistent pain. However, reliable clinical tests to detect such instability are lacking. Purpose To determine the diagnostic accuracy of the resisted anterior drawer (RAD) test for detecting lateral elbow instability in patients with LE. Methods Consecutive adult patients diagnosed with LE underwent standardized clinical examination followed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The RAD test was considered positive when pain during resisted wrist extension, with the elbow in extension, decreased by at least 1 point on a visual analogue scale (VAS) with anteromedial stabilization of the radial head. MRI-defined instability was defined as the presence of lateral collateral ligament (LCL) injury, posterior sagging, or ulnohumeral joint-line opening of grade ≥1. Diagnostic indices were calculated with 95% confidence intervals and likelihood ratios, and the continuous reduction in pain was evaluated with receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Results A total of 500 elbows were analyzed (mean age: 51 years). MRI evidence of instability was present in 57.4% of elbows. The RAD test demonstrated a sensitivity of 95.8% (95% CI 92.8-97.6%), specificity of 82.2% (95% CI 76.5-86.7%), and overall accuracy of 90.0% (95% CI 87.1-92.3%), with positive and negative likelihood ratios of 5.4 and 0.05. The area under the ROC curve for the reduction in pain was 0.92 (95% CI 0.90-0.95). The magnitude of pain reduction during the RAD maneuver correlated with the severity of MRI-defined instability (Spearman ρ = -0.71). Increasing MRI severity was associated with a higher number of corticosteroid infiltrations, whereas symptom duration showed only a weak association with structural instability. Conclusion In this Level III diagnostic study, the RAD test showed high sensitivity and good specificity for MRI-defined lateral elbow instability in patients with LE, and the magnitude of pain reduction was correlated with MRI-defined severity. These findings suggest that the RAD test may be a useful screening maneuver for instability-related pain in patients with LE. A prospective, blinded cohort study with an independent reference standard is required to confirm its clinical utility. Level of evidence Level III, Diagnostic Study.

title: Defining and predicting outcomes of a work-injuries rehabilitation program through multivariate baseline phenotypes and longitudinal modeling.
authors: Bayattork M, Carter T, Walton DM.
abstract: Objective To characterize short-term pain and health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL) recovery trajectories in injured workers undergoing standardized musculoskeletal rehabilitation. We also examined whether multidimensional baseline phenotypes derived from brief self-report measures predicted these trajectories and subsequent recovery. Methods Adults with work-related musculoskeletal injuries were enrolled at entry into a community-based rehabilitation program (N = 146), of whom 134 contributed to pain and 138 to HRQoL trajectory analyses. Participants were classified into one of 4 latent profiles at intake from a prior analysis: Localized/Resilient (57.0%), Mood-Dominant (21.8%), Neurosensory-Dominant (12.7%), and Complex/Central (8.5%). Pain (Numeric Pain Rating Scale, NPRS) and HRQoL (EQ-5D-5L index) were measured at baseline, 4, and 8 weeks; self-rated global recovery, self-reported return-to-work status, and administrative discharge/ongoing-care codes were collected at 8 weeks. Growth mixture modeling defined NPRS and EQ-5D-5L trajectories. Odds ratios (ORs) quantified associations between baseline classes and "No Recovery/No Improvement" trajectories, as well as point outcomes. Results Three pain trajectories (Rapid Recovery 34.1%, Incomplete Recovery 42.2%, No Recovery 23.7%) and two QoL trajectories (Good QoL 86.2%, No Improvement 13.8%) were identified. Compared with the Localized/Resilient baseline class, odds of NPRS No Recovery were higher in the Mood-Dominant (OR 3.97, 95%CI 1.32-11.92), Neurosensory‑Dominant (OR 10.99, 3.20-37.38), and Complex, Central (OR 22.67, 4.76-107.90) classes, with similarly graded increases for EQ‑5D‑5L No Recovery (ORs 9.00, 7.50, and 150.00, respectively), although estimates for the small Complex/Central subgroup were imprecise. The Complex /Central class also had higher odds of self-reported "not fully returned to work" (OR 4.18, 1.05-16.64) and being coded as "requires ongoing care" (OR 5.74, 1.93-17.11) relative to Localized/Resilient, whereas self-rated global recovery showed no significant between-class differences. Conclusions Brief, fully self-reported, multivariate phenotypes obtained at program entry stratify acutely injured workers into likely rehabilitation outcomes in the short term. These findings support the potential value of integrating mechanism-informed phenotyping with trajectory modeling to inform stratified, risk-guided musculoskeletal rehabilitation.

title: Common acetabular fracture patterns in patients with femoroacetabular impingement.
authors: Garlapaty AR, Townsley S, Touhey DC, Walz JW, Duren D, Cook JL, Crist BD.
abstract: Introduction The incidence of acetabular fractures is rising, affecting both younger and elderly patient populations. Developmental abnormalities such as femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) and hip dysplasia alter hip biomechanics, potentially predisposing younger patients to fracture. FAI, resulting from a cam and/or pincer deformity, is common, affecting 25% of asymptomatic males and 5% of asymptomatic females, and has been linked to hip pain and early osteoarthritis. However, the relationship between FAI morphology and acetabular fracture pattern remains unclear. Methods Patients, 18-55 years old, treated between 2005 and 2023 for acetabular fracture, hip dislocation, or femoral head fracture were reviewed for FAI morphology using the Judet and Letournel classification systems. Statistical comparisons were conducted using Fisher's exact tests and unpaired t-tests, with significance set at p Results A total of 294 patients (72%) exhibited plain radiographic FAI morphology, while 115 (28%) served as controls. The most common fracture pattern in both groups was posterior wall (PW) fractures (23.1% FAI, 31.3% control). Male FAI patients were significantly more likely to experience transverse fractures (p = 0.032, OR=4.6) and posterior column plus PW fractures (p = 0.035, OR=2.5) than controls. Among FAI patients, posterior column fractures were significantly more likely to occur in females (p = 0.011, OR=19). A total of 31 (27.0%) control patients and 63 (21.4%) FAI patients experienced complications. Conclusions In our data set, FAI patients accounted for 72% of patients undergoing acetabular fracture ORIF. FAI patients most commonly sustained posterior wall fractures, but male FAI patients had a significantly higher rate of transverse and posterior column plus PW. FAI patients experienced a complication rate of 21.4% compared to 27.0% in non-FAI patients.

title: CORR Insights®: Is the Parkinson Disease Diagnosis-to-Surgery Interval Associated With 5-year Vascular and Periprosthetic Outcomes After TKA? A Nationwide Large-database Study.
authors: Meermans G.

title: Bowel and Bladder Dysfunction and Patient-Reported Outcomes in Patients Undergoing a Sacrectomy for a Primary Bone Tumor an Observational Study From the Primary Tumor Research and Outcomes Network (PTRON).
authors: Ludwig TE, Rhines LD, Reynolds J, Gokaslan ZL, Lazary A, Dea N, Fisher CG, Luzzati A, Gasbarrini A, Rampersaud YR, Clarke MJ, Disch AC, Cecchinato R, Boriani S, Mummaneni PV, Tobert DG, Barzilai O, Goodwin CR, Netzer C, Laufer I, Verlaan JJ, Charest-Morin R.
abstract: Study DesignProspective cohort.ObjectiveThe primary objective was to describe bowel and bladder (BB) function by nerve root sacrifice following a Sacrectomy. Secondary objectives were to compare patient reported outcomes (PROs) based on BB function at 12 months, and to assess surgeon-patient reported BB function concordance.MethodsData from AO Spine Knowledge Forum Tumor Primary Tumor Research and Outcomes Network (PTRON) registry included patients who underwent a sacrectomy (S1-S5) for a primary bone tumor, with at least one PRO reported at baseline and 12 months. BB function was recorded at baseline and 12 months. PROs included EQ-5D, SOSGOQv2.0, SF-36, leg/back NRS, ECOG.ResultsEighty-one patients were included. Bilateral S1-S2 sacrifice was associated with complete BB dysfunction; preservation of at least one S3 root was associated with preserved BB function in more than half of cases. Distal S4-S5 resections often preserved function, but about one-third had BB dysfunction. Agreement between surgeon-patient reported BB function was moderate (κ 0.39-0.45). At 12 months, patients with preserved BB function reported higher EQ-5D (0.70 vs 0.60, p=0.025) and SOSGOQv2.0 (83.5 vs 67.5, p=0.031), better ECOG (p= 0.028) and lower leg pain (0.5 vs 4.5, p=0.013).ConclusionA substantial proportion of patients experience BB dysfunction after sacrectomy, particularly with more cranial resections. This dysfunction aligned with worse PROs, greater pain, and poorer performance status. Agreement between surgeon- and patient-reported BB outcomes was moderate, emphasizing the importance of incorporating patient-reported measures into follow-up and counseling.

title: Association Between Early Joint Awareness and Falls After Total Hip Arthroplasty.
authors: Wada O, Nagai K, Igeta M, Mori A, Mizuno K.
abstract: Background The Forgotten Joint Score-12 (FJS-12) is a patient-reported outcome measure of joint awareness after total hip arthroplasty (THA). Falls after THA remain clinically important. However, longitudinal evidence regarding the associations among early FJS-12, subsequent falls, and later recovery of joint unawareness remains limited. Methods This retrospective cohort study used a prospectively maintained institutional database from a single Japanese institution. Consecutive patients who underwent primary THA between January 2021 and December 2023 were included. FJS-12 was assessed at 3 and 12 months postoperatively, and falls occurring between 3 and 12 months postoperatively were identified at the 12-month visit based on patients' self-report over this 9-month interval. Modified Poisson regression was used to examine the association between FJS at 3 months and subsequent falls. Multiple linear regression was used to examine the association between fall occurrence and FJS at 12 months, adjusting for FJS at 3 months. Results Overall, 623 patients were analyzed (mean age 70.8 years; 85.2% female). Ninety-nine patients (15.9%) experienced at least 1 fall between 3 and 12 months postoperatively. Lower FJS at 3 months was associated with a higher risk of subsequent falls. Fall occurrence was associated with lower FJS at 12 months, independent of FJS at 3 months and other covariates. Conclusions Early postoperative joint awareness was associated with subsequent falls after THA, and falls were associated with lower FJS at 12 months. The FJS-12 may provide additional patient-reported information when assessing postoperative fall risk.

title: Assessment of Curve Flexibility in Idiopathic Scoliosis Patients With Severe Scoliosis (Cobb Angle ≥ 90<sup>o</sup>): Comparison Between the Supine Traction Radiograph Versus the Physician Supervised Supine Side Bending Radiographs.
authors: Chan CYW, Chandren JR, Tan EYW, Chandirasegaran S, Chiu CK, Kwan MK.
abstract: Study designRetrospective study.ObjectiveTo analyze the flexibility of severe scoliosis with cobb angle ≥90 o , comparing between the supine traction radiograph versus the physician supervised supine side bending film.Methods72 severe idiopathic scoliosis patients between 2015 to 2023 in a single academic institution who underwent single-staged posterior spinal fusion with curves more than ≥90 o with available anteroposterior, traction and side bending radiographs were recruited.Results58 patients had severe curves in the main thoracic (MT) region, with mean preoperative Cobb angle of 107.3±16.6° and postoperative Cobb angle of 51.2±15.5°. 18 patients had severe curves at thoracolumbar/lumbar (TL/L) region, with mean preoperative Cobb angle of 99.8±8.2° and postoperative Cobb angle of 45.2±12.8°. The correction rates for MT and TL/L curve is 52.7±11.1° and 55.0±11.1° respectively. No significant differences were observed between sidebending (SB) and traction radiographs in assessing MT curve flexibility (34.7±12.4% vs. 34.5±11.8%, respectively; p=0.907) or in the corresponding correction indices (1.7±0.5 vs. 1.7±0.9, respectively; p=0.461). However, TL/L curves had a significant difference in flexibility comparing SB (46.0±12.6%) and traction radiographs (42.0±11.5%) (p=0.008) and comparing the side bending correction index (SBCI) (1.2±0.2) and traction correction index (TCI) (1.4±0.3) (p=0.010). The SBCI for TL/L curve was closer to 1, indicating that the Cobb angle on SB radiographs for TL/L curves could more accurately predict the postoperative Cobb angle.ConclusionIn severe TL/L curves, physician-supervised supine side bending (PSSB) radiographs may provide a more accurate assessment of curve flexibility, as reflected by a correction index closer to 1. These findings suggest that PSSB radiographs may be a useful radiographic assessment for evaluating TL/L curve flexibility and guide preoperative planning in patients with severe idiopathic scoliosis.

title: Aspirin is safe and effective for prevention of deep vein thrombosis following acetabular fracture surgery.
authors: Dinesh A, Poursalehian M, Billow D, Peirish RW, Cereijo C, Padubidri A, Patterson B, Vallier HA.
abstract: Background Patients with acetabular fractures are at significant risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), yet the optimal chemoprophylactic agent remains undefined. Emerging evidence from elective arthroplasty and general orthopaedic trauma populations suggests that aspirin (ASA) may be a safe and effective alternative to traditional anticoagulants. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of ASA compared to other anticoagulants for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prevention following acetabular fracture surgery. Methods A retrospective cohort analysis was performed using a global, web-based health research network that provides on-demand access to de-identified, real-world data from electronic health records and claims. Adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent surgical treatment for acetabular fractures between January 2014 and December 2025 and received VTE prophylaxis within 14 days of surgery were identified. Patients were stratified into ASA (n = 1189) and other anticoagulant (n = 5478) cohorts. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed to balance baseline characteristics, yielding 1174 patients per cohort. Rates and odds of DVT, emergency department (ED) visits, deep infection, stroke, and readmission were assessed at 14-, 30-, and 90-day postoperative intervals. Temporal trends in VTE prophylaxis utilization were also analyzed. Results Compared to other anticoagulants, ASA was associated with significantly lower odds of DVT at 14 days (1.11% vs. 2.22%; odds ratio [OR]: 0.494; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.253-0.967; P = 0.036), 30 days (1.45% vs. 2.73%; OR: 0.524; 95% CI: 0.290-0.950; P = 0.030), and 90 days (2.56% vs. 4.34%; OR: 0.577; 95% CI: 0.365-0.913; P = 0.018). ASA was also associated with significantly lower odds of ED visits at 90 days (OR: 0.741; 95% CI: 0.570-0.963; P = 0.024). There were no significant differences in deep infection, stroke, or readmission rates. ASA utilization increased from 7.2% in 2014-39.5% in 2025. Conclusions ASA is safe and effective for DVT prevention following acetabular fracture surgery and is associated with fewer ED visits compared to other anticoagulants. These findings support the growing adoption of ASA as a VTE prophylactic agent in the acetabular fracture population.

title: Total Knee Arthroplasty as the Initial and Definitive Treatment for the Multiligament Injured Knee.
authors: Williams WA, Mason EM, Daniel AV, Holliday CL, Courington RM, Langford JR, Kupizewski SJ, Stuart MJ, Levy BA, Haidukewych GJ.
abstract: Background Multiligament knee injuries (MLKIs) are complex injury patterns that pose challenges for patients and surgeons alike. The objective of this study was to evaluate the clinical and functional perioperative outcomes of a cohort of patients with evidence of pre-existing knee osteoarthritic changes that underwent total knee arthroplasty (TKA) as the initial and definitive treatment for MLKI. Methods Patients from 2 tertiary care centers that underwent TKA as primary treatment for their MLKI within 1 year from their initial time of injury were retrospectively identified for study inclusion.
