Range of motion, and Knee Society Scores were evaluated for all patients. Perioperative complications as well as TKA component types and degrees of implant constraint were also analyzed. Results Twelve patients met study inclusion criteria. Mean follow-up time was 40 months (range 24 to 86 mos). Mean time from MLKI to TKA was 5 months (range 3 days to 11 months). Mean age was 61 years (range 51 to 78). Mean postoperative knee range of motion was 1-106 degrees at last follow-up. Knee Society Scores improved by an average of 129 points at last follow-up. Two patients required rotating hinge TKA components with all others requiring lesser degrees of implant constraint. There were no instances of postoperative knee instability and no patients required revision TKA surgery at last follow-up. Conclusions TKA is a viable primary treatment option for MLKI in older patients with pre-existing multicompartmental knee osteoarthritis. In this patient population, TKA may allow for improved function and adequate stability of the multiligament injured knee. Study design Retrospective case series. Level of evidence IV.

title: Tibiofemoral and patellofemoral kinematics after kinematic versus mechanical alignment in varus TKA-a dynamic knee rig study.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Simon JM, Siedow TM, Thorwächter C, Petri TE, Bauer L, Holzapfel BM, Müller PE, Niethammer TR.
abstract: Introduction Kinematic alignment (KA) in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) of the varus knee shows promising clinical outcomes by preserving individual joint anatomy. However, it remains unknown whether this results in knee joint kinematics that more closely resemble the native baseline condition than mechanical alignment (MA). Therefore, this study evaluated the direct influence of KA versus MA on tibiofemoral and patellofemoral kinematics and contact biomechanics in the varus knee during a standardized dynamic muscle-loaded squat. Materials and methods Seven fresh-frozen human cadaveric knee specimens with constitutional varus (-1.4° to -8.3°) were tested in a dynamic knee rig (30° to 130° flexion) under muscle-controlled loading. Kinematics, retropatellar contact area, peak pressure, and quadriceps force were continuously recorded across three successive states within the same specimen: native, KA TKA, and MA TKA using a medial-pivot implant design. Statistical analysis was performed using one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping, including non-parametric SnPM1D ANOVA and pairwise SnPM{F} tests for kinematics, and paired-samples SPM{t} tests for contact mechanics and quadriceps force. Results Between alignment techniques (KA vs. MA), no statistically significant differences emerged regarding kinematics and patellofemoral biomechanics following Holm-Bonferroni correction (all p adj > 0.05). Descriptively, KA displayed a trend toward unphysiological anterior femoral translation in deep flexion (100°-120°, p = 0.028; p adj = 0.084) and persistent patellar medialization (delta of up to 5 mm) compared to MA, though these did not retain statistical significance post-adjustment. Both TKA techniques significantly reduced patellar contact area (p adj Conclusions KA was not shown to restore native knee kinematics or patellofemoral mechanics more closely than MA. Descriptive kinematic variations suggest that KA does not automatically optimize functional joint mechanics when using standard implant geometries.

title: The Effect of EVOLVE Radial Head Arthroplasty Stem Tilt on Clinical Outcomes.
journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
authors: Tat J, Kheiran A, Grewal R, Athwal GS, Faber KJ, Drosdowech DS, King GJW.
abstract: Introduction Radial head arthroplasty (RHA) mal-alignment can occur when there is excessive tilt of the radial head stem relative to the radial canal. The etiology, clinical significance and management for increased RHA tilt is poorly understood. Our primary objective was to compare clinical outcomes in patients with excessive radiographic RHA tilt to controls. A secondary objective was to determine the relationship between radiographic stem alignment measurements and clinical outcomes. Methods We performed a retrospective chart review of patients who underwent a smooth stem RHA (EVOLVE, Wright Medical) between 1999 - 2021 for acute radial head fractures requiring isolated RHA. Patient demographics, clinical outcomes scores (PREE, QuickDASH, MEPI), range of motion, complications, reoperations, and radiographic measurements were compared between patients with excessive RHA tilt and controls. Radial head alignment was assessed using several parameters including radial neck-shaft angle, lateral overhang distance RHA implant, proximal radioulnar joint angle, radial neck length, radial neck width, radial neck cut angle, radial tuberosity width, and radiocapitellar line. Excessive RHA tilt was defined as patients with a high-neck shaft angle (greater than 1 Standard Deviation above the mean), while controls had a neck-shaft angle less than 1 Standard Deviation. Regression modelling was used to determine whether the radiographic alignment parameters correlate with of outcomes (PREE, QuickDASH, MEPI), complications and reoperations. A subgroup analysis compared radiographic tilt at 6 weeks and 1 year postoperatively. Results Sixty-one patients were included in the study, 10 patients with mal-alignment of the RHA and 51 patients in the control group. There was no significant difference in patient characteristics between groups (age, gender, handedness, smoking, time to surgery, follow-up time) (p>0.01). The tilt group demonstrated greater neck-shaft angles, RHA lateral overhang, PRUJ angles, and implant lucency, with shorter radial neck lengths and lower radial neck cut angles (all p 2 =0.14, F 1,54 =9.7, p=0.003) and MEPI scores (R 2 =0.10, F 1,53 =7.3, p=0.009). Excessive tilt was more commonly observed at late rather than early follow-up. Conclusion A cohort of patients with excessive RHA tilt cohort had worse overall clinical outcomes scores when compared to the control group, however they did not demonstrate higher rates of complications or revision surgery. In this patient cohort, excessive implant tilt developed late after surgery rather than in early follow-up.

title: The Deep Medial Collateral Ligament: Part 2, Structural Properties and Failure Characteristics.
journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
authors: Super JT, Murray IR, Wilebski BJ, Carlson MR, Retzer NK, Tollefson LV, Gaye CE, LaPrade CM, LaPrade RF.
abstract: Background The deep medial collateral ligament (dMCL) has traditionally been described as a capsular thickening deep to the superficial medial collateral ligament; however, recent investigations suggest a more extensive anteromedial course with a more important role in knee stability. Despite this, its structural properties and failure characteristics are not well described. Purpose To quantify the structural properties of the dMCL, including load to failure, stiffness, displacement, and failure location. Study design Descriptive laboratory study. Methods Ten fresh-frozen cadaveric knees (mean age, 63.4 ± 4.7 years; range, 58-70 years; all males; 5 right, 5 left knees; mean body mass index, 26.2 ± 1.9 kg/m 2 ) were dissected to isolate the dMCL while preserving its meniscofemoral and meniscotibial attachments. Specimens were mounted in a 6 degrees of freedom robotic system and subjected to preconditioning and then uniaxial load-to-failure testing. Load, displacement, stiffness, and failure location were recorded. Results The mean load to failure of the dMCL was 242.9 ± 86.6 N, with a mean stiffness of 25.3 ± 14.3 N/mm and a median displacement at failure of 12.4 mm (range, 8.9-31.8 mm). Failure occurred predominantly within the meniscotibial portion (9/10 specimens), with only 1 failure in the meniscofemoral portion, and none of the specimens failed at the femoral or tibial osseous attachments. Conclusion When the expanded anteromedial course of the dMCL is included, its measured load to failure was higher than values previously reported using more restricted anatomic definitions. Failure occurred predominantly within the meniscotibial portion. These findings characterize the isolated structural properties and predominant failure pattern of the dMCL and may provide reference data for future biomechanical evaluation of medial knee reconstruction techniques. Clinical relevance Quantification of the structural properties of the dMCL provides a biomechanical basis for surgical reconstruction and fixation strategies. These data may assist in graft selection and fixation strength requirements in anatomic medial knee reconstructions, particularly in patients with anteromedial rotatory instability.

title: Synovial plica syndromes: a comprehensive overview from embryology to pathology.
authors: Cerezal A, Cogolludo G, Canga A, Encinas-Ullán CA, Pérez-Carro L, Cruz A, Cerezal L.
abstract: Synovial plicae are folds of synovial tissue in the knee, hip, elbow, and shoulder, representing embryonic remnants of synovial septa. They are usually asymptomatic, but trauma, repetitive microtrauma, or prior surgery can render them thickened and fibrotic, producing pain and mechanical symptoms collectively termed plica syndrome. It is easily overlooked or misdiagnosed because the symptoms are nonspecific and other intra-articular disorders often coexist. This review addresses the embryology, histology, anatomy, clinical presentation, imaging, and treatment of synovial plicae across these joints, with emphasis on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features. MRI is the preferred imaging modality for evaluating suspected plica syndrome, characterizing the fold and associated abnormalities, and excluding alternative causes of joint pain. Pathologic plicae appear thickened and irregular, with increased signal intensity and frequently associated focal synovitis or adjacent chondral damage. Plica thickness alone has limited diagnostic value, as measurements overlap between symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals. Establishing a diagnosis of symptomatic plica syndrome requires correlation of the imaging findings with the clinical presentation. When joint effusion is absent, magnetic resonance (MR) or computed tomography (CT) arthrography improves delineation of the synovial folds and associated lesions. Plica syndrome occurs most often in young, physically active patients, and management is initially conservative. When symptoms are refractory, arthroscopic resection relieves symptoms, particularly when the plica is the only abnormality and the cartilage is preserved. Most outcome data derive from the knee and the elbow.

title: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome following posterior instrumented correction and fusion of scoliosis managed with structured nutritional escalation.

title: Skin color representation in orthopedic literature.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Goyal RK, Adio AA, Nadiminti H, Black EM, Khan AZ, Horneff JG, Hill BW, Abboud JA.
abstract: Introduction Underrepresentation of skin color in educational materials can undermine diagnostic accuracy and contribute to disparities in orthopedic care for minority populations. While underrepresentation of darker skin types has already been identified in orthopedic literature, this study assessed whether underrepresentation is apparent in open access journals, is uniform across all orthopedic subspecialties, differs between figure types, and has shifted over time as awareness of skin of color disparities has grown. Materials and methods 40,674 figures were accessed from 14 open-access orthopedic journals and assigned a subspecialty and a country of origin based on author affiliation. Automatic filters narrowed the dataset to 4,809 figures. Each figure was processed by a GPT-4o artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline to obtain skin presence (yes/no), figure type (clinical, intraoperative, illustration), Fitzpatrick skin type (I-VI), and a confidence score (1-5). Agreement was high with human review for skin presence and figure type and moderate with a board-certified dermatologist for skin tone, with disagreement biased toward darker ratings. 2,025 skin-containing figures were analyzed. Results Among 2,025 figures, most depicted light skin (65.6%, Fitzpatrick I-II), 29.6% medium (III-IV), and only 4.8% dark (V-VI). This demonstrated severe overrepresentation of light skin (p Conclusions Within open-access orthopedic literature, dark skin is consistently underrepresented and falls short of US and diverse-population benchmarks, regardless of figure type or subspecialty. This systemic pattern narrows the implicit norm of who an orthopedic patient appears to be and warrants editorial attention given documented disparities in orthopedic care.

title: Serum Calprotectin Demonstrates Moderate Diagnostic Performance for Detecting Periprosthetic Joint Infection in Hip and Knee Arthroplasty.
authors: Schelling MH, Schwarze J, Gosheger G, Schneider KN, Bockholt S, Theil C.
abstract: Background Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a serious complication after total hip and knee arthroplasty, with limited accuracy of conventional biomarkers. This study assessed serum calprotectin (CP) alongside established markers in revision arthroplasty. Methods This retrospective single-center study included 399 patients (232 total knee arthroplasty, 167 total hip arthroplasty). Based on Musculoskeletal Infection Society 2018 criteria, 132 patients were diagnosed with PJI and 267 were classified as non-PJI. All patients underwent serum CP, C-reactive protein (CRP), and interleukin-6 (IL-6) testing; microbiological analyses were performed when indicated. Results Serum CP was significantly higher in PJI than aseptic revisions (median 11,700 ng/mL [interquartile range 8080-18,675] vs 5,440 ng/mL [interquartile range 3600-8300], P Conclusions Serum calprotectin demonstrated moderate diagnostic performance and may may complement conventional serum markers in selected cases in which conventional serum markers are inconclusive.

title: Sclerostin downregulation in aseptic loosening.
authors: Alimy AR, Goedecke E, Ocokoljic A, Ries C, Beil FT, Rolvien T.
abstract: Aims Aseptic loosening is one of the leading indications for revision surgery after total hip and knee arthroplasty, yet its diagnosis and underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined. In this exploratory study, we investigated synovial fluid biomarkers and periprosthetic bone tissue characteristics to identify molecular signatures associated with aseptic loosening. Methods A total of 40 patients were included across three groups: primary osteoarthritis (OA; n = 13), aseptic loosening (n = 15), and other aseptic revisions (n = 12). Routine blood tests and synovial cytology were obtained. Synovial fluid underwent targeted proteomic profiling. Trabecular bone was assessed by histomorphometry, quantitative backscattered electron imaging, and immunofluorescence. Results Routine blood (CRP, white blood cell (WBC) count) and synovial (WBC count and differential) analyses showed no differences between groups, underscoring their limited diagnostic utility. In contrast, bone-focused multiplex synovial fluid profiling identified sclerostin as the strongest discriminatory marker, with significantly lower levels in aseptic loosening than in OA and other aseptic revisions. Dickkopf-1 showed a concordant but weaker reduction, reaching significance versus OA. Histomorphometric analysis of periprosthetic trabecular bone samples demonstrated preserved microarchitecture and turnover across groups. However, quantitative backscattered electron imaging revealed enlarged osteocyte lacunae specifically in aseptic loosening. Immunofluorescence confirmed reduced sclerostin expression within periprosthetic bone, mirroring synovial fluid findings. Synovial sclerostin demonstrated promising diagnostic potential, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.82 for differentiating aseptic loosening from other revision indications. Conclusion This study showcases osteocyte dysregulation as a key feature of aseptic loosening, and suggests that reduced osteocyte-derived sclerostin may reflect adaptive responses to abnormal mechanical and inflammatory stimuli at the implant-bone interface. Larger prospective studies are required to validate these findings, but osteocyte-derived sclerostin may represent a promising biomarker and potential therapeutic target in aseptic loosening.

title: Patients With Critical Humeral Bone Loss Have Similar Patient-Reported Outcomes to Patients Without Critical Humeral Bone Loss After Arthroscopic Shoulder Stabilization at a Mean Follow-Up of 7 Years.
authors: Gilbert R, Lin RT, Dadoo S, Liu A, Cong T, Popchak A, Lesniak BP, Rodosky M, Hughes JD, Lin A.
abstract: Purpose To compare long-term patient-reported outcomes (PROs) between patients with and without critical humeral bone loss (CHBL) and to compare long-term PROs among patients with CHBL who underwent arthroscopic Bankart repair (ABR) alone versus those who received a remplissage augmentation (ABR + R). Methods A retrospective review included patients aged 13 to 50 years who underwent ABR or ABR + R for anterior shoulder instability from 2007 to 2023. Exclusion criteria included 20% glenoid bone loss, off-track Hill-Sachs lesion, concomitant pathology, or revision surgery. CHBL was defined as humeral head defect extension below the 90° equator. Western Ontario Shoulder Index, pain Visual Analog Scale, and Subjective Shoulder Value were collected at the final follow-up. PROs and recurrence rates were compared between cohorts and within the CHBL subgroup. Results Three hundred eighty-four patients were included (mean age 23 ± 9 years (range: 13-49), 78% men), of which 99 (26%) were successfully contacted for PROs: 129 (34%) with CHBL and 255 (66%) without CHBL. The CHBL cohort was older (25 vs 22 years, P P P = .08), but, within the CHBL cohort, recurrence was significantly lower after ABR + R than ABR alone (9% vs 32%, P P > .05). In a multivariable linear regression, only recurrent instability was an independent predictor of inferior PROs; the presence of CHBL was not an independent predictor. Among CHBL patients, PROs were similar between ABR and ABR + R. Conclusions Patients with CHBL had similar long-term PROs to those without CHBL after ABR or ABR + R at a minimum follow-up of 1 year. Furthermore, the addition of remplissage was found to be associated with a reduced rate of recurrent anterior shoulder instability in patients with CHBL. Level of evidence Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Outside-In Medial Collateral Ligament Release Shows Superior Evidence for Safe Medial Joint Space Widening and Functional Recovery in Knee Arthroscopy: A Systematic Review.
authors: Rezaee H, Ayati Firoozabadi M, Salkhori O, Sahebi M, Mortazavi SMJ.
abstract: Purpose To compare various medial collateral ligament (MCL) release techniques used during knee arthroscopy by evaluating their anatomical targets, biomechanical effects, medial joint space widening, clinical and functional outcomes, and associated complications. Methods A comprehensive literature search was performed in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between January 2000 and June 2025. Eligible studies focused on MCL release in adult knee arthroscopy patients and reported clinical and functional outcomes. Data on medial joint space opening, knee instability, functional scores, and complications were extracted. Results Thirteen studies were included, with the outside-in technique, especially the percutaneous pie-crusting method, being the most extensively studied. The outside-in technique consistently achieved the greatest joint space widening, with increases ranging from 2.5 to 12 mm. The inside-out technique showed moderate joint space expansion (3-7 mm). Functional outcomes improved significantly across all techniques. The outside-in technique reported a Lysholm score increase from 48.2 to 80, a visual analog scale score decrease from 5.6 to 1.8, and an International Knee Documentation Committee score rise from 51.4 to 82.2. The inside-out technique showed a moderate improvement in Lysholm score from 59.3 to 85.7, with no significant differences in instability or long-term complications. Subperiosteal release also enhanced Lysholm scores from 50 to 92.5, with minor increases in joint laxity that resolved over time. All techniques showed low complication rates, with transient needle tract pain and mild ecchymosis being the most common side effects. Conclusions MCL release techniques, especially the outside-in percutaneous pie-crusting method, improve medial joint space visualization and medial joint space during knee arthroscopy, aiding meniscal repair, partial meniscectomy, meniscal root repair, and other procedures. These techniques are generally safe but cause temporary ligamentous laxity similar to a grade I MCL sprain, so they are not entirely "benign." Surgeons must weigh inducing controlled trauma against potential drawbacks of a tighter joint because the risk-benefit balance varies case by case. Level of evidence Level IV, systematic review of Level III and IV studies.

title: Open-Source and Commercial 3-Dimensional Computed Tomography Methods Show Limited Agreement for Classifying Acetabular Morphology in Patients Undergoing Hip Arthroscopy.
authors: Ellingwood AA, Grewal RS, Gass HM, Chen A, Woo D, Beasley BVL, Bomar JD, Parvaresh KC, Upasani VV, Schmitz MR.
abstract: Purpose To compare acetabular morphology classifications derived from a validated open-source (freely available) method with those derived from commercially available software in patients undergoing hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement syndrome. Methods We analyzed preoperative 3-dimensional computed tomography imaging in patients with femoroacetabular impingement syndrome using open-source and commercial software. The open-source method calculated acetabular coverage across 5 regions and generated z -scores relative to an internal normative database. Hips with z -scores ≥2 or ≤-2 were classified as abnormal. The commercial method categorized hips as normal, undercovered, or overcovered based on published thresholds (lateral center-edge angle, Tönnis angle, coverage percentage, and crossover sign) and focal depth mapping. The primary outcome was categorical agreement between methods. Results Seventy-six hips (55 women, 21 men; mean age 35.5 ± 12.3 years) were included. The open-source method classified 58/76 hips as normal, 10/76 as dysplastic, and 8/76 as overcovered. The commercial method classified 14/76 hips as normal, 29/76 as undercovered, and 33/76 as overcovered. A total of 23/76 hips were classified the same in both systems and called agreed. Disagreements (53/76 hips) fell into 3 categories: (1) essentially similar despite different labels because of borderline z -scores or small focal areas (n = 24), (2) disagreements driven by Tönnis angle alone (n = 8), and (3) true disagreements (n = 21). Notably, 5 hips (6.6%) showed opposite classifications (e.g., dysplastic vs overcovered). Subanalysis of z -scores showed that 69.8% of disagreements reflected borderline morphology ( z -scores of ±1-2). Conclusions Although both open-source and commercial methods provide 3-dimensional classification of acetabular morphology, categorical agreement was limited. Most disagreements reflected borderline morphology or small focal areas of uncertain clinical relevance. A minority showed true classification opposites. Clinical relevance Awareness of the methodological differences between open-source and commercial 3-dimensional computed tomography platforms may help surgeons appropriately interpret acetabular morphology classifications during preoperative planning for patients undergoing hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement syndrome.

title: Open and endoscopic decompression for cubital tunnel syndrome: long-term clinical outcomes, prognostic factors, and comparison of anterior transposition techniques.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Ertem H, Şireci C, Al F, Alyousef A, Çiçek İB, Ertem K.
abstract: Background/objective The optimal surgical treatment for cubital tunnel syndrome (CuTS) remains controversial, and comparative evidence regarding endoscopic-assisted anterior transposition is lacking. This study compared the clinical and functional outcomes of open and endoscopic decompression, evaluated open versus endoscopic-assisted anterior transposition, and identified patient-related prognostic factors associated with postoperative outcomes. Methods Fifty-six patients who underwent surgery for CuTS between 2010 and 2023 were retrospectively reviewed. Nineteen patients underwent open in situ decompression and 37 underwent endoscopic decompression. Outcomes were assessed using Quick DASH, VAS, Wilson-Krout grading system, patient satisfaction, and job change. An additional comparative analysis was performed in patients requiring anterior transposition because of intraoperative ulnar nerve instability (open, n = 16; endoscopic-assisted, n = 11). Smoking, body mass index (BMI), occupation, and preoperative McGowan grade were evaluated as prognostic factors. Results Median follow-up was 138 months (range, 56-180) in the open group and 76 months (range, 27-156) in the endoscopic group. No statistically significant differences were detected between open and endoscopic decompression in postoperative Quick DASH, VAS, Wilson-Krout grades, patient satisfaction, job change, or complication rates. Among patients undergoing anterior transposition, median follow-up was 148 months (range, 60-180) after open transposition and 105 months (range, 50-156) after endoscopic-assisted transposition. No statistically significant differences were detected in postoperative Quick DASH, VAS or Wilson-Krout grades between patients who underwent open anterior transposition and those who underwent endoscopic-assisted anterior transposition. Increasing preoperative McGowan grade was associated with worse postoperative Quick DASH, VAS, and Wilson-Krout outcomes. Smoking and higher BMI were associated with less favorable Wilson-Krout outcomes, whereas occupation had no significant effect on postoperative recovery. Conclusions No statistically significant differences were detected in long-term clinical and functional outcomes between open and endoscopic decompression for CuTS. Similarly, no statistically significant differences were detected between open and endoscopic-assisted anterior transposition. Greater preoperative disease severity was associated with less favorable postoperative outcomes. Given the retrospective design and limited sample size, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence or non-inferiority between the surgical techniques.

title: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in chronic and relapsing musculoskeletal pain: pearls for clinical practice.
authors: Di Martino A, Scaglione F, Graziosi A, Tranquilli Leali P.
abstract: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the principal pharmacological option for inflammatory musculoskeletal pain and are frequently treated as an interchangeable class from which any agent may be selected. This narrative review examines the pharmacological basis of that assumption and organises the evidence around three questions: which molecule, at what dose, and in which formulation. Four observations follow from the available data. COX selectivity is an incomplete predictor of clinical risk, since a non-selective agent may carry a cardiovascular profile comparable to that of the coxibs while a coxib may reduce events across the whole gastrointestinal tract; risk is therefore better assigned to individual molecules at defined doses than to selectivity classes. Comparative efficacy is dose-dependent rather than uniformly equivalent, so equivalence between agents applies only at comparable analgesic doses, and apparent non-response is frequently sub-therapeutic dosing. Organ-specific risk differs in kind as well as in degree across the cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, renal, hepatic and haemostatic axes, and proton pump inhibitors protect the upper gastrointestinal tract only. Modified-release formulations alter onset and peak-to-trough fluctuation, but no evidence indicates that they attenuate class-level organ toxicity. Contraindications lying outside the cardiorenal and gastrointestinal axes are stated, together with the clinically relevant drug interactions and the regulatory restrictions applying to individual agents.

title: Myofascial trigger point needling intervention for patellar tendinopathy unresponsive to PRP injection therapy: a case report.
authors: Liu W, Zhan Q, Zheng X, Chen Y, Chai S.
abstract: Rationale Patellar tendinopathy (PT) is a common sports injury characterized by persistent pain and limited mobility, which may progress to complete rupture of the patellar tendon. Common treatments, such as platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection and medication, have limitations, including limited efficacy. Therefore, exploring effective alternative therapies is of practical significance. Patient concerns The patient is a 17-year-old male soccer player who experienced left knee pain for over a year following training. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed signs consistent with patellar tendinopathy. The patient had previously undergone standardized drug therapy, PRP injection therapy, and eccentric exercises, but the results were unsatisfactory. Diagnoses Patellar tendinopathy. Interventions The patient underwent three weeks of myofascial trigger point (MTrP) needling therapy (also termed trigger point dry needling), administered three times per week to eight active MTrPs around the knee. Outcomes After 3 weeks of treatment, the patient's patellar tendon pain resolved, and motor function improved. Ultrasound revealed the disappearance of hypoechoic and heterogeneous echoic areas around the patellar tendon. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient had returned to full training without recurrence of knee pain. Lessons In this single case, MTrP needling was associated with rapid pain relief and improved ultrasound appearance. While these findings are promising, they are preliminary and hypothesis-generating. For PT unresponsive to PRP therapy, this intervention may be a potential therapeutic option that warrants further investigation in controlled trials.

title: Multiparametric quantitative MRI in knee osteoarthritis: evidence and requirements for interpretation and reporting.
authors: Jia Y, Liu L, Zhao B, Zhang X, Sun R, Guo X.
abstract: Quantitative MRI can characterize cartilage and other joint tissues beyond visible structural damage, but its contribution to individual management of knee osteoarthritis remains uncertain. This narrative review examines the evidence needed to interpret quantitative measurements, combine parameters, and report their uncertainty. An initial PubMed search in June 2026 was supplemented on 14 September 2026 by an updated PubMed search and broader Embase and Web of Science searches. Targeted full-text assessment addressed incremental value, outcome timing, validation, and measurement error. Selected development studies found better discrimination with integrated diffusion and relaxation measurements than with individual parameters, whereas other combined imaging models did not improve on simpler comparators. Longitudinal associations were outcome-specific, and independent external validation was limited. Treatment studies showed inconsistent agreement between imaging changes and symptomatic benefit. We propose a five-step interpretation framework that establishes the clinical question, verifies technical adequacy, assesses morphology and comparable reference data, evaluates measurement uncertainty, and separates observations from clinical inferences. Two hypothetical scenarios illustrate its application. Quantitative MRI currently provides its strongest support as a controlled research measurement. Demonstrated reproducibility, an appropriate comparator, and evidence of added decision value are required before a quantitative finding can justify patient-level diagnostic, prognostic, or treatment-response claims.

title: Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw After Dental Extractions During High-Dose Denosumab Therapy in a Patient With Paget's Disease: A Case Report.
authors: Zamani T, Mosannen Mozaffari P, Anvari K, Anbiaee N, Famili K, Mirzaei A, Fallah Toosi F, Shafiee A.
abstract: Patients with Paget's disease who receive high-dose denosumab may develop medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw, particularly after dental extractions. Pre-treatment dental assessment, careful risk communication, accurate staging, and coordinated conservative and surgical management are essential. Platelet-rich fibrin may be used only as an adjunct, not as an established standard treatment.

title: MRI-based assessment of greater tuberosity exposure in massive rotator cuff tears: a systematic review of current evidence and methodological gaps.
authors: Herrmann J, Limmer J, Neubauer D, Lehmeyer T, Oberfeld J, Rudert M, List K, Hochberger F.
abstract: Background Massive rotator cuff tears (MRCTs) lack a standardized and reproducible imaging-based definition. A recent Delphi consensus introduced greater tuberosity exposure (GTE) as a defining criterion for MRCTs, proposing that MRCTs be classified by either involvement of at least two rotator cuff tendons or ≥ 67% GTE on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Purpose To evaluate the role of GTE in the MRI-based definition and structural characterization of MRCTs and to describe the extent and methodological maturity of the evidence available for GTE and established MRI-derived parameters. Methods A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from database inception to February 17, 2026, and updated on October 9 and 11, 2026 with supplementary citation searching, in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies were included if they investigated MRCTs using MRI-based or MRI-transferable imaging and reported structural definitions, measurement methods, or associations with irreparability, structural healing, or clinical outcomes. Prognostic studies were assessed using the Quality In Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tool. Findings were synthesized narratively; no meta-analysis was performed due to substantial heterogeneity in study designs, imaging protocols, and outcome definitions. The synthesis described the extent and methodological maturity of the available evidence and did not compare diagnostic or prognostic performance between parameters. Results A total of 34 studies were included. No study evaluated GTE as a quantitative MRI-derived parameter. Only two studies addressed footprint coverage on imaging, one qualitatively and one by a semi-quantitative five-zone score of residual tendon attachment; neither measured GTE as a defined exposure parameter or applied predefined thresholds. In contrast, MRCTs were consistently characterized using indirect structural parameters, primarily tendon involvement and tear size. Established MRI-derived variables-including tear size, tendon retraction, fatty infiltration, muscle atrophy, and superior humeral migration-were assessed using established measurement frameworks based on defined anatomical landmarks, notwithstanding methodological heterogeneity in imaging protocols and thresholds across studies. These parameters were frequently evaluated in relation to irreparability, structural healing, and functional outcomes, whereas no study evaluated a direct quantitative MRI-based measure of GTE in relation to a clinical or structural endpoint. Conclusion No standardized and outcome-validated MRI-based method for quantifying GTE was identified within the scope of this review. Despite its conceptual appeal as a direct representation of footprint deficiency, GTE has not yet undergone standardized measurement development or outcome-based validation. The evidence base for established MRI-derived parameters is more extensive and methodologically mature, with operationalized measurement methods and reported outcome associations; this does not imply clinical inferiority of GTE. Future research should focus on developing reproducible MRI-based measurement techniques for GTE and evaluating its diagnostic and prognostic relevance in dedicated validation studies. Study design Systematic review; Level of evidence, 3. Individual included studies ranged from Level II to Level V.

title: Longitudinal remodeling of acylcarnitine signatures before and after arthroplasty for osteoarthritis: A 7-year cohort study.
authors: Sõber-Williams EK, Kilk K, Kals J, Märtson A, Prommik P, Tootsi K.
abstract: Objective Total joint arthroplasty (TJA) is the most effective treatment for end-stage osteoarthritis (OA). Although systemic acylcarnitine alterations have been reported in OA, long-term metabolic changes after TJA remain poorly understood. Existing metabolomic studies are cross-sectional and have not compared post-TJA changes with age- and sex-matched controls. We examined metabolic markers before and 7 years after TJA to assess long-term systemic metabolic changes relative to healthy aging controls. Method Fasting serum acylcarnitines were measured using liquid chromatography mass-spectrometry in a longitudinal cohort of participants with end-stage OA undergoing TJA (n = 70) and in age- and sex-matched healthy controls (n = 82) at baseline and 7-year follow-up. Acylcarnitine concentrations were compared between groups and longitudinally within participants, with analyses adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, hypertension status, and corrected for multiple comparisons. Results A total of 70 patients (age 62 ± 7) with severe OA who were undergoing TJA and 82 matched controls without OA were included in the study. Forty-eight acylcarnitine measures and ratios passed quality control. Fifteen acylcarnitines changed differently between groups over follow-up; six measures differed at baseline and 12 at follow-up. Five baseline differences normalized, whereas 11 new between-group differences emerged. After adjustment for baseline metabolite concentrations, seven acylcarnitines showed differential longitudinal change: four short-chain species (C5-OH, C5-DC, C5-M-DC, C5:1-DC) and three long-chain species (C14:2-OH, C16:2, C18:1). The four short-chain species increased 19.8-32.0% more in the TJA group than in controls. Free carnitine (C0) declined relative to controls, with a 24.8% lower longitudinal change (ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.62-0.91). Several medium- and long-chain acylcarnitines that were lower at baseline normalized toward control concentrations. Total acylcarnitine/free carnitine increased 32.3% more in the TJA group (ratio 1.32, 95% CI 1.17-1.50), with the baseline group difference resolving by follow-up. Conclusion TJA was associated with partial normalization of select circulating acylcarnitines; however, persistent abnormalities in hydroxy- and dicarboxy-acylcarnitines suggest ongoing alterations in lipid handling. Reduced carnitine buffering capacity and shifts toward alternative oxidation pathways further indicate incomplete restoration of systemic fatty-acid metabolism. Overall, these findings support pathway-specific metabolic remodeling rather than full metabolic normalization following TJA.

title: Long-term functional and orthopaedic outcomes in patients with severe pelvic ring injury requiring REBOA: A two-center matched cohort study.
authors: Yoon YC, Song HK.
abstract: Background Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) is used for life-threatening hemorrhage, but evidence has largely focused on acute outcomes. Long-term functional and orthopaedic outcomes among survivors treated with REBOA remain poorly characterized. Methods This retrospective two-center matched cohort included 98 adults with severe, hemodynamically unstable pelvic ring injuries who survived at least 24 h; hospital survivors required at least 12 months of follow-up. Forty-nine REBOA-treated patients were matched 1:1 to 49 non-REBOA patients by major Young-Burgess category, Injury Severity Score, and age. The primary outcome was functional status among hospital survivors, categorized as good/fair/poor. Deep surgical site infection (SSI) after definitive pelvic fixation was the key secondary outcome, and nonunion was exploratory. Main models used a propensity-score linear predictor based on age, Injury Severity Score, initial systolic blood pressure, and lactate. Results Seventy-five patients survived hospitalization (30 REBOA; 45 non-REBOA); median follow-up was 19 months. Good/fair/poor outcomes were 16.7%/46.7%/36.7% in REBOA survivors and 51.1%/37.8%/11.1% in non-REBOA survivors. REBOA exposure was associated with worse functional status after adjustment (common odds ratio [cOR], 3.14; 95% CI, 1.11-8.92; P = 0.032). Among 68 definitive-fixation survivors, deep SSI occurred in 44.0% versus 9.3% (adjusted OR, 7.01; 95% CI, 1.88-31.07; P = 0.003); all observed events occurred within 60 days. Nonunion occurred in 26.7% versus 6.7% (adjusted OR, 9.09; 95% CI, 2.00-53.71; P = 0.004). Sensitivity analyses for deep SSI were directionally consistent. Conclusions Among hospital survivors, REBOA exposure was associated with poorer long-term functional recovery and a higher burden of deep SSI. Nonunion was more frequent but remained exploratory. These findings characterize a high-risk orthopaedic survivor phenotype but do not establish a direct causal effect of REBOA.

title: How Does Hematopoietic Stem Cell Gene Therapy Affect Hip Dysplasia in Mucopolysaccharidosis Type I Hurler Syndrome? Radiological Outcomes at a Minimum 4-year Follow-up.
authors: De Pellegrin M, Cossutta M, Consiglieri G, Contisciani F, Filisetti C, Tucci F, Morosini C, Mellone R, Romeni S, Aiuti A, Bernardo ME.
abstract: Background Mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS IH), or Hurler syndrome, is a lysosomal disorder caused by glycosaminoglycan accumulation due to an α-L-iduronidase deficiency. It is characterized by progressive skeletal impairment and impaired cognitive development. Hip dysplasia is a major skeletal manifestation for which conventional treatments (allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation with or without enzyme replacement therapy) does not prevent progression. Questions/purposes Among patients with MPS IH, does hematopoietic stem cell gene therapy (HSC-GT) result in (1) longitudinal improvement in bony measurements of hip dysplasia, specifically the acetabular index (the angle between the Hilgenreiner line and the line drawn from the Y-cartilage to the lateral edge of the acetabular roof) and migration percentage (the proportion of the femoral head lateral to a Perkins line drawn from the lateral edge of the acetabular roof); (2) improvement in the cartilaginous acetabular index and migration percentage, accounting for the cartilaginous components of the acetabular roof and femoral head; and (3) an increase in the proportion of patients with an acetabular index and cartilaginous acetabular index within published norms? Methods Between 2018 and 2019, 8 patients (6 males, 2 females) with MPS IH received OTL-203, an HSC-GT, in a Phase I/II clinical trial. All patients met the trial eligibility criteria, including absence of a suitable allogeneic donor and a Developmental Quotient or Intelligence Quotient score ≥ 70. Median (range) age at treatment was 23.5 months (14 to 34). All patients had dysplastic hip morphology at baseline, with abnormal acetabular index values and reduced femoral head coverage. This secondary analysis used prospectively collected orthopaedic and skeletal data from the same trial cohort, including hip radiographs and MRIs obtained during multidisciplinary follow-up. All patients completed the 5-year follow-up and entered the approved long-term follow-up program (up to 15 years after HSC-GT); no patients were lost to follow-up. One patient with pretreatment bilateral hip dislocation underwent hip surgery and was excluded from the subsequent longitudinal analysis, with radiological data retained up to surgery. One additional patient had missing radiographic assessments because behavioral difficulties precluded imaging; all other patients had 4-year assessments available. Hip dysplasia was assessed at baseline and 1, 2, 3, and 4 years after HSC-GT using acetabular index and migration percentage on radiographs and MRIs, as well as cartilaginous acetabular index and cartilaginous migration percentage on MRI. Radiological measurements were compared with published age- and sex-specific normative values. Mean ± SD age at last follow-up was 5.8 ± 0.5 years. Results Radiographic acetabular index and migration percentage decreased longitudinally (acetabular index: fixed effect estimate = -2.7° per year [95% CI -3.5° to -1.9°]; p Conclusion These findings suggest that hip dysplasia may stabilize or improve after OTL-203 treatment, supporting continued radiological surveillance in young children after HSC-GT. Longer-term prospective multicenter studies are needed to assess durability and clinical relevance and to compare outcomes with bone marrow transplantation. Level of evidence Level IV, therapeutic study.

title: High-Strength Tape for Cable Structure Reconstruction During Arthroscopic Repair of L-Shaped Rotator Cuff Tears.
authors: Liu S, Ren Y, Jia Y, Ye N, Dou Z, Jia J, Na Y.
abstract: With the innovation and progressive maturation of arthroscopic techniques, the advantages of minimally invasive surgery and accelerated rehabilitation have made arthroscopy a preferred option for patients with rotator cuff injuries. However, for complex rotator cuff tears, such as "L-shaped" tendon tears, the risk of postoperative retear remains considerable. The cable structure, serving as a "suspension bridge" within the rotator cuff, is a critical load-bearing component of the shoulder joint. This structure is frequently compromised in "L-shaped" rotator cuff tears. In this report, we describe an arthroscopic technique using high-strength tape to restore the cable structure and treat "L-shaped" rotator cuff tears. The key steps include using high-strength tape to reduce the retracted tendon stump and restore the cable structure, thereby re-establishing mechanical integrity, reducing tension on the repaired tendon, and minimizing the cutting effect of sutures on the tendon. Finally, the sutures from the medial-row anchor are employed to perform a "Margin Convergence" repair of the longitudinal tear component.

title: Gait kinematics and toe-clearance in younger and healthy older adults: A comparison accounting for walking speed.
authors: Sato H, Kamide N, Sakamoto M, Ando M, Shiba Y.
abstract: Age-related reductions in walking speed often confound the interpretation of gait alterations in older adults. This study compared lower-limb kinematics and trip-related parameters between younger and healthy older adults after controlling for body size and sex and adjusting for walking speed. Data from 325 older adults (mean age 72 (SD 4) years) and 100 younger adults (mean age 22 (SD 2) years) were analyzed using quantitative gait analysis. Propensity score matching (1:1 ratio) was performed to pair participants by sex, height, and weight, yielding 76 matched pairs. Kinematic parameters (sagittal plane motion of the pelvis, hip, knee, and ankle) and trip-related parameters (minimum toe clearance [minTC] and probability of tripping [POT]) were compared using ANCOVA with walking speed as a covariate. Regardless of walking speed, older adults exhibited significantly greater peak anterior pelvic tilt and hip flexion than younger adults. During maximum-effort walking, older adults demonstrated significantly higher minTC and lower POT than younger adults. Regression analysis showed that peak knee flexion was more strongly associated with walking speed in older adults, whereas cadence was more strongly associated with walking speed in younger adults. These findings suggest differences between younger and older adults in the gait parameters associated with walking speed. They also indicate that healthy older adults do not necessarily exhibit less favorable toe-clearance-related biomechanical indicators during fast walking than younger adults.

title: Factors associated with tocilizumab primary failure in the treatment of giant cell arteritis.
authors: de Boysson H, Adoukonou NE, Dumont A, Orvain T, Boutemy J, Delacotte C, Gallou S, Hankard A, Maigné G, Silva NM, Philip R, Trenec M, Rocamora A, Deshayes S, Aouba A.
abstract: Objectives Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is the most common systemic vasculitis in adults over 50. Tocilizumab (TCZ), the first biologic approved in GCA, enables glucocorticoid-sparing remission, but reliable predictors of treatment outcome at initiation are lacking. We aimed to identify baseline and follow-up predictors of TCZ failure in GCA. Methods In this retrospective single-centre cohort study, consecutive GCA patients receiving their first TCZ course at Caen University Hospital (2014-2024) were included, excluding early withdrawal ( Results Of 91 patients, TCZ was successful in 43 (47%) and failed in 48 (53%). Baseline multivariable analysis identified three predictors of failure: CRP > 63.5 mg/L (OR 3.40; 95% CI 1.26-9.77; P Conclusions Baseline CRP, LVV and prior relapses can be combined into a simple predictive score to stratify the probability of TCZ response in GCA. Complete metabolic extinction on FDG-PET/CT during treatment further identifies patients at risk of failure.

title: Distal Clavicle Plate Combined With EndoButton Device for the Treatment of Neer Type IIB Distal Clavicle Fractures.
authors: Zhu T, Huang C, Fan H, Hu X, Fu Y, Dong H, Zhang Y.
abstract: The present article describes a surgical technique for the management of Neer type IIB distal clavicle fractures using a distal clavicle plate combined with an EndoButton device. The procedure consists of stepwise arthroscopic evaluation and exposure, fracture reduction, conoid ligament reconstruction, and plate fixation. This combined approach allows for concurrent management of intra-articular lesions, provides stable fixation, reduces the risk of iatrogenic clavicle fractures, and facilitates early postoperative rehabilitation. Nevertheless, it has certain limitations: the approach is not minimally invasive, its indications are relatively narrow, and it requires advanced arthroscopic expertise. All in all, this surgical approach is applicable to both acute and chronic Neer type IIB distal clavicle fractures.

title: Clinical outcomes after fully visualized transforaminal endoscopic spine surgery in patients with lumbar disc herniation stratified by paraspinal muscle degeneration: A retrospective cohort study.
authors: Wang L, Shi B, Zhang W, Ma X, Cao B, Xiao H, Zhang H.
abstract: Objective To evaluate pain and functional outcomes after fully visualized transforaminal endoscopic spine surgery in patients with lumbar disc herniation (LDH) stratified by preoperative paraspinal muscle degeneration, and to examine whether degeneration grade was associated with 2-year outcomes. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 129 patients with single-level LDH who underwent surgery between December 2021 and December 2023 and had complete preoperative, 1-month, 6-month, and 2-year follow-up data. Two blinded spine surgeons independently graded bilateral multifidus fatty infiltration from 0 to 4 on axial T2-weighted MRI at the mid-disc level; linearly weighted kappa was 0.967(95% CI, 0.937 to 0.989). Longitudinal outcomes were analyzed using covariate-adjusted patient-level random-intercept mixed-effects models with degeneration grade treated as a categorical factor, followed by adjusted 2-year regression and post hoc sensitivity analyses. Results Of 136 screened patients, 129 were included after excluding 2 with incomplete records and 5 lost to follow-up. The cohort included 64 men and 65 women, with a mean age of 57.36 ± 11.63 years; grades 0-4 included 13, 25, 33, 32 and 26 patients, respectively. All grades improved substantially. In covariate-adjusted mixed models treating grade as a factor, the grade effect was significant for back pain VAS (P Conclusions Fully visualized transforaminal endoscopic spine surgery was associated with substantial pain relief and functional improvement across all multifidus degeneration grades. More severe degeneration showed modest prognostic associations with residual back pain and disability, but the estimated effects were smaller than published minimal clinically important differences. These findings should inform cautious counseling and hypothesis generation rather than be used as a standalone surgical decision rule.

title: Clinical findings associated with diagnosing lumbar foraminal stenosis: systematic review.
authors: Ekedahl H, Av Kák Gustafsson ME, Larsson C.
abstract: Purpose To determine the diagnostic value of history taking and clinical examination tests for diagnosing lumbar radicular pain due to foraminal stenosis (FS) as established using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Method An electronic search of PubMed, CINAHL, Embase and MEDLINE was conducted. Studies with diagnostic accuracy of FS using dichotomous index tests (patient history measures and clinical examination tests) were included. The risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS 2) tool. Diagnostic value of index test was analyzed using proportions of positive findings (sensitivity). Specificity was not obtained. The results of all patients with FS were compared with all patients of a different specific diagnosis, disc herniation (DH) or central spinal stenosis (CSS), by comparing the proportion of positive findings for each index test. Results A total of 2,491records were identified. After title and abstract screening, 1,951 records were excluded, and 84 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Finally, 15 studies were included. No study investigating accuracy of tests for patients with recess stenosis was found. In the included studies, 737 subjects had FS, and 10 different index tests were found (2 patient history measures and 8 clinical examination tests). Of the 15 included studies, overall risk of bias was judged as low in two studies, while remaining studies had some concerns primarily due to unclear risk in the index test and flow and timing domains. Applicability concerns were generally low across studies. The index tests with highest average proportion of positive findings in detecting FS were Leg pain at rest (74%; 4 studies, n = 190) and Lumbar extensions test (66%; 11 studies, n = 537); and the test with the lowest proportion of positive findings was Straight leg raise (SLR; 33%; 10 studies, n = 471). Conclusion This review concluded that SLR has the lowest ability to detect lumbar foraminal stenosis, whereas positive Lumbar extension test and Leg pain at rest have the highest ability to detect the diagnosis. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given methodological uncertainties and limited diagnostic accuracy evidence.

title: Care Hotel With Virtual Monitoring as an Alternative Recovery Pathway for Outpatient Total Joint Arthroplasty: Safety and Patient Experience.
authors: Kumar J, Fawcett MA, Ma RT, Sherman CE, Spencer Gardner LS, Ledford CK, Chadha RM, Springer BD.
abstract: Background As total hip (THA) and knee arthroplasty (TKA) transition toward outpatient care, medical centers need to create models to support same-day discharge (SDD) for all patients, particularly those traveling long distances. A care hotel (CH) with virtual monitoring represents a novel postoperative recovery pathway, and our study evaluates patient safety and experience of this alternative model. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 5324 primary THA and TKA patients from a single tertiary referral center between July 2021 and April 2025. Of these, 590 cases (11%) utilized the CH pathway and were compared to traditional inpatient (IP), and SDD cohorts. Outcomes included demographic characteristics, 30-day emergency department (ED) utilization, hospital readmission rates, and patient-reported experience metrics. Results The 30-day ED return rate for CH patients was significantly lower than IP group (3.9 vs 6.8%, P = .006). The CH ED return rate was also lower than SDD; however, not statistically significant (3.9 vs 5.5%, P = .15). Among those returning to the ED, hospital readmission rates were 47.8% for CH, 39.3% for IP and 31.8% for SDD ( P > .22). Patient satisfaction among responders was high, with 94% of CH patients reporting they would be likely or very likely to recommend the alternative recovery pathway. Conclusions The CH provides a safe, well-received recovery pathway for THA and TKA patients with low ED utilization, acceptable readmission rates, and high patient satisfaction among responders. The CH model may represent a scalable strategy to expand access for outpatient THA and TKA while preserving hospital resources.

title: CT-based navigation for acetabular cup placement in supine and lateral positions: a simulated surgery study using patient-specific 3D-printed pelvic models.
authors: Liang L, Nemati HM.
abstract: Purpose Accurate acetabular cup placement is critical for the success of total hip arthroplasty (THA). The aim of this study was to evaluate the accuracy and precision of a CT-based, AI-driven navigation tool for acetabular cup placement in supine and lateral patient positions, using a patient-specific 3D-printed pelvic model with an embedded acetabular cup rim as a physical measurement reference. Methods Twenty-six patient-specific pelvic models were generated from preoperative CT data. A virtual acetabular cup was added to each pelvic mesh, cropped to the rim, and 3D-printed together with the bone, yielding a physical cup reference embedded in the printed pelvis. The ground-truth cup orientation and position were defined within the planning application by overlaying a cup component template on the embedded rim. Each model was tested once in supine and once in lateral position in a paired design. Ten cases were repeated three times per position to assess intra-session precision. Outcomes were surface matching root-mean-square error (RMSE), cup anteversion, inclination, and depth errors. Analyses included two one-sided tests (TOST) for equivalence (±0.5 mm), Bland-Altman agreement, Levene's test, and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Results Mean alignment-point RMSE was 0.26 mm (supine) and 0.28 mm (lateral); mean independent test-point RMSE was 0.30 mm in both positions, with TOST confirming equivalence within ±0.5 mm. Mean absolute anteversion error was 0.67° (supine) and 0.44° (lateral), with comparable inclination errors. Mean absolute cup depth error remained well below ±3 mm. Bland-Altman analyses showed narrow 95% limits of agreement between positions. All ICC(3,1) values for cup orientation exceeded 0.99 in both positions. Conclusions The evaluated navigation tool achieved sub-millimeter surface matching, small cup placement errors, and excellent intra-session precision in both supine and lateral positions. The embedded-rim phantom enabled direct measurement of cup orientation and seating depth on the printed model and is applicable to other CT-based navigation systems.

title: Blockade of the Succinate-SUCNR1 Metabolic Axis Helps Restore Mitochondrial Homeostasis and Prevents Structural Failure in Overuse-Induced Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy in a Mouse Model.
journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
authors: Yan D, Fang D, Wang X, Wu D, Zhang Y, Zhao Q.
abstract: Background Rotator cuff repair failures are primarily driven by intrinsic tissue degeneration. While mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in this cascade, the specific metabolic signals driving structural tendon failure remain poorly defined. The succinate-SUCNR1 axis may function as a critical metabolic checkpoint in this process. Hypothesis The authors hypothesized that the succinate-SUCNR1 axis is clinically hyperactivated in rotator cuff tears (RCTs), and that targeted blockade of this axis would mitigate overuse-induced tissue degeneration and preserve ultimate biomechanical integrity. Study design Controlled laboratory study. Methods Human supraspinatus specimens (10 RCTs, 10 controls) were analyzed for succinate levels, SUCNR1 expression, and histological severity. A murine treadmill overuse model was established in wild-type (WT) and Sucnr1 -deficient ( Sucnr1 -/-) mice (21 per group) to evaluate histological degeneration, pathological neovascularization, and biomechanical properties (ultimate failure load and stiffness). Mechanistically, senescent human tendon stem cells (hTSCs) (n = 6) were treated with a selective SUCNR1 antagonist (Compound 20) to evaluate mitochondrial bioenergetic rescue via seahorse analysis. Results In RCT specimens, tissue degeneration strongly correlated with succinate accumulation and SUCNR1 upregulation (Pearson r = 0.81; P Sucnr1 deficiency protected mice from overuse-induced tendinopathy, significantly suppressing inflammatory infiltration and aberrant neovascularization while maintaining collagen architecture. Sucnr1 ablation prevented the significant loss of tendon stiffness and ultimate failure load observed in the WT overuse group ( P Conclusion The succinate-SUCNR1 axis is a potent driver of structural failure. Targeting this axis may help restore mitochondrial homeostasis and break the "inflamm-aging" cycle, potentially reducing retear rates after rotator cuff repair. Clinical relevance Pharmacological blockade of SUCNR1 represents a promising, biology-preserving strategy to improve intrinsic tendon quality. By helping restore mitochondrial homeostasis and halting the degenerative cascade, targeting this axis may reduce structural failure rates after rotator cuff repair.

title: Biological Augmentation of Arthroscopic Partial-Thickness Bursal-Sided Rotator Cuff Repair Using Minced Autologous Glenohumeral Ligament Tissue Particles.
authors: Liu H, Wang X, Mao H, Shen W.
abstract: Rotator cuff tears are associated with high retear rates and limited healing capacity after repair. We describe an arthroscopic biological augmentation technique using minced autologous glenohumeral ligament tissue during double-row partial-thickness bursal-sided rotator cuff repair. Ligament tissue is harvested, processed into particulate grafts, and implanted within a suture-bridge construct to create a stable, biologically active interpositional layer at the repair site. This technique provides a simple and fully autologous method to enhance the local healing environment during rotator cuff repair.

title: Arthroscopic Marrow-Stimulating Procedure for Full-Thickness Knee Cartilage Lesions.
authors: M J, C R J, Subramaniam P S R, Thomas AK, M C A.
abstract: Articular cartilage defects remain challenging to treat because cartilage is avascular, sparsely cellular and has limited intrinsic healing potential. If left untreated, these lesions may progress to degenerative osteoarthritis, resulting in persistent pain and functional limitation. Marrow stimulation techniques such as drilling and microfracture are commonly used to promote repair by accessing subchondral bone marrow elements. Although these procedures are simple and widely practiced, their clinical benefits are often limited to the short- to mid-term, and they may disrupt the subchondral bone plate, potentially compromising future cartilage restoration options. Nanofracture represents an evolution of traditional microfracture, using smaller-diameter (1 mm) and deeper (9 mm) perforations to enhance marrow access while minimizing trabecular bone compaction. This article describes an arthroscopic nanofracture technique using a curved guide and depth-controlled wire, allowing precise, evenly spaced perforations and improved access to challenging regions such as the posterior femoral condyles and tibial plateau without added surgical morbidity. By preserving subchondral architecture and ensuring consistent marrow stimulation, nanofracture may improve the biological quality of repair tissue.

title: Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction With Preservation of the Tibial Insertion of the Hamstring Tendons and Double-Pulley Technique.
authors: Liu Z, Yang Y, Hu L, Su S, Huang P.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury is one of the most common knee disorders, occurring mostly in sports-related injuries. After injury, knee stability is compromised, leading to further damage to surrounding structures, such as meniscal tears, cartilage wear, and other lesions. Therefore, timely and effective repair of the injured ACL is critical. At present, a variety of surgical techniques are available for ACL reconstruction, with substantial differences in graft selection and fixation methods, and no universal consensus has been reached in the academic community. Hamstring tendons are among the most commonly used autografts. Preservation of the tibial insertion of the hamstring tendons has been proven to provide distinct biological and mechanical advantages. This technical note introduces an ACL reconstruction technique using a double-pulley system, which allows effective intraoperative adjustment of tension in each bundle of the reconstructed ACL to achieve highly uniform tension across all bundles. Furthermore, the native tibial insertions of the hamstring tendons (gracilis and semitendinosus) are preserved, maximizing blood supply to the reconstructed ligament. This approach facilitates the ligamentization of the graft and shortens the tendon-bone healing period.

title: Altered Cognitive Control and Cortical Oscillatory Dynamics in Athletes With ACL Reconstruction During Decision-Making Under Uncertainty.
journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
authors: Jiménez-Martínez J, Gutiérrez-Capote A, Alarcón-López F, Cárdenas-Vélez D.
abstract: Background Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury induces neuroplastic changes within the central nervous system (CNS) that may persist beyond reconstruction and rehabilitation. Purpose/hypothesis The purpose was to compare neurocognitive performance and cortical oscillatory activity between open-skill athletes (eg, soccer, basketball, or handball players) without ACL injury history and athletes with ACL reconstruction (ACLR) during a probabilistic go/no-go task. It was hypothesized that athletes with ACLR would exhibit poorer behavioral performance and less efficient oscillatory dynamics, particularly higher theta and lower suppression of beta and alpha power oscillations after goal stimulus onset. Study design Controlled laboratory study. Methods A total of 90 open-skill athletes (45 non-ACLR, 45 ACLR) performed a probabilistic go/no-go task while electroencephalographic recording was performed. Time-frequency analysis targeted midfrontal theta (4-7 Hz), left-lateralized central beta (15-25 Hz), and posterior alpha (8-12 Hz) oscillations during prestimulus and target stimulus windows. Linear mixed-effects models examined group differences in cognitive performance and oscillatory power. Results Athletes with ACLR showed slower response times and lower accuracy ( d = 0.75-1.09). Midfrontal theta power was attenuated for the ACLR group during the prestimulus phase ( d = 0.60) yet elevated during target phase trials ( d = 0.48), indicating a shift from proactive to reactive cognitive control in athletes with ACLR. Left-lateralized central beta ( d = 0.61) and posterior alpha suppression ( d = 0.55) were reduced, reflecting impaired motor cortical disinhibition and less efficient visual-attentional resource deployment, especially under high uncertainty conditions. Conclusion Athletes with ACLR showed persistent alterations in the cortical oscillatory mechanisms associated with conflict monitoring, motor preparation, and attentional allocation under uncertainty. These neurocognitive alterations may compromise adaptive motor responses in sport contexts characterized by high uncertainty and cognitive mental demand, potentially increasing reinjury risk. These findings support the integration of neurocognitive assessment into return-to-sport protocols. Clinical relevance Alterations in cortical oscillatory dynamics during decision-making under uncertainty may reflect reduced efficiency in cognitive control, motor preparation, and attentional allocation, which are not detected by standard assessments. Exercise professionals should consider integrating these assessments into return-to-sport protocols to address the persistent CNS alterations that may underlie reinjury risk in athletes with ACLR.

title: A simple independent high-strength suture augmentation significantly improves tendon biomechanical properties in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
authors: Dung TC, Elsheikh R, Kha TD, An NT, Makram AM, Chanh PT, Nam NH, Huy NT.
abstract: Purpose The all-inside anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) technique heavily depends on continuous graft stability, making graft preparation critical. Graft augmentation techniques have been proposed to enhance stability in ACLR. This biomechanical study investigated whether an independent high-strength suture augmentation, applied parallel to the tendon graft, improves construct properties. Methods Thirty-eight specimens were allocated to three groups: Suture (n = 10; No. 2 non-absorbable braided polyethylene), Graft (n = 13; bovine tendon), and Graft+Suture (n = 15; combined construct). All specimens underwent uniaxial tensile testing, including a preconditioning phase from 0 to 350 N followed by a load-to-failure test at 50 mm/min to determine elongation (mm), ultimate failure load (UFL, in N), and construct stiffness (N/mm). Statistical analysis was performed using one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc analysis. Results The Graft+Suture group exhibited significantly lower elongation (2.72 ± 0.51 mm) compared with both the Graft group (4.44 ± 1.59 mm; MD -1.71 mm, 95% CI -2.86 to -0.56; p = 0.002) and the Suture group (7.77 ± 1.37 mm; MD -5.05 mm, 95% CI -6.29 to -3.81; p Conclusion In this in vitro bovine model, independent high-strength suture augmentation significantly improved tendon graft biomechanical properties, producing higher UFL and stiffness, while reducing elongation. These findings suggest a potential strategy for graft reinforcement, though a more cautious interpretation is warranted pending in vivo and clinical validation. Level of evidence Not applicable.

title: A feasible and cost-effective method to induce distal radius fractures in full-length forearm human cadaveric specimens.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Krüger J, Terndrup M, Thomsen MG, von Keudell A, Andersen JA, Maleitzke T.
abstract: Introduction Reported rates of loss of reduction in nonoperatively treated distal radius fractures (DRF) range from 17 to 71%. Thus, realistic biomechanical models are warranted to test novel immobilization devices that prevent loss of reduction in nonoperative fracture management. Currently available human cadaveric specimen models have several limitations: (i) disrupted soft tissue integrity, (ii) difficulty in replicating complex fracture patterns, and (iii) high technical demands and costs. Therefore, the aim of this study was to establish a feasible and accessible method for inducing DRFs, that accurately reflects in-vivo biomechanical fracture conditions in tissue-intact cadaveric specimens, suitable for testing of novel immobilization devices. Materials and methods Fifteen upper extremity cadaveric specimens were included. Specimens were prepared as full‑length forearm models. Using a repurposed strength training tower as a vertical drop tower, fractures were induced by proximally administering 120-135 J impacts. CT scans were performed pre- and post-fracture induction. All fractures were classified according to the AO/OTA classification. Results DRFs were successfully induced in all 15 specimens. A single 120 J impact produced a DRF in 11 out of 15 cases (73%). A second impact was administered in 4 out of 15 specimens (27%). Eleven of the 15 induced DRFs (73%) were classified as AO/OTA type C fractures, most commonly 2R3C3.2. Concomitant distal ulnar fractures were present in 6 cases, concomitant carpal fractures in 9 specimens. The overall cost of the setup amounted to 947 €. Conclusions This study presents a feasible, cost-effective method to induce DRFs in tissue-intact, full-length human cadaveric forearm specimens. The setup consistently produces DRFs, predominantly AO/OTA type C, which can, with certain limitations, be utilized for biomechanical testing of immobilization devices, while also being uited for surgical and anatomical education.

title: Visually detectable pointer deviation of the nextar surgical navigation system with c-arm, o-arm and ct imaging: a bench-top study using a two-dimensional phantom.
authors: Zaccaria R, Suero E, Lampert C, Simon D, Neudeck R, Hauck S, Weigert A, Reidler P, Böcker W, Wegener B.
abstract: Background The accuracy of surgical navigation systems is critical for their safe and effective clinical use. This bench-top study evaluated whether a positional deviation of the pointer tip from a 1-mm target could be detected on the display of the NextAR surgical navigation system (Medacta International SA, Switzerland) when image-to-patient registration was based on C-arm, O-arm or CT imaging, and whether such a detectable deviation depended on the distance between the fiducial reference marker and the target. The endpoint was a visual observation of the pointer on the display and not an independently measured target registration error (TRE). Methods A flat two-dimensional phantom (millimetre graph paper on a wooden board) carried two parallel rows of 20 steel nails with 1-mm heads. Adjacent nails were 10 mm apart and the rows 120 mm apart. The fiducial was fixed midway between the rows at the start of the grid and defined the origin. The phantom was imaged with a Ziehm Vision RFD 3D C-arm, a Medtronic O-arm MVS O2 and a Siemens SOMATOM Drive CT. Ten image acquisitions, each followed by a new image-to-patient registration, were performed per modality. For each nail within the imaged volume, the tip of a navigated pointer was placed on the nail head and the operator visually inspected the NextAR three-dimensional display for a deviation. NextAR provides no numerical deviation value. No artificial registration error was introduced, and the pointer tip was not independently measured. The primary endpoint, visually detectable pointer deviation (hereafter detectable deviation), was a visible offset of the pointer tip from the centre of the nail head on the display. The threshold of about 1 mm is an approximate limit given by the size of the nail head and the millimetre grid and was neither calibrated nor independently measured. Results are descriptive, with exact two-sided Clopper-Pearson 95% confidence intervals. Results No detectable deviation was observed in any acquisition (0/10 per modality; exact 95% CI 0-30.9%; overall 0/30, 95% CI 0-11.6%). The maximum fiducial-to-target distances evaluated were 143 mm with C-arm, 152 mm with O-arm and 199 mm with CT imaging. The intervals refer to acquisitions under fixed bench-top conditions. Conclusions Under the controlled conditions of this two-dimensional bench-top experiment, no deviation was visible on the NextAR display with any of the three imaging modalities. Because the endpoint was a visual assessment limited to about 1 mm and was not independently measured against an external reference, the study does not establish submillimetre accuracy, equivalence between modalities, absence of distance-related effects, or clinical reliability. Verification in anatomically appropriate cadaveric and clinical settings is required. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Unilateral Biportal Endoscopy Versus Percutaneous Endoscopic Interlaminar Discectomy for Highly Migrated Lumbar Disc Herniation: A Retrospective Comparative Study With Quantitative MRI-Based Decompression Analysis.
authors: Wang S, Guan J, Liu T, Yan L, He X, Wang N, Tian Y.
abstract: Study designRetrospective comparative cohort study.ObjectiveTo compare the perioperative, clinical, and radiographic outcomes of unilateral biportal endoscopy (UBE) and percutaneous endoscopic interlaminar discectomy (PEID) in the treatment of highly migrated lumbar disc herniation (HMLDH).MethodsA total of 128 patients with single-level HMLDH who underwent UBE (n = 63) or PEID (n = 65) between June 2022 and January 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. All patients completed a minimum follow-up period of 2 years. Perioperative variables, complications, and reoperation events were analyzed. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). Radiographic decompression was quantitatively assessed using the postoperative dural sac cross-sectional area (DSCA) expansion rate measured on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).ResultsCompared with PEID, UBE was associated with a significantly shorter operative time, less endoscopic hemostasis time, and lower fluoroscopy time. Intraoperative blood loss was lower in the PEID group. Early postoperative back pain was significantly lower in the PEID group, whereas no significant between-group differences were observed in long-term VAS or ODI outcomes. The overall complication rate was significantly lower in the UBE group. In addition, UBE achieved a significantly greater DSCA expansion rate and a lower rate of residual disc fragments than PEID.ConclusionUBE and PEID achieved comparable long-term clinical outcomes in patients with HMLDH. UBE demonstrated advantages in perioperative efficiency, radiographic decompression, and reduced radiation exposure. Furthermore, UBE was associated with a lower overall complication rate, primarily attributable to a lower incidence of postoperative nerve root irritation.

title: Tranexamic Acid Administration is Associated With Lower Transfusion Rates and Wound Complications Following Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty for Periprosthetic Joint Infection.
authors: Kumaran P, Wier J, Telang SS, Liu SH, Becerra J, Lieberman JR, Heckmann ND.
abstract: Background Tranexamic acid (TXA) is widely used in total joint arthroplasty, but data on its efficacy in periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) of the knee are scarce. We assessed TXA efficacy in revision total knee arthroplasty (TKA) for PJI. Methods A national database was queried for patients ≥18 years undergoing stage-one revision TKA for PJI from 2016 to 2023. Patients with and without TXA exposure were propensity matched. Multivariable logistic regression assessed primary outcomes (postoperative transfusion, bleeding complications, and wound complications) and secondary outcomes (thromboembolic complications). Results Overall, 13,247 TXA patients were matched 1:1 to 13,247 non-TXA patients on comorbidities, Charlson Comorbidity Index, demographics, hospital characteristics, and preoperative transfusion rates, all with standardized mean differences P P P = .563).
