Odds of aggregate venous thromboembolism (aOR: 0.97, 95% CI: 0.82-1.13, P = .874), deep vein thrombosis (aOR: 1.00, 95% CI: 1.00-1.01, P = .309), and pulmonary embolism (aOR: 1.06, 95% CI: 0.83-1.34, P = .639) were similar. Conclusions TXA was associated with lower rates of transfusion and aggregate wound complications, without increased venous thromboembolism risk, during revision TKA for PJI.

title: The effect of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists on bone metabolism: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials of predominantly first-generation agents.
authors: Safargar M, Ahmadi N, Prabahar K, Zandi R, Kord-Varkaneh H.
abstract: Background Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) improve cardiometabolic outcomes, but their isolated effects on human bone remodeling remain uncertain because prior syntheses pooled heterogeneous study designs and active antidiabetic comparators. This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified the effects of GLP-1RAs versus placebo on densitometric, biochemical, and inflammatory markers of bone metabolism in randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Methods Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and PubMed/MEDLINE were searched from inception through May 12, 2026 for randomized placebo-controlled trials of GLP-1RAs or dual incretin agonists administered for 12 to 52 weeks. Eleven trials provided compatible data for random-effects meta-analysis and one additional trial was synthesized narratively, comprising 11 trials of first-generation agents (exenatide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) and one trial of second-generation semaglutide (1.0 mg/week), with zero eligible placebo-controlled trials identified for semaglutide 2.4 mg/week or tirzepatide. Weighted mean differences (WMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) bone mineral density (BMD), bone turnover markers, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), and evidence certainty was rated using GRADE. Results Compared with placebo, GLP-1RA treatment reduced lumbar spine BMD (WMD: -0.02 g/cm 2 , 95% CI: -0.03 to -0.00, I 2 = 0.0%; 3 trials, N = 222; Moderate certainty) and increased the bone resorption marker C-terminal telopeptide (CTX) (WMD: 0.05 μg/L, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.08, I 2 = 72.5%; 6 trials, N = 439; Low certainty), while reducing serum hs-CRP (WMD: -0.49 mg/L, 95% CI: -0.97 to -0.00, I 2 = 0.0%; 4 trials [5 arms], N = 340; Low certainty). No significant differences were observed for femoral neck BMD (WMD: 0.01 g/cm 2 , 95% CI: -0.02 to 0.04, I 2 = 68.9%; 5 trials [6 arms], N = 323; Very Low certainty), total hip BMD (WMD: 0.00 g/cm 2 , 95% CI: -0.02 to 0.03, I 2 = 70.8%; 5 trials [6 arms], N = 382; Low certainty), or procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide (P1NP) (WMD: -1.24 μg/L, 95% CI: -3.61 to 1.13, I 2 = 0.0%; 5 trials, N = 399; Moderate certainty), and leave-one-out exclusion of the single semaglutide trial did not alter the direction or significance of any pooled estimate. Conclusions Treatment with predominantly first-generation GLP-1RAs over 12 to 52 weeks increases osteoclastic bone resorption and induces a small, borderline reduction in lumbar spine BMD while preserving hip BMD and lowering systemic inflammation. Because existing placebo-controlled RCTs largely reflect earlier-generation agents with moderate weight loss, these findings cannot be extrapolated to higher-potency anti-obesity therapies such as semaglutide 2.4 mg/week or tirzepatide, which require dedicated long-term skeletal safety trials.

title: Serum urate and the risk of incident osteoarthritis: A prospective cohort study.
authors: Wang J, Zhang Y, Zhang X, Xing X, Wang Z, Ding C, Cai G.
abstract: Objectives Serum urate has been implicated in joint inflammation and may contribute to osteoarthritis (OA) development. This study aimed to examine the associations between serum urate and the incidence of knee, hip, and hand OA in a large population-based cohort. Methods This prospective cohort study included 43,1530 UK Biobank participants (mean age 56 years, 55% women) who were free of knee, hip, and hand OA at baseline with available serum urate measurements. Both linear and non-linear associations between serum urate levels and incident OA were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models. Potential mediation by biomarker of inflammation (IL-β, IL6, CRP, and TNF) and cartilage metabolism (CILP, COMP, CRATC1, and MMP1) was evaluated. Results Over a median follow-up of 14 years, 29,686 (6.88%), 19,040 (4.41%), and 11,696 (2.76%) participants developed knee, hip, and hand OA, respectively. Per 1 standard deviation increase serum urate was associated with a higher risk of incident OA (knee: hazard ratio [HR]=1.08, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.06-1.10; hip: HR=1.05, 95% CI: 1.03-1.07; hand: HR=1.04, 95% CI: 1.01-1.07). Non-linear associations were not observed for hip or hand OA, whereas a non-linear association was identified for knee OA. The relationships between serum urate and the risk of OA were partially mediated by inflammatory (proportion of mediation: 4.21%-15.14%) and cartilage metabolism biomarkers (proportion of mediation: 3.86%-16.33%). Conclusion Higher serum urate was associated with an increased risk of OA across knee, hip, and hand joints. Inflammatory and cartilage metabolic pathways may partly mediate this relationship.

title: Return to play and performance in Division I collegiate pitchers following ulnar collateral ligament surgery: a retrospective case series.
authors: King BW, Westbrooks B, Bailey EP, Sharp C, Aspang JSU, Hammond K, Danilkowicz RM.
abstract: Background The purpose of this study was to evaluate return to play, postoperative performance, and career advancement in National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I baseball players following ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) surgery. Methods NCAA Division I pitchers undergoing UCL surgery between 2015 and 2024 were identified using the Tommy John List. Outcomes included return to play, level of return to play, advancement to professional baseball, and pre- and postoperative earned run average (ERA), walks and hits per innings pitched (WHIP), strikeout-to-walk ratio, and innings pitched per season. Comparisons were made between performance outcomes from all preoperative seasons versus all postoperative seasons for pitchers who returned to Division I. Results A total of 264 pitchers were included, with 239 (90.5%) returning to play following UCL surgery. Return-to-performance analysis included 156 pitchers who returned to play at the Division I level. The only significant difference in pre- and postoperative performance for the full cohort was an increase in innings pitched per season (median difference, 6.25; P=0.002). Subgroup analysis of Power 5 pitchers demonstrated significantly higher postoperative ERA (median difference, 0.42; P=0.01) and WHIP (median difference, 0.05; P=0.03), along with a significant increase in innings pitched per season (median difference, 7.94; P=0.01). Conclusions Division I pitchers returned to play at high rates following UCL surgery. Among those who returned to Division I, no significant differences were observed in postoperative ERA, WHIP, or strikeout-to-walk ratio for the full cohort. However, Power 5 conference pitchers displayed small but statistically significant increases in postoperative ERA and WHIP. Level of evidence: IV.

title: Open-Wedge High Tibial Osteotomy With Complete Tibial Tubercle Osteotomy to Preserve Patellar Height.
authors: Miyasaka T, Kayama T, Kubota D, Arakawa S, Saito M.
abstract: Distalization of the tibial tubercle is a concern during open-wedge high tibial osteotomy, particularly when a large correction is required, considering the potential for patella baja and patellofemoral problems. This Technical Note describes the use of open-wedge high tibial osteotomy combined with complete tibial tubercle osteotomy to maintain the position of the tibial tubercle during correction. Performing tibial tubercle osteotomy first allows placement of a thin retractor beneath the fragment during the transverse osteotomy, helping to protect the fragment and reduce the risk of an incomplete osteotomy. Temporary fixation of the tibial tubercle to the proximal tibial fragment before wedge opening is a key step in maintaining the original position of the tubercle and preventing distalization during correction. This technique is a practical option for selected patients requiring substantial varus correction when preservation of patellar height is desired.

title: Musculoskeletal Disorder Risk in Motorcycle Operators: Development and Validation of a Targeted Screening Scale.
journal: Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine
authors: Zguira MS, Ayed A, Houas MA, Dergaa I, Moula S, Ceylan HI, Bragazzi NL, Stefanica V, Kasmi S, Rebai H, Douzi W.
abstract: Objective To develop and validate a musculoskeletal disorder screening scale for motorcycle operators. Methods In a cross-sectional study, 140 Tunisian operators rated pain in nine body regions on a four-point scale. Results Two factors separated upper-body from lower-body regions and explained 67.5 percent of the variance. Cronbach alpha reached 0.910 and 0.881. The two-factor model outperformed the one-factor model (chi-square difference 67.92, p Conclusions The scale shows a coherent two-factor structure and high internal consistency, with model fit short of the approximation-error threshold.

title: Moral Dissonance Is Greater When Clinicians Act Contrary to Evidence, Experience, and Values Than When They Disappoint the Patient.
authors: Azib N, Spier JD, Ring D, Razi A, and the Science of Variation Group, and the Science of Variation Group and Members of the Science of Variation Group include:.
abstract: Background Most musculoskeletal visits, tests, and treatments are optional. Specialists may experience moral dissonance when patient requests are difficult to reconcile with evidence, experience, and professional values. This dissonance may arise when clinicians feel torn between acquiescing to a request they view as unsupported and declining the request while worrying about disappointing the patient. Understanding the specific factors associated with greater moral dissonance, either in the form of acquiescence or disappointment, may inform efforts to improve both patient and clinician experiences when guiding patients toward effective health strategies. Questions/purposes (1) Is the severity of moral dissonance experienced by musculoskeletal specialists greater when acquiescing to patient requests that are contrary to evidence, experience, and values compared with disappointing the patient by declining a request? (2) What scenario factors are associated with the severity of moral dissonance? Methods We invited members of the Science of Variation Group (SOVG), an international collaborative of musculoskeletal surgeons who participate in monthly survey-based experiments addressing variation in care, to complete an online survey- and scenario-based experiment between April 12 and May 4, 2025. The SOVG is open to all musculoskeletal surgeons, but its active participants are mostly White academic surgeons (54%) in the US and Europe (26%), which is not representative of the average musculoskeletal surgeon. Our experiments are therefore designed to measure associations rather than to estimate rates or prevalence. The analysis depends on variation in how surgeons judge and respond to the same clinical scenarios and should be reproducible in any sample of surgeons with sufficient variation in opinions. Of approximately 200 SOVG members who typically participate in at least one survey annually, 68% (135) of surgeons completed at least one scenario. Participants reviewed 11 clinical scenarios with randomized elements, including patient age, patient gender, and combinations of clinical presentation and patient request. Participants were then randomly assigned to rate moral dissonance as either pressure to act contrary to evidence, experience, and values ("Imagine you give the patient what they want. To what degree do you feel like you are acting contrary to your values and best evidence?") or as a feeling of disappointing the patient ("To what degree do you feel like you're letting the patient down if you can't offer a diagnosis and treatment?"). Both items were rated on a scale from 0 ("I don't feel it at all") to 100 ("I feel it strongly"). Multilevel mixed-effects linear regression models were used to identify factors associated with levels of distress, accounting for surgeon-level nesting. Regression coefficients represent the estimated difference in moral dissonance on the 0-to-100 rating scale associated with each factor compared with the reference category. Positive coefficients indicate higher moral dissonance and negative coefficients indicate lower moral dissonance. For categorical variables, the coefficient represents the average difference in moral dissonance between that category and the reference category, adjusted for the other variables in the model. Results Levels of moral dissonance were higher when rated as acting contrary to evidence, experience, and values (median [IQR] 70 [40 to 90]) than when rated as disappointing the patient (40 [20 to 70]); the group medians differed by 30 points on the 0-to-100 scale. In the multilevel mixed-effects regression model, disappointing the patient was associated with a 21-point lower moral dissonance score than acting contrary to evidence, experience, and values (regression coefficient -21 [95% confidence interval (CI) -27 to -15]). Relative to requests for electrodiagnostic testing for pain with typing, moral dissonance ratings were higher for requests for carpal tunnel release despite normal electrodiagnostic testing results (regression coefficient 6.7 [95% CI 0.9 to 13]) and surgical excision of a wrist ganglion for symptoms consistent with a wrist ganglion (regression coefficient 7.1 [95% CI 1.3 to 13]). These coefficients indicate approximately 7-point higher moral dissonance ratings on the 0-to-100 scale compared with the reference scenario. Moral dissonance ratings were lower than in the reference scenario for requests for proximal median nerve release for nonspecific forearm pain (regression coefficient -14 [95% CI -20 to -8.2]) and surgery for distal biceps tendinopathy (regression coefficient -14 [95% CI -20 to -7.9]), indicating approximately 14-point lower ratings than the reference scenario. Conclusion The finding that moral dissonance was greater when rated as acquiescing to care that conflicts with evidence, experience, and values than when rated as disappointment suggests that the source of distress may be the surgeon's sense of responsibility for potentially reinforcing unhelpful beliefs, exposing patients to low-value care, or contributing to overuse. The variation by clinical presentation and patient request suggests that distress may be greatest when requested care is discretionary but still clinically plausible, making it harder to decline. Clinical relevance These findings suggest that surgeons may reduce moral dissonance by strategizing and practicing specific communication steps when patients request discretionary but plausible care, such as curiosity about the concern and goal driving the request, validation of that concern, and introducing options that might better achieve the patient's goals while introducing less potential harm and false hope.

title: Minimally Invasive Zadek Osteotomy vs Open Achilles Debridement for Insertional Achilles Tendinopathy in Athletes: A Retrospective Comparative Cohort Study.
authors: Genuth G, Stavrou P, Brown C, Iselin LD.
abstract: Background Insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT) is a common cause of posterior heel pain in athletic populations and may require surgical intervention following failed conservative management. Minimally invasive Zadek osteotomy (MIS Zadek) has emerged as an alternative to traditional open Achilles tendon debridement with Haglund resection, with potential advantages in recovery and complication profile. Methods A retrospective comparative cohort study was performed including 50 athletic patients with IAT (25 MIS Zadek, 25 open surgery) treated between 2022 and 2024 at a single high-volume centre. All patients participated in regular sports activity and failed at least 6 months of nonoperative treatment. The primary outcome was time to return to sport. Secondary outcomes included return-to-sport rate, Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) physical function (PF), PROMIS pain interference (PI), and postoperative complications. Multivariable regression analysis was performed to adjust for potential confounders. Results Return to sport was achieved in 100% of MIS patients (25/25) and 92% of open patients (23/25; P = .49). Time to return to sport was shorter following MIS Zadek (4.3 ± 1.2 vs 6.1 ± 1.5 months; mean difference -1.8 months, 95% CI -2.6 to -1.0; P P P = .02; Cohen d = 0.69), with a similar pattern for PROMIS PI (47.2 ± 5.5 vs 51.1 ± 6.0; mean difference -3.9, 95% CI -7.1 to -0.7; P = .02; Cohen d = 0.67). By 18 months, PROMIS PF improved further in both groups with comparable outcomes (59.4 ± 4.9 vs 57.8 ± 5.2; mean difference +1.6, 95% CI -1.4 to 4.6; P = .29), and PROMIS PI similarly converged (44.8 ± 4.9 vs 46.3 ± 5.1; mean difference -1.5, 95% CI -4.4 to 1.4; P = .30). Complication rates were lower in the MIS group (2/25, 8%) compared with the open group (6/25, 24%; P = .25), although this difference did not reach statistical significance. Conclusion MIS Zadek osteotomy was associated with faster return to sport and improved early recovery compared with open surgery; with the numbers available, no significant difference in long-term functional outcomes could be detected. Complications were numerically less frequent following MIS Zadek osteotomy, although this difference did not reach statistical significanceLevel of Evidence:Level III, retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Management of recurrent medial ankle pain after total ankle replacement arthroplasty: the role of medial malleolar anterolateral corner resection in resolving bone-to-implant impingement.
authors: Jung SO, Suh JS, Choi JY.

title: Lateral unicompartmental knee arthroplasty retaining partial internal fixation for traumatic osteoarthritis: a case report.
authors: Xu WB, Zhang HL, Wei LY, Huang ZY, Tao K, Ling J, Wang SC.
abstract: Background Post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) following tibial plateau fractures presents a clinical challenge, particularly in younger patients with high functional demands. This article aims to present the results of lateral unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (LUKA) retaining partial internal fixation in PTOA. Case presentation A 55-year-old female patient developed PTOA of the lateral compartment one year following operation for a tibial plateau fracture. The patient reported a one-year history of knee pain and experienced walking difficulties in the past eight weeks. The patient underwent LUKA under spinal anesthesia combined with nerve block. Strategically, instead of complete removal of the existing hardware, three critical screws beneath the tibial plateau were shortened and re-tightened to provide structural reinforcement while avoiding interference with prosthetic implantation. The patient was able to ambulate independently shortly after surgery. At the 3-month follow-up, knee function was satisfactory, with the Knee Society Score improving from 62 to 92. At the 6-month follow-up, no significant persistent pain or major complications such as prosthetic loosening, fracture, or wear. Conclusion This case demonstrates that LUKA with retention of partial internal fixation may represent a feasible strategy in carefully selected patients with PTOA and osteoporosis. This innovative approach preserves critical structural support, minimizes iatrogenic bone loss, and is associated with encouraging short-term clinical outcomes, offering a novel perspective for managing complex post-traumatic knees. However, long-term follow-up is necessary to verify these results.

title: Lambrinudi-Type Arthrodesis and Plantar Fasciectomy in the Treatment of Rigid Cavovarus Deformity.
authors: Ruiz R, Susdorf R, Hintermann B.
abstract: Background While using a standard triple arthrodesis in treating rigid cavovarus deformity, the talus often remains extended, leading to anterior ankle impingement and overload. The primary goal of this study was to test our hypotheses that the talus would adopt a more normal flexion position with a Lambrinudi-type triple arthrodesis and that the foot morphology would become more normal by combining it with a plantar fasciectomy. Additionally, the aim was to evaluate whether outcomes differ between neurogenic and non-neurogenic feet. Method Seventeen patients (17 feet; neurogenic [N], 11 feet; non-neurogenic [NN], 6 feet) who underwent a Lambrinudi-type arthrodesis combined with a plantar fasciectomy at our institution from 2016 to 2023, with at least 2 years of follow-up, were included. We prospectively collected radiographic and clinical data to evaluate changes in foot and ankle morphology. Results With the numbers available, no significant difference could be detected between the N and NN groups in clinical outcomes. The VAS scale decreased by 6.5 ± 0.3 points after surgery ( P g = 6.6 [4.9-8.4]), and the EFAS score increased by 31.5 ± 0.9 points ( P g = -8.7 [-10.9 to -6.5]). All radiographic measurements improved significantly ( P P = .024, Hedges g = -0.8 [-1.5 to -0.1]). The foot length increased from 122 ± 16 mm preoperatively to 134 ± 12 mm postoperatively (plus 10.1%, P g = -0.9 [-1.5 to -0.2]). Conclusion A Lambrinudi-type arthrodesis combined with a complete plantar fasciectomy was an effective method for correcting a rigid cavovarus deformity in both N and NN feet. It was intended to unload the anterior tibiotalar joint by flexing the talus and changing the flexion forces, and it increased foot length by 10.1%. It also was associated with significant clinical improvements across all measured outcome domains. Level of evidence Level IV, prospective case series.

title: Integration of weight-bearing computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging for advanced musculoskeletal statistical shape modeling of the foot and ankle.
journal: International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery
authors: Requist MR, Moreno E, Reddy C, Peterson AC, Mills MK, Lenz AL.
abstract: Purpose Statistical shape models (SSMs) from three-dimensional (3D) medical imaging describe morphology variation in normal and pathologic anatomy. Within the foot and ankle, weight-bearing computed tomography (WBCT) is used to characterize skeletal deformity but poorly visualizes soft tissue. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides improved evaluation of soft tissue structures but less accurate bone visualization. This methodologic analysis describes and tests reliability of a novel process to generate SSMs from coregistered MRI and WBCT structures. This method is illustrated via two example models: a combined musculoskeletal model and a distal tibia growth plate model. Methods Bilateral WBCTs and T1-weighted DIXON MRIs of the lower legs were collected from 14 individuals aged 8 to 18 with no prior lower limb surgery in a control group and hereditary neuropathy group. Bones were segmented from WBCT and manually aligned in MRI space. Alignment reliability was evaluated with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Six muscles were segmented semi-automatically and the distal tibia growth plate was manually segmented from MRI. Following cropping, size normalization, and alignment multi-domain SSMs were generated. SSMs were evaluated qualitatively through comparison with expected anatomy and quantitively by calculation of compactness, generalization, and specificity. Results The alignment method demonstrated excellent reliability with an intrarater ICC of 1 and interrater ICC of 0.999. The musculoskeletal model demonstrated expected atrophy in neuromuscular disease and the preliminary growth plate model showed variation in metaphyseal thickness. Both models demonstrated compactness, specificity, and generalization comparable to published SSMs, requiring 11 and 12 modes to account for 95% of population variance. Conclusion This method allows for application of shape modeling to novel questions in musculoskeletal morphology through simultaneous modeling of bone and soft tissue anatomy. Limitations include manual registration and MRI resolution. This analysis presented examples of muscle and growth plate models, but has broader applications in musculoskeletal analysis.

title: Increased risk of infection and reoperation following total knee arthroplasty in patients under 40.
authors: Daley A, Yarden J, Diaz-Coto S, Moschetti W.
abstract: Background Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is increasingly performed in younger patient populations. This study aimed to compare perioperative outcomes between patients under 40 and those over 65, stratified by surgical indication. Methods This retrospective study used the Epic Cosmos dataset to identify primary TKA patients under 40 years old (n = 3,177) or over 65 (n = 698,662). Patients were stratified by surgical indication (primary osteoarthritis, post-traumatic osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, avascular necrosis, and multiple indications) using ICD-10 codes. Outcomes included superficial wound dehiscence, infection, readmission, and ipsilateral reoperation, assessed at 90 days and 1 year postoperatively. Differences between age groups were assessed using adjusted odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) derived from multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for sex, body mass index, comorbidity burden, insurance status and smoking status with significance set at p Results Surgical indications differed significantly between cohorts (standardized proportions difference 0.939, p 65 compared to 64.6% in patients Conclusion Patients under 40 undergoing Total Knee Arthroplasty are at increased risk for prosthetic joint infection, superficial wound problems and ipsilateral reoperation at 90 days and 1 year when compared to those over the age of 65, independent of smoking status and comorbidity burden. Those with multiple indications for surgery are also at increased risk for infection and same-side reoperation at both time points.

title: How Much Do Horizontally Referenced and Interteardrop-referenced Acetabular Coverage Indices Differ During Standing in Adults With Hip Pain?
authors: Cousins R, Wagner M, Rao M, Pun SY, Smit K, Beaulé P, Grammatopoulos G.
abstract: Background Acetabular coverage is conventionally assessed using the lateral center-edge angle (LCEA) and acetabular index. However, on standing radiographs, these measurements may be referenced either to the pelvis or to the weightbearing horizontal. Whether selection of these reference lines leads to clinically relevant differences in acetabular coverage interpretation is uncertain. Questions/purposes (1) How do horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced LCEA and acetabular index measurements compare in patients with nonarthritic hip pain? (2) How are the magnitude and direction of pelvic obliquity associated with differences between horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced acetabular coverage measurements? (3) What are the magnitude and direction of pelvic obliquity in young adults undergoing assessment for unilateral nonarthritic hip pain? (4) How are hip-length discrepancy measures based on the lesser trochanter and hip center of rotation associated with the magnitude and direction of pelvic obliquity? Methods In this retrospective comparative study, 598 patients evaluated at a tertiary-referral young-adult hip clinic between June 2021 and June 2025 were identified; 10% (60 of 598) were excluded for bilateral hip involvement or prior procedures, 5% (28 of 598) for insufficient radiographs, and 3% (17 of 598) for age 50 years or older, leaving 493 patients age 16 to 49 years with unilateral nonarthritic hip conditions and standing AP pelvic radiographs to be included. The mean ± SD age was 35 ± 8 years; 39% (191 of 493) were male. Diagnoses included dysplasia; cam-type, mixed, and pincer-type femoroacetabular impingement; isolated labral tears; and other nonarthritic hip conditions. In each hip, LCEA and acetabular index were measured using horizontal and interteardrop-referenced measurements, and classification disagreement was assessed using LCEA ( 40°) and acetabular index ( 10°) categories. Associations between pelvic obliquity magnitude and measurement-difference magnitude were assessed using linear regression, with directional relationships assessed graphically. Pelvic obliquity was measured as the angle between the interteardrop and horizontal reference lines, with direction defined relative to the clinically evaluated side. Hip-length discrepancy measures based on the lesser trochanter and hip center of rotation were compared across pelvic obliquity magnitude and direction groups. After interrater standardization, each patient was randomly allocated to one of two observers, who performed all measurements for that patient; a third observer reviewed a random sample. Interobserver intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.69 to 0.87. Results Mean ± SD absolute differences between horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced measurements were 2° ± 1° for both LCEA and acetabular index. Classification disagreement occurred in 14% (69 of 493) using LCEA-based categories and 10% (51 of 493) using acetabular index-based categories, most notably when interteardrop-referenced LCEA indicated borderline dysplasia and horizontally referenced LCEA indicated normal coverage (29% [28 of 95]). Each 1° increase in pelvic obliquity magnitude was associated with an approximately 1° greater measurement difference for LCEA (β = 0.89 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 0.93]; R2 = 0.86; p Conclusion These findings indicate that horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced measurements can yield discordant acetabular coverage estimates and radiographic classifications for the same patient. As standing radiographs become more widely incorporated into hip evaluation, comparison of horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced LCEA and acetabular index measurements may provide additional information by revealing pelvic-obliquity-associated differences in measured coverage while standing. In patients with appreciable pelvic obliquity, these differences may warrant consideration when interpreting acetabular morphology and discussing the relative indications for treatment or procedural options because they may lead clinicians to disagree about whether the same hip meets thresholds used in treatment planning. Future work should correlate measurements based on horizontal referencing and interteardrop referencing in patients with appreciable pelvic obliquity with clinical and surgical outcomes to (1) determine whether acetabular indices measured using the interteardrop line or floor-based horizontal reference confer superior clinical value and (2) define procedure-specific thresholds for relevant diagnostic subgroups. Level of evidence Level III, diagnostic study.

title: Global research landscape, intellectual structure, and thematic evolution of robot-assisted surgical management of pelvic urinary tract fistulas: a bibliometric and knowledge-mapping analysis.
authors: Wu G, Li D, Liu H, Fan C, Du G, Tian J.
abstract: Robot-assisted surgery has been applied to a range of pelvic urinary tract fistulas, but the literature is dispersed across urology, gynecology, colorectal surgery, and reconstructive practice. We examined how this literature developed, how its contributing communities interact, and whether its clinical themes converge. English-language articles and reviews indexed in the Science Citation Index Expanded within the Web of Science Core Collection from inception to 1 August 2026 were screened for clinical or technical relevance. The final corpus contained 104 publications, comprising 85 articles and 19 reviews, published between 2005 and 2026. Publication and disciplinary trends, geographic collaboration, historical foundations, reference-based networks, Author Keyword themes, thematic evolution, and journal citation pathways were analyzed. Output remained low and uneven, although higher annual counts became more frequent after 2021. Urology remained the principal disciplinary setting, with broader participation from gynecology, reproductive health, and surgery. Authors from 31 countries or regions contributed; the United States led in both publication output and citations, while international collaboration remained concentrated within a limited network. Historical and thematic analyses identified vesicovaginal fistula repair as the main intellectual and conceptual backbone; colovesical, ureteral, rectourinary, and congenital applications formed smaller, partly separate streams. The literature has acquired a recognizable cross-specialty structure, but its principal clinical strands have not yet converged into a comparable evidence base. Future studies should prioritize multicenter designs and consistent reporting of anatomy, prior treatment, reconstruction, and clinically relevant outcomes.

title: Genetic susceptibility to anterior cruciate ligament rupture in females: a systematic review of female-stratified candidate-gene evidence and the absence of genome-wide studies.
authors: Edmonds CJ, Browne GJ, Khan WS, McDonnell SM.
abstract: Objective To systematically synthesise and critically appraise genetic association studies reporting female-stratified evidence for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture. Design Systematic review. Data sources Web of Science, Scopus, Ovid MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to 21 December 2025, which was the predefined search date for this review. Eligibility criteria for selecting studies Human genetic association studies reporting female-stratified ACL rupture outcomes or extractable female-only data were included. Studies reporting combined-sex analyses without extractable female data were excluded. Due to predefined heterogeneity in phenotypes, populations and genetic models, findings were synthesised narratively. Results 19 studies met the inclusion criteria, predominantly small candidate-gene case-control designs. Importantly, these publications did not represent 19 independent cohorts. The largest prospective cohort included 790 women at risk at baseline, of whom 58 sustained an incident ACL injury and 732 remained without incident injury. COL5A1 rs12722 was the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant. Positive single-variant estimates principally concerned CC homozygotes under a recessive model and arose from South African samples with documented participant reuse. Separate allelic associations were also reported. Independence of this signal was limited by probable cohort overlap, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence. Evidence for other collagen, proteoglycan, inflammatory and extracellular matrix remodelling genes was inconsistent. No female-stratified genome-wide association studies were identified. Conclusions COL5A1 rs12722 is the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant, but independent replication is not established. Positive recessive estimates concern CC homozygotes and should not be extended to heterozygotes. Small samples, participant reuse, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence limit certainty. Female-stratified associations do not establish sex-specific effects. Evidence derives predominantly from women of European ancestry, and generalisability to other ancestries remains unknown. Current findings do not support genetic screening for ACL rupture risk in female athletes; adequately powered, female-stratified genomic studies with rigorous phenotyping and independent replication across diverse ancestries are needed.

title: From Hunterian to Hunterian: the posterior malleolar fracture.
journal: Annals of the Royal College of Surgeons of England
authors: Bates S, Mason LW.
abstract: Background The posterior malleolar fracture (PMF) is now understood through three-dimensional imaging and mechanism-based classification, yet this understanding is not new. We argue that its central mechanism (rotation of an axially loaded talus within the ankle mortise) was inferred by Bonnin three-quarters of a century ago, obscured by an era of radiographic, size-based description, and later confirmed and made visible by computed tomography (CT). This continuity is frequently overlooked in the wider literature. Methods We present a narrative review of the primary historical literature alongside contemporary CT-based and cadaveric studies. Results Bonnin's cadaveric experiments showed that a rotating, axially loaded talus behaves as a wedge within the mortise, splitting the posterior tibial margin (the injury we now term a rotational pilon fracture) and he held that damage to the plafond, not the size of the fragment, determined the prognosis. Attention later shifted to the proportion of articular surface involved - a quantity poorly measured on radiographs and divorced from mechanism. CT has since reintroduced the mechanism in living patients: the Mason-Molloy classification describes three pathomechanical types that confirm and refine Bonnin's observations, and management has moved from size thresholds to classification-guided fixation. Conclusions Bonnin and Mason, two Hunterian Professors separated by more than half a century, performed essentially the same investigation with the tools available to them and reached the same conclusion. Recognising that the modern classification visualises a mechanism Bonnin had already inferred (rotation of a loaded talus) restores a continuity the wider literature has largely missed.

title: Epigallocatechin-3-gallate attenuates PAR-2-mediated inflammatory signaling and preserves markers of mitochondrial integrity in osteoarthritic chondrocytes.
authors: Patnaik R, Banerjee Y.
abstract: Epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), the principal catechin of green tea, exhibits broad anti-inflammatory properties; however, its effect on protease-activated receptor-2 (PAR-2)-mediated signaling in osteoarthritis (OA) has not been investigated. Here, we report that EGCG (5-10 µM) dose-dependently suppresses PAR-2 expression at both mRNA and protein levels in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated human chondrocytes derived from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. This upstream inhibition attenuated ERK1/2 phosphorylation (pERK/total ERK ratio reduced below basal levels at 10 µM) and produced concordant suppression of three functionally linked effector arms: (i) pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, MCP-1), with near-maximal inhibition at 10 µM and a saturation plateau at 20 µM; (ii) the SOX4-ADAMTS-5 catabolic axis (81.9% and 66.2% protein reduction, respectively); and (iii) RANK/RANKL surface expression. EGCG also restored mitochondrial membrane potential and biomass to near-homeostatic levels. Crucially, small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated PAR-2 silencing reduced LPS-induced TNF-α by ~38% and substantially blunted EGCG's incremental efficacy, supporting PAR-2 as a predominant, though not exclusive, mediator of EGCG's anti-inflammatory action. The effective concentrations employed are physiologically attainable through dietary green tea consumption, as documented by a comprehensive survey of EGCG content across 36 commercial varieties. These findings support PAR-2 as a candidate upstream target of EGCG in OA chondrocytes and suggest a mechanistic model involving PAR-2 → ERK1/2 → TNF-α/SOX4/ADAMTS-5, through which a dietary polyphenol exerts coordinated anti-inflammatory and anti-catabolic effects, while preserving structural and thermodynamic markers of mitochondrial integrity.

title: Emphysematous osteomyelitis of the lower extremity: Prevalence, imaging features, interobserver agreement and clinical outcomes in a 16-hospital cohort.
authors: Conlan M, Faunce W, Negatu D, Reeves A, Seykora T, Eutsler E, Lee M, Chen S.
abstract: Purpose To estimate emphysematous osteomyelitis (EO) observed prevalence, compare 3-month major adverse events (death or major amputation) between EO and nonemphysematous osteomyelitis (NEO), and assess interobserver agreement for key imaging features. Methods In this retrospective 16-hospital study, radiology-report text screening followed by manual report review identified CT and MRI examinations demonstrating lower-extremity osteomyelitis. EO was defined as intraosseous gas without direct bone-to-air communication. Forty-five EO cases met criteria, and 180 NEO cases were randomly sampled in a 4:1 ratio for prognostic comparison. Associations with 3-month major adverse events were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression. Three radiologists independently reviewed 90 cases (45 EO, 45 NEO) to assess interobserver agreement. Results Of the 1417 imaging examinations that identified lower-extremity osteomyelitis, 45 (3.2%) met the study's EO inclusion criteria. Major adverse events occurred within 3 months in 33.3% (15/45) of EO cases and 12.8% (23/180) of nonemphysematous osteomyelitis cases. EO (adjusted OR, 3.22; 95% CI, 1.46-7.12; p = .004) and peripheral artery disease (adjusted OR, 3.11; 95% CI, 1.38-7.03; p = .006) were independently associated with higher odds of death or major amputation within 3 months. Agreement for intraosseous gas was substantial on CT (κ = 0.71) and almost perfect on MRI (κ = 0.81). Conclusion EO is uncommon but associated with worse 3-month outcomes. Our findings support consideration of EO as a potential imaging marker of short-term adverse outcomes in patients with lower-extremity osteomyelitis.

title: Embedded incus into the external auditory canal following temporal bone fracture.
authors: Obeidat M, Sbeitan O, Obeidat GB, Mugdadi TH, Al-Mashagbah MMA.

title: Early (<3 months) versus late (≥3 months) periprosthetic femoral fractures after hip arthroplasty: fracture characteristics and treatment patterns.
authors: Qiu C, Zhang K, Wang Q, Zhang R, Li W.
abstract: Background To describe and compare injury context, fracture morphology, bone stock, and treatment patterns between periprosthetic femoral fractures (PFFs) occurring Methods We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients hospitalized for their first documented PFF episode after total hip arthroplasty or hemiarthroplasty at a tertiary orthopedic referral hospital from January 2021 through December 2025. Early PFF was defined as P values were interpreted descriptively, and absolute percentage-point differences with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported for selected binary contrasts. A 6-month cutoff was examined post hoc as a sensitivity analysis. Results Among 132 patients, 126 had a usable month-based interval; 23 (18.3%) had early PFF and 103 (81.7%) had late PFF. Low-energy injury was recorded in 23/23 (100.0%) early PFFs and 86/102 (84.3%) late PFFs, corresponding to an absolute difference of 15.7 percentage points (95% CI, 0.2-24.0). Vancouver B2/B3 fractures occurred in 8/23 (34.8%) versus 22/102 (21.6%) patients (absolute difference, 13.2 percentage points; 95% CI, -5.1-34.7). Surgery was performed in 21/23 (91.3%) versus 88/103 (85.4%), and ORIF was the most frequent treatment in both groups. At the 6-month cutoff, multiple fracture categories and treatment strategies remained represented in both timing groups. Conclusions In this cohort, a 3-month operational grouping suggested a difference in recorded injury context, while both timing groups included multiple fracture morphologies, bone-stock categories, and treatment strategies. Timing may provide useful contextual information at presentation but should be interpreted together with Vancouver classification, implant stability, bone stock, and patient condition. These observations require validation in larger cohorts with finer timing resolution.

title: Different osteoarthritis progression rates within early-stage knee osteoarthritis: a retrospective cohort study using machine learning cluster analysis from the osteoarthritis initiative database.
authors: Song JW, Kim SE, Ro DH.
abstract: Background Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a heterogeneous disease with varying progression rates among patients within the same severity grade. This study aimed to identify clinically interpretable radiographic phenotypes among knees with baseline Kellgren and Lawrence (KL) grade 2 osteoarthritis and to compare their 4-year radiographic progression patterns using baseline radiographic features, lifetime exercise patterns, and demographic characteristics. Methods Data of patients with baseline KL grade 2 from the Osteoarthritis Initiative database were retrieved. Unsupervised clustering was performed using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) for dimensionality reduction, followed by hierarchical density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (HDBSCAN) to identify distinct subgroups. The proportion of knees progressing to KL grade ≥ 3 within 4 years was compared between subgroups, followed by a survival analysis until knee replacement or progression to KL grade 4. Results A total of 1997 knees with a mean follow-up of 103.3 months (maximum, 108 months) were included. A total of seven subgroups were identified and classified into accelerated osteoarthritis progression (AOP) group and slow osteoarthritis progression (SOP) group according to whether their 4-year KL grade progression proportions were above or below the training-set average. In a supportive long-term survival analysis, the AOP group also showed significantly earlier progression to knee replacement or KL grade 4 than the SOP group (training set, P Conclusions Within baseline KL grade 2 knees, clinically interpretable radiographic phenotypes, including lateral JSN, medial JSN with subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte-dominant changes without JSN, and chondrocalcinosis-dominant patterns, were associated with different 4-year KL grade progression rates. These findings support viewing KL grade 2 knee OA as a heterogeneous radiographic stage that may be further stratified into phenotype-based subgroups with different short-term radiographic prognoses.

title: Arthroscopic autologous iliac crest cancellous bone grafting for Hepple stage V osteochondral lesions of the talus: a retrospective case series.
journal: Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research
authors: Zhang ZH, Xue C, Su CF, Gao SH, Oliva F, Maffulli N, Migliorini F, Feng SM.
abstract: Background Evidence regarding arthroscopic autologous iliac crest cancellous bone grafting for Hepple stage V osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLTs) remains limited. This study assessed short-term clinical outcomes, postoperative imaging findings, and perioperative characteristics of this technique. Methods This retrospective case series included 23 patients undergoing arthroscopic autologous iliac crest cancellous bone grafting between March 2020 and July 2024. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) demonstrated subchondral cystic changes in all lesions, which were classified as Hepple stage V OLTs. The primary outcome was the European Foot and Ankle Society (EFAS) score at final follow-up. Secondary outcomes included the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain score during walking, the American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society (AOFAS) score, Karlsson Ankle Functional Score (KAFS), 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36) pain domain score, Tegner score and ankle range of motion (ROM). Postoperative radiographs and available CT scans were reviewed to assess graft position and subchondral healing; MRI findings were also evaluated when available. Operative time, concomitant lateral ligament repair, and complications were documented. Paired comparisons were performed using the paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test, as appropriate after assessment of normality. Results Mean follow-up was 21.0 ± 8.7 months (median, 18.0 months; Q1-Q3, 13.0-24.0), and mean lesion area was 1.94 ± 0.38 cm 2 . Median operative time was 75.0 min (Q1-Q3, 67.5-86.0), and five patients underwent concomitant lateral ligament repair. The median EFAS score improved from 9.0 (Q1-Q3, 8.0-10.0) preoperatively to 19.0 (Q1-Q3, 18.0-20.0) at final follow-up (P Conclusions Arthroscopic autologous iliac crest cancellous bone grafting was associated with improvements in pain, function, and activity in patients with Hepple stage V OLTs at short-term follow-up. Postoperative CT demonstrated graft incorporation in all patients who underwent CT assessment. These preliminary findings support the feasibility of this technique for appropriately selected cystic lesions, although larger comparative studies with longer follow-up are warranted.

title: Arthroscopic Scapholunate Osseous Ligament Anchor-Based Round-Block Repair for Scapholunate Instability.
authors: de Villeneuve Bargemon JB, Goorens CK, Merlini L, Audiffret L.
abstract: Scapholunate instability remains difficult to treat, particularly in lesions involving detachment of the dorsal intercarpal ligament from the scaphoid. We describe the Scapholunate Osseous Ligament Anchor-based Round-block technique, an arthroscopic anchor-based repair designed to reinsert and retension the dorsal capsuloligamentous complex. The procedure allows dynamic assessment of reduction and may be combined with additional palmar stabilization when needed. This modular technique may represent a useful arthroscopic option for selected patterns of scapholunate instability.

title: Arthroscopic Biologic Meniscal Root Repair With Iliotibial Band Autograft Augmentation.
authors: Piontek T, Rubczak S, Bulinski P, Naczk J, Głowacki J, Bąbik B, Banach A.
abstract: This paper presents a description of a surgical technique-a modified Henning-Piontek procedure-used for meniscal root salvage. The method is intended for difficult, chronic injuries with loss of continuity of the meniscal root. Such cases would most often result in total or subtotal meniscectomy, which, as is well known, significantly accelerates the degenerative changes in the knee. This technique aligns with the "save the meniscus" approach practiced and promoted by the authors. It involves the use of an iliotibial band graft to create a bridge between the damaged meniscus and the anatomical attachment site of the meniscal root. This enables anatomical repair of the meniscal root, facilitates healing, and preserves the natural structure of the joint.

title: Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion Versus Cervical Disc Arthroplasty for Cervical Degenerative Disc Disease: Alarming Rates of Bias.
authors: Davood J, Avetisian H, Rusu D, Napolitano M, Khorsandi J, Prasad A, Borna J, Noorvash J, Kahen N, Lindgren A, Karakash WJ, Mason TW, Wang JC, Hah RJ, Alluri RK.
abstract: Study DesignCross-Sectional.ObjectivesWhether cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA) or anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) yields better outcomes in cervical degenerative disc disease remains unsettled, and clinicians turn to evidence syntheses for guidance. These syntheses, however, may contain spin, a reporting bias that presents an intervention as more effective or safer than the data support. This study sought to characterize how often spin appears in reviews comparing ACDF and CDA, which forms it takes, and whether methodological quality, journal impact factor, or citation rate predicts spin outcomes.MethodsPubMed, Web of Science, and Embase were searched for systematic reviews and meta-analyses directly comparing ACDF and CDA. Each article was assessed for spin using the Yavchitz classification system and for methodological quality (AMSTAR-2). Logistic and Poisson regression assessed whether study AMSTAR-2 rating, journal impact factor, and yearly citations predicted spin outcomes.Results77 articles were included. Spin was identified in 49 (63.6%); all spin-positive reviews favored CDA. The most frequent types were claiming benefit despite high risk of bias (39.0%), overemphasis on efficacy (26.0%), and selective safety reporting (15.6%). AMSTAR-2 ratings were poor: 83.1% were critically low, 15.6% low, and 1.3% high. Lower AMSTAR-2 rating independently predicted spin (OR 0.182, 95% CI 0.048-0.689, p = 0.012); impact factor and citations did not.ConclusionsSpin is prevalent in reviews comparing CDA with ACDF and uniformly favors CDA. Greater methodological rigor and balanced reporting are needed for evidence syntheses to reliably inform clinical decisions.

title: All-Inside Posterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using Achilles Allograft and Suture Tape Augmentation.
authors: Md Yusoff BAH, Zhafri A, Ramlan MKR, Nik Kamaruzman NKA, Omar A, Mohamad N, Azwan Aziz M.
abstract: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) reconstruction is challenged by graft elongation and delayed biological integration, often necessitating slow rehabilitation and carrying a risk of arthrofibrosis. This technical report describes an all-inside technique augmented with the modified internal bracing to address these limitations. The technique involves integrating a FiberTape within a quadrupled Achilles tendon allograft, creating a load-sharing composite. An all-inside, retrograde socket method was used for anatomic PCL reconstruction in the knee, with suspensory fixation on both femur and tibia. The graft-tape construct was simultaneously tensioned. The technique provides immediate biomechanical stability by mitigating graft micromotion, elongation, and tunnel abrasion. By closely replicating native PCL stiffness, this construct facilitates an accelerated, protective rehabilitation protocol focused on early motion and quadriceps activation, thereby aiming to reduce failure rates and postoperative stiffness. This method represents a synergistic evolution in PCL reconstruction, combining synthetic reinforcement with biological healing.

title: Access to pharmacological management for osteoporosis by older people with hip fractures in long-term care: A nationwide cross-sectional study.
authors: Inacio MC, Cuthbert AR, Fernando RL, Caughey G, Eshetie T, Crotty M.
abstract: Objectives To examine whether individuals who had a hip fracture while accessing long-term care (LTC) in a facility or at home, or while waiting for LTC, received recommended pharmacological management for osteoporosis before and in the year after fracture. Design A population-based cross-sectional study using the National Historical Cohort of the Registry of Senior Australians. Setting and participants Older people hospitalised with a hip fracture while accessing or waiting for facility or home-based LTC in Australia between 01/01/2012 and 31/12/2018. Methods Utilisation of pharmacological management for osteoporosis (i.e., bisphosphonates, denosumab, teriparatide, strontium) before and one year after hip fracture was examined using linked pharmaceutical, hospital, and aged care data. Logistic regression models examined the associations between individual and LTC setting characteristics and accessing pharmacological management in the year after fracture. Results Of the 52,233 (71.3% female, 87.7 median age) hip fractures that occurred during the study period, 58.3% (n = 30,441) were in individuals receiving facility-based LTC, 14.6% (n = 7603) were receiving home-based LTC, and 27.2% (n = 14,189) were waiting for LTC. Forty three percent (N = 22,622 of 52,233) had received pharmacological management for osteoporosis at any time prior to hip fracture and 21% received it in the previous year. One-year post fracture, 39% of the 30,768 individuals who were still alive had received pharmacological management for osteoporosis. Older age, male gender, having dementia, receiving facility-based LTC, and not receiving pharmacological management prior to fracture were associated with lower receipt of pharmacological management after fracture. Conclusions and recommendations These results highlight that the use of pharmacological management for osteoporosis for older people experiencing a hip fracture while in or waiting for LTC remains low, despite clinical guideline recommendations. Brief summary Of the 52,233 older Australians who had a hip fracture while receiving or waiting for long-term care between 2012 and 2018, 43% had received pharmacological management for osteoporosis at any time prior to fracture. In the year after fracture, 39% of the 30,768 individuals who were still alive received pharmacological management for osteoporosis. These national estimates highlight that access to pharmacolocical management for osteoporosis in long-term care recipients following hip fracture remains low, despite clinical guideline recommendations.

title: Using double-bundle Achilles tendon-bone allograft for reconstruction of compound loss of lateral malleolus and lateral ankle ligaments: A rare case report.
authors: Chiu H, Chen JH.
abstract: Rationale Composite defects of the lateral ankle, involving bone loss, ligament disruption, and soft tissue compromise, cause profound mechanical instability and are difficult to reconstruct with techniques that address bone or ligaments alone. Patient concerns We report a 26-year-old woman who presented with progressive right ankle pain, recurrent giving-way, and peroneal tendon subluxation 7 years after a high-energy crush injury that required flap coverage. Diagnoses Lateral malleolar loss with a distal fibular bony defect measuring approximately 5 × 3 × 2 cm and chronic varus instability; complete anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) and calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) rupture; and peroneal tendon dislocation were confirmed by stress radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging. Interventions Single-stage reconstruction with a cryopreserved Achilles tendon-bone allograft. The calcaneal bone block was contoured and fixed to the fibular stump with a 4.5-mm cannulated screw to reconstitute the lateral malleolus. The tendon was split into 2 bundles (7 mm × 30 mm for the ATFL and 7 mm × 40 mm for the CFL) for anatomic ATFL and CFL reconstruction and secured with interference screws at the talar and calcaneal footprints. The peroneal tendons were reduced after bony restoration. Postoperative rehabilitation used an Aircast® brace with non-weight-bearing ambulation for the first 3 weeks, partial weight-bearing from week 3, full weight-bearing by week 6, and brace discontinuation at week 12. Outcomes At the final follow-up of 16 months, the patient ambulated pain-free with a stable ankle. Radiographs demonstrated successful incorporation of the bone allograft, and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed intact ATFL/CFL grafts with maintained peroneal tendon reduction. Functional scores were Karlsson-Peterson 87 and American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society ankle-hindfoot 90. Lessons A double-bundle Achilles tendon-bone allograft enables simultaneous reconstruction of lateral malleolar bone and lateral ligaments, avoiding donor-site morbidity and achieving durable stability in complex, previously reconstructed ankles. This approach should be considered when both osseous and ligamentous deficits coexist.

title: Ultrasound-guided needling release combined with platelet-rich plasma injection for refractory heel pain: A case report.
authors: Chen B, Yang Y, Mao F.
abstract: Refractory heel pain is a clinically challenging condition of multifactorial origin, often complicating both diagnosis and treatment. No standard therapy exists for refractory heel pain, and clinical experience is limited. We report the efficacy of ultrasound-guided needling release of calcific deposits combined with autologous platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection and systematic rehabilitation in a patient with refractory heel pain. A 57-year-old self-employed female patient presented with a 3-year history of recurrent redness, swelling, and pain in the right heel, with symptoms worsening after activity. In the month prior to admission, pain had progressively worsened, limiting her ability to stand, walk, and perform daily activities. Refractory right heel pain (chronic calcifying Achilles tendinitis, Achilles tendinopathy, plantar fasciitis with bone spur formation). The procedure involved ultrasound-guided fenestration and disruption of calcifications at the Achilles tendon insertion, followed by intralesional PRP injection and a 6-month staged rehabilitation program. At 1 week postoperatively, Visual Analog Scale (VAS) decreased to 3, and the patient could walk independently. At 1 month, VAS was 2, and she returned to work and daily activities. At 3 months, VAS was 1, American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society score improved to 90, and pain was largely resolved. The favorable outcome persisted at 6-month follow-up. The combination of ultrasound-guided precise lesion management, PRP-based biological repair, and systematic rehabilitation offers a minimally invasive, safe, and effective strategy for refractory heel pain, serving as a valuable clinical reference for similar cases.

title: Transperineal ultrasound evaluation of pelvic floor structure after different modes of delivery and its predictive value for postpartum rehabilitation outcomes.
authors: Liu C, Wang T.
abstract: This study aimed to investigate the impact of different modes of delivery on pelvic floor structure in primiparous women and to evaluate the predictive value of transperineal ultrasound parameters for poor pelvic floor muscle strength at 6 to 12 months postpartum. Clinical data of 214 primiparous women who delivered at our hospital from May 2024 to December 2025 were retrospectively collected, including 165 in the vaginal delivery group and 49 in the cesarean section group. Pelvic floor ultrasound parameters at 6 to 8 weeks postpartum were compared between groups. The primary outcome was poor pelvic floor muscle strength at 6 to 12 months postpartum, defined as an Oxford grade ≤ 3. Logistic regression analysis was used to identify associated ultrasound predictors, and receiver operating characteristic curves were used to evaluate predictive performance. Because only 12 poor-strength events occurred in the cesarean section group, multivariable results in that subgroup were considered exploratory. The vaginal delivery group showed significantly greater bladder neck mobility (BNM), urethral rotation angle, levator ani hiatus area, and incidence of cystocele compared with the cesarean section group (P < .05). Poor pelvic floor muscle strength was also more frequent in the vaginal delivery group (43.6% vs 24.5%, P = .015). In the vaginal delivery group, BNM (odds ratio [OR] = 1.38), levator ani hiatus area during Valsalva maneuver (OR = 1.20), and levator ani avulsion (OR = 3.15) were independently associated with poor pelvic floor muscle strength (P < .01). In the exploratory cesarean section subgroup analysis, only BNM reached statistical significance (OR = 1.52, P = .040), with imprecise estimates due to the small number of outcome events. The combined model in the vaginal delivery group achieved an area under the curve of 0.86, with a sensitivity of 81.9% and a specificity of 78.5%. Vaginal delivery was associated with more pronounced short-term pelvic floor structural changes than cesarean section. Early postpartum transperineal ultrasound parameters showed potential for risk stratification of subsequent poor pelvic floor muscle strength after vaginal delivery; however, prospective multicenter studies with external validation are required before routine screening or treatment decisions based on the model can be recommended.

title: Total hip arthroplasty improves global sagittal and coronal spinal imbalance and spinopelvic mobility : a prospective cohort study.
authors: Leung TKC, Chan PK, Cheung A, Luk MH, Lau LCM, Cheung WK, Chiu KY, Fu H.
abstract: Aims The impact of total hip arthroplasty (THA) on global spinal alignment is under-reported. This study prospectively evaluates the effect of THA on coronal and sagittal global spinal balance and spinopelvic kinematics using dynamic whole-body EOS radiographs. Methods We prospectively studied 163 patients (62 male, 101 female; mean age 68.4 years (SD 9.1)) undergoing primary unilateral THA for end-stage osteoarthritis. Full-body EOS images were acquired preoperatively and at a six-month follow-up in standing, relaxed-seated, and deep-seated postures. The primary outcome was change in sagittal vertical axis (SVA). Secondary outcomes included changes in pelvic tilt (PT), sacral slope (SS), proximal femoral angle (PFA), and coronal parameters (C7-central sacral vertical line (C7-CSVL), limb length discrepancy (LLD), and pelvic obliquity (PO)). Preoperative SVA > 50 mm defined sagittal imbalance; C7-CSVL > 20 mm defined coronal imbalance. Statistical analysis employed paired non-parametric tests and multivariate regression. Results In the 58 patients with preoperative sagittal imbalance (SVA > 50 mm), mean SVA improved significantly from 77.9 mm (SD 24.4) to 59.9 mm (SD 36.1; p Conclusion THA improves global sagittal and coronal spinal imbalance, restoring spinopelvic mobility by increasing hip flexion and reducing compensatory pelvic tilt. These dynamic postoperative changes challenge the static assumptions underpinning current hip-spine classifications. Preoperative and postoperative analysis of global dynamic spinopelvic balance and mobility are crucial for managing hip-spine syndrome.

title: The diagnostic value of quantitative 99mTc-MDP SPECT/CT fusion imaging in the differential diagnosis of spinal infections.
authors: Wang J, Wang J, Jia Y, Shi Z, Ma P, Liu H, Zhao Q, Niu N.
abstract: Aims To investigate the value of quantitative 99m Tc-labelled methylene diphosphonate ( 99m Tc-MDP) single-photon emission CT (SPECT)/CT fusion imaging in the differential diagnosis of spinal infections. Methods A total of 90 patients with confirmed spinal infections, prior to any clinical treatment, underwent 99m Tc-MDP SPECT/CT fusion imaging. The maximum, mean, and minimum standardized uptake values (SUVmax, SUVmean, SUVmin), bone metabolic volume (MBV), total bone uptake (TBU), and CT Hounsfield unit (HU) values were measured in both affected and normal vertebrae. Multidimensional comparisons of SPECT/CT parameters were performed, including within-subject analyses comparing affected and adjacent normal vertebrae in the same infection type, as well as inter-group comparisons across different types of spinal infections. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis to determine the area under the curve (AUC) and optimal cut-off values, while the linear associations between quantitative SPECT/CT parameters of affected vertebrae and laboratory biomarkers were evaluated. Results The median SUVmax of affected vertebrae in pyogenic spondylitis (PS) was 21.17 (IQR 17.19 to 22.01), significantly higher than that observed in spinal tuberculosis (STB) (17.57 (IQR 15.02 to 18.98)) and brucellar spondylitis (BS) (15.63 (IQR 14.28 to 16.90)). SUVmax demonstrated strong diagnostic performance in differentiating PS from BS, with an AUC of 0.852, yielding 95.0% sensitivity and 71.7% specificity at an optimal cut-off value of 18.51. Similarly, CT HU values showed moderate discriminative ability for distinguishing BS from STB, achieving an AUC of 0.741, with 80.0% sensitivity and 65.0% specificity at a cut-off of 706 HU. Furthermore, a strong positive correlation was observed between SUVmax and CT HU values across all three infection groups. In addition, SUVmax exhibited a significant positive correlation with serum inflammatory markers in patients with PS. Conclusion Quantitative 99m Tc-MDP SPECT/CT fusion imaging enables objective assessment of spinal infection severity, thereby facilitating the differential diagnosis of distinct aetiological types of spondylitis.

title: Temporal Effects on Intraoperative Bacterial Contamination of Surgical Gloves in Noninfection Orthopaedic Trauma Cases.
authors: Amirhekmat A, Shimabukuro J, Bittencourt C, Beyer RS, Learned JR, Scolaro JA, Lim PK.
abstract: Objectives Surgical site infections (SSIs) are among the most serious complications in orthopaedic trauma surgery, contributing to patient morbidity, mortality, and substantial financial costs. With direct inoculation from intraoperative bacterial contamination being a large contributor to these infections, the temporal dynamics of intraoperative bacterial colonization on surgical gloves in orthopaedic trauma cases was investigated. Methods Surgical glove bacterial cultures were taken by firmly pressing the operating room staff member's gloved fingertips onto a sheep's blood agar plate. Cases, without known preexisting infection, were chosen from a single level 1 trauma center at random between 2023 and 2025. Samples were obtained at 2 intraoperative time points: (1) immediately after draping and (2) after implant placement but before final irrigation. These samples were compared with negative controls of freshly donned, but unused sterile gloves. Glove imprints were then incubated for 2 weeks, and bacterial isolates were identified using MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry. Results Of 276 total gloves sampled, 70 (25.4% 70/138) demonstrated bacterial growth, compared with 0 controls (0%, 0/138 P Conclusions Intraoperative surgical gloves demonstrated high rates of bacterial contamination, particularly with longer procedure times. Routine glove changes after draping, after final implant placement, and after >75 minutes of operating time may be a simple, low-cost strategy to reduce potential SSI risk. Level of evidence Prognostic Level IV. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

title: Technical Tricks to Improve Iliosacral Screw Safety Using Three-dimensional Computed Tomography Imaging.
authors: Zuelzer DA, Routt MLC.
abstract: Summary This technical note describes a method used to facilitate iliosacral screw fixation with three-dimensional (3D) computed tomography (CT) imaging. Preoperative pelvis CT scans were used to generate 3D reconstructions, which were then manipulated into inlet and outlet orientations. The inlet position for S1 was achieved when the anterior cortex of the S1 body became superimposed on itself; the outlet position was when the S1 nerve root tunnel was viewed en face. On the fluoroscopic inlet view of S1, multiple cortical densities were often visible and could be difficult to distinguish as S1 versus other sacral segments. 3D CT helped distinguish the position and shape of the anterior cortical limit of S1 by referencing preoperative 3D CT inlet images that were reproduced intraoperatively on fluoroscopy using the appearance of the anterior pelvic ring and the relative obliquity of the obturator foramen. This technique was especially valuable in the setting of common posterior pelvic anatomic variations-including asymmetry, degenerative osteophytes, severe sacral slope, and dramatic cortical recesses of the upper sacral segment. These variations were often difficult to anticipate with conventional plain film or standard CT imaging alone, underscoring the potential clinical utility of this technique.

title: Surgical management and short-term clinical and radiological outcomes in patients with cervical spondylodiscitis: A single-center retrospective study.
authors: Noh J, Lee S, Oh Y, Eun J.
abstract: Cervical spondylodiscitis (CSD) is a rare but increasingly prevalent spinal infection that may cause rapid neurological deterioration because of its nonspecific clinical presentation. This study aimed to evaluate the short-term clinical and radiological outcomes of surgically treated CSD and to explore whether the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-to-surgery interval was associated with postoperative neurological recovery. This retrospective single-center cohort study included 25 consecutive patients who underwent surgical management for CSD between January 2016 and December 2025. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the visual analogue scale and modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score. Radiological outcomes were evaluated by measuring the local cervical kyphosis angle. Patients were stratified according to the MRI-to-surgery interval (≤24 vs >24 hours). Surgical treatment significantly improved pain, neurological function, inflammatory markers, and cervical sagittal alignment. Mean visual analogue scale scores decreased from 6.0 to 3.4 (P 24 hours after MRI acquisition (P = .518); however, the timing analysis was limited by the small subgroup sizes and baseline differences in neurological status. Surgical management of CSD was associated with significant short-term clinical and radiological improvement. Although postoperative outcomes did not differ significantly according to the MRI-to-surgery interval, these findings should not be interpreted as supporting delayed surgery once surgical indications are established.

title: Suprascapular nerve block with versus without ultrasound-guided T2 erector spinae plane block for chronic shoulder pain: A retrospective comparative study.
authors: Yu S, Nam S, Lee K, Kim JI, Kim J.
abstract: Suprascapular nerve block (SSNB) is widely used for chronic shoulder pain but may provide suboptimal analgesia because of incomplete coverage of the shoulder's sensory innervation. High thoracic (T2) erector spinae plane block (ESPB) provides broad craniocaudal spread and may complement SSNB. This study evaluated whether SSNB with T2 ESPB was associated with improved clinical outcomes compared with SSNB without T2 ESPB in patients with chronic, conservative-refractory shoulder pain. This retrospective comparative study included 84 adult patients with chronic shoulder pain lasting at least 3 months despite conservative treatment at a tertiary academic hospital. Patients underwent ultrasound-guided SSNB without T2 ESPB (n = 57) or SSNB with T2 ESPB (n = 27). The primary outcome was the proportion of responders, defined as achieving a ≥30% reduction in numeric rating scale (NRS) pain score at 4 weeks. Secondary outcomes included NRS pain score at 4 weeks, patient global impression of change (PGIC), and procedure-related adverse events. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to adjust for potential confounders. At 4 weeks, the responder rate was higher in the SSNB with T2 ESPB group than in the SSNB without T2 ESPB group (59.3% vs 17.5%, P < .001). The combined group also had a lower mean NRS pain score (3.9 ± 2.8 vs 5.2 ± 2.6, P = .049) and higher PGIC scores (median [IQR], 4 [4-5] vs 4 [3-4]; P = .010). In multivariable analysis, SSNB with T2 ESPB remained associated with a positive response (OR 5.931, 95% confidence interval: 2.01-17.50, P = .001). No procedure-related adverse events were identified. SSNB with T2 ESPB was associated with better short-term clinical outcomes than SSNB alone in patients with chronic shoulder pain. Prospective randomized, dose-matched studies are needed to confirm these findings and clarify the specific contribution of T2 ESPB.

title: Supervised physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises provide limited additional benefit at 24 months in braced adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis: a randomized trial.
authors: Zhang X, Liang M, Huang Y, Lin B, Lin Y, Yang Y, Wang X, Huang X, Liao B.
abstract: Aims Physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises (PSSE) are used as an adjunct to bracing in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS), although evidence for their long-term benefit remains limited. This randomized trial assessed whether supervised PSSE provide clinically important radiological and patient-reported benefits compared with self-directed exercise in patients with AIS undergoing brace treatment. Methods Patients with AIS (major Cobb angle 25° to 45°; Risser grade 0 to 2) were recruited from a tertiary scoliosis centre between December 2018 and December 2022. Patients were randomized to supervised Schroth-based PSSE, consisting of physiotherapist-led sessions plus daily home exercises, or to self-directed general exercise. The co-primary outcomes were change in major Cobb angle and change in health-related quality of life measured using the Chinese Brace Questionnaire-34. A 5° between-group difference in Cobb angle was prespecified as the minimal clinically important difference (MCID). To provide a clinically anchored interpretation, 24-month radiological outcomes were classified as improved (> 5° decrease), stable (-5° to +5°), or worsened (> 5° increase), and compared using adjusted ordinal logistic regression in intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol (PP) analyses. Results Supervised PSSE resulted in a greater reduction in major Cobb angle than self-directed exercise at 24 months (adjusted between-group difference -3.23° (95% CI -3.51 to -2.96); p Conclusion Supervised PSSE provided a statistically significant but clinically modest radiological benefit over self-directed exercise. This did not translate into a higher likelihood of clinically meaningful radiological improvement. No sustained clinically meaningful quality-of-life benefit was shown.

title: Successful treatment of knee osteoarthritis pain with alcohol neurolysis of genicular nerves based on new anatomical landmark: A case report.
authors: Ahn SH, Boudier-Revéret M, Lee EC, Doan HN, Chang MC.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a major cause of chronic knee pain and disability. Genicular nerve neurolysis is a minimally invasive treatment option for patients whose pain persists despite conventional therapies. However, landmark-guided genicular nerve neurolysis can miss some articular branches. We report a patient with persistent knee OA pain who was successfully treated with alcohol neurolysis of the genicular nerves using newly proposed landmarks. A 77-year-old man continued to have right-knee pain (Numeric Rating Scale [NRS] 7) despite an intra-articular steroid injection. The patient was diagnosed with severe knee OA. He underwent fluoroscopy-guided alcohol neurolysis of the superolateral, superomedial, and inferomedial genicular nerves using 50% alcohol mixed with 2% lidocaine; needle placement was adjusted posteriorly according to newly proposed landmarks derived from cadaveric anatomy. The knee pain decreased to NRS 3 at 1, 3, and 6 months after the procedure without complications. This case shows that genicular nerve alcohol neurolysis, with posteriorly adjusted new landmarks, can markedly reduce knee OA pain, highlighting its potential clinical utility.

title: Sit-to-stand performance and gait symmetry in older adults with sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity: A cross-sectional comparative study of lower limb motor function.
authors: Li Z, Liu Y, Liu N.
abstract: Sarcopenic obesity (SO), characterized by the concurrent presence of diminished muscle mass and excessive adiposity, poses an increased risk to physical function, balance, and fall susceptibility in older adults. Although sarcopenia alone has been linked to mobility impairments, the specific effects of elevated body fat on sit-to-stand (STS) performance and gait symmetry have not been thoroughly investigated.
