Fifteen CAI(23.5 ± 2.9 years, 11 M/4F), fifteen coper(24.1 ± 3.4 years, 12 M/3F) and fifteen healthy participants(25.5 ± 3.5 years, 11 M/4F) performed single-leg drop landings from 30 cm. Total centre of pressure movement during 1-second and 3-second(TOTEX 1s &TOTEX 3s ), mediolateral sway distance(D ML ), peak vertical GRF(peak vGRF) and root-mean-square of mediolateral GRF in the first 0.4 s(RMS_ML_0.4) were recorded via force plate. Surface electromyography recorded muscle activity 200 ms before landing among tibialis anterior(TA), peroneus longus(PL) and gastrocnemius lateralis(GL). Pre-activation timing was calculated using the Teager-Kaiser energy operator(TKEO). Statistical analysis involved one-way ANOVA(α = 0.05) and Tukey post-hoc testing. Compared to healthy participants, CAI individuals displayed earlier TA(270 ± 73 ms vs. 85 ± 53 ms, p ML (55.6 ± 15.7 mm vs. 39.5 ± 9.0 mm, p ML (42.7 ± 7.0 mm vs. 55.6 ± 15.7 mm, p = 0.008) compared to CAI individuals. CAI exhibited postural control deficits and ineffective feedforward control, shown by lower PL activity despite early pre-activation. Rate of force production training is advised. Increased GL activation may serve as a compensatory response in copers after initial ankle sprain.

title: Embedding muscle attachment sites in statistical shape models can estimate hip muscle attachment sites in patients with hip dysplasia.
authors: Kim N, Wissman MM, Harris MD, Besier T.
abstract: Manual selection of muscle attachment points on musculoskeletal models is time-consuming and susceptible to human error. Statistical shape modelling can accurately predict bone morphology and has the potential to predict regional muscle attachment sites. This study evaluated the variability of manually selected muscle attachment points across a cohort of 20 hip dysplasia patients. Attachment points were compared against the regional attachment sites embedded in a shape model (using a SOMSO anatomical model). Variability of manually selected points was calculated using Euclidean distances between points. Muscle segmentations from each individual were projected onto the surface bone of a shape model and compared to the SOMSO-embedded muscle regions using a Dice Score. Manually selected muscle attachment points varied 4 to 5 mm across all muscles on both the femur and pelvis. Muscles that showed high overlap of regional attachment areas across individuals demonstrated strong agreement with the SOMSO-embedded regions of the shape model. These findings suggest that embedding muscle attachment footprints within a statistical shape model can predict muscle attachment sites within the variability observed from manually selected points. Therefore, this approach can provide a rapid and robust approach to identify patient-specific muscle attachments sites.

title: Development and validation of a model using thoracic vertebrae data from low-dose CT scans for detecting AI-QCT-defined lumbar osteoporosis.
authors: Zhang Y, Rong C, Zhang Y, Wang Z, Xiao H, Chen J, Liang Y, Yang X, Xie W.
abstract: Despite evidence supporting opportunistic lumbar osteoporosis screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT), a clinically deployable screening strategy is lacking. This study aimed to develop and validate a model using thoracic bone mineral density (BMD) from LDCT for opportunistic screening. This multi-center, cross-sectional study included 18,298 adults who underwent LDCT with coverage from T1 to L2 at 134 Chinese health check-up centers. Outcome was defined as "artificial intelligence quantitative computed tomography (AI-QCT) defined lumbar osteoporosis" based on a mean L1-L2 BMD 3 by phantom-less AI-QCT system. Five machine learning models were trained on T1-T12 BMD (n = 11,065) and evaluated internally (n = 4743) and externally (n = 2490). Performance metrics included accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, Brier score, F1 score and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC). AI-QCT-defined lumbar osteoporosis was present in 1730 (9.5%) participants. Higher thoracic BMD was inversely associated with the AI-QCT-defined lumbar osteoporosis. T12 exhibited the strongest association: each 1 mg/cm 3 increment reduced odds by 21.9% (OR: 0.781, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.769, 0.793, P < 0.001). Logistic regression was selected as the final model. In external validation, it achieved an AUC of 0.993 (95% CI: 0.991, 0.996), AUPRC of 0.922 (95% CI: 0.887, 0.951), F1 score (0.813), sensitivity (0.975), and specificity (0.963). AI-QCT-derived thoracic BMD showed potential for identifying AI-QCT-defined lumbar osteoporosis. Integrating phantomless AI-QCT into lung cancer screening may enable large-scale opportunistic screening, but prospective validation against independent standards is required.

title: Construction of a quality evaluation index system for waterless surgical hand antisepsis in operating rooms.
authors: Yang S, Yuan X, Yin X, Zhou W, Zhou H, Miao L, Zhang G, Zhang X.
abstract: Objective To develop and obtain expert consensus on a quality evaluation index system for waterless surgical hand antisepsis in operating rooms and to assign hierarchical weights to the finalized indicators. Methods Guided by the Donabedian structure-process-outcome model, candidate indicators were generated through a structured literature review and semi-structured interviews. A three-round expert consultation was conducted: Rounds 1 and 2 were used to screen and refine indicators, and Round 3 was used for AHP-based pairwise weighting. Twenty-two eligible experts received the Round-1 questionnaire; 20 returned valid questionnaires and constituted the panel retained for Rounds 2 and 3, in which all 20 responded. Expert authority was assessed using Cr = (Ca + Cs)/2. In Round 3, individual expert authority coefficients were normalized to obtain expert-specific weights, and pairwise judgments were aggregated using a weighted geometric mean before AHP weight calculation and consistency testing. Results The valid response rates were 90.9% (20/22), 100% (20/20), and 100% (20/20) in Rounds 1, 2, and 3, respectively. The panel mean expert authority coefficients (Cr) were 0.883, 0.895, and 0.900. Kendall's coefficients of concordance for the two indicator-screening rounds were 0.242 and 0.334, respectively (both P Conclusion This study produced a consensus-based and hierarchically weighted quality evaluation index system for waterless surgical hand antisepsis. The framework may support standardized quality assessment and future quality-improvement work; however, the present study establishes expert consensus and relative priorities rather than clinical effectiveness, psychometric reliability, or causal effects. Multicenter clinical validation is required before broad implementation.

title: Comparative Effectiveness of Intravenous, Oral, and Topical Tranexamic Acid in Elective Spine Surgery: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
authors: Hammadeh BM, Sabet CJ, Al-Qunbar A, Sabbah L, Mohammad AK, Hasan Z, Kikhia A, Al-Barbarawi MK.
abstract: Study DesignSystematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis.ObjectiveTo compare the efficacy and safety of intravenous (IV), oral, topical, and combined IV+topical tranexamic acid (TXA) in reducing perioperative bleeding and transfusion requirements in elective spine surgery, and to identify the optimal administration route.MethodsWe searched Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, and CENTRAL from inception to February 20, 2026, for RCTs evaluating TXA routes in elective spine procedures. A Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis was performed. Primary outcomes were length of stay (LOS), blood loss, and drainage volume; secondary outcomes included hemoglobin levels, operative time, complications, transfusion requirements, and coagulation parameters. Treatment rankings were estimated using Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking Curve (SUCRA). Trial sequential analysis (TSA) assessed evidence robustness.ResultsTwenty-five randomized controlled trials were included. Combined IV+topical TXA ranked highest for reducing LOS (SUCRA 97.1%; mean difference -2.46 days vs. control, 95% CrI -4.15 to -0.81), intraoperative blood loss (SUCRA 83.9%; MD -122.8 mL, 95% CrI -202.2 to -43.6), postoperative day 1 hemoglobin preservation (SUCRA 96.5%; MD +0.99 g/dL, 95% CrI 0.43-1.57), and drainage volume (SUCRA 83.4%; MD -191.3 mL, 95% CrI -311.6 to -74.8). Oral TXA ranked first for total blood loss (SUCRA 83.8%; MD -421.2 mL, 95% CrI -691.9 to -156.6), closely followed by combined IV+topical TXA (SUCRA 82.2%). No route significantly increased complications or adversely affected coagulation. TSA suggested insufficient evidence for definitive conclusions on several outcomes.ConclusionsCombined IV+topical TXA ranked highest for reducing hospital stay, intraoperative blood loss, and drainage volume in elective spine surgery, and no route was associated with a detected increase in reported complications. These findings suggest that combined IV+topical TXA is a promising option; however, TSA indicated that the available evidence is insufficient to establish definitive route superiority or safety, and further high-quality trials are needed.

title: Clinical decision-making for decompression-level selection in multilevel degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis: a retrospective cohort study.
authors: Long Y, Li L, Zhong Y, Li C, Yang S, Wang G, Sun H, Si J, Li J, Zhang Y.
abstract: Purpose To characterise changes in decompression-level selection during sequential preoperative assessment in patients with multilevel degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis (DLSS) and to describe postoperative outcomes and subsequent events involving initially untreated candidate levels. Methods This retrospective single-centre cohort included 168 patients with two to four MRI-defined candidate levels who underwent endoscopic decompression. Planned decompression levels were reconstructed before walking load testing (WLT), after WLT, after selective nerve root block (SNRB) when performed, and at the final preoperative assessment. Postoperative clinical outcomes and subsequent events involving initially untreated candidate levels were recorded during 24 months of follow-up. Results Planned level sets changed after WLT in 72/168 patients (42.9%), and final plans differed from initial imaging-informed plans in 87/168 patients (51.8%). Among 55 patients undergoing SNRB, post-WLT plans were modified in 22 (40.0%). All final planned levels were decompressed. At 24 months, 143 patients (85.1%) completed follow-up, with a model-estimated 38.44-point improvement in the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI); 123/143 (86.0%) achieved the ODI threshold for patient acceptable symptom state (PASS). Among 231 initially untreated candidate levels, five underwent delayed decompression, with a 24-month Kaplan-Meier estimate of 2.6% (95% CI 1.1-6.0). Conclusion Sequential incorporation of imaging, functional assessment, and selective diagnostic procedures was associated with changes in planned decompression levels in patients with multilevel DLSS. This study describes surgical decision-making and the subsequent clinical course of initially untreated candidate levels after selective decompression planning.

title: Care-Need Level Worsening After Hip Fracture Surgery in Kyoto, Japan: Population-Based Cohort Study.
journal: Journal of the American Medical Directors Association
authors: Sasaki K, Takahashi Y, Nishikawa Y, Toyama M, Kohno A, Sakai M, Ueshima H, Shimamoto T, Tateyama Y, Kato G, Iwami T, Nakayama T.
abstract: Objectives To describe 3-year transitions of care-need level after hip fracture surgery and identify factors associated with subsequent nonfatal worsening among day-180 survivors. Design Retrospective cohort study using linked administrative medical and long-term care insurance claims. Setting and participants Adults aged ≥75 years in Kyoto City, Japan, who underwent hip fracture surgery between 2013 and 2018. The day-180 landmark cohort included 6556 patients who survived to day 180 and were not certified as care-need level 5 before surgery or at the landmark. Methods Follow-up started at day 180. The primary estimand was subsequent nonfatal care-need level worsening among patients alive and still at risk at the landmark; death after the landmark was treated as a competing event. We estimated cumulative incidence functions and Fine-Gray models with covariate-by-log-time interactions. Supplementary analyses examined a death-inclusive composite end point and alternative landmarks. Results The cumulative incidence of worsening was 10.6% at 12 months, 28.3% at 24 months, and 37.4% at 36 months after surgery. Longer initial claims-based rehabilitation continuity during the postoperative 6 months was associated with a lower incidence of subsequent nonfatal worsening (adjusted subdistribution hazard ratio per month, 0.961; 95% CI, 0.941-0.982). The supplementary composite end point analysis showed no clear association between rehabilitation continuity and worsening or death (hazard ratio, 0.988; 95% CI, 0.972-1.006). Associations of higher Hospital Frailty Risk Score and preoperative care-need levels with worsening varied over time. Conclusions and implications Among day-180 survivors after hip fracture surgery, preoperative frailty and care-need levels showed time-varying associations with subsequent nonfatal worsening. Longer initial claims-based rehabilitation continuity was associated with lower incidence of nonfatal worsening but should be interpreted as a claims-based association, not evidence of a causal effect or mortality-inclusive benefit. These findings support ongoing risk assessment and periodic reassessment of care needs beyond the early postoperative period.

title: Cable-routing geometry as a design variable for multiplanar hip assistance in a single-actuator soft exosuit.
authors: Kwon J, Park S, Driscoll HG, Lee G.
abstract: Cable-driven soft exosuits for gait assistance are predominantly sagittal-plane devices, yet pathological gait involves coordinated deviations across all three anatomical planes. This study experimentally evaluated whether cable-routing geometry alone, within a single-actuator hip exosuit, can produce measurable multiplanar hip effects during walking. Ten healthy, exosuit-experienced male adults walked on a treadmill under five conditions: one matched unpowered control and four powered configurations that paired single-plane and multi-plane cable routing with hip-flexion and hip-extension assistance. Three-dimensional hip kinematics were compared across conditions, and exosuit-generated hip torques were estimated from subject-specific musculoskeletal models. Multi-plane routing produced phase-dependent kinematic changes concentrated in the transverse plane. Relative to unassisted walking, multi-plane flexion assistance increased hip internal rotation (3.6°, p = 0.0002), multi-plane extension assistance increased hip external rotation (1.8°, p = 0.0095), and single-plane flexion assistance produced a smaller but significant increase in external rotation (1.1°, p = 0.0463). Frontal-plane differences were not significant for any comparison with unassisted walking, so the hypothesized larger frontal-plane deviations under multi-plane routing were not supported. Multi-plane routing also produced greater sagittal-plane hip excursion than single-plane routing. Overall gait-trajectory similarity between single-plane and multi-plane routing was comparable in most comparisons and differed significantly only in the hip frontal plane during extension assistance. The estimated torques indicated that multi-plane routing introduced larger frontal- and transverse-plane components while the sagittal-plane component remained dominant. These findings show that cable-routing geometry alone can shape phase-localized hip kinematics, reaching significance in the transverse plane, without adding actuators. The effect magnitudes were small and near the measurement uncertainty of the capture system. The all-male, exosuit-experienced sample limits generalizability, so relevance to clinical populations remains to be tested. Cable-routing geometry is therefore proposed as a candidate rather than an established design variable for multi-dimensional assistance in soft exosuits.

title: Biomechanical link between knee osteoarthritis and lumbar spine loading: An experimental and simulation-based analysis.
authors: Jamshidian A, Rouyin A, Nazemi H, Arjmand N, Farahmand F.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and low back pain (LBP) frequently co-occur, yet their biomechanical link remains unclear. This exploratory study investigated whether KOA gait is associated with altered trunk muscle forces and lumbar loading. Motion-capture and ground-reaction-force data were collected from eight individuals with mild-to-moderate medial KOA and ten healthy controls. Participant-scaled OpenSim models were used to estimate trunk muscle forces and lumbar joint reaction forces (JRFs). Between-group comparisons used Mann-Whitney U tests with false-discovery-rate correction. Walking speed did not differ between groups, whereas stride length was shorter in KOA (q = 0.033). Proximal kinematic differences were limited: no pelvic variable remained significant after correction, and only mean thoracic lateral bending differed (q = 0.032), with a small absolute magnitude. Mean knee angle differed between groups (q = 0.014), with additional differences in peak knee and ankle kinematics (q ≤ 0.006). Model-predicted mean and peak multifidus, longissimus, and iliocostalis forces were greater in KOA, whereas internal oblique forces were lower (all q < 0.05). Mean and peak lumbar compression were greater in KOA at all six levels from T12-L1 to L5-S1 (all raw p < 0.001; q < 0.05), and anterior-posterior JRFs were greater at selected levels. These higher muscle forces and JRFs, despite limited group-level proximal kinematic differences, may reflect attenuation or cancellation of heterogeneous individual gait adaptations during averaging, even though these adaptations may still influence internal mechanical demands.

title: Arthroplasty centers logistically separated from general orthopedic departments were associated with a more successful implementation of a standardized day-case setup : A Danish cohort study of 6718 procedures from a fast-track multi-center collaboration.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Jensen CB, Danielsen O, Varnum C, Jakobsen T, Andersen MR, Bieder MJ, Overgaard S, Jørgensen CC, Kehlet H, Gromov K.
abstract: Background Day-case hip and knee arthroplasty can reduce bed occupancy and improve cost-effectiveness, which is crucial for addressing the increasing demand among hip and knee osteoarthritis patients. This study investigated how different arthroplasty center setups were associated with the implementation and day-of-surgery (DOS) discharge rates of a standardized day-case setup. Materials and methods We included unilateral primary hip and knee arthroplasty patients from seven fast-track arthroplasty centers, all implementing a standardized day-case setup in September 2022 with identical eligibility and discharge criteria. Centers were categorized as: Satellite Arthroplasty Centers (SACs): Only primary arthroplasties, separate logistics. Elective Arthroplasty Centers (EACs): Complex primaries, revisions, separate logistics. Arthroplasty Unit Orthopedic Departments (AUOs): Primary and revision procedures, integrated into a general orthopedic department. We compared DOS discharge rates from September 2022 to September 2023 with a baseline period (July 2019-December 2019) using crude percentages. We compared the DOS discharge rate for day-case-eligible patients in study period between the center types using mixed effects models. Results We included 6718 patients (1357 SAC, 4309 EAC, 1052 AUO) during the study period and 3974 in the baseline period. DOS discharge rates increased post-implementation across all centers (SAC: 3.9% to 30%, EAC: 5.5% to 23%, AUO: 7.4% to 14%). Compared with AUOs (36%), successful DOS discharge among eligible patients was more likely in SACs (54%; adjusted OR 3.0, 95% CI 1.3-7.1; adjusted risk difference 25 percentage points, 95% CI 5.9-44) and EACs (60%; adjusted OR 3.8, 95% CI 1.7-8.5; adjusted risk difference 31 percentage points, 95% CI 13.8-48). Conclusions Arthroplasty centers with logistics separate from the general orthopedic department, SACs and EACs, were associated with higher rates of successful DOS discharge among eligible patients during implementation of a standardized day-case pathway, despite integrated arthroplasty units, AUOs, having higher day-case surgery use before implementation.

title: Anterior-Only Stabilization of Traumatic Subaxial Cervical Spine Injuries: Why Constructs Fail and Why Most Survive-A Systematic Review.
authors: Alwady D, Aly MM, Bransford R, Joaquim A, Costachescu B, Popescu EC, Bin Shebreen A, Baeesa S, Bin Dajim N, Salem K, Riew KD.
abstract: Study DesignSystematic review.ObjectivesTo characterize mechanical failure rates and candidate risk signals for failure after anterior-only stabilization for traumatic subaxial cervical spine injuries.MethodsWe searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to June 1, 2026 for studies evaluating mechanical construct failure or candidate risk signals after anterior-only stabilization for subaxial fractures. Narrative synthesis reported crude event fractions and study-specific odds ratios without pooling. Risk of bias and evidence certainty were assessed using ROBINS-I and GRADE (PROSPERO CRD420261420216).ResultsSix studies were included: five retrospective clinical cohorts (659 patients) and one nationwide registry (1,486 patients). Crude failure fractions were 5.8% (38/659) overall and 8.1% (33/405) in a morphology-focused descriptive subset, excluding separable stiff-spine cases. The separately analyzed registry recorded implant failure in 0.9% (14/1,486), implant malposition in 1.0% (15/1,486). Candidate risk signals included posterior tension-band injury (bilateral facet dislocation, posterior longitudinal ligament [PLL] injury, and facet fracture), compression endplate fracture, older age, and C7-T1 involvement; AO Spine Type C morphology was associated with registry implant failure. Compression endplate fracture and older age were each associated with failure in two cohorts; the remaining signals in one. In three cohorts with specific timing, failures were identified within seven postoperative weeks. Evidence certainty was very low.ConclusionsMechanical failure appears uncommon in selected anterior plate-based cohorts. Each candidate risk signal was supported by one or two studies; effects may depend on patient selection and surgical technique. We propose a hypothesis-generating construct-survival framework balancing mechanical demand against construct capacity until fusion and requiring prospective validation.

title: Adequately increased postoperative medial proximal tibial angle can prevent medial joint space narrowing after open-wedge high tibial osteotomy: a 3-year cohort study.
authors: Chiba D, Maeda S, Sasaki E, Tsushima T, Kimura Y, Tsuda E, Ishibashi Y.
abstract: Purpose This study aimed to investigate the longitudinal relationship between postoperative medial proximal tibial angle (pMPTA) and joint space narrowing or osteophyte formation during a 3-year follow-up period after medial open-wedge high tibial osteotomy (MOWHTO). Methods This retrospective cohort study included 133 knees of 101 patients (58 female patients; 77 female knees) who underwent MOWHTO [mean age: 57.5 ± 7.9 years; body mass index: 26.3 ± 4.0 kg/m 2 ; 32 patients (19 female patients) underwent bilateral surgeries]. On the basis of plain radiograph until 1 month postoperatively (Post Op), pMPTA and change in MPTA (ΔMPTA) (i.e., [pMPTA] - [preoperative MPTA]) were measured. Additionally, the medial and lateral femorotibial joint space widths (MJSW/LJSW) and osteophyte area (MOPA/LOPA) were measured at Post Op, and the JSW and OPA were remeasured at 3-year follow-up (3Y). Amount of changes in JSW and OPA were measured using the following formula: Δ = [JSW 3Y or OPA 3Y ] - [JSW Post Op or OPA Post Op ]. If ΔMJSW was ≤ -0.3 mm, we defined medial knee osteoarthritis as progressed (p-mOA). Results Forty-seven (35.3%) patients were diagnosed with p-mOA. Both pMPTA and ΔMPTA positively correlated with ΔMJSW. Receiver operating characteristic curves of pMPTA detected p-mOA, and the cut-off of pMPTA was 90°. Generalized estimation equations revealed that those with Conclusions Only in those with nonradiographic OA, correcting pMPTA with Level of evidence III.

title: A Simple Knot Technique to Simultaneously Prevent Medial-Row Suture Loosening and Lateral-Row Anchor Failure in Double-Row Rotator Cuff Repair.
authors: Wang W, Gao M, Wang Y, Li S.
abstract: We describe a simple knot-tying technique to augment fixation during double-row rotator cuff repair. After standard lateral-row anchor placement and suture tensioning, the remaining suture limbs are secured with a surgeon's knot positioned flush against the bone-anchor interface. This knot serves as a mechanical stopper: when the retracted cuff exerts medial traction on the medial-row sutures, the knot blocks suture slippage at the lateral bone surface, generating a counterforce that neutralizes pullout forces and maintains footprint compression. No additional implants are required. This technique is particularly valuable in osteoporotic bone or massive cuff tears, where lateral-row anchor fixation is prone to early failure.

title: A Comprehensive Review of the Physical Examination of the Elbow in the Throwing Athlete.
authors: Eskew JR, Soth BT, Alawa J, McGrath TM, Wanich T, Cirino CM, Carr JB.
abstract: Elbow pain is a significant source of morbidity in overhead throwing athletes, arising from a spectrum of pathologies including ulnar collateral ligament injury, valgus extension overload, medial epicondylitis, ulnar neuritis, radiocapitellar pathology, and more. Accurate diagnosis requires a systematic physical examination combined with advanced imaging. This technical note describes a comprehensive examination protocol for the throwing athlete's elbow.

title: What Is the 40-year Survivorship of Periacetabular Osteotomy Free From Conversion to THA?
authors: Hirt J, Roshardt J, Siebenrock KA, Ganz R, Steppacher SD, Tannast M.
abstract: Background Periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) is a widely accepted technique for the surgical treatment of symptomatic acetabular dysplasia with reproducibly favorable short- and midterm outcomes. Long-term follow-up studies are essential because PAO is performed in young patients with the aim of preserving the native hip for many decades. However, follow-up of 30 years remains scarce, and no study has reported 40-year outcomes after PAO. Questions/purposes (1) What is the cumulative 40-year survivorship free from conversion to THA? (2) How did hip function change and osteoarthritis progress during follow-up of the surviving hips? (3) Which preoperative factors were associated with conversion to THA? (4) What clinically relevant thresholds can be identified for preoperative factors associated with conversion to THA? Methods This was a retrospective case series of a consecutive, single-surgeon cohort followed longitudinally and previously reported at 10, 20, and 30 years. Between 1984 and 1987, a total of 75 hips (63 patients) were treated with PAO for acetabular dysplasia at the Department of Orthopaedic Surgery of the Inselspital Bern by the originator of the procedure. Of those, 57% (43 of 75) of hips had reached the endpoint (conversion to THA or arthrodesis) before our previous report on this group (published at a minimum of 27 years). Over the entire follow-up, 5 hips (4 patients) in which the patient died with the hip preserved were treated as competing events. Since the previous report, a further 8 hips were converted and 8 hips (6 patients) were lost to follow-up, leaving 11 hips (7 patients) with complete clinical and radiographic follow-up here, all at a minimum of 36 years. During the study period (1984 to 1987), the only indication for PAO was hip dysplasia with closed triradiate cartilage. The study group here consisted of 83% (52 of 63) women, the median (range) patient age at surgery was 26 years (12 to 55), and the median (range) BMI was 22 kg/m2 (16 to 28). A total of 27 hips had previous surgery to attempt sufficient coverage. Clinical and radiographic follow-up was performed at 10-year intervals, at 10, 20, 30, and 40 years after PAO. Survivorship free from conversion to THA was estimated using a competing-risks analysis with death without conversion treated as a competing event. Twelve patients underwent bilateral PAO and contributed two hips each. Because two hips from the same patient are not independent observations, all confidence intervals (CIs) and p values were calculated using a robust variance estimator with the patient as the clustering unit. Clinical scores, hip ROM, and osteoarthritis grade were described at each follow-up. Preoperative factors associated with conversion to THA were analyzed using Cox proportional hazards regression with a robust variance estimator clustered on patient. Thresholds for predictive factors were identified using maximally selected rank statistics. This approach tests every observed value of a factor as a potential dividing line and selects the value producing the greatest difference in survivorship between the two resulting groups. Results At 40 years, the survivorship free from conversion to THA was 27% (95% CI 12% to 39%). Merle d'Aubigné-Postel and Harris hip scores improved during the first decade after surgery and remained above the preoperative level at each follow-up visit. Two preoperative factors were independently associated with a higher risk of conversion to THA: a higher Tönnis osteoarthritis grade (HR 2.3 per 1-grade increase [95% CI 1.4 to 3.9]; p Conclusion PAO provides durable joint preservation in acetabular dysplasia and can delay THA for decades, with 27% of hips remaining free from conversion at 40 years. Preoperative osteoarthritis and a positive anterior impingement test result were associated with conversion to THA. Older age was also associated with conversion, with a threshold of 28 years, although age was related to the degree of joint degeneration at presentation. Patient selection should therefore be based primarily on the preoperative condition of the joint, with younger age at surgery as an additional consideration. Level of evidence Level III, therapeutic study.

title: Weightbearing CT in the Evaluation of Athletic Foot and Ankle Injuries.
authors: Brué J, Micicoi L, de Cesar Netto C.
abstract: Purpose of review Subtle foot and ankle injuries in athletes, including syndesmotic sprains, ligamentous Lisfranc injuries, osteochondral lesions of the talus, and proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures, may be underestimated or misclassified on conventional imaging. This review summarizes the current role of weightbearing CT (WBCT) in their evaluation, focusing on quantitative parameters, recent technical advances, and their potential influence on clinical decision-making. Recent findings Recent evidence has shifted WBCT from qualitative assessment toward reproducible three-dimensional quantification. Volumetric assessment and distance mapping improve characterization of syndesmotic instability, while external-rotation stress can reveal abnormalities not evident during neutral standing. In the midfoot, triplanar realignment and side-to-side comparison improve the reliability of Lisfranc measurements and support detection of subtle instability. Distance mapping permits reproducible quantification of osteochondral lesion surface area, depth, and volume and may improve consistency in surgical planning. WBCT has also characterized sport-specific alignment patterns and a morphologic and bone-density phenotype associated with proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures. Semiautomated segmentation and deep-learning methods may further reduce observer dependence and analysis time. WBCT provides three-dimensional measurements under physiologic load that complement clinical examination and conventional imaging in selected athletic foot and ankle conditions. Its greatest current value lies in characterizing subtle instability, malalignment, and osseous morphology when these findings may alter treatment planning. However, most available evidence is retrospective and derived from symptomatic or injured cohorts. Prospective studies are needed to validate diagnostic thresholds, determine whether WBCT-derived parameters predict injury or outcomes, and define their role in routine athletic screening and return-to-sport decision-making.

title: Union rate and time to union following platelet-rich plasma therapy in fracture nonunion: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Regmi A, Saini R, Baral S, Jain VK, Kulshrestha S, Iyengar KP.
abstract: Background Fracture nonunion remains a challenging clinical problem associated with prolonged disability and repeated surgical interventions. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been proposed as a biological adjunct to enhance bone healing; however, clinical evidence remains inconsistent. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of PRP in the management of fracture nonunion. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO Registration: CRD420261366849). PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception to March 2026. Studies evaluating PRP in fracture nonunion and reporting union rate or time to union were included. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to compare PRP with control interventions. Risk ratios (RR) were calculated for union rates and standardized mean differences (SMD) for time to union. Additional single-arm analyses were performed to estimate pooled outcomes in PRP-treated cohorts. Results Twenty-one studies comprising 877 patients were included. Two comparative studies (n = 119) demonstrated a higher likelihood of union with PRP (RR 1.17, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01-1.36, p Conclusion PRP was associated with higher union rates in the limited comparative evidence, although no statistically significant difference in time to union was demonstrated. Heterogeneity in PRP protocols, methodological limitations, and the small comparative evidence base limit the certainty of these findings. PRP may have a potential role as a biological adjunct in fracture nonunion management, but further well-designed randomized controlled trials are required before definitive clinical recommendations can be made.

title: Temporary percutaneous trans-tibiofibular K-wire stabilization of selected unstable ankle fractures.

title: Surgeon Ergonomics of Lateral Lumbar Interbody Fusion Across Four Patient Positions: A Proof-of-Concept Simulation Study Using Motion Capture and Electromyography.
authors: Louie PK, Jeong AY, Laynes RA, Ali MA, Yamanouchi K, Nguyen KT, Leveque JC, Nemani VM, Bansal A.
abstract: Study DesignProof-of-concept simulation-based biomechanical pilot study.ObjectivesTo compare surgeon posture and muscle activity across four lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF) positions and rank them by overall ergonomic burden.MethodsFive right-handed spine surgeons (case volumes 15 to 500 or more) each simulated a single-level LLIF on a synthetic model in four positions, three using direct vision (lateral decubitus, prone seated, prone lateral) and one using a camera and monitor (prone camera). Whole-body motion capture and surface EMG were recorded simultaneously, analyzed by surgical phase, and summarized per surgeon.ResultsNeck-flexion intensity was greatest in lateral decubitus and lower in every prone position, with the same ranking in all five surgeons (exact Friedman p=3.0e-06, Kendall W=1.00). Arm elevation was highest in prone seated. Across four summaries of posture and muscle activity, prone camera was the most favorable position in every surgeon, while the others reordered by measure. All positions scored medium-to-high risk. No two-position comparison reached adjusted significance, as expected at this sample size. ConclusionsPatient position in LLIF does not appear to change patient outcome, but it changes what the operation costs the surgeon. Lateral decubitus loaded the neck in every surgeon regardless of case volume or preference, prone seated loaded the shoulder, and prone camera was most favorable overall . Surgeons can reduce their exposure through position and setup, and ergonomics offers an objective way to compare setups when patient outcomes cannot separate them. These are proof-of-concept findings in five surgeons and require confirmation in a larger sample.

title: Segmental Arthroscopic Hip Labral Reconstruction Using a Peroneus Longus Allograft.
authors: Kody MT, Banffy MB.
abstract: Arthroscopic hip labral reconstruction has become an important tool for treating irreparable labral pathology, particularly in the revision setting. Restoration of the acetabular labrum is critical for hip stability, load distribution, and maintenance of the joint suction seal. Segmental labral reconstruction allows focal defects to be addressed while preserving healthy native labral tissue. This technical note describes a reproducible technique for segmental labral reconstruction using a peroneus longus allograft. The use of a peroneus longus allograft provides consistent graft sizing and avoids donor-site morbidity. This technique emphasizes a stepwise approach, including appropriate patient selection, portal placement, graft preparation, controlled graft delivery, and secure fixation to restore labral function and stability. Segmental reconstruction is particularly useful for focal irreparable defects and may help restore joint mechanics and the suction seal while avoiding unnecessary circumferential reconstruction.

title: ScaffoldForge: Bioinspired generative design of 3D-printed bone scaffolds via conditional diffusion for large segmental bone defect reconstruction.
authors: Zhang Y, Zhang H, Yang H.
abstract: We present ScaffoldForge, a 3D conditional diffusion framework for the generative design of bone scaffolds. ScaffoldForge maps a set of standardized trabecular descriptors (bone volume fraction BV/TV, trabecular thickness Tb.Th, trabecular spacing Tb.Sp, trabecular number Tb.N, connectivity density Conn.D, structure model index SMI, degree of anisotropy DA, and permeability k) to a 3D scaffold architecture in a single forward pass. A multi-objective conditioning mechanism couples these descriptors through adaptive instance normalization, and a physics-constrained loss adds empirical penalties for stiffness, manufacturing feasibility, and perfusion, evaluated on the denoiser's reconstruction of the clean scaffold so that the penalties carry gradient. To address the scarcity of paired geometry-property data, we describe a procedural pipeline whose generated scaffolds reproduce the morphometric distributions of real micro-CT references. In an in silico evaluation on three benchmark datasets, ScaffoldForge attains an estimated 56.6 MPa compressive strength (8.2% over topology optimization; paired t-test, p = 0.043, n = 5 seeds) and reduces design-time cost from 8,400-12 seconds per design, a 700× speedup. Generated structures are diverse rather than memorized, and morphometric accuracy holds across all seven shape descriptors. Three analyses probe the reliability of these results given the small training corpus. Equivalence testing replaces the earlier argument from non-significant difference tests: the procedural and real descriptor distributions are equivalent at a medium margin of 0.5 standard deviations for all seven descriptors, but the 50 available real reference volumes cannot establish equivalence at a strict 0.3-standard-deviation margin for five of them. A classifier two-sample test shows that generated scaffolds retain a measurable but shrinking signature of the procedural generator. Enlarging the corpus from 250 to 2,050 scaffolds leaves in-distribution accuracy nearly unchanged while reducing the cross-dataset descriptor error on unseen anatomy from 0.079 to 0.058, which localizes the cost of the small corpus in generalization rather than in fit. We further illustrate a CT-to-scaffold pipeline for personalized generation. All results are computational; physical, biological, manufacturing, and regulatory validation remain future work.

title: Sarcopenic obesity and pain sensitivity, central sensitization-related symptoms, and physical function among patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty: A cross-sectional study.
authors: Tanaka S, Miura J, Saito Y, Kajiwara Y, Tomooka Y, Fujita S, Mibu A, Imai R, Yamada K, Tokunaga M, Ushida T, Nishigami T.
abstract: Background Sarcopenic obesity is associated with poor physical function in patients with knee osteoarthritis (OA). However, its association with pain sensitivity and central sensitization-related symptoms remains unclear. Objective To investigate pain-related characteristics and physical function associated with sarcopenic obesity in patients with end-stage knee OA undergoing total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Methods This cross-sectional study included patients undergoing TKA. Patients were categorized into four body composition phenotypes based on the Japanese Working Group on Sarcopenic Obesity criteria: no obesity/sarcopenia, obesity, sarcopenia, and sarcopenic obesity. The primary outcomes were pain intensity, pain sensitivity, and central sensitization-related symptoms, assessed using pain intensity at rest and during movement, pressure pain thresholds (PPTs) at the affected knee and forearm, and the Central Sensitization Inventory-9 (CSI-9). The secondary outcomes were physical function and disability, assessed using quadriceps strength, Timed Up and Go (TUG), and Oxford Knee Score (OKS). Analyses of covariance were adjusted for age, sex, Kellgren-Lawrence grade, C-reactive protein, Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index, and Life-Space Assessment. Exploratory pairwise comparisons were performed between the sarcopenic obesity group and the other groups. Results Among 636 patients, 55 had sarcopenic obesity. Compared with the no obesity/sarcopenia and obesity groups, the sarcopenic obesity group had higher CSI-9 scores (adjusted mean differences, 3.89 [95% CI, 0.96-6.82] and 3.47 [0.58-6.37], respectively) and lower affected-knee PPTs (-0.64 [-1.15 to -0.13] and -0.52 [-0.88 to -0.16] kgf/cm², respectively). Corresponding differences versus the sarcopenia group were 1.28 (-2.32 to 4.88) for CSI-9 and -0.33 kgf/cm² (-1.17 to 0.52) for PPT. Compared with the no obesity/sarcopenia group, the sarcopenic obesity group also had lower quadriceps strength (-0.06 kgf/kg [-0.11 to -0.01]) and slower TUG performance (2.14 s [0.22-4.06]). Conclusions Differences in pain-related characteristics and physical function were observed across body composition phenotypes. Exploratory comparisons showed higher CSI-9 scores and lower affected-knee PPTs in patients with sarcopenic obesity than in those with no obesity/sarcopenia and obesity. However, the mechanisms underlying these differences remain unclear because neuropathic-like pain was not assessed. Further studies incorporating neuropathic-like pain assessment are needed to clarify associations between body composition phenotypes and pain-related characteristics.

title: Rural and Urban Hospitals Demonstrate Different Patterns of Declining Inpatient Arthroplasty Volume, 2013-2023.
authors: Byrne AR, Pachipala K, Cecere RA, Follett LY, Sarpong NO.
abstract: Background Total joint arthroplasty has shifted rapidly from inpatient to outpatient settings. We evaluated whether inpatient Medicare arthroplasty volume changed differently across rural and urban hospitals from 2013 to 2023. Methods Medicare Inpatient Hospitals-by Provider and Service files were analyzed. Hospitals with reportable Medicare Severity Diagnosis-Related Group 469/470 volume were classified as urban (Rural-Urban Commuting Area 1-3) or rural (Rural-Urban Commuting Area 4-10). A two-way fixed-effects model with hospital and year fixed effects assessed rural-urban differences in volume change using 2013 as reference. Persistence of reportable inpatient volume was evaluated among hospitals observed in 2013. Results The cohort included 25,002 hospital-year observations across 2911 hospitals. The mean volume declined from 203 to 59 cases at urban hospitals and from 84 to 37 at rural hospitals between 2013 and 2023. Rural hospitals had greater relative declines before 2020, but the association reversed thereafter; rural × year difference-in-differences estimates were +63.4 cases in 2020, +104.2 in 2021, +118.3 in 2022, and +121.0 in 2023 (all P P Conclusions Inpatient arthroplasty declined substantially in both settings. Urban hospitals remaining observable experienced larger post-2020 volume declines, whereas rural hospitals were more likely to disappear from the reportable inpatient dataset. These patterns suggest different geographic manifestations of the national transition away from inpatient arthroplasty.

title: Robotic navigation strategies for PFNA fixation: impact on one-time guide pin success rate and anteversion angle accuracy - a retrospective cohort study.
authors: Huang YY, Tang GX, Chen YF, Li HL, Huang B, Chen WM, He LX.
abstract: This study evaluated the clinical efficacy of three navigation strategies (full robotic navigation, robotic navigation for the main nail only with freehand anteversion, and conventional freehand technique) in PFNA fixation for intertrochanteric fractures, analyzed factors affecting anteversion angle accuracy, and quantified the learning curve of robot-assisted surgery. A retrospective review was conducted on 121 intertrochanteric fracture cases managed with PFNA. We categorized patients into three groups by navigation strategy: G1 (double navigation, n = 41), G2 (single navigation, n = 40), and G3 (non-navigation, n = 40). Perioperative parameters (fluoroscopy time span, total fluoroscopy times, number of attempts, visible intraoperative blood loss, etc.) were compared among groups. The main metric assessed was the attempt frequency for anteversion determination (reflecting one-time success rate). Within G1, Spearman correlation and multivariable linear regression explored the associations between anteversion error and medullary canal diameter, as well as fluoroscopy times for main nail insertion. Curve estimation was used to evaluate learning curves for fluoroscopy time span and main nail insertion time. Baseline characteristics were similar across the three groups, with no significant differences (P > 0.05). The number of attempts to determine anteversion in G1 (1.22 ± 0.48) was significantly lower than in G2 (4.30 ± 2.49) and G3 (3.98 ± 1.93) (both P < 0.001). Regarding overall surgical efficiency, fluoroscopy time span in G1 (65.95 ± 8.71 min) was 12.0 min shorter (15.4% reduction, P < 0.05) than in G3 (77.93 ± 29.98 min), total fluoroscopy times (40.63 ± 7.89) were 16.3 fewer (28.6% reduction, P < 0.001); visible intraoperative blood loss (99.8 ± 91.2 mL) was 119.5 mL less (54.5% reduction, P < 0.001), and blood transfusion volume (0.73 ± 1.45 units) was significantly lower than in G3 (2.14 ± 1.72 units, P = 0.002). Compared with G2, G1 also showed significantly reduced fluoroscopy time span, total fluoroscopy times, and visible intraoperative blood loss (all P < 0.05). Main nail insertion time in G2 (43.78 ± 6.94 min) was significantly longer than in G3 (34.65 ± 17.59 min, P = 0.002), whereas G1 (37.80 ± 6.43 min) was not significantly different from G3. Within G1, anteversion error showed a strong negative correlation with medullary canal diameter (r = - 0.807, P < 0.001). Multiple regression identified medullary canal diameter as the only independent predictor of anteversion error (β = - 0.781, P < 0.001). Learning curve analysis demonstrated a marked reduction in fluoroscopy time span with robotic case order (R² = 0.644, P < 0.001), with the quadratic model providing the best fit. Full robotic navigation (double navigation) significantly improves anteversion-angle positioning efficiency (fewer attempts), reduces fluoroscopy time span and exposure frequency (suggesting lower radiation exposure), and decreases visible intraoperative blood loss. However, anteversion accuracy still depends on patient anatomy, particularly medullary canal diameter, necessitating consideration during preoperative planning. Moreover, the learning curve showed rapid early improvement, followed by a gradual plateau.

title: Remnant preservation and stump suturing in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction reduce tibial tunnel widening without compromising tunnel placement: A computed tomography-based randomised controlled trial.
authors: El-Desouky M, Elkalyoby AS, Rashwan AS, Gaballah AI, Abdelrazek BH.
abstract: Purpose Tunnel widening remains a concern following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction because it may adversely affect graft incorporation and complicate revision surgery. Remnant preservation has been proposed as a strategy to reduce tunnel widening, but its effect on postoperative tunnel remodelling remains uncertain. This study aimed to determine whether remnant preservation with tibial stump suturing reduces tunnel widening without compromising tunnel placement accuracy. Methods In this prospective randomised controlled trial, 179 patients undergoing primary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction were randomised to remnant-preserving reconstruction with tibial stump suturing ( n = 88) or conventional stump resection ( n = 91). Standardised three-dimensional computed tomography was performed at 2 weeks and 1 year postoperatively. Tibial and femoral tunnel widening were calculated as the percentage change in tunnel diameter between scans, and tunnel placement accuracy was assessed using the computed tomography-based quadrant method. The incidence of clinically significant tunnel widening (>20%) was also compared. Results Baseline tunnel diameters were comparable between groups. At 1-year follow-up, remnant-preserving ACL reconstruction resulted in significantly less tibial tunnel widening than stump resection (14.58 ± 4.49% vs. 19.74 ± 4.36%, p 20%) (11.4% vs. 25.3%; relative risk, 0.45; p = 0.016). Femoral tunnel widening was similar between groups (18.23 ± 2.92% vs. 18.35 ± 2.59%, p = 0.766). No clinically relevant differences in tunnel placement were observed between groups. Conclusion Remnant-preserving ACL reconstruction with tibial stump suturing selectively reduces tibial tunnel widening at 12 months without compromising anatomic tunnel placement accuracy. These findings support the use of remnant preservation when preservation of tibial tunnel integrity is a surgical consideration. Level of evidence Level I. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07236593; registration date: November 15, 2025 (retrospectively registered).

title: Radial head arthroplasty restores axial construct stiffness in a Monteggia-like injury model: a biomechanical study.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
authors: Weber MM, Hockmann JP, Rosenkranz TA, Leschinger T, Müller LP, Rausch V.
abstract: Introduction Monteggia-like lesions are rare but complex elbow injuries involving fractures of both the proximal ulna and the radial head. While the influence of ulnar alignment and soft tissue integrity on radial head stability has been extensively studied, the effect of radial head integrity on the stability of ulnar fixation remains poorly understood. Given the high rates of nonunion and revision surgery after proximal ulna fractures, improved understanding of forearm biomechanics in these combined injuries is highly clinically relevant as it influences the surgical strategy in primary care of these injuries. Accordingly, this study aimed to evaluate the biomechanical impact of radial head resection and radial head arthroplasty on forearm stiffness in a simulated Monteggia-like injury model. We hypothesized that radial head resection would reduce construct stiffness compared with both the native state and radial head arthroplasty, and that arthroplasty would partially restore stiffness toward native levels MATERIALS AND METHODS: Eight fresh-frozen human cadaveric elbow specimens were biomechanically tested under axial loading. After baseline testing in the native state, a standardized segmental comminution model was created and stabilized using locking plate osteosynthesis. Sequential testing was then performed after radial head resection and after implantation of a modular radial head prosthesis. Specimens were loaded cyclically up to 450 N for 1,000 cycles with the elbow positioned at 30° of flexion. Construct stiffness was calculated and compared between testing conditions. Results Mean construct stiffness in the native state was 49.3 ± 4.29 N/mm and decreased significantly after creation and fixation of the ulnar defect (36.05 ± 6.71 N/mm). Radial head resection resulted in a further significant reduction in stiffness (25.83 ± 6.65 N/mm). Following radial head arthroplasty, stiffness increased to 33.8 ± 7.89 N/mm, representing a significant improvement compared with the resection state (p ≤ 0.0026). No significant difference was observed between stiffness after prosthesis implantation and the condition with intact radial head and stabilized ulna. Conclusion Radial head integrity significantly contributes to forearm stiffness in Monteggia-like lesions. Radial head arthroplasty partially restores biomechanical stability after resection and may alter load distribution in a manner that could be relevant for fixation durability. These findings support the need to address the radial column to optimize stability in complex elbow injuries. Level of evidence Biomechanical study.

title: Patients Undergoing Proximal Hamstring Repair Have High Rates of Return to Work and Favorable Outcomes: A Systematic Review.
authors: Bindra A, Gillinov SM, Girardi KG, Lord KT, Kodra JD, Lee MS, Atadja L, Norman MB, Moran J, Surucu S, Jimenez AE.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate return-to-work (RTW) rates and functional outcomes after surgical repair of proximal hamstring tendon avulsion injuries. Methods This systematic review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews. PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Scopus were searched in April 2025 for studies reporting RTW outcomes after surgical repair of proximal hamstring avulsions. Eligible studies involved human subjects undergoing open or endoscopic repair and reporting RTW rates or patient counts. No minimum follow-up duration was required. Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data, with discrepancies resolved by a third. Study quality was assessed using the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies criteria. Results Six studies (229 patients) met inclusion criteria. Four studies reported an overall RTW rate ranging from 89% to 100%, whereas 2 studies stratified outcomes by Workers' Compensation (WC) status, showing lower RTW rates among WC patients (70.0%-86.3%) compared with non-WC patients (92.5%-94.1%). Return-to-sport rates, when reported, ranged from 58% to 100%. Study-level RTW and return-to-sport outcomes were summarized descriptively without pooled estimates because of heterogeneity in study design, surgical approach, injury chronicity, WC status, and outcome definitions. Complication rates were low overall, with retear or reoperation occurring in 0% to 5.8% of cases. Clinically relevant patient improvement thresholds were only reported in 1 study. Conclusions In this study, most patients undergoing surgical repair for proximal hamstring avulsion injuries return to work with favorable functional outcomes and low complication rates. Level of evidence Level IV, systematic review of Level III and IV studies.

title: Patient experiences with a prescription-based digital health application (DiGA) for knee disorders: a qualitative study in german orthopaedic care.
authors: Burgert S, Raab N, Kornfeld T, Knitza J, Boy K, Schwarz J, May S, Heinze M, Mühlensiepen F.
abstract: Background Musculoskeletal disorders are among the leading causes of chronic pain, functional limitations, and reduced quality of life worldwide. Prescription-based digital health applications (DiGAs) have the potential to improve outpatient care, enhance treatment adherence, and address structural challenges such as shortages in physiotherapy services. However, real-world evidence on the use of DiGAs from the patient perspective in orthopaedic settings within the German healthcare context remains limited. This study aimed to explore acceptance, perceived potential, and challenges associated with DiGA use among patients with knee joint disorders. Methods An exploratory qualitative study was conducted at an academic outpatient clinic for orthopaedics and trauma surgery in Germany. Ten adult patients (aged 18-65 years) with anterior cruciate ligament rupture or meniscal injury and a prescribed DiGA ("Orthopy") were recruited. Semi-structured telephone interviews were conducted at the time of prescription (n = 10) and approximately two to three weeks later (n = 6; one follow-up interview took place after twelve weeks). All four participants who withdrew completed a dropout questionnaire. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis according to Kuckartz. Main categories were derived deductively from the research question; subcategories were developed inductively from the data. Baseline and follow-up interviews of the six completing participants were compared within and across cases. Sociodemographic and clinical data were collected to contextualise findings. Trustworthiness was supported by iterative coding, an intra-coder consistency check, and team discussion of the coding frame. Coding was performed by a single researcher. Results Participants were generally open to using the DiGA and valued its flexibility, location independence, and its role in bridging gaps in physiotherapy. The DiGA was primarily perceived as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for conventional therapy. Perceived key strengths included structured exercise guidance, educational content, and easy integration into daily routines, particularly in prehabilitation. Challenges included limited personalisation, insufficient adaptation of feedback, and limited motivational benefit when the app was used without accompanying professional guidance. Additional barriers comprised administrative delays in activation, usability issues among less digitally literate users, and insufficient physician guidance. Data privacy concerns played a minor role. Interviewed participants did not report serious safety concerns during the short observation period. Conclusions Participants perceived the DiGA as a suitable complement to physiotherapy in orthopaedic care, particularly for prehabilitation and continuity of care. Better personalisation, usability, and integration into existing care structures could further enhance its perceived value. Long-term adherence, clinical effectiveness, safety, and sustainable implementation remain to be established. Future research should address these questions and patient-centred design. Trial registration The study was registered in the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00036514) on 10 April 2025, after data collection had begun in January 2025 (retrospective registration).

title: Occult Skeletal Stress Injuries of the Wrist and Vitamin D Deficiency: A Case Series.
authors: Harrison K, Kavolus MW, Lourie GM.
abstract: Stress reactions occur from repetitive loads that weaken the bone and are often associated with nutritional deficiencies and metabolic dysfunction. More commonly, these injuries are reported in the lower extremities, with less literature on stress fractures in the upper extremities. Seven patients presented with chronic, atraumatic wrist pain that did not improve with conservative measures. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated increased signal on T2, suggestive of carpal stress reaction. Patients had documented low vitamin D levels or levels obtained after MRI confirmation of stress injury. All patients showed improvement in symptoms after targeted vitamin D supplementation and nutritional management; none of the patients required surgical intervention. Stress reactions in the hand and wrist are relatively uncommon. These injuries, and underlying metabolic abnormalities, can be missed easily without a careful history and work-up. Recognizing these injuries and correcting contributing factors can help avoid more catastrophic skeletal stress injuries in the lower extremities, such as the tibia or femoral neck.

title: No significant differences between large language model prompting strategies and human experts in summarisation of 'the formal EU-US meniscus rehabilitation consensus: An ESSKA-AOSSM-AASPT Initiative'.
authors: Lindskog J, Öttl F, Yu Y, Paterno MV, Giordano A, Rambaud A, Prill R, Królikowska A, Samuelsson K, Hamrin Senorski E.
abstract: Purpose This study aimed to evaluate the interpretive and applicative performance of three conditions applied to the formal EU-US, ESSKA-AOSSM-AASPT consensus on meniscus rehabilitation: (1) single-pass prompting, (2) sequential chain-of-thought prompting and (3) human expert-written output. Methods This exploratory comparative study evaluated three conditions applied to two parts of the formal EU-US ESSKA-AOSSM-AASPT meniscus rehabilitation consensus: (1) single-pass prompting, (2) sequential chain-of-thought prompting using ChatGPT (GPT-5.1), Claude (Sonnet 4.5), and Gemini (3.0), and (3) human expert-written output from three collaborating human experts. For each part, three tasks were assessed: generation of summaries, application of summaries to three predefined clinical scenarios, and resistance to three predefined misinterpretation queries. Three blinded senior sports physiotherapists evaluated summary quality using five QUEST categories and rated the clinical application and misinterpretation resistance responses. Median ratings were compared using Friedman and post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Gwet's AC2 coefficient with quadratic weights was used to assess inter-rater agreement for each QUEST category and for the clinical application and misinterpretation resistance items. Results Across consensus parts, no statistically significant differences were identified between large language model prompting strategies and human expert outputs for QUEST categories, clinical application, and misinterpretation resistance queries. Sequential chain-of-thought prompting received higher numerical reviewer ratings than single-pass prompting for ChatGPT and Gemini, particularly for quality of information and trust and confidence, although differences were not statistically significant. Inter-rater agreement ranged from substantial to almost perfect (Gwet's AC2 = 0.79-0.99). Conclusion No statistically significant differences in reviewer ratings were observed between ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and human expert output, with generally high ratings for summaries and responses to clinical scenarios. Large language models may therefore represent a potential adjunct for summarisation and interpretation of sports medicine consensus recommendations to inform rehabilitation decision-making. Level of evidence Level V.

title: Modified Suture-Gripping Technique for Arthroscopic Meniscal Suturing.
authors: Sasaki R, Muroya N, Nishimura T, Hayashi T, Kaneda K, Nagashima M, Kobayashi S, Morioka H.
abstract: Meniscal preservation is essential for the maintenance of knee function. The suture-gripping technique, using a suture shuttle, enables accurate needle insertion from inside the joint and flexible withdrawal of the suture from outside the capsule, thereby facilitating meniscal repair of the anterior segment. Using a continuous suturing technique with this method is possible, and we described a modified approach. We recently recognized that ARTHRO-PIERCE, a device originally designed for hip arthroscopy, can be used to perform the same suture-gripping technique principles for meniscal repair. The ARTHRO-PIERCE has a sharper tip-when compared with a suture shuttle holding a suture at its tip-that improves penetration, a more rigid shaft that improves reach and trajectory toward the anterior horn and anterior body, and robust suture grasping without relying on a loop mechanism than a conventional suture shuttle. Here, we describe the step-by-step surgical technique. This technique expands the versatility of the suture-gripping technique for anterior meniscal suturing with improved device handling and secure suture control.

title: Methods for Computed Tomography-Based Glenoid Bone Loss Measurement Show High Interobserver Consistency but Variable Accuracy.
authors: Nair AV, Rajan A, Veerendra K, M P, Yoo YS, Kumar BA, Rashid S, Dalapathi A, Jetty T, Sadda SR, Khan PS.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the reliability of computed tomography (CT)-based glenoid bone loss calculation methods in shoulder instability by assessing interobserver agreement using 3-dimensional virtual bone models and to identify the technique that provides the most optimal balance for clinical application. Methods Between January 2023 and June 2023, normal shoulder CT scans without evidence of instability or prior surgery were retrieved from institutional archives. Virtual anteroinferior glenoid bone defects of predefined sizes (10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 30%, 35%, and 40%) were created on a standardized en face glenoid view using CT console-based segmentation tools, establishing a controlled reference standard. Four senior musculoskeletal radiologists independently measured glenoid bone loss on both 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional reconstructions using 4 established techniques (Sugaya, PICO, Hamamoto, and Parada). Interobserver reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), and agreement with the predefined defect size was evaluated using Bland-Altman analysis. Results The PICO method showed the highest interobserver reliability (ICC = 0.995) but showed systematic overestimation with the largest mean bias (+6.93 mm) and wide limits of agreement, reflecting proportional bias. The Sugaya method showed both high reproducibility (ICC = 0.854) and minimal bias (-1.06 mm), making it the most balanced technique. The Hamamoto method showed good reliability (ICC = 0.952) but a tendency to overestimate (+4.04 mm). The Parada method showed poor reproducibility (ICC = 0.223) despite moderate accuracy (-2.85 mm). Conclusions The Sugaya method showed the most favorable combination of accuracy and interobserver reliability for CT-based glenoid bone loss measurement in a controlled virtual model. The PICO method, despite excellent interobserver consistency, showed systematic overestimation. The Hamamoto method showed acceptable reliability with moderate overestimation, whereas the Parada method showed poor reproducibility. Clinical relevance Reliable glenoid bone loss estimation is vital for surgical planning in shoulder instability. According to our study, the Sugaya method offers the most accurate and reproducible measurements, helping surgeons make better-informed decisions and avoid inappropriate procedures.

title: Limited-Incision Kager's Fascia Flap Coverage Versus Open Repair for Acute Achilles Tendon Rupture: A Retrospective Comparative Study.
authors: Liu C, Wang Z, Fang X, Zhang W, Zhu L, Jiang H, Tan W, Zhou M, Li Z, Yang X, Li P, Chen X, Luo S, Xie Z, Wang X.
abstract: Purpose There is ongoing debate within the medical community regarding the optimal surgical technique for repairing Achilles tendon ruptures. Therefore, this study aimed to compare a novel limited-incision Kager's fascia flap coverage technique with conventional open repair for acute Achilles tendon rupture. Methods Ninety patients surgically treated for acute closed Achilles tendon rupture between January 2017 and December 2021 were retrospectively followed, including 41 with limited-incision Kager's fascia flap coverage technique and 49 with traditional open surgical suture. Functional outcomes were evaluated at 12 months postoperatively using the American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) ankle-hindfoot score and the Achilles Tendon Total Rupture Score (ATRS). Color Doppler ultrasound examination of Achilles tendon blood supply was performed at 3 months postoperatively to assess hemodynamic parameters. To evaluate the influence of age on outcomes, patients were divided into ≥ 50 years and Results The limited-incision Kager's fascia flap coverage group demonstrated superior outcomes compared with the traditional open surgery group. At 12-month follow-up, the fascia flap group had significantly higher AOFAS scores (91.43 ± 2.74 vs. 84.80 ± 2.85) and ATRS scores (94.56 ± 2.45 vs. 86.26 ± 3.15) than the control group (both p Conclusion The limited-incision Kager's fascia flap coverage technique for treating acute closed Achilles tendon ruptures shows certain efficacy, improving limb function, reducing surgery-related injuries, and potentially promoting Achilles tendon healing by enhancing local blood supply at the rupture site, thereby improving clinical outcomes and outperforming traditional open surgery. Simultaneously, the technology demonstrates good efficacy across different age groups.

title: Lateral Extra-articular Tenodesis With All-Suture Knotless Anchor.
authors: Lucina L, Tierney S, Patel RM.
abstract: Although many patients have had satisfactory outcomes from arthroscopic anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, persistent rotational instability and graft failure still occur. Therefore, the anterolateral ligament complex has been a newer focus of research. The addition of the lateral extra-articular tenodesis to augment anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction has been found to increase stabilization and reduce rerupture rates. We describe our surgical technique for performing a modified Lemaire lateral extra-articular tenodesis with an all-suture knotless anchor.

title: Intramedullary nailing versus locking plate fixation for proximal humerus fractures: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
authors: Dhillon J, Porter K, Ngoue M, Kirby K, Mierisch C, Hansen L, Krumrey J.
abstract: Proximal humerus fractures (PHFs) are common in the elderly and may require surgical fixation, yet controversy persists regarding the optimal technique-open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) versus intramedullary nailing. This study synthesizes high-quality randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evidence to determine the relative efficacy, safety, and functional outcomes. A systematic review was performed by searching PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and Embase through February 2026. Eligible RCTs compared intramedullary nailing and plate fixation for PHFs, evaluating range of motion (ROM), strength, complications, reoperation rates, and patient-reported outcomes (PROs). Six RCTs comprising 404 PHFs were included (204 nails, 200 plates). Mean patient age was 69.3 years (nail) and 68.5 years (plate), with average follow-up of 30.6 months. There were no significant differences between intramedullary nailing and locking plate fixation in DASH score (MD, -0.66; 95% CI, -11.94 to 10.62; P=.91), VAS pain (MD, -0.40; 95% CI, -0.93 to 0.13; P=.14), Constant score (MD, 1.33; 95% CI, -2.72 to 5.37; P=.52), or ASES score (MD, 0.74; 95% CI, -5.25 to 6.74; P=.81). Complication rates (RR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.21-2.25; P=.53) and reoperation rates (RR, 1.5; 95% CI, 0.49-4.59; P=.48) were also not significantly different between fixation methods. In a post hoc fracture-type analysis, nail fixation was associated with higher Constant scores in 3- and 4-part fractures (MD, 6.87; 95% CI, 3.02-10.73; P=.0005), whereas no significant difference was observed in 2-part fractures (MD, -2.43; 95% CI, -5.32 to 0.46; P=.10). Intramedullary nailing and locking plate fixation provide no statistically significant difference in functional and clinical outcomes for PHFs. Complication and reoperation rates varied across studies, with no significant pooled differences between fixation methods. Further high-quality randomized studies are needed to clarify whether specific patient or fracture subgroups may benefit from one fixation strategy over the other.

title: Hemiarthroplasty with a long femoral stem and proximal cement augmentation for a myeloma-related pathological femoral neck fracture: a case report.
authors: Shang Z, Wu C, Liu J.
abstract: Background Pathological femoral neck fractures are a frequent skeletal complication of multiple myeloma due to extensive osteolytic bone destruction. However, extensive proximal femoral invasion with massive cavitary destruction leading to femoral neck fracture is clinically uncommon, and optimal surgical management remains challenging because of poor bone quality and high mechanical failure risk. Case presentation We report a patient with a known history of multiple myeloma who sustained a low-energy fall resulting in a pathological fracture of the right femoral neck. Imaging demonstrated diffuse osteolytic involvement of the pelvis and proximal femur with severe osteoporosis and degenerative hip changes. Given the patient's poor general condition and multiple comorbidities, a multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion involving orthopaedics, hematology, cardiology, endocrinology, and neurology was conducted to formulate an individualized perioperative strategy. Bipolar hemiarthroplasty was performed using a long femoral stem with distal press-fit fixation, combined with debridement of tumor-infiltrated tissue, proximal cement augmentation of osteolytic bone defects, and supplemental plate and cerclage cable fixation. This reconstructive strategy was selected as an alternative to proximal femoral replacement to achieve immediate mechanical stability and facilitate early mobilization. Intraoperative autologous blood salvage and reinfusion were used as part of the perioperative blood-management strategy, with no immediate procedure-related complications observed. Results The patient was followed for 15 months after surgery. At the latest follow-up, she remained ambulatory with satisfactory hip function and a Harris Hip Score of 84 points. Follow-up radiographs demonstrated stable reconstruction without prosthetic loosening, dislocation, periprosthetic fracture, or other major implant-related complications. Conclusion Hemiarthroplasty with a long femoral stem, proximal cement augmentation, and supplemental fixation may represent a viable option for selected patients with multiple myeloma-related pathological femoral neck fractures and extensive osteolytic destruction. Careful assessment of bone loss and individualized multidisciplinary planning are important for balancing mechanical stability and perioperative risk.

title: Four large language models in parent-oriented education for pediatric flexible flatfoot: Quality, readability, hallucination, and reproducibility.
authors: Servet E, Unat B, Bilgin MA, Karabulut Ç, Gönder N.
abstract: Purpose Parents increasingly consult large language model (LLM) chatbots about pediatric flexible flatfoot, a common condition that rarely requires treatment and in which the clinical task is chiefly communication. We compared four LLMs on the quality, readability, and reproducibility of parent-oriented answers. Methods This was a cross-sectional, comparative content analysis of AI-generated text. No patients, clinical records, or human participants were involved; the units of analysis were parent-oriented questions and the chatbot responses they generated. Twenty parent-oriented questions were submitted in triplicate to ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, and Gemini in independent, memory-disabled sessions (240 responses). Two blinded pediatric orthopedic surgeons scored responses (Mika grade, four-point Likert, and a hallucination taxonomy; PEMAT-P, DISCERN, and QUEST on pooled material). Readability used five indices. Between-model differences were tested with Friedman and Dunn-Bonferroni post-hoc tests; agreement and reproducibility used intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Results All five readability indices differed between models (P Conclusions Clinical-quality scales did not reliably distinguish the four LLMs, whereas readability differed substantially; none met recommended readability standards, and output was only moderately reproducible. Model choice should be guided by readability and actionability, under clinician oversight. Significance of study For a condition managed mainly through parent education, LLM selection should rest on readability and actionability rather than presumed clinical accuracy, with output used under clinician oversight. Level of evidence V (cross-sectional comparative content analysis of AI-generated text; no human participants).

title: Endplate-to-endplate cement contact and 24-month outcomes after unilateral percutaneous vertebroplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures: a single-center retrospective cohort study.
authors: Zhang K, Xia L, Wang Z.
abstract: Background Bone cement distribution may influence load transfer and late structural failure after vertebral augmentation. However, the association between endplate contact and clinical outcomes remains difficult to estimate due to confounding factors. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 620 patients who underwent unilateral percutaneous vertebroplasty (PVP) for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures (OVCFs) at a single institution. Cement distribution was classified as contact with neither endplate (group I), the superior endplate only (group II), the inferior endplate only (group III), or both endplates (group IV). The primary outcome was time to postoperative vertebral refracture within 24 months. Secondary outcomes included longitudinal visual analogue scale (VAS) scores, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), vertebral recompression, radiographic restoration, cement leakage, and perioperative measures. Confounding was addressed using stabilized multinomial inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW). Repeated outcomes were analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE), and time to refracture was analyzed using Cox regression. Restricted cubic splines, subgroup analyses, and 10-fold cross-validation were performed. Results Among 620 patients, 150 refractures (24.2%) occurred. Event rates were 30.9%, 26.6%, 25.7%, and 15.2% in groups I-IV, respectively (log-rank P = 0.0069). After weighting, the maximum standardized mean difference (SMD) decreased from 0.231 to 0.053. At 24 months, group IV had lower adjusted VAS scores (mean difference, -0.72; 95% confidence interval ( CI ), -0.93 to -0.51) and ODI scores (mean difference, -6.75; 95% CI , -8.35 to -5.15) than group I. In the Cox model, group IV was associated with a lower refracture hazard (hazard ratio ( HR ), 0.40; 95% CI , 0.25-0.64).
